aminoguanidine.description: Aminoguanidine (developmental name Pimagedine) is a chemical compound with the formula $CH6N4$. Mechanistically it is best known as the first identified inhibitor of Advanced Glycation End Products (AGEs), acting as a "carbonyl trap" that intercepts reactive carbonyl species and prevents protein cross-linking. It is also a selective inhibitor of Inducible Nitric Oxide Synthase (iNOS) and of Diamine Oxidase (DAO). In the adrenochrome literature, aminoguanidine is used as a reagent to stabilize Adrenochrome by forming Adrenochrome monoaminoguanidine. Nitric Oxide Pathway (vs. Methylene Blue) Aminoguanidine and Methylene blue are frequently compared because they act at different steps of the same NO–Cyclic Guanosine Monophosphate (cGMP) vasodilation cascade: Aminoguanidine acts upstream — it selectively inhibits Inducible Nitric Oxide Synthase, blocking overproduction of Nitric Oxide during inflammation. Methylene blue acts downstream — it inhibits Soluble Guanylyl Cyclase, blocking cGMP generation even when NO is already present. [!info] Selective iNOS inhibition Because aminoguanidine spares the endothelial isoform (eNOS), it is theorized to halt inflammatory vasodilation without abolishing normal blood-pressure regulation — unlike non-selective NOS blockade. This complementarity has been explored in Septic Shock, refractory Vasoplegic Shock, acute heart-transplant rejection (restoring myocyte contractility via lowered cGMP), and thermal injury (reducing vascular hyperpermeability). Therapeutic Roles and Safety Aminoguanidine prevented diabetic renal, retinal, and neural complications in experimental models, and reached phase III trials for Diabetic Nephropathy (as Pimagedine) but was not approved due to safety concerns: Pro-oxidant activities. Inhibition of Nitric Oxide Synthase. Potential DNA damage by free radical production. Risk of autoimmune reactions and Vitamin B6 depletion. It is today primarily an experimental/laboratory tool, not an approved broad clinical therapy. [!warning] Histamine intolerance (oral) Oral aminoguanidine potently inhibits gut Diamine Oxidase, the enzyme that degrades dietary histamine. This can cause severe acute Histamine Intolerance — headaches, flushing, hives, and tachycardia after histamine-rich foods (aged cheese, cured meats, fermented foods). IV administration bypasses gut DAO but still affects systemic DAO. Oral vs. Intravenous Oral: well absorbed; historically studied (Pimagedine tablets) for chronic AGE inhibition in diabetes. IV / intraperitoneal: used in experimental animal models of septic shock and ischemia–reperfusion injury for rapid iNOS blockade. Documents Dietary Advanced Glycation End Products and Aging A study with long-term (24–30 weeks) administration of Aminoguanidine (an inhibitor of AGE formation) showed prevention of the age-related Cardiac Hypertrophy and arterial stiffness. Adrenochrome is very unstable due to its o-quinone and, therefore, is usually stabilized by conventional derivation with Hydrazine, e.g., Aminoguanidine, Semicarbazide, phenylhydrazine, o-nitrophenylhydrazine, p-nitro phenylhydrazine and 2,4-dinitrophenylhy... GOPS Protocol Aminoguanidine moiety of the hybrid molecule provides AGE inhibition and carbonyl trapping in the glyco-oxidative proteostasis shield strategy. Aminoguanidine: An AGE Product Inhibitor A review of aminoguanidine (Pimagedine) as the first AGE inhibitor, detailing its prevention of age-related cardiac enlargement, arterial stiffening, and diabetic complications (albuminuria, survival) via carbonyl trapping and cross-link inhibition. Contrasts aminoguanidine (upstream iNOS inhibition) with methylene blue (downstream sGC inhibition) on the NO–cGMP cascade; oral vs IV pharmacokinetics and DAO/histamine safety. Connections Adrenochrome: Stabilized by aminoguanidine to form Adrenochrome monoaminoguanidine. Adrenochrome monoaminoguanidine: The stable derivative formed. Hemostatics: The resulting derivative is used as a hemostatic. Advanced Glycation End Products: Inhibited by aminoguanidine (carbonyl trap). Glycation: Prevented by its action as a carbonyl trap. Cross-linking: Aminoguanidine prevents AGE-induced protein cross-linking. Inducible Nitric Oxide Synthase: Selectively inhibited (upstream NO blockade). Nitric Oxide / Soluble Guanylyl Cyclase / Cyclic Guanosine Monophosphate: NO-pathway targets shared with methylene blue. Diamine Oxidase / Histamine Intolerance: Gut DAO inhibition → histamine sensitivity. Methylene blue: Complementary downstream NO-pathway agent. Very Low Density Lipoprotein: Aminoguanidine reduced VLDL adhesion to vessel walls in animal models. Albuminuria: Reduced by aminoguanidine in diabetic clinical trials. Acetyl-L-Carnitine: Cited alongside aminoguanidine as a cross-link-preventing agent. Alagebrium: ALT-711, a thiazolium cross-link "breaker" developed by the same sponsor as Pimagedine. Carnosine: A fellow glycation/cross-link inhibitor mentioned with aminoguanidine. Atherosclerosis: Aminoguanidine improved blood flow in peripheral vascular disease. Diabetic Nephropathy: Phase III target indication (unapproved). Vitamin B6: Depleted by aminoguanidine (safety concern).

complex_i.description:
Complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase) is the first and largest enzyme complex of the mitochondrial electron transport chain. It oxidizes NADH, transfers electrons to ubiquinone, and pumps protons, contributing to the proton-motive force that drives ATP synthesis. Its inhibition is a central mechanism of Mitochondrial Dysfunction in Parkinson's Disease.

Structure & Function

Complex I is a ~1 MDa L-shaped assembly of ~45 subunits (14 conserved mitochondrial-encoded core subunits plus nuclear-encoded accessory proteins). The membrane arm houses the proton pumps; the peripheral arm contains the NADH-binding and flavin (FMN) and iron-sulfur cluster electron-transfer chain. Electrons flow NADH → FMN → Fe-S clusters → ubiquinone, coupled to translocation of four protons per NADH.

Inhibition and Parkinson's Disease

Post-mortem PD substantia nigra shows a specific ~30–35% reduction in complex I activity, independent of Lewy Bodies distribution, supporting mitochondrial failure as an early pathogenic event. The prototypic inhibitor is MPP+, the active metabolite of MPTP, which binds the ND2/ND4 region and blocks electron flow; the herbicide Paraquat and rotenone act similarly. Loss of complex I elevates Oxidative Stress via increased superoxide and depletes ATP, preferentially killing Neuromelanin-rich SNpc neurons.

Relation to Neuromelanin & Selective Vulnerability

Dopaminergic neurons have high baseline oxidative demand and accumulate iron within neuromelanin granules, amplifying complex I–derived radical formation. The combination of metabolic stress, Alpha-Synuclein Aggregation, and impaired Mitophagy creates a feed-forward loop of damage. This explains why agents that inhibit complex I produce parkinsonism and why mitochondrial resilience is a therapeutic target.

Pathology & Clinical Relevance

Mitochondrial enhancers (e.g., inhibitors of the MPT pore, PGC-1α activators, Coenzyme Q10) and complex I–sparing strategies have been trialed in PD. Complex I activity in platelets/monocytes is explored as a peripheral biomarker. The complex I story integrates the toxic, genetic, and aging axes of PD pathogenesis.

Connections

MPTP: Toxin metabolized to MPP+ causing parkinsonism.
Paraquat: Herbicide inhibiting complex I.
Mitochondrial Dysfunction: Core PD mechanism via complex I loss.
Parkinson's Disease: Disorder with reduced nigral complex I.
Oxidative Stress: Consequence of complex I inhibition.
Neuromelanin: Pigment amplifying redox stress in SNpc.
Alpha-Synuclein Aggregation: Interacts with mitochondrial failure.

caspase_6.description:
Caspase-6 is an effector (executioner) caspase activated during the terminal execution phase of Apoptosis. Although less studied than Caspase-3, it occupies a distinctive role in dismantling the nuclear envelope through cleavage of lamin A/C, making it a principal driver of the morphological collapse that defines apoptotic cell death.

Structure & Activation

Caspase-6 is produced as an inactive zymogen (~33 kDa) with a short prodomain. Unlike initiator caspases, it lacks DED or CARD recruitment domains and is instead activated by upstream initiators — Caspase-8 (extrinsic) and Caspase-9 (intrinsic) — as well as by feedback amplification from Caspase-3. Mature caspase-6 is a heterotetramer of large (p18) and small (p11) subunits sharing the conserved catalytic dyad (Cys-His) and substrate specificity for aspartate residues, particularly the (V/E)T/D motif.

Mechanism of Action

A signature substrate is nuclear lamin A, an intermediate-filament protein underpinning the nuclear lamina. Caspase-6 cleaves lamin A at a conserved site, severing the lamina meshwork and precipitating nuclear envelope breakdown, chromatin condensation, and DNA fragmentation. Caspase-6 also processes other structural and signaling proteins, including keratin 18, huntingtin, and the amyloid precursor protein, implicating it in both apoptosis and non-apoptotic proteolytic events. Its activation can therefore propagate cellular demolition even when caspase-3 is partially inhibited, providing a backup execution route.

Physiological & Pathological Function

Caspase-6 is pivotal for the ordered demolition of cells during development and homeostasis. In disease, its nuclear-targeting activity is co-opted in chemotherapy-induced apoptosis of tumors. Conversely, caspase-6-mediated cleavage of neuronal structural proteins has been implicated in Neurodegeneration (e.g., axonal degeneration in Alzheimer's and Huntington's disease models), illustrating that the same protease serves both tumor suppression and tissue injury depending on context. In Cancer, robust caspase-6 activation generally favors therapy response, whereas its suppression contributes to apoptotic resistance.

Clinical & Research Relevance

Because caspase-6 can execute apoptosis independently of caspase-3, it is a candidate target for overcoming caspase-3-resistant malignancies. Small-molecule caspase-6 activators and peptides that disrupt its inhibitory interactions are under preclinical investigation. Conversely, caspase-6 inhibitors are explored neuroprotectively. Biomarkers of caspase-6 activity (e.g., circulating cleaved cytokeratin-18 fragments) reflect epithelial tumor cell death and are used as pharmacodynamic readouts in early-phase trials.

6_hydroxydopamine.description:
6-hydroxydopamine (6-OHDA) is a structurally dopamine-like neurotoxin that is selectively taken up by catecholaminergic neurons and used extensively in research to model Parkinson's Disease. It destroys these neurons through the generation of reactive oxygen species and the disruption of Mitochondrial Dysfunction.

Overview

6-OHDA is a hydroxylated analogue of dopamine lacking the meta-hydroxyl required for normal catecholamine function. Because it is recognized by the high-affinity catecholamine uptake systems, 6-OHDA is concentrated specifically in dopaminergic and noradrenergic neurons, where it exerts selective toxicity. For this reason it cannot cross the blood–brain barrier and must be injected directly into the brain (e.g., into the Substantia Nigra Pars Compacta or striatum) to produce a lesion.

Mechanism of Action

Once inside the neuron, 6-OHDA undergoes rapid auto-oxidation, generating superoxide radicals, hydrogen peroxide, and hydroxyl radicals via Fenton chemistry. It also inhibits mitochondrial respiration at Complex I and Complex IV, depleting ATP and triggering Oxidative Stress. The combination of oxidative damage to DNA, proteins, and lipids, together with energetic failure, culminates in apoptotic and necrotic cell death. Injected unilaterally, 6-OHDA produces the classic rotational model in which rats turn away from the lesioned side when challenged with dopamine agonists such as amphetamine.

Physiological & Experimental Relevance

The 6-OHDA lesion model has been instrumental in delineating the anatomy of the Nigrostriatal System, validating the efficacy of L-DOPA and dopamine agonists, and testing neuroprotective and cell-replacement strategies. It faithfully reproduces the loss of striatal dopamine terminals and the motor deficits (akin to Bradykinesia) seen in PD, although it does not recapitulate the intraneuronal Lewy Bodies that define human disease.

Pathology & Clinical Relevance

As a tool, 6-OHDA has clarified that oxidative stress and mitochondrial impairment are sufficient to kill dopaminergic neurons, supporting the Oxidative Stress and Mitochondrial Dysfunction hypotheses of PD. It is also a cautionary reminder that environmental or endogenous catechols with redox-cycling potential could contribute to selective neuronal vulnerability. Comparative work with MPTP and rotenone has refined understanding of which mitochondrial targets are most critical in parkinsonism.

hif_1.description:
HIF-1α (Hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha) is a transcription factor that mediates cellular responses to low oxygen (hypoxia). It regulates metabolic reprogramming, including the shift to Glycolysis (the Warburg Effect), and is a key driver of Angiogenesis via VEGF.

Sirtuin Regulation
SIRT3 negatively regulates HIF-1α by promoting its prolyl hydroxylation and degradation, suppressing aerobic glycolysis
SIRT6 represses HIF-1α to regulate glycolysis and lipid metabolism
SIRT2 can destabilize HIF-1α, contributing to tumor-suppressive functions

Clinical Relevance

HIF-1α is frequently overexpressed in Cancer and linked to poor prognosis. It is a therapeutic target in Renal Cell Carcinoma, glioblastoma, and Breast Cancer.

genome_stability.description:
Overview

Genome stability is the property of a cell or organism to preserve the integrity of its genetic information across replication, repair, and cell division. It depends on accurate DNA Repair, telomere maintenance, and the silencing of mobile genetic elements. Loss of genome stability is one of the Hallmarks of Aging and is a major driver of cancer and age-related degeneration.

Sirtuin-Dependent Maintenance

A key contributor is SIRT6, which deacetylates Histone H3 at lysine 9 (H3K9) on telomeric chromatin, promoting the recruitment of factors that maintain Telomere structure and function. SIRT6 also suppresses LINE-1 retrotransposon activity, limiting the insertional mutagenesis and DNA damage caused by retrotransposition.

[!important]
SIRT6-deficient cells exhibit marked genomic instability, telomere dysfunction, and premature cellular Senescence (Michishita et al., 2008; Van Meter et al., 2014). This demonstrates that a single histone deacetylase coordinates multiple layers of genome protection.

Mechanistic Layers
DNA repair — Homologous recombination repair and NHEJ (via DNA-PKcs) correct double-strand breaks.
Telomere maintenance — H3K9 deacetylation and shelterin function prevent erosion and fusion of chromosome ends.
Repeat silencing — Retrotransposon repression (LINE-1, HERV) prevents insertional damage; its failure during aging triggers innate immune signaling via the cGAS-STING axis.
Epigenetic fidelity — faithful DNA Methylation maintenance by DNMT1 and UHRF1 preserves repressive marks that stabilize the genome.

Pathology

Genomic instability underlies cancer initiation, replicative senescence, and progeroid syndromes. Interventions that enhance SIRT6 activity or suppress retrotransposition (e.g., NRTIs) are being explored to restore genome stability in aging.

inducible_nitric_oxide_synthase.description:
Inducible Nitric Oxide Synthase (iNOS, NOS2) is the cytokine-inducible isoform of Nitric Oxide Synthase. Unlike the constitutive endothelial (eNOS) and neuronal isoforms, iNOS is expressed in macrophages and many cells after inflammatory stimulation and generates sustained, high-output Nitric Oxide.

Role in Pathology

Excess iNOS-derived NO drives pathological Vasodilation and Hypotension in Septic Shock and Vasoplegic Shock, impairs myocardial contractility in acute heart-transplant rejection, and contributes to vascular hyperpermeability after burns.

Aminoguanidine (Selective Inhibitor)

Aminoguanidine is a relatively selective iNOS inhibitor — it blocks NO production upstream while sparing eNOS, theoretically halting inflammatory vasodilation without abolishing normal blood-pressure regulation. This contrasts with Methylene blue, which blocks NO signaling downstream at Soluble Guanylyl Cyclase.

[!info] Upstream vs downstream
Aminoguanidine (iNOS inhibition) and methylene blue (sGC inhibition) target opposite ends of the same NO–Cyclic Guanosine Monophosphate cascade and have been studied as complementary agents.

Documents
Aminoguanidine selectively inhibits iNOS (upstream NO synthesis); methylene blue inhibits sGC (downstream). Compared across vasoplegia, transplant rejection, and burns.

xbp1.description:
X-box binding protein 1 (XBP1) is a transcription factor that plays a crucial role in the unfolded protein response (UPR) and regulates hepatic autophagy by activating TFEB. Its spliced form, XBP1s, also modulates inflammatory and metabolic gene programs; SIRT6 regulates XBP1 to alleviate endoplasmic reticulum stress in the liver.

Structure and Function
XBP1 is a bZIP transcription factor in the unfolded protein response (UPR).
Its active form (XBP1s) arises from IRE1-mediated alternative splicing of XBP1 mRNA during ER Stress.
As a member of the C/EBP family of transcription factors, XBP1 binds to UPRE on its target genes (Zhang et al.).
XBP1s drives UPR target genes as the principal UPR transcription factor.

Autophagy Connection
XBP1s transcriptionally activates autophagy genes including Beclin1 and LC3B.
XBP1 deficiency impairs autophagy and sensitizes cells to ER stress.
XBP1 regulates hepatic autophagy by activating TFEB.



SIRT6 alleviates endoplasmic reticulum stress by regulating XBP1, complementing its H3K9 deacetylation at glycolytic promoters to limit inflammatory and metabolic dysfunction in the liver (Szczęsny-Małysiak et al., 2026). SIRT6 thereby connects XBP1 biology to hepatic metabolic homeostasis.

gdf15.description: Growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15) is a distant member of the TGF-β superfamily. Unlike classical TGF-β ligands, GDF15 does not signal through canonical SMAD2/3 pathways; instead it is a stress-responsive secretory factor induced by the Integrated Stress Response (ISR) and acts as a mitokine that communicates local mitochondrial dysfunction to distal tissues. In the context of aging, GDF15 has emerged as one of the most robust circulating biomarkers of senescence burden and Senescence, linking mitochondrial stress, the Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype, and systemic inflammaging to age-related functional decline. [!info] Core senescence-relevant facts GDF15 is consistently elevated in plasma with age and is a component of multi-protein senescent-cell and frailty biomarker panels. It is induced by the same stress axes that drive senescence (DNA Damage Response, p53, mitochondrial ISR via ATF4/CHOP). It is secreted by senescent cells and is itself listed among canonical Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype factors. Circulating GDF15 is predictive of mortality, frailty, and multiple age-related diseases, independent of classical risk factors. Overview GDF15 is a 34-kDa secreted protein synthesized as a precursor, cleaved in the Golgi, and released as a mature dimer. Under basal conditions its expression is low in most adult tissues, with higher constitutive production in the placenta, prostate, and certain epithelial barriers. Expression is dramatically induced by diverse cellular stresses — mitochondrial dysfunction, endoplasmic reticulum stress, oxidative stress, genotoxic damage, and oncogene activation — positioning GDF15 as a generalized "stress alarm" cytokine. Because mitochondrial dysfunction and unresolved cellular stress are hallmarks of Aging and drivers of Senescence, GDF15 levels rise as organisms age and serve as a peripheral readout of accumulated senescent burden. Structure & Domains Belongs to the TGF-β superfamily based on a conserved cysteine-knot motif, but is phylogenetically distant from the BMP/GDF subfamily and lacks standard bioactive pro-domain processing typical of other family members. Synthesized as a 308-aa pre-proprotein; the N-terminal signal peptide and propeptide are cleaved to yield the mature ~12–15 kDa C-terminal dimer. Does not engage the conventional TGF-β receptor/SMAD2/3 axis. Its high-affinity receptor is the glial-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF) family receptor α-like protein GFRAL, which heterodimerizes with the RET co-receptor in the Brainstem and selected peripheral neurons to mediate anorexia and weight loss. The orphan status of GFRAL in many peripheral tissues implies additional, less-characterized receptors or non-canonical signaling modalities relevant to its metabolic and inflammatory effects. Mechanism of Action & Pathways ISR / ATF4 / CHOP induction GDF15 transcription is a canonical downstream target of the Integrated Stress Response. Mitochondrial perturbation (e.g., impaired biogenesis, ETC dysfunction, fusion/fission imbalance) activates the OMA1–DELE1–HRI axis, driving phosphorylation of eIF2α and selective translation of ATF4. ATF4 then induces CHOP and directly transactivates GDF15 (alongside FGF21, another mitokine). This places GDF15 at the apex of the retrograde mitochondrial-to-nuclear stress communication circuit described in Mitohormesis. Senescence and DNA damage axes p53-dependent induction: GDF15 is induced by p53 downstream of DNA damage and oncogenic stress, and exhibits pro-apoptotic activity in transformed cells. This is the same p53 axis that enforces senescence arrest, explaining why senescent cells upregulate GDF15. DDR / cGAS–STING overlap: Persistent DNA damage and cytosolic mtDNA leakage activate the cGAS-STING Pathway, a potent SASP inducer. Cells under these conditions upregulate GDF15, coupling mitochondrial-ISR signaling to the senescence program. NF-κB / inflammasome: SASP amplification via NF-κB and the NLRP3 Inflammasome reinforces GDF15 secretion, integrating it into the inflammatory secretome of senescent cells. Receptor signaling (GFRAL/RET) Mature GDF15 binds GFRAL in the area postrema and nucleus of the solitary tract of the Brainstem, activating RET and downstream ERK/PI3K-Akt pathways to suppress Appetite and increase Energy expenditure. This explains the anorexia and weight loss seen in mitochondrial disease, cancer cachexia, and during Metformin therapy — contexts where circulating GDF15 is markedly elevated. GDF15 is now recognized as both a product of and a contributor to the senescent phenotype: SASP component: GDF15 is catalogued among canonical Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype factors. acetyl_coa.description:
Acetyl-CoA

Overview: Acetyl-coenzyme A (Acetyl-CoA) is a central metabolic hub: the two-carbon acetyl unit is carried by coenzyme A and feeds oxidative phosphorylation, biosynthesis, and epigenetics. It is generated from pyruvate (pyruvate dehydrogenase), fatty-acid β-oxidation, amino-acid catabolism, and acetate (via acetyl-CoA synthetase).

Role in Energy Metabolism: Acetyl-CoA enters the citric acid (TCA) cycle in the Mitochondria, where condensation with oxaloacetate forms citrate. Its oxidation drives NAD+ and FADH₂ production and ultimately ATP synthesis. The acetyl-CoA/CoA and NAD+/NADH ratios are key metabolic sensors.

Role in Epigenetics: Acetyl-CoA is the obligate acetyl donor for Histone Acetylation, catalyzed by histone acetyltransferases (HATs); the opposing reaction is performed by Sirtuins (NAD+-dependent deacetylases) and HDACs. Thus the availability of acetyl-CoA directly couples nutrient state to chromatin state and gene expression. High acetyl-CoA favors open, transcriptionally active chromatin; sirtuin-mediated deacetylation is energy- and Caloric Restriction-linked.

Cross-talk with Autophagy: Nutrient sufficiency raises acetyl-CoA, which can inhibit Autophagy via mTOR activation, whereas fasting lowers acetyl-CoA and promotes autophagic flux. This positions acetyl-CoA as a metabolic switch between anabolism and catabolism.

Longevity Relevance: The acetyl-CoA pool integrates diet, exercise, and Sirtuins activity. Interventions that modulate acetyl-CoA availability (e.g., Nicotinamide Riboside, caloric restriction, Mitohormesis) influence downstream acetylation and stress-resistance pathways relevant to Longevity.

Role in Senescence and the SASP: In cellular senescence, mitochondrial metabolism is a functional checkpoint for the senescence-associated secretory phenotype. Mitochondrial pyruvate entry via the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier feeds a citrate–acetyl-CoA export axis (mitochondrial citrate carrier SLC25A1 → cytoplasmic ACLY) that supplies the acetyl-CoA pool used to place H3K27ac at SASP loci. Inhibiting SLC25A1 or MPC (e.g., with CTPI2) collapses this pool, removes H3K27ac from SASP enhancers, and selectively suppresses SASP expression while leaving viability and mtDNA-driven signaling intact. Exogenous acetate can bypass the block via ACSS2, restoring acetylation and SASP — confirming acetyl-CoA availability, not mitochondrial integrity, is the limiting step.

[!important] Source: Mitochondrial metabolism and epigenetic crosstalk drive SASP
Mitochondrial pyruvate metabolism regulates senescence-associated chromatin via acetyl-CoA export. Mice treated with CTPI2 showed reduced age-related Frailty and improved healthspan, positioning the citrate–acetyl-CoA axis as a druggable node for SASP modulation.

transposable_elements.description:
Transposable elements (TEs), colloquially "jumping genes," are DNA sequences capable of changing their position within a genome. They comprise roughly 45% of the human genome and are normally kept transcriptionally silent.

Types & Mechanisms
Retrotransposons (Class I) move via a "copy-and-paste" RNA intermediate that is reverse-transcribed:
LTR elements — including endogenous retroviruses (HERVs).
Non-LTR elements — autonomous LINE-1 (L1) and non-autonomous Alu (SINEs) that depend on L1 machinery.
DNA transposons (Class II) move by a "cut-and-paste" mechanism using a transposase; most are inactive in humans.



[!important] Derepression during aging
TEs are silenced by Heterochromatin, DNA methylation, and repressive histone marks (e.g. H3K9me3). Age-related Epigenetic Alterations and heterochromatin erosion — including declining SIRT6 and loss of Piwi/KRAB-ZNF control — allow TE reactivation. Mobilized LINE-1 elements cause insertional mutagenesis and Genomic Instability, and their cytoplasmic cDNA activates the cGAS-STING Pathway, fueling Inflammaging and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype.

TE reactivation is therefore both a marker and a driver of Senescence, and nucleoside reverse-transcriptase inhibitors have been explored to suppress it.

Documents
Describes loss of heterochromatin-based silencing and reactivation of transposable elements as a conserved feature of aging.
Centenarian SIRT6
Links SIRT6-mediated repression of LINE-1/transposable elements to genome stability and exceptional longevity.

Connections

cellular_reprogramming.description:
Cellular Reprogramming is the conversion of one cell type into another—most famously the reset of Somatic Cells to a pluripotent state to generate Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells (iPSCs) using the Yamanaka Factors (OSKM: Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc). It is fundamentally an Epigenetic Remodeling process that erases somatic memory and installs a new identity.

Mechanisms

Reprogramming proceeds through defined phases: an early "stress" phase, a mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition (Mesenchymal-to-Epithelial Transition), and late stabilization of the pluripotency network (Oct4–Sox2–Nanog). It requires global erasure of somatic DNA Methylation, reconfiguration of histone marks (loss of H3K9me3/H3K27me3 at pluripotency loci, gain of H3K4me3/H3K27me3 bivalency), chromatin opening, and X-chromosome reactivation. MET is essential because fibroblasts are mesenchymal while iPSCs are epithelial.

Methods

Beyond transcription-factor delivery (retroviral, sendai viral, episomal, mRNA, or protein), reprogramming can be achieved by small molecules (e.g., GSK3β and MEK inhibitors), CRISPR-based locus activation, and chemical-only ("RNA-free") protocols. Efficiency remains low and stochastic, limited by incomplete epigenetic remodeling and persistence of partially reprogrammed intermediates.

Applications

Reprogramming underpins Regenerative Medicine, Disease Modeling (patient-specific iPSC lines carrying disease alleles), drug screening, and developmental studies. Partial Reprogramming—transient, incomplete reset—has emerged as a Rejuvenation strategy: it restores youthful transcriptomic and epigenetic profiles in aged cells and tissues (e.g., in vivo OSKM expression in mice) without teratoma risk from full dedifferentiation.

cardiac_hypertrophy.description:
Cardiac Hypertrophy is an adaptive enlargement of cardiomyocytes in response to increased workload, neurohumoral stimulation (e.g., Angiotensin II, endothelin-1), or mechanical stress. While initially compensatory—preserving stroke volume—sustained pathological hypertrophy progresses to heart failure, cardiomyopathy, and increased risk of arrhythmias. Distinguishing physiological hypertrophy (exercise-induced, reversible, benign) from pathological hypertrophy (pressure overload, maladaptive) is central to cardiovascular medicine.

Mechanisms of Hypertrophic Growth

Pathological hypertrophy is driven by neurohumoral axes (renin–angiotensin–aldosterone, sympathetic) and mechanical stretch, activating signaling nodes including calcineurin–NFAT, MAPKs, and AKT–mTOR. These converge on transcription factors (e.g., GATA4, NFAT, MEF2) that induce fetal gene reprogramming (atrial natriuretic peptide, β-myosin heavy chain). Concurrently, mitochondrial dysfunction, increased ROS, and impaired autophagy worsen contractile and energetic reserve.

Sirtuin Connections

Multiple sirtuins oppose pathological remodeling:
SIRT1 protects against Cardiac Hypertrophy by deacetylating FoxO1 and FOXO3a, suppressing pathological gene expression programs, and activating PGC-1α-driven mitochondrial biogenesis; it also promotes cardiac autophagy. Its effect is dose-dependent (dual): low (2.5×) or moderate (7.5×) overexpression attenuates Ang II-induced hypertrophy (reduced apoptosis, promoted autophagy, PKC-ζ inhibition), whereas high (12.5×) overexpression exacerbates it via Akt/PDK1 membrane localization (Wu et al., 2022).
SIRT3 deficiency exacerbates Cardiac Hypertrophy by increasing mitochondrial ROS and impairing OXPHOS, lowering the heart's bioenergetic reserve.
SIRT7 represses Cardiac Hypertrophy by deacetylating GATA4, a key transcription factor for hypertrophic gene expression. SIRT7 knockout mice develop spontaneous cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis, highlighting its essential role.
SIRT6 attenuates Cardiac Hypertrophy through Histone H3 K9 deacetylation and suppression of NF-κB-dependent inflammatory signaling, limiting pathological inflammation in the myocardium. Mechanistically, SIRT6 inhibits isoproterenol-induced hypertrophy via autophagy (FoxO3 nuclear retention through Akt attenuation), decreases p300 → NF-κB p65 acetylation, blocks IGF–Akt signaling via c-Jun, and suppresses STAT3 (Wu et al., 2022).
SIRT2 protects against agonist-induced hypertrophy by deacetylating the transcription factor NFATc2; its loss reduces AMPK signaling, promoting aging-related and Ang II-induced hypertrophy (Wu et al., 2022).
SIRT5 prevents age-related cardiac hypertrophy (Wu et al., 2022).
SIRT4 is an adverse player — overexpression aggravates Ang II-induced hypertrophy by inhibiting MnSOD (SOD2) activity (Wu et al., 2022).

Together, the sirtuin family integrates nutrient sensing (NAD⁺) with cardiomyocyte growth, bioenergetics, and inflammation.

Physiological Protection and Interventions
Caloric Restriction and Intermittent Fasting attenuate Cardiac Hypertrophy via SIRT3/NAD+-dependent pathways, improving mitochondrial function and redox balance.
Exercise-induced physiological hypertrophy engages distinct, SIRT1/PGC-1α-associated pathways that enhance (rather than impair) cardiac capacity.
Impaired Autophagy contributes to pathological hypertrophy; SIRT1 promotes cardiac autophagic flux, clearing damaged organelles.

Clinical Relevance

Hypertrophy is a major risk factor for heart failure with reduced or preserved ejection fraction. NAD⁺ precursor supplementation and SIRT1/SIRT3 activation are investigated as cardioprotective strategies to limit maladaptive remodeling. The multiple sirtuin checkpoints make the NAD⁺–sirtuin axis an attractive target for preventing progression from hypertrophy to failure.

neurodegeneration.description: Neurodegeneration is the progressive loss of structure or function of neurons, including death of neurons. It is a key feature of diseases like Alzheimer's Disease and Parkinson's Disease, often linked to Oxidative Stress and AGEs. Definition Neurodegeneration is the progressive loss of structure or function of neurons, including the death of neurons. Role of Oxidative Stress The brain is particularly vulnerable to Oxidative Stress due to its high oxygen consumption, high lipid content (prone to Lipid Peroxidation), and relatively low antioxidant defenses. Oxidative damage to Proteins (leading to aggregation) and Mitochondria (leading to energy failure) are central drivers of neurodegenerative processes. Related Conditions Alzheimer's Disease: Characterized by Amyloid Beta plaques and Tau Protein tangles, both linked to oxidative damage. Parkinson's Disease: Involves the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the Substantia Nigra, often driven by mitochondrial dysfunction. Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS): Linked to mutations in Superoxide Dismutase (SOD1) and oxidative damage to motor neurons. Oxidative Stress in Alzheimer's Disease: Metal- and Aβ-Catalyzed ROS In Alzheimer's Disease, oxidative stress precedes and drives amyloid plaque formation. Amyloid Beta (Aβ) peptides (particularly the Aβ1–42 isoform) bind redox-active metals (Cu^2+ and Fe^3+) through histidine residues at positions 6, 13, and 14. The Aβ–metal complex reduces Cu^2+ to Cu^+ and Fe^3+ to Fe^2+, which then reduce molecular oxygen to superoxide and Hydrogen Peroxide via Fenton chemistry. This process, termed "Aβ-associated redox cycling," generates stoichiometric amounts of H2O2 in the presence of reducing agents such as vitamin C and dopamine. Elevated H2O2 then oxidizes nearby Lipids (producing Malondialdehyde and 4-HNE), Proteins (carbonyl formation), and Nucleic Acids (8-oxo-dG). Tau Protein hyperphosphorylation is both a consequence and amplifier of this oxidative environment: H2O2 inhibits PP2A (the main tau phosphatase) through oxidation of its catalytic cysteine, promoting tau aggregation into neurofibrillary tangles. Oxidized tau seeds propagate trans-synaptically in a prion-like manner, spreading oxidative pathology across neural networks. Parkinson's Disease: Dopamine Oxidation and Complex I Deficiency Parkinson's Disease is characterized by the selective loss of Dopaminergic Neurons in the Substantia Nigra pars compacta, where three intersecting oxidative mechanisms converge. First, Dopamine itself is inherently unstable: its catechol ring undergoes Autoxidation in the presence of iron or MAO to form dopamine quinones, superoxide, H2O2, and the neurotoxic metabolite 6-OHDA. Dopamine quinones covalently adduct to Cysteine residues on Alpha-synuclein (αSyn), stabilizing its toxic oligomeric forms and impairing proteasomal degradation. Second, Mitochondria Complex I activity is reduced by ~30–40% in the Substantia Nigra of PD patients, causing energetic failure and increased electron leakage to oxygen, amplifying superoxide production. This Complex I defect can be reproduced by environmental toxins like MPTP (through its metabolite MPP+) and Rotenone, both of which selectively inhibit Complex I and induce parkinsonism in humans and animal models. Third, Neuroinflammation driven by activated microglia releases Nitric Oxide and ROS that further damage adjacent dopaminergic neurons. Peroxynitrite, formed from the reaction of NO with superoxide, nitrates Alpha-synuclein at tyrosine residues (particularly Tyr-39, Tyr-125, and Tyr-133), promoting its aggregation into Lewy Bodies, the pathological hallmark of PD. Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis: SOD1 Mutations and Excitotoxicity Mutations in Superoxide Dismutase (SOD1) account for ~20% of familial ALS cases. While the initial hypothesis implicated loss of SOD1 enzymatic activity (i.e., impaired superoxide scavenging), subsequent research established that mutant SOD1 gains a toxic function: aberrant copper-mediated chemistry that generates hydroxyl radicals and peroxynitrite, and the formation of insoluble intracellular aggregates that impair the proteasome and autophagic pathways. More than 180 distinct SOD1 mutations have been identified, with the A4V and G93A variants being the most studied. Mutant SOD1 also triggers ER stress by binding to the ER chaperone Derlin-1 and activating the Unfolded Protein Response (UPR), leading to motor neuron apoptosis. Concurrently, loss of the astrocytic glutamate transporter EAAT2 in ALS leads to excitotoxic Ca^2+ overload in motor neurons, which activates NADPH Oxidase (NOX2) and Calpain, unleashing further ROS production and proteolytic damage.

melanogenesis.description:
Melanogenesis is the biosynthesis of melanin pigments, best characterized in cutaneous Melanocytes but also operative—in modified form—in neuromelanin-producing neurons. The pathway converts the amino acid L-Tyrosine into a heterogeneous polymer through a cascade of oxidations and cyclizations catalyzed chiefly by Tyrosinase. Understanding melanogenesis is central to neuromelanin research because the same catecholamine-handling chemistry that makes skin pigment also generates the Aminochromes that polymerize into Neuromelanin in the Substantia Nigra Pars Compacta.

The Core Enzymatic Cascade
Tyrosinase initiation: Tyrosinase hydroxylates L-Tyrosine to L-DOPA, then oxidizes L-DOPA to dopaquinone.
Branch point: Under low cysteine, dopaquinone cyclizes to dopachrome, rearranges (via dopachrome tautomerase/TRP2 and DHICA oxidase/TRP1) to indoles, and polymerizes into Eumelanin. Under high cysteine, it forms cysteinyldopas and ultimately Pheomelanin.
Regulation: The MC1R/cAMP axis promotes eumelanogenesis; ASIP/Agouti opposes it.

Neuromelanogenesis in the Brain

In dopaminergic neurons, the substrate is not tyrosine alone but the catecholamines Dopamine, L-DOPA, and Norepinephrine themselves. Their auto-oxidation and enzyme-catalyzed oxidation yield dopaquinone, aminochromes, and quinone methides that covalently cross-link proteins, lipids, and metals into the insoluble, granular Neuromelanin. This process is partly non-enzymatic and accelerates with age and catecholamine turnover. Unlike skin melanin (exported in melanosomes), neuromelanin remains intracellular, accumulating lifelong and interacting with Lysosomal Dysfunction.

Protective vs. Pathological Roles

Melanogenesis produces a redox-active polymer: eumelanin can buffer free radicals (protective), yet the quinone intermediates and pigment-bound iron can promote Oxidative Stress (pathological). The balance determines whether pigment shields the neuron or contributes to its vulnerability in Parkinson's Disease.

Research Relevance

Melanogenesis enzymes (tyrosinase, TRP1/2) and their inhibitors are studied both for pigmentation disorders and as probes of neuromelanin formation. Modeling neuromelanogenesis in vitro helps dissect how Alpha-synuclein and pigment co-localize in Lewy Bodies.

L-Tyrosine - amino acid precursor of the pathway.
L-DOPA - intermediate and also a neuromelanin precursor.
Neuromelanin - brain pigment formed by neuronal melanogenesis.
Eumelanin - black/brown end-product in skin.
Pheomelanin - red/yellow cysteine-derived product.
MC1R - master regulator of eumelanin vs. pheomelanin fate.

regulated_cell_death.description:
Overview

Regulated cell death (RCD) encompasses genetically encoded pathways by which cells die in a controlled manner, in contrast to unregulated necrotic death. Major forms include Apoptosis, Necroptosis, Pyroptosis, Autophagic Cell Death, and Ferroptosis, each with distinct molecular machinery and physiological functions.



Ferroptosis is a regulated, iron-dependent cell death pathway in which cells lose their ability to regulate fats and eventually die, distinct from unregulated necrosis or other programmed death programs. It was discovered and named (originally "oxytosis") by Pam Maher in 2001. The hallmark mechanism is accumulation of lipid peroxides to toxic levels, normally kept in check by Glutathione via glutathione peroxidase 4.

[!info] Druggable and regulatable
Because ferroptosis is druggable and genetically regulatable, it has become a promising therapeutic target alongside cellular senescence for supporting healthy aging and clearing dysfunctional cells.

Context & Clinical Relevance

RCD is increasingly linked to neurodegeneration and age-related diseases. The relationship between cell death programs and Cellular Senescence is central to tissue homeostasis: senescence arrests potentially damaged cells, while regulated death clears them. In cancer, evading RCD is a hallmark, and reactivating death programs — through BH3 mimetics, necroptosis inducers, or ferroptosis sensitizers — is a major therapeutic strategy.

Therapeutic Directions

The druggability of ferroptosis (e.g., via GPX4 or system xc− inhibition) and its interplay with senescence and immunotherapy make it an active area of translational research for clearing dysfunctional cells in aging and disease.

Documents
Could this enzyme help remove "zombie" cells from our tissues?
This document introduces ferroptosis as a regulated, iron-dependent death pathway distinct from necrosis and apoptosis, framing it alongside cellular senescence as a druggable target for healthy aging.

Necroptosis: Regulated necrotic-like death pathway.

immune_aging.description:
Immune Aging, also known as Immunosenescence, refers to the gradual deterioration of the Immune System with age. It is characterized by a decline in both innate and adaptive immune responses, making older individuals more susceptible to infections, reduced vaccine efficacy, and a higher risk of chronic inflammatory diseases.

Key Features
Thymic Involution: The shrinking of the thymus, leading to reduced production of naïve T cells.
Inflammaging: A state of chronic, low-grade systemic inflammation.
Senescence: Accumulation of senescent immune cells with a Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype (SASP).
Altered Cell Dynamics: Changes in the proportions and functions of various immune cell subsets.

Clinical Implications
Immune aging is a major driver of age-related morbidity and mortality, contributing to conditions such as Atherosclerosis, Cancer, and increased severity of viral infections like COVID-19.

Therapeutic Strategies
Interventions targeting immune aging include autophagy inducers like Rapamycin, Metformin, and Spermidine, as well as lifestyle changes such as Dietary Restriction and Exercise.

retinal_pigment_epithelium.description:
Overview

The retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is a monolayer of hexagonal, heavily pigmented epithelial cells situated between the photoreceptor outer segments and Bruch's membrane/choriocapillaris. As a critical component of the blood-retina barrier, the RPE performs multiple essential functions: phagocytosis of shed photoreceptor outer segments (POS), regeneration of 11-cis-retinal via the visual cycle (RPE65), transepithelial transport of ions, nutrients, and metabolites, secretion of growth factors (PEDF, VEGF), and absorption of stray light by melanin granules. RPE dysfunction is central to the pathogenesis of age-related macular degeneration (AMD), retinitis pigmentosa, and other retinal dystrophies.

Structure & Microanatomy
Apical microvilli: Interdigitate with photoreceptor outer segments; mediate phagocytosis via αvβ5 integrin and MERTK signaling
Basal lamina: Secretes collagen IV, laminin, and fibronectin forming Bruch's membrane
Tight junctions: ZO-1, occludin, claudin-19 form the outer blood-retina barrier
Melanosomes: Mature melanosomes absorb scattered light; lipofuscin accumulates with age (A2E, lipofuscin fluorophores)
Mitochondria-rich: High metabolic demand for phagocytosis and visual cycle

Key Functions

Phagocytosis of Photoreceptor Outer Segments

Photoreceptors shed ~10% of their outer segments daily. RPE recognizes phosphatidylserine on POS via MFG-E8 and αvβ5 integrin, triggering MERTK-dependent phagocytosis. Lysosomal degradation requires RPE65, LRAT, and cathepsins. Defects cause retinitis pigmentosa (MERTK, RPE65) and AMD (impaired clearance).


All-trans-retinal released from bleached rhodopsin is reduced to all-trans-retinol by RDH8/12 in photoreceptors, transported to RPE via IRBP, esterified by LRAT, isomerized to 11-cis-retinol by RPE65 (isomerohydrolase), oxidized to 11-cis-retinal by RDH5/RDH11, and transported back to photoreceptors. RPE65 mutations cause Leber congenital amaurosis (LCA2) and retinitis pigmentosa.

Blood-Retina Barrier & Transport

Apical (apical Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, BEST1 Cl⁻ channel) and basolateral transporters maintain ionic homeostasis, remove metabolic waste (lactate, CO₂), and supply glucose (GLUT1), fatty acids, and vitamin A. BEST1 mutations cause Best vitelliform macular dystrophy.


PEDF (anti-angiogenic, neurotrophic) — apical secretion

CFH, CFB, C3 — complement regulation; CFH Y402H variant major AMD risk factor

Clinical Relevance

Age-Related Macular Degeneration (AMD)
Dry AMD (Geographic Atrophy): RPE atrophy precedes photoreceptor loss; driven by oxidative stress, complement dysregulation (CFH, C3, ARMS2/HTRA1), lipofuscin toxicity (A2E), and impaired autophagy.
Wet AMD (Neovascular AMD): RPE-derived VEGF drives choroidal neovascularization (CNV) through Bruch's membrane breaks. Anti-VEGF therapy (aflibercept, ranibizumab, faricimab) is standard-of-care.
Risk variants: CFH Y402H (OR ~3-7), ARMS2/HTRA1, C3, APOE, TIMP3.

Retinitis Pigmentosa & Leber Congenital Amaurosis

RPE65, LRAT, RDH5, MERTK, RLBP1 mutations cause autosomal recessive RP/LCA. RPE65 gene therapy (voretigene neparvovec/AAV2-RPE65, Luxturna®) approved 2017 — first FDA-approved gene therapy for inherited retinal disease.



iPSC-RPE transplantation (subretinal delivery) in clinical trials for dry AMD (NCT02903576, NCT03102138, NCT04339764) and Stargardt disease. Key challenges: immune rejection, subretinal fibrosis, integration with host Bruch's membrane, and functional maturation. Polarized monolayer formation, phagocytic competence, and RPE65 expression are release criteria.

Other RPEopathies
Best disease (BEST1): Subretinal fluid accumulation, lipofuscin deposition
Central serous chorioretinopathy (CSCR): RPE pump dysfunction, choroidal hyperpermeability

disc.description:
The Death-Inducing Signaling Complex (DISC) is a multi-protein assembly that forms during the initiation of the Extrinsic Pathway of Apoptosis.

Assembly
The DISC forms on the intracellular tails of death receptors (e.g., Fas, DR4, DR5, TNFR1) following ligand binding.
Receptor Trimerization: Ligand binding causes receptors to cluster.
Adaptor Recruitment: The adaptor protein FADD (and sometimes TRADD) is recruited to the receptor's death domain.
Caspase Recruitment: FADD then recruits pro-Caspase-8 (or Caspase-10) molecules through death effector domain interactions.


The primary function of the DISC is to facilitate the proximity-induced auto-activation of Caspase-8. Once activated, caspase-8 is released into the cytoplasm to activate executioner caspases like Caspase-3.



List of documents that mention this entity
Apoptosis in cancer from pathogenesis to treatment
Binding of the death ligand to the death receptor results in the formation of a binding site for an adaptor protein and the whole ligand-receptor-adaptor protein complex is known as the DISC \[\].
In the Extrinsic Pathway, initiator Caspase-8 and Caspase-10 are activated through the formation of a death-inducing signal complex (DISC) in response to engagement of extracellular ligands (e.g. Fas or TNF ) by cell surface receptors (Figure 1).

Connections
Extrinsic Pathway: The central activation platform for death receptor-mediated apoptosis.
FADD: The core structural adaptor of the DISC.
Caspase-8: The enzyme activated within the DISC.
Intrinsic Pathway: Linked to the DISC via Bid cleavage.

arterial_aging.description:
Overview

Arterial aging refers to the progressive structural and functional deterioration of large elastic arteries with age, most prominently manifesting as arterial stiffening and impaired endothelium-dependent vasodilation. It is a central contributor to systolic hypertension, isolated systolic hypertension, and the rising cardiovascular risk of aging populations. Mechanistically, arterial aging is driven by the accumulation of oxidative stress, low-grade inflammation, and cellular senescence within the vessel wall, and is held in check by competent Autophagy.

Mechanism / Structure

With age, autophagic flux in vascular cells declines. Impaired autophagy permits damaged mitochondria, misfolded proteins, and lipid aggregates to accumulate, promoting endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, and vascular stiffening. The loss of nitric-oxide (NO)-mediated relaxation follows from this oxidative and inflammatory burden, as endothelial NO bioavailability falls.

[!info] Autophagy as the defender of vascular youth
Autophagy prevents arterial aging by clearing damaged mitochondria and aggregates that would otherwise drive endothelial dysfunction and stiffening. Enhancing autophagy — pharmacologically or via caloric restriction — rescues endothelial function in preclinical models.



Spermidine reverses features of arterial aging, including large elastic artery stiffening, and restores NO-mediated endothelial function in aged vessels. These vascular benefits are linked to spermidine-induced autophagy, which clears damaged mitochondria and reduces vascular oxidative stress and inflammation. By improving endothelium-dependent vasodilation, spermidine counteracts the stiffening that propagates systolic hypertension and cardiovascular risk with age, supporting it as a candidate vascular-rejuvenation intervention.

Clinical & Research Significance

Arterial aging underlies much of the systolic hypertension and arterial stiffness seen in older adults and predicts adverse cardiovascular events independently of traditional risk factors. Interventions that restore autophagic competence — such as spermidine, caloric restriction, or other autophagy enhancers — are promising but remain largely preclinical. The key translational challenge is demonstrating durable human vascular benefit and defining the optimal timing and intensity of autophagy modulation.

Documents
Knowledge-graph triple contexts (spermidine reverses arterial aging; autophagy prevents arterial aging) were the source material for this note.
Connections
Autophagy: Competent autophagic flux defends against arterial stiffening and endothelial dysfunction.
Spermidine: Induces autophagy that reverses arterial aging features and restores NO-mediated function.

anti_inflammatory.description:

elastin.description: Elastin is a highly elastic structural protein of the ECM that provides resilience, recoil, and compliance to tissues subject to repeated mechanical stress—including skin, lungs, arteries, ligaments, and vocal cords. Elastin is one of the longest-lived proteins in the human body (half-life of decades), and its progressive degradation and crosslinking with age are fundamental drivers of tissue stiffening, skin ageing, and cardiovascular disease. Structure & Biosynthesis Gene: ELN is located on chromosome 7q11.23. Deletions or mutations cause Williams syndrome (supravalvular aortic stenosis, connective tissue abnormalities). Protein: Elastin is a ~72 kDa soluble precursor (tropoelastin) that is secreted by fibroblasts, smooth muscle cells, and chondrocytes. Tropoelastin monomers are cross-linked by Lysyl Oxidase (LOX) on microfibrillar scaffolds (composed of fibrillin-1 and fibrillin-2) to form insoluble elastin polymers. Crosslinking: Elastin crosslinks include desmosine and isodesmosine, unique amino acids formed by LOX-mediated oxidative deamination of lysine residues. These crosslinks give elastin its extraordinary elasticity and durability. Turnover: Elastin has an extremely slow turnover rate in adult tissues. In healthy human arteries, elastin half-life is estimated at 70+ years, making it one of the most stable proteins in the body. This longevity makes elastin particularly vulnerable to cumulative damage from glycation, oxidation, and proteolysis. [!important] Longest-Lived Structural Protein Elastin's extreme longevity (decades) means that damage from glycation, oxidation, and proteolysis accumulates over a lifetime without efficient repair, making it a central player in ageing-related tissue deterioration. Tissue Distribution & Function Skin: Elastin fibres in the dermis provide elasticity and resilience. Loss of elastin integrity manifests as sagging, wrinkles, and loss of skin recoil. Lungs: Elastin in alveolar walls enables lung expansion and recoil during breathing. Elastin degradation is the hallmark of emphysema. Arteries: Elastic lamellae in large arteries (aorta, carotids) enable pulsatile recoil and maintain blood pressure during diastole. Elastin fragmentation drives arterial stiffening. Ligaments & tendons: Elastin provides elasticity and recoil, particularly in ligaments subject to repeated stretching (e.g., ligamentum flava of the spine). Other: Vocal cords, bladder, uterus, and cornea all contain elastin essential for their mechanical function. Degradation & Proteases Elastin is resistant to most proteases but is degraded by a specialised set of elastinolytic enzymes: MMP-12: The most potent elastinolytic MMP. MMP-12 is the only MMP that can effectively degrade insoluble elastin at physiological concentrations, making it the principal elastase in macrophage-mediated tissue remodelling. MMP-2: Gelatinase A has moderate elastinolytic activity. MMP-9: Gelatinase B degrades elastin, particularly in inflammatory lung disease. MMP-3: Stromelysin-1 degrades elastin as part of its broad substrate repertoire. Neutrophil elastase: A serine protease from neutrophil granules; potent elastinolytic enzyme prominent in pulmonary inflammation. Cathepsins: Cathepsin S and cathepsin L contribute to elastin degradation in the vasculature and skin. Elastin Fragmentation & Elastokines Degradation of elastin generates bioactive fragments called elastin-derived peptides (EDPs) or elastokines, which have potent signalling activities: EBP receptor: EDPs bind the elastin-binding protein (EBP), a complex of spliced Gal-3, elastin-binding protein, and Neu-1 sialidase on the cell surface. MMP amplification: EDP–EBP signalling upregulates MMP expression (including MMP-2, MMP-9, MMP-12), creating a positive feedback loop of elastin degradation. Inflammation: EDPs are chemotactic for monocytes and macrophages, promoting inflammatory cell recruitment to degraded elastic tissues. Senescence: EDP-mediated MMP upregulation in dermal fibroblasts contributes to the aged fibroblast phenotype and paracrine senescence. [!warning] Positive Feedback Loop Elastin fragmentation → EDP generation → EBP signalling → MMP upregulation → further elastin degradation. This feed-forward loop accelerates tissue deterioration in ageing, COPD, and atherosclerosis. Age-Related Changes Glycation & AGEs Elastin accumulates advanced glycation end-products (AGEs) over the lifespan. AGE crosslinks stiffen elastin fibres, reduce elasticity, and make elastin resistant to normal remodelling. The Maillard reaction generates these crosslinks progressively, contributing to arterial stiffening and loss of skin compliance. Oxidative Damage Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS) from UV radiation, cigarette smoke, and inflammatory cells damage elastin through direct oxidation and by upregulating elastinolytic MMPs. UVA-induced singlet oxygen is a major driver of solar elastosis (photoaging).

serum.description: Serum is the clear, pale-yellow liquid fraction of Blood that remains after coagulation, with a composition nearly identical to Plasma but lacking clotting factors such as Fibrinogen, Prothrombin, and Factor VIII. It constitutes approximately 50–55% of total Blood volume and serves as a versatile medium for transport, immune defense, and clinical diagnostics. Overview Serum is obtained by allowing whole Blood to clot for 30–60 minutes at room temperature, then removing the clot by centrifugation (1,000–2,000 g for 10–15 minutes). The resulting supernatant is serum. Unlike Plasma, which is prepared by adding anticoagulants (e.g., heparin, citrate, EDTA) to prevent clotting, serum retains the full complement of soluble factors released during coagulation, including Platelet-derived growth factors and proteolytic enzymes generated by the clotting cascade. The yield from whole Blood is approximately 45–55% of the original volume. Composition Serum is an aqueous solution (≈91–92% water) containing a complex mixture of proteins, electrolytes, nutrients, hormones, and waste products. The total protein concentration of serum is approximately 60–80 mg/mL, with the two major fractions being: Albumin (~35–50 mg/mL): The most abundant serum protein, synthesized in the liver. It maintains Oncotic Pressure, transports hydrophobic molecules (free fatty acids, bilirubin, drugs, thyroid hormones), and serves as an antioxidant via its free thiol group at Cys34. Globulins (~20–35 mg/mL): A heterogeneous group subdivided into α₁, α₂, β, and γ fractions. The γ-globulins correspond to immunoglobulins (Antibodies), produced by B lymphocytes. Additional proteins include complement factors (C3, C4), transferrin, haptoglobin, lipoproteins (HDL, LDL, VLDL), and acute-phase reactants such as C-Reactive Protein and serum amyloid A. Electrolytes Serum electrolyte concentrations are tightly regulated: Electrolyte Normal Range (mM) ------------- ------------------- Sodium (Na⁺) 135–145 Potassium (K⁺) 3.5–5.0 Chloride (Cl⁻) 98–106 Bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) 22–26 Calcium (Ca²⁺) 2.2–2.6 Phosphate (PO₄³⁻) 0.8–1.5 Magnesium (Mg²⁺) 0.7–1.0 Other Components Serum carries nutrients (glucose, amino acids, fatty acids, vitamins), metabolic waste products (Urea, Creatinine, Bilirubin), hormones (thyroid hormones, cortisol, insulin, catecholamines), cytokines, growth factors, and circulating nucleic acids. It also contains numerous enzymes, including transaminases (ALT, AST), Alkaline Phosphatase, Gamma-Glutamyl Transferase (GGT), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), and Creatine Kinase (CK). Functions Transport and Carrier Function Serum serves as the primary vehicle for distributing nutrients, hormones, and drugs throughout the body. Albumin and carrier globulins (e.g., Thyroid-Binding Globulin, Sex Hormone-Binding Globulin, Corticosteroid-Binding Globulin) solubilize and deliver hydrophobic cargo. Many therapeutic drugs circulate largely bound to serum proteins, which affects their pharmacokinetics, volume of distribution, and elimination half-life. Immune Defense Serum contains Antibodies (IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE, IgD) that neutralize pathogens, opsonize targets for phagocytosis, and activate complement. The Complement System (classical, lectin, and alternative pathways) mediates direct lysis of microbes, opsonization, and chemotaxis. Serum immunoglobulins are the basis of humoral immunity and passive immunotherapy (e.g., intravenous immunoglobulin, or IVIG). pH Buffering Serum bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻/CO₂ system) is the primary extracellular buffer, maintaining pH 7.35–7.45. Albumin and phosphate provide secondary buffering capacity. Imbalances manifest as metabolic alkalosis or acidosis, with characteristic changes in serum HCO₃⁻ and anion gap. Water and Electrolyte Balance Serum composition reflects whole-body fluid and electrolyte homeostasis. The Kidneys regulate serum sodium, potassium, chloride, and bicarbonate concentrations through reabsorption, secretion, and excretion. Disturbances in serum electrolytes are common in renal disease, endocrine disorders, and diuretic therapy. Clinical Significance Diagnostic Biomarkers Serum is the most widely used sample type in clinical laboratory medicine. Key biomarkers include: Troponin I and Troponin T: Cardiac-specific markers for Myocardial Infarction (MI) and myocardial injury. C-Reactive Protein (CRP): Acute-phase reactant; elevated in Inflammation and infection. Creatinine and Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN): Markers of renal function; the BUN:creatinine ratio aids differential diagnosis of Acute Kidney Injury. Glucose: Diagnostic for Diabetes Mellitus (fasting, postprandial, and HbA1c). ALT (alanine transaminase), AST (aspartate transaminase), GGT (gamma-glutamyl transferase): Markers of Hepatocellular Injury and cholestasis. Autoantibodies: Antinuclear antibodies (ANA), rheumatoid factor (RF), anti-TPO, anti-tTG — serological hallmarks of autoimmune disease. Tumor markers: PSA (prostate), CA-125 (ovarian), CEA (colorectal), AFP (hepatocellular), CA 19-9 (pancreatic).

covid_19.description:
COVID-19 (coronavirus disease 2019) is an infectious respiratory disease caused by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). It ranges from asymptomatic infection to severe viral pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and multi-organ involvement, with systemic inflammation and immune dysregulation as central features.

Etiology & Pathophysiology

COVID-19 results from SARS-CoV-2 infection of angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2)-expressing cells, driving inflammatory and oxidative stress pathways. Dysregulated immune responses, lymphopenia, and cytokine release contribute to severe lung injury and extrapulmonary complications.

Sirtuin Involvement (Wu et al., 2022)
SIRT1: An unbalanced p53/SIRT1 axis impacts lymphocyte homeostasis in COVID-19 — persistently activated p53 due to low SIRT1 may contribute to lymphopenia; increased SIRT1 may alleviate pathogenesis.
SIRT3: Serum SIRT3 levels are associated with clinical outcome/prognosis, markedly lower in severe versus mild/moderate patients, suggesting SIRT3 as a prognostic marker.

Therapeutic Implications

Sirtuin modulation (particularly SIRT1 activation to restore p53 balance and lymphocyte homeostasis) is proposed as a strategy to mitigate immune dysfunction in COVID-19, while serum SIRT3 may serve as a severity biomarker.

french_paradox.description:
The French paradox is the epidemiological observation that populations in France have relatively low rates of coronary heart disease and Atherosclerosis despite consuming a diet rich in saturated fats, low physical activity, and high rates of tobacco use. The term was popularized in the 1980s–1990s and has been partly attributed to the moderate consumption of red wine, which contains Resveratrol and other Polyphenols with antioxidant properties. The paradox has been central to the study of resveratrol and red wine's cardioprotective effects.

Key Observations

[!info] Source: Berrougui et al., Atherosclerosis 2009
The "French paradox" — the paradoxical observation that a low incidence of CVD could co-exist with a high-fat diet intake and moderate consumption of red wine — was a primary impetus for research on resveratrol.
Low CVD incidence despite high saturated fat intake
Moderate red wine consumption is a cultural norm in France and a distinguishing dietary factor between French and other Western populations
Red wine contains Resveratrol and other Polyphenols

Resveratrol, a Stilbene polyphenol found in grape skin, was identified as a candidate mediator of the observed cardiovascular benefits

Proposed Mechanisms
Resveratrol: Inhibits Lipid Peroxidation, enhances Cholesterol Efflux, upregulates ABCA1
Other polyphenols: Polyphenolic compounds in red wine have antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties
HDL effects: Non-alcoholized red wine increases plasma HDL in rats
Cholesterol reduction: Red wine polyphenols reduce total plasma Cholesterol in hamsters

Epidemiological Evidence
Wine consumption has been inversely correlated with CVD risk in multiple populations
The WHO MONICA project documented declining coronary heart disease mortality in France
Animal studies confirm the protective effect of wine polyphenols on plasma lipids

Scientific Impact

The French Paradox spurred extensive investigation into:
The Sirtuin system and SIRT1 activation by dietary polyphenols
Antioxidant mechanisms of red wine polyphenols in endothelial protection
The role of Nitric Oxide in wine's vasodilatory effects
Oxidative Stress modulation by dietary Polyphenols

Criticisms and Nuances
Some researchers attribute the paradox partly to dietary pattern differences (e.g., lower processed food intake, higher vegetable consumption) rather than wine alone
The Mediterranean Diet as a whole — not just red wine — likely drives the cardiovascular benefit
Later large-scale studies have questioned whether moderate alcohol confers net cardiovascular benefit, though polyphenol-specific effects remain of interest

Documents
Berrougui et al., Atherosclerosis 2009
French paradox identified as primary impetus for resveratrol research; red wine polyphenols inhibit atherosclerotic progression.
The Sirtuin System The Holy Grail of Resveratrol?
The French Paradox reflects the reduced incidence of Cardiovascular Disease found in some French populations with moderate wine consumption despite a high-fat intake, low exercise, and increased tobacco use.

Connections
Resveratrol — Key polyphenol in red wine attributed to the French paradox; central to its study since the 1980s–1990s


Atherosclerosis — Red wine polyphenols inhibit atherosclerotic progression
HDL — Red wine increases plasma HDL levels
Cholesterol — Red wine polyphenols reduce plasma cholesterol

Mediterranean Diet — Distinguishing dietary factor; the diet as a whole likely drives the benefit
Stilbene — Polyphenol class of resveratrol in grape skin
Sirtuins — Sirtuin system and SIRT1 activation by dietary polyphenols

cd157.description: CD157 (also known as BST-1, bone marrow stromal cell antigen 1) is a glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored ectoenzyme encoded by the BST1 gene on chromosome 4p15. It is a member of the ADP-ribosyl cyclase family, alongside CD38, and catalyzes the conversion of NAD+ to cyclic ADP-ribose (cADPR) and ADP-ribose, both of which are calcium-mobilizing second messengers. The enzyme can also produce Nicotinamide as a byproduct of its NAD+ glycohydrolase activity. Structure & Domains CD157 is a GPI-anchored protein of approximately 33 kDa (unglycosylated), tethered to the outer leaflet of the plasma membrane via a GPI anchor. Its single catalytic domain is structurally homologous to CD38, sharing a conserved (β/α)₈ TIM barrel fold characteristic of the ADP-ribosyl cyclase family. The active site contains a catalytic triad comprising Glu179, Trp184, and Thr188, which coordinates substrate binding and catalysis. The enzyme possesses 3–4 N-glycosylation sites that contribute to proper folding, stability, and surface expression. Unlike CD38, which is a type II transmembrane protein, CD157 lacks a transmembrane domain and relies entirely on its GPI anchor for membrane attachment, conferring distinct lateral mobility and membrane microdomain localization. Mechanism of Action CD157 exhibits three distinct enzymatic activities, with the relative ratios varying across species and cell types: NAD+ glycohydrolase — Hydrolyzes NAD+ to ADP-ribose and Nicotinamide, representing the predominant activity in most contexts. ADP-ribosyl cyclase — Cyclizes NAD+ to form cADPR, a cyclic nucleotide second messenger. cADPR hydrolase — Hydrolyzes cADPR to ADP-ribose, terminating the calcium-mobilizing signal. cADPR is a potent calcium second messenger that activates ryanodine receptors on the Endoplasmic Reticulum, triggering Ca²⁺ release into the cytosol. This calcium signal is critical for diverse cellular processes, including muscle contraction, secretion, gene expression, and cell migration. The balance between CD157's cyclase and hydrolase activities determines the amplitude and duration of cADPR-mediated calcium signals. Physiological Function Immune System CD157 is expressed on Monocytes, Macrophages, Neutrophils, and bone marrow stromal cells. It promotes B Cell growth and differentiation, partly through its enzymatic production of cADPR and consequent calcium signaling. CD157 also functions as a cell adhesion molecule, facilitating interactions with Integrins on adjacent cells. In Neutrophils, CD157 regulates migration and transendothelial extravasation, contributing to leukocyte trafficking during Inflammation. CD157 is expressed in the brain, where its cADPR-producing activity contributes to neuronal calcium homeostasis. Given that CD38-mediated cADPR signaling regulates oxytocin release and social behavior, CD157 may play complementary roles in the central nervous system. The BST1 locus has been linked to Parkinson's Disease susceptibility, suggesting a role in Dopaminergic Neurons survival and function. Bone Marrow Stromal Support As its name suggests, CD157 is highly expressed on bone marrow stromal cells, where it supports hematopoiesis by providing trophic signals to developing hematopoietic progenitors. The enzymatic production of cADPR and ADP-ribose within the bone marrow Microenvironment influences progenitor cell proliferation and differentiation. Pathology & Clinical Relevance Parkinson's Disease The BST1 gene is a well-established GWAS risk locus for sporadic Parkinson's Disease. Multiple independent studies have identified single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) at this locus, including rs11724635 and rs4698412, that confer increased disease risk. The mechanism is thought to involve altered CD157 expression or enzymatic activity, which may affect Dopaminergic Neurons vulnerability to age-related stressors. Reduced cADPR production could impair calcium buffering and mitochondrial function in substantia nigra neurons, while excess NAD+ consumption may deplete cellular NAD+ reserves, compromising Sirtuins and other NAD+-dependent enzymes. CD157 is overexpressed in synovial fibroblasts from patients with Rheumatoid Arthritis, where it may contribute to the hyperproliferative and invasive phenotype of the synovial lining. The BST1 locus has also been associated with Inflammatory Bowel Disease, implicating CD157 in intestinal immune homeostasis. Cancer CD157 expression has been documented in certain cancers, where it may influence the Tumor Microenvironment through modulation of NAD+ metabolism and calcium signaling. In some contexts, CD157 overexpression on tumor-associated stromal cells could suppress antitumor immunity by depleting local NAD+ or by generating immunosuppressive adenosine downstream of ADP-ribose metabolism.

bleomycin.description:
Bleomycin is a glycopeptide antibiotic that causes DNA double-strand breaks via iron-mediated free-radical generation. Clinically it is used as a chemotherapeutic (e.g., in lymphoma and testicular cancer regimens).

Use as a Senescence Inducer

[!info] Source: Repurposing apigenin for senomorphic effect in antiaging pipelines
In the apigenin study, PSC27 prostate stromal cells were treated with a sub-lethal dose of bleomycin (50 μg/mL; "BLEO"), producing a canonical senescence phenotype after 8–10 days — elevated SA-β-Gal, reduced BrdU incorporation, and increased DDR foci. BLEO-induced senescence was used to screen and characterize apigenin's senomorphic suppression of the SASP.

Bleomycin is a standard tool for generating therapy-induced senescence (TIS) in vitro, alongside ionizing radiation and topoisomerase II inhibitors such as Mitoxantrone.



List of documents that mention this entity
Cellular Senescence in IPF (Baurzhan et al., 2026)
The bleomycin model shows senescent alveolar epithelial cells precede fibrotic remodeling, though it incompletely recapitulates chronic human IPF.

bak.description:
Overview
BAK (Bcl-2 homologous antagonist/killer) is a pro-apoptotic Bcl-2 family effector that resides constitutively embedded in the outer mitochondrial membrane of healthy cells. Unlike the mostly cytosolic BAX, BAK is activated in situ by BH3-only proteins (e.g., Bid), whereupon it oligomerizes to form the pores that drive Apoptosis.

Structure & Activation
BAK contains BH1–BH3 domains and is held in check by anti-apoptotic partners such as Bcl-2 and Mcl-1. Displacement by activators (Bim, Bid, Puma, Noxa) liberates BAK to assemble large β-barrel pores. BAK and BAX are functionally redundant at the membrane yet operate from distinct cellular compartments.

Mechanism of Action & MOMP
Activated BAK hetero-oligomerizes with BAX and additional BAK subunits, permeabilizing the outer membrane and releasing Cytochrome c and Smac DIABLO. This initiates the Caspases cascade and the execution phase of death. The resulting leakage also amplifies Reactive Oxygen Species and can trigger Mitophagy via Parkin.

Phosphorylation-Dependent Licensing

BAK is maintained in an inactive state on the mitochondria through inhibitory phosphorylation at Tyr108. For BAK to be activated, it must be dephosphorylated at this site. This "licensing" is mediated by the PTPN5 (STEP), along with PTPN2 and PTPN23. In K-RAS mutated cancers (e.g., colon cancer), hyperactive ERK1/2 phosphorylates and inactivates PTPN5, locking BAK in its inactive state and providing profound resistance to apoptosis. Genetic loss or downregulation of PTPN2 and PTPN23 is common in T-cell leukemias and epithelial cancers, raising the threshold for BAK activation.

Physiology, Redox & Longevity
BAK-mediated permeabilization intersects with Mitochondrial Dysfunction, senescent-cell survival, and Inflammaging. Cells that downregulate BAK/BAX resist death and contribute to the Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype in aging. Senotherapeutics and Nicotinamide Riboside-associated metabolic remodeling influence these pathways, positioning BAK as a longevity-relevant node linking apoptosis, mitophagy, and redox control.

[!info] Source: document - Complex I drives glutamine-dependent TCA cycle to support viability of MYChigh breast cancer cells (NAD+)
Metformin induces conformational BAK activation (exposing the N-terminal neoepitope) preferentially in MYC^high^ TNBC cells, with 40–60% of cells staining BAK-positive at 72h. BAX is not activated under the same conditions. In breast epithelial cells, BAK conformational activation reflects mitochondrial apoptotic sensitization rather than execution of Apoptosis — downstream events (BAX activation, caspase cleavage) require additional stimuli. This MYC-dependent BAK priming positions Complex I inhibition as a sensitization strategy for combination therapies.

methylfolate.description:
Methylfolate — chemically L-5-methyltetrahydrofolate (5-MTHF) — is the active, methylated circulating form of Folate. It is the predominant folate species in plasma and the sole folate derivative that can cross the blood–brain barrier, making it central to CNS methylation and monoamine metabolism.

Chemical Structure and Source

Methylfolate is a reduced tetrahydrofolate bearing a methyl group at the N5 position. Dietary folates are first reduced and methylated intracellularly, a final step catalyzed by MTHFR (methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase). Unlike folic acid (the synthetic oxidized form), 5-MTHF requires no reductive activation and is directly usable, which is why it is the preferred supplemental form in individuals with MTHFR impairments.

Mechanism in the Methylation Cycle

Methylfolate donates its methyl group to Homocysteine via Methionine Synthase (using MethylB12 as cofactor), producing Methionine and regenerating tetrahydrofolate. Methionine is then converted to S-Adenosylmethionine (SAMe), the universal methyl donor for COMT and all other methyltransferases. Thus methylfolate sits upstream of the methyl-group pool that COMT (Catechol-O-methyltransferase) consumes to inactivate catecholamines.

Interaction with COMT and Sensitivity

Individuals carrying slow COMT variants (Val158Met Met/Met) have reduced catechol-methylating capacity. High-dose Methylfolate supplementation can flood the cycle with methyl groups, accelerating catecholamine turnover and producing "overmethylation" symptoms: anxiety, irritability, rage, insomnia, and palpitations. This is most pronounced when methylfolate is combined with MethylB12. Clinical guidance often recommends starting at very low doses (e.g., 100–400 µg) and tapering, with monitoring for mood changes.

Clinical and Research Relevance

5-MTHF is used to lower elevated homocysteine, support pregnancy (neural tube defect prevention), and as adjunctive therapy in depression and schizophrenia where methylation and SAMe availability are compromised. The MTHFR C677T polymorphism markedly reduces methylfolate generation, making direct 5-MTHF supplementation the standard intervention.

COMT How to Optimize Your Supplements for Your COMT Genotype
Some people with slow COMT enzyme function have side effects from Methylated Vitamins (Methylfolate, MethylB12), Methyl Donor supplements, and COMT Inhibitors supplements.
