thrombospondin_1.description:
Overview

Thrombospondin-1 (TSP-1, encoded by THBS1) is a large matricellular glycoprotein that modulates cell-matrix interactions, cell adhesion, survival, inflammation, and angiogenesis. It is secreted by platelets, endothelial cells, and macrophages, particularly under stress.

Structure & Domains

TSP-1 is a homotrimer containing multiple functional domains, including the N-terminal domain, procollagen-like and type I (properdin-like) repeats, EGF-like repeats, and a C-terminal domain. These domains mediate binding to diverse receptors including CD36, CD47, integrins, and proteoglycans.



The CD36 receptor binds thrombospondin-1, and this interaction activates FYN kinase and p38 MAPK signaling that influences cell adhesion, survival, and inflammation. Thrombospondin-1 thus acts as a CD36 ligand that shapes macrophage behavior. The directionality is ligand binding to intracellular signaling.

[!warning] Receptor promiscuity
Thrombospondin-1 has many other receptors (e.g., Integrins, CD47), so CD36 is one node in a broader network rather than the sole mediator of TSP-1 function.

Physiological & Pathological Roles

TSP-1-CD36 signaling can influence macrophage phagocytosis, Angiogenesis, and platelet function, expanding CD36's role beyond lipid uptake. TSP-1 is a major anti-angiogenic factor in the tumor microenvironment and is implicated in thrombosis, wound healing, and age-related inflammation.

pufa.description:
PUFA

Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) are fatty acids containing two or more cis double bonds. Key members include arachidonic acid (AA, 20:4), adrenic acid (AdA, 22:4), dihomo-γ-linolenic acid (DGLA, 20:3), docosahexaenoic acid (DHA, 22:6), eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA, 20:5), and linoleic acid (LA, 18:2). Their bis-allylic methylene groups make them exquisitely prone to lipid peroxidation.

Role in Ferroptosis

When esterified at the sn-2 position of membrane phospholipids (PL-PUFAs), PUFAs become the direct substrates for iron-dependent peroxidation—the execution step of Ferroptosis. The abundance and species of membrane PL-PUFAs (shaped by enzymes such as ACSL4 and, newly, Acid ceramidase) are major determinants of cellular ferroptosis sensitivity.

[!info] Source: Acid ceramidase modulates the lipid profile… (Soriano-Castell et al., 2026)
Acid ceramidase over-expression in replicatively senescent fibroblasts increased membrane PL-PUFA content (notably all arachidonic acid-containing PLs), creating a pro-ferroptotic profile. ACase knockdown lowered PL-PUFAs and protected against RSL3-induced Ferroptosis independently of GPX4/GSH and iron—because less PUFA substrate means less LPO.

mir_378.description:
Overview

miR-378 (miR-378a) is a ~22-nucleotide MicroRNA that regulates gene expression post-transcriptionally by binding target mRNA 3'-UTRs. It is notable for being co-transcribed with its host gene and for dual roles in mitochondrial energy metabolism and, in aging tissues, in the repression of SIRT1 as part of a pro-inflammatory miRNA network.

Genomic Locus & Family
miR-378a is encoded within the first intron of the PPARGC1B gene (PGC-1β) on chromosome 5q32, tying its expression to metabolic/mitochondrial biogenesis programs.
Paralogs (miR-378b–i) share a common seed sequence; the miR-378 family is conserved across mammals.


Metabolic targets: ERRγ (ESRRG), GABPA, and CRAT/MED13 — through which miR-378 modulates a metabolic shift and counterbalances PGC-1β activity (Carrer et al., PNAS 2012).
SIRT1: in the context of vascular and cartilage aging, miR-378 is reported among microRNAs that suppress SIRT1 translation via 3'-UTR binding, contributing to reduced deacetylase activity.
Additional context-dependent targets include apoptosis and angiogenesis regulators (e.g., SUFU, FUS-1, TUSC2).

Role in Senescence, Aging & Disease

[!info] Metabolism–inflammation crosstalk
Because miR-378 sits inside the PGC-1β locus, its dysregulation couples mitochondrial/metabolic decline with the SIRT1–NF-kappaB inflammatory axis relevant to Inflammaging.
Aging vasculature & cartilage: upregulated alongside miR-217 and miR-543, converging on SIRT1 loss, RelA/p65 hyperacetylation, and sustained inflammatory signaling (SASP).
Cardiac & metabolic disease: modulates cardiomyocyte survival, hypertrophy, and systemic energy homeostasis; studied in obesity and heart failure.
Cancer: context-dependent oncogenic or tumor-suppressive behavior depending on tissue.
Epigenetics link: via SIRT1 suppression, miR-378 indirectly influences Histone Modification states (e.g., H4K16 acetylation) and chromatin-based gene silencing.

Therapeutic Relevance

miR-378 is a proposed target of LNA antagomirs (with miR-217 and miR-543) to de-repress SIRT1 in aged endothelial and cartilage tissue.

sk61_2.description:
S6K1/2 (ribosomal protein S6 kinase 1 and 2; p70S6K/p85S6K) are AGC-family serine/threonine kinases that function as primary downstream effectors of mTORC1. They phosphorylate ribosomal protein S6 and a battery of translational regulators to promote protein synthesis, and they provide negative feedback that dampens upstream PI3K-Akt-IRS1 signaling.

Activation

mTORC1 phosphorylates and activates S6K1 at Thr389 (Thr389 in S6K1; analogous site in S6K2) . Active S6K1/2 then phosphorylates:
Ribosomal protein S6 — enhances translation of 5'-TOP mRNAs.
IRS1 (e.g., Ser1101) — negative feedback that desensitizes Insulin Signaling and PI3K-Akt signaling .
eIF4B, PDCD4 — translational regulators.

Role in Rapamycin Hormesis (mTOR-PI3K Incoherent Bivalent Motif)

In the mass-action model of Cerrillo, Vidakovic & Míguez (2026), S6K1/2 is central to the rapamycin Incoherent Bivalent Motif:
Active S6K1/2 inactivates mTORC2 (via mSIN1 phosphorylation)  — one branch of the incoherent loop.
S6K1/2-mediated IRS1 phosphorylation is the downstream-controlled node of the backward (mTORC1→IRS1) link.
The Michaelis-Menten constant for mTORC1→S6K1/2 activation is significantly lower than other interactions (narrow distribution, low median), placing this link in the Saturated Enzymatic Regime that maximizes hormesis probability .

Thus S6K1/2 is the kinetic "hinge" whose saturation makes the backward reaction thresholded, enabling rapamycin's inverted-U dose response (peak ~1 nM).

Physiological and Pathological Roles
Cell growth / hypertrophy: Drives ribosomal biogenesis and protein synthesis.
Metabolic disease: S6K1-mediated IRS1 phosphorylation creates negative feedback contributing to Insulin Resistance and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus.
Aging: Part of the mTOR-driven aging axis; inhibition mirrors benefits of Rapamycin and Caloric Restriction.

The Biochemical Basis of Hormesis

Incoherent Bivalent Motif — the motif in which S6K1/2 is the saturated hinge

keap1.description: Keap1 (Kelch-like ECH-associated protein 1) is a redox-sensitive protein that functions as a sensor for oxidative stress and regulates the degradation and nuclear translocation of NRF2. Domain Architecture Keap1 is a 624-amino acid protein with modular structure comprising five distinct domains: an N-terminal BTB (Broad-Complex, Tramtrack, and Bric-à-Brac) domain, an intervening linker region (IVR), a central BTB and C-terminal Kelch (BACK) domain, and six C-terminal Kelch repeats forming a β-propeller structure. The BTB domain mediates Keap1 homodimerization and recruitment of Cullin3 (Cul3) and RBX1 to form a functional Cullin-RING E3 ubiquitin ligase complex. The Kelch repeats bind directly to the NRF2 ETGE and DLG motifs, tethering Nrf2 for ubiquitination. Mechanism of Nrf2 Regulation Under basal conditions, Keap1 constitutively targets Nrf2 for K48-linked polyubiquitination and proteasomal degradation, maintaining low Nrf2 protein levels and preventing spurious activation of the Antioxidant Response Element (ARE) transcriptome. The Keap1-Cul3-E3 ligase complex cycles Nrf2 with a half-life of approximately 20 minutes. Keap1 functions as a substrate adaptor, positioning Nrf2 for ubiquitination at specific lysine residues in its Neh1 domain. The dimeric nature of Keap1 allows simultaneous binding of two Nrf2 molecules via the high-affinity ETGE and lower-affinity DLG motifs, creating a "hinge-and-latch" mechanism that is disrupted by electrophiles. Redox-Sensitive Cysteine Sensors Keap1 is distinguished by its exceptional cysteine content (27 cysteines in human Keap1), with several residues serving as redox-sensitive sensors. Critically, Cys151 in the BTB domain is required for Nrf2 activation by most electrophiles; Cys273 and Cys288 in the IVR are essential for regulation by certain heavy metals and oxidants; and Cys226, Cys434, and Cys613 contribute to overall redox sensitivity. Modification of these cysteines by electrophiles, ROS, or reactive nitrogen species induces conformational changes that impair Keap1's ability to ubiquitinate Nrf2, leading to Nrf2 stabilization and nuclear translocation. Conformational Changes and Nrf2 Dissociation Electrophile modification of Keap1's sensor cysteines, particularly Cys151, causes conformational rearrangements within the BTB domain that disrupt the Keap1-Cul3 interaction or alter the spatial orientation of the Kelch domain relative to the E3 ligase. This reduces the ubiquitination efficiency of Nrf2 bound via the DLG motif while retaining ETGE binding. Newly synthesized Nrf2 molecules are no longer efficiently ubiquitinated and instead accumulate, translocate to the nucleus, and activate ARE-driven gene expression. Connection to Adrenochrome and Electrophile Sensing In the context of the Adrenochrome Pathway, adrenochrome and its redox-cycling products act as electrophiles that can modify Keap1 sensor cysteines, thereby activating the NRF2 stress response. This Keap1-Nrf2-adrenochrome axis represents a feed-forward adaptive mechanism: electrophilic Aminochromes induce their own detoxification by upregulating NQO1, HO-1, and glutathione-synthesizing enzymes. Therapeutic targeting of Keap1 with small-molecule electrophiles (e.g., Sulforaphane, Dimethyl fumarate) is an active strategy to boost endogenous antioxidant defenses in neurodegeneration, Diabetes, Chronic Kidney Disease, and Aging. puma.description:
Puma (p53 upregulated modulator of apoptosis), also known as BBC3, is a potent pro-apoptotic BH3-only member of the Bcl-2 family.

Mechanism
Puma is a major downstream target of the p53 tumor suppressor protein. Upon DNA damage or other cellular stresses, p53 induces the expression of Puma. Puma then localizes to the mitochondria where it neutralizes anti-apoptotic proteins (like Bcl-2 and Bcl-xL) and potentially activates Bax and Bak to trigger the Intrinsic Pathway.


Deficiency in Puma or the p53 pathway leads to evasion of Apoptosis and promotes carcinogenesis. Restoring Puma expression is a potential therapeutic strategy.

lipid_peroxidation.description: Lipid peroxidation is the free radical chain reaction in which radicals abstract hydrogen from the polyunsaturated fatty acids of Cell Membranes, producing reactive aldehydes such as Malondialdehyde and 4-Hydroxynonenal. It is a central execution pathway of Oxidative Stress, damaging membranes, proteins, and DNA, and is a key process in Atherosclerosis. Initiation, Propagation, and Termination Lipid peroxidation proceeds through three classical phases. Initiation occurs when a radical—most notably Hydroxyl Radicals (•OH), Peroxynitrite (ONOO⁻), or a ferryl complex—abstracts hydrogen from a bis-allylic methylene (–CH₂–) of a PUFA. The resulting carbon-centered radical (L•) is resonance-stabilized by adjacent double bonds. Propagation is rapid and self-sustaining: L• reacts with O₂ at near-diffusion-limited rates (k ≈ 10⁸ M⁻¹s⁻¹) to form a lipid peroxyl radical (LOO•), which abstracts H from an adjacent PUFA, generating a lipid hydroperoxide (LOOH) and a new L•. Each initiator can oxidize dozens to hundreds of lipids. LOOH decomposes via the Fenton Reaction (LOOH + Fe²⁺ → LO• + OH⁻ + Fe³⁺), yielding alkoxyl radicals (LO•) that branch new chains—exponential amplification. Termination occurs when two radicals recombine (L• + L• → L–L; 2 LOO• → LOOL + O₂, Russell mechanism). Chain-breaking Antioxidants such as Vitamin E (k ≈ 10⁶ M⁻¹s⁻¹) intercept LOO•, donating H to form a stable tocopheroxyl radical; Ascorbic Acid regenerates α-tocopherol at the membrane–water interface. [!info] Source: Berrougui et al., Atherosclerosis 2009 Lipid peroxidation is characterized by the formation of conjugated dienes, lipid hydroperoxides, TBARS, and aldehydes. In LDL, oxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acids produces conjugated dienes (measured at 234 nm) and alters the apoB protein moiety. In HDL, lipid peroxidation alters phospholipid fluidity, modifies apoprotein structure, and decreases PON1 activity. Major Products and Reactivity Primary products are lipid hydroperoxides, which fragment into secondary aldehydes: Malondialdehyde (from PUFAs with ≥3 double bonds), 4-Hydroxynonenal (4-HNE, from n-6 PUFAs), acrolein, and F2-Isoprostanes (non-enzymatic prostaglandin-like compounds from arachidonic acid). 4-HNE and MDA form covalent adducts with protein cysteine/histidine/lysine and DNA (M₁dG lesions), while 4-HNE at low concentrations activates the NRF2/ARE protective pathway—an example of redox signaling. Conjugated Dienes: Early markers; measured at 234 nm Malondialdehyde (MDA): End-product; measured by TBARS assay Reactive aldehydes: Cross-link with proteins (e.g., apoB) Enzymatic vs Non-Enzymatic Pathways Enzymatic peroxidation is catalyzed by stereoselective oxidoreductases. Lipoxygenases (LOX) incorporate molecular oxygen at specific positions of arachidonic acid, producing signaling molecules such as Leukotrienes and Hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acids (HETEs). Cyclooxygenases (COX-1 and COX-2) mediate the bis-dioxygenation of arachidonic acid to Prostaglandin G₂, initiating the prostanoid cascade. Non-enzymatic peroxidation is unregulated and produces isomeric products (Isoprostanes) that serve as in vivo biomarkers of oxidative damage. Role of Polyunsaturated Fatty Acids PUFAs, particularly Arachidonic acid (20:4, n-6) and Docosahexaenoic acid (22:6, n-3), are highly susceptible to peroxidation due to the presence of multiple bis-allylic methylene groups. The lability increases geometrically with the number of double bonds: DHA, with six double bonds, is ~10-fold more oxidizable than linoleic acid (18:2). Neuronal membranes are enriched in DHA, rendering neural tissue especially vulnerable to Lipid Peroxidation cascades. Physiological and Pathological Consequences Peroxidation inserts polar groups into the bilayer, increasing permeability, fluidity, and fusion tendency. In Mitochondria, cardiolipin peroxidation (driven by Reactive Oxygen Species at Complex III) facilitates cytochrome c release and Apoptosis. In Atherosclerosis, oxLDL formation via lipid peroxidation is an initiating event: oxLDL is cleared unregulated by Macrophage scavenger receptors (SR-A, CD36 Receptor), forming foam cells; 4-HNE-modified proteins in plaques activate NF-κB. In Neurodegenerative Diseases, elevated MDA and 4-HNE in CSF and tissue of Alzheimer's Disease, Parkinson's Disease, and Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis indicate neuronal injury. 4-HNE adduction of the astrocytic glutamate transporter GLT-1 (EAAT2) impairs clearance, causing excitotoxicity. Iron-dependent peroxidation also drives Ferroptosis, a regulated necrotic cell death. Role in Atherosclerosis LDL lipid peroxidation produces Oxidized LDL, which is taken up by Macrophages to form Foam Cells Lipid peroxidation markers correlate with Atherosclerosis progression Connection to Catecholamine-Induced Oxidative Damage Catecholamine autoxidation provides an initiating radical source that can trigger myocardial lipid peroxidation.

histone_acetyltransferase.description:
Histone Acetyltransferase (HAT) is a class of enzymes that transfer an acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to specific lysine residues on histone tails. This modification is a key component of the epigenetic regulation of gene expression.

Classification

HATs are grouped into families based on sequence and function:
GNAT family (Gcn5, PCAF, p300/CBP-associated factor): acetylate nucleosomal histones and many transcription factors.
MYST family (MOF, Tip60, HBO1): linked to dosage compensation, DNA repair, and replication licensing.
p300/CBP: large, versatile co-activators that acetylate histones and a broad set of non-histone substrates, integrating signaling with transcription.
Nuclear receptor co-activators (SRC-1, ACTR): recruited by ligand-bound nuclear receptors.

Mechanism of Action & Impact on Chromatin

Acetylation neutralizes the positive charge of the histone tail, reducing its affinity for the negatively charged DNA. This causes nucleosomes to loosen, transitioning chromatin from a condensed state to a more "open," transcriptionally active state known as Euchromatin. HATs thus function as transcriptional co-activators.

Regulation of Transcription

By opening DNA, HATs allow transcription factors and RNA polymerase II to access promoter and enhancer regions. They act in dynamic opposition to Histone Deacetylases (HDACs). Signal-dependent recruitment of HATs (e.g., by p300/CBP downstream of growth-factor or stress pathways) couples extracellular cues to gene activation.

Role in Aging and Disease

The HAT/HDAC balance is often disrupted in Aging:
Neurodegeneration: Reduced histone acetylation is observed in Alzheimer's Disease and related Neurodegenerative Diseases, where HAT activators and HDAC inhibitors are explored as therapies.
Longevity Pathways: Metabolic regulators such as AMPK and Sirtuins intersect with HAT-controlled pathways, linking diet and environment to the Epigenome.
Cancer: Aberrant HAT activity (e.g., translocations involving p300/CBP in lymphoma) contributes to oncogenesis.

berberine.description:
Berberine is a bioactive isoquinoline alkaloid (specifically a quaternary ammonium berberine cation) extracted from the rhizomes and bark of plants in the genus Berberis, as well as Coptis chinensis, Hydrastis canadensis (goldenseal), and Phellodendron. It imparts a characteristic yellow color to these botanicals and has a long history in traditional medicine systems across Asia.

Chemical Properties & Structure

Structurally, berberine is a positively charged, planar heterocycle built from a fused berberine skeleton; it is not a phenol and contains no catechol (ortho-dihydroxyphenyl) moiety. This is pharmacologically important: because it lacks the 1,2-dihydroxybenzene arrangement that COMT recognizes, berberine is neither a substrate nor an inhibitor of COMT. By contrast, many flavonoids such as Quercetin and Luteolin are catechols that compete for COMT and can reduce its activity.

Mechanism of Action

Berberine exerts effects through multiple targets. It activates AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), thereby improving insulin sensitivity, enhancing skeletal muscle glucose uptake, and suppressing hepatic gluconeogenesis. It modulates the gut microbiota (enriching butyrate producers and Akkermansia), inhibits intestinal α-glucosidases, and downregulates pro-inflammatory NF-κB and TNF-α signaling. It also interacts with mitochondrial complexes and may influence lipid metabolism via PPARα/γ. These pleiotropic actions explain its studied benefits in type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, and Anti-inflammatory contexts.



For individuals carrying slow COMT variants (e.g., Val158Met Met/Met), catechol-containing supplements and flavonoids can accumulate or inhibit methylation, producing overstimulation. Because berberine is non-catecholic, it is frequently recommended as a safe Anti-inflammatory and metabolic alternative that does not burden the Methylation Cycle or interact with COMT.

Clinical & Research Relevance

Randomized trials report berberine lowers fasting glucose and HbA1c comparably to metformin in some cohorts, and improves lipid panels. It is generally well tolerated, though it can cause mild gastrointestinal upset and may interact with CYP3A4-metabolized drugs. Its role in psychiatric or cognitive comorbidity linked to Dopamine and COMT is indirect and not established as a monotherapy.

vcam_1.description: Vascular cell adhesion protein 1 (VCAM-1) is a protein that mediates the adhesion of lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, and basophils to vascular endothelium. Its expression is upregulated in response to pro-inflammatory stimuli and is a marker for Endothelial Dysfunction and early Atherosclerosis linked to chronic Inflammation. Redox Regulation of VCAM-1 Expression and Function Transcriptional Regulation by Oxidative Stress VCAM-1 expression is primarily regulated at the transcriptional level by binding of NF-κB (specifically the p65/p50 heterodimer) to two κB response elements within the VCAM-1 promoter. Oxidative Stress potently activates NF-κB through degradation of its inhibitory subunit IkappaBalpha — a process mediated by the IκB kinase (IKK) complex, whose activity is enhanced by Reactive Oxygen Species. In endothelial cells, Exogenous H₂O₂ (Hydrogen Peroxide) and Lipid hydroperoxides directly induce VCAM-1 transcription, independently of cytokine stimulation. Additionally, TNF-alpha and IL-1β — both of which signal through ROS-dependent pathways — synergistically upregulate VCAM-1 via p38 MAPK and JNK activation, which stabilize VCAM-1 mRNA by binding HuR (an RNA-binding protein) to its 3'-UTR. NADPH Oxidase-Dependent VCAM-1 Induction The endothelial NADPH Oxidase isoforms Nox1 and NOX4 are major sources of ROS that regulate VCAM-1 expression. Oxidized LDL (Oxidized LDL), via binding to lectin-like oxidized LDL receptor-1 (Lox-1), activates Nox4, producing Hydrogen Peroxide that diffuses to the nucleus and potentiates NF-κB binding to the VCAM-1 promoter. Shear stress — the frictional force of blood flow — suppresses endothelial Nox activity and VCAM-1 expression at physiological levels (15–40 dyn/cm²), whereas oscillatory or low shear stress (characteristic of atherosclerotic-prone regions) enhances Nox expression and VCAM-1 upregulation. This mechano-redox coupling explains the focal distribution of early atherosclerotic lesions at arterial bifurcations. VCAM-1/VLA-4 Interactions and Leukocyte Recruitment VCAM-1 binds to the integrin VLA-4 (α₄β₁ integrin, also known as CD49d/CD29) expressed on monocytes, lymphocytes, eosinophils, and basophils. This interaction mediates firm adhesion and transendothelial migration of leukocytes into the subendothelial space — a critical step in Inflammation and Atherosclerosis. The VCAM-1/VLA-4 binding triggers outside-in signaling within leukocytes, activating Rac1 and macrophage NADPH oxidase, generating ROS that facilitate matrix degradation by MMP-9 (Gelatinase B) during diapedesis. The binding affinity of VLA-4 for VCAM-1 is enhanced under oxidizing conditions due to disulfide bond rearrangement in the integrin extracellular domain. Soluble VCAM-1 (sVCAM-1) as a Biomarker Proteolytic cleavage of membrane-bound VCAM-1 by ADAM-17 (TACE — TNF-α converting enzyme) releases soluble VCAM-1 (sVCAM-1) into the circulation. sVCAM-1 levels are elevated in Cardiovascular Disease, Diabetes Mellitus, Hypertension, and Rheumatoid Arthritis, serving as a biomarker of Endothelial Dysfunction and systemic Oxidative Stress. sVCAM-1 also retains functional activity — it promotes monocyte chemotaxis and induces endothelial NADPH Oxidase activation in a feed-forward loop. Therapeutic Modulation of VCAM-1 via Redox Pathways Several clinically used drugs inhibit VCAM-1 expression through antioxidant mechanisms: Statins (e.g., Atorvastatin, Rosuvastatin): Reduce VCAM-1 expression by inhibiting Rac1 geranylgeranylation (blocking Nox activation) and by upregulating endothelial Nitric Oxide Synthase (eNOS), whose product NO inhibits NF-κB. PPARα agonists (Fibrates: Fenofibrate, Gemfibrozil): Suppress VCAM-1 by interfering with NF-κB transactivation in a PPARα-dependent manner. PPARγ agonists (Thiazolidinediones: Pioglitazone): Downregulate VCAM-1 through transrepression of NF-κB and AP-1 pathways. N-Acetylcysteine (NAC): Directly inhibits VCAM-1 transcription by scavenging ROS and replenishing Glutathione. Resveratrol and dietary polyphenols: Suppress VCAM-1 via SIRT1 activation and NRF2-dependent HO-1 induction, which degrades the pro-oxidant heme required for Nox function. VCAM-1 in Neuroinflammation and Multiple Sclerosis In the central nervous system, VCAM-1 is expressed on cerebral Endothelial Cells and facilitates entry of encephalitogenic T cells across the Blood-brain barrier (BBB) into the CNS parenchyma in Multiple Sclerosis. Natalizumab (Tysabri) — a humanized monoclonal antibody against α₄ integrin (the VLA-4 subunit) — blocks VCAM-1/VLA-4 interactions, reducing T-cell trafficking into the CNS. The therapeutic efficacy of natalizumab underscores the critical role of VCAM-1 in neuroinflammatory disease. Oxidative Stress at the BBB upregulates VCAM-1 through local TNF-alpha and IL-1β production by activated Microglia, further promoting immune cell infiltration.

bcl_xl.description:
Bcl-xL (B-cell lymphoma-extra large, BCL2L1) is a potent anti-apoptotic member of the Bcl-2 family of proteins that regulates programmed cell death by inhibiting mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP) and Cytochrome c release. It is a major regulator of the Intrinsic Pathway of apoptosis, a critical survival factor in senescent cells, and a key target for senolytic therapeutics.

Overview

Bcl-xL is a major regulator of the intrinsic (mitochondrial) apoptotic pathway. Alongside Bcl-2, Bcl-w, A1-Bfl-1, and Mcl-1, it blocks the mitochondrial release of cytochrome-c, opposing pro-apoptotic family members that promote such release. It is frequently overexpressed in cancer and upregulated as part of the senescent cell anti-apoptotic pathways (SCAPs).

Mechanism of Action

Bcl-xL localizes to the mitochondrial outer membrane where it sequesters pro-apoptotic effectors BAX and BAK, preventing their oligomerization and the subsequent release of Cytochrome c. It also binds BH3-only proteins (Bim, Bad, Puma), neutralizing their pro-apoptotic signaling. In senescent cells, Bcl-xL upregulation contributes to apoptosis resistance.

Regulation

Bcl-xL activity is modulated by phosphorylation and protein dynamics:
Polo kinase 3: Phosphorylates Bcl-xL at Ser49 during cell cycle progression and checkpoints.
CDK1: Phosphorylates Bcl-xL during mitotic arrest, providing a link between mitosis and Apoptosis.
Retrotranslocation: Bcl-xL can block the mitochondrial translocation of Bax by re-directing it back to the cytoplasm.

Role in Cancer
Overexpression: Bcl-xL is frequently overexpressed in various cancers, including leukemia, breast cancer, and non-small-cell lung cancer.
Resistance: High levels of Bcl-xL contribute to resistance against chemotherapy and radiotherapy by sequestering pro-apoptotic proteins like Bax and Bak.
Drug Target: It is a primary target of BH3 mimetics such as ABT-737 and ABT-263.



Inhibition of Bcl-xL (e.g., by ABT-263) causes thrombocytopenia (low platelet count) because Bcl-xL is essential for the survival of mature platelets.


[!info] Source: COMT × Fisetin Research Evaluation
Fisetin binds the hydrophobic groove of Bcl-xL with pharmacologically preferred selectivity over Bcl-2. Computational modeling confirms favorable binding energies (Bcl-2:fisetin = −22.2 to −35.1 kcal/mol depending on ionization state). PI3K-Akt pathway inhibition by fisetin further suppresses Bcl-xL expression in senescent endothelial cells (Ji et al. 2025, PMID: 38789909). This dual mechanism — direct binding + transcriptional suppression — underlies fisetin's senolytic activity.

Other compounds targeting Bcl-xL include Navitoclax (ABT-263) and ABT-737, which are BH3 mimetics developed as anticancer agents.

park7.description:
PARK7 (also known as DJ-1) is a multifunctional protein that plays a critical role in cellular protection against oxidative stress and glycation.

Function in Glycation Prevention

Historically characterized as a protein deglycase, biochemical evidence indicates that PARK7 primarily functions as a glutathione-independent glyoxalase. It stereospecifically detoxifies free Methylglyoxal and Glyoxal directly into L-lactate and Glycolic acid, respectively, preventing these reactive intermediates from forming irreversible Advanced Glycation End Products (AGE) crosslinks on Cysteine, Lysine, and Arginine residues.

Loss-of-function mutations in PARK7 lead to significant tissue-specific accumulation of novel AGEs and are strongly linked to early-onset familial Parkinson's Disease.

[!info] Source: DJ-1 / Glycation Defense Trace
PARK7/DJ-1 occupies Line 1 of a three-layer enzymatic AGE defense system (Prevent → Repair → Degrade). Its GSH-independent glyoxalase activity is critical because the canonical Glyoxalase System (GLO1/GLO2) consumes Glutathione — under Oxidative Stress, when Methylglyoxal levels are highest, glutathione is depleted and DJ-1 becomes the last line of defense.

The Adrenochrome Double Hit


Adrenochrome-driven Oxidative Stress creates a double hit: it depletes Glutathione that GLO1/GLO2 need, AND it activates DJ-1 through Cys106 oxidation. If PARK7 is also mutated, the result is an AGE explosion — tissue-specific accumulation of novel AGEs linked to early-onset Parkinson's Disease.

hypochlorous_acid.description: Hypochlorous acid (HOCl) is a weak acid that forms when chlorine dissolves in water. In biology, it is a highly reactive species generated by activated Neutrophils via the enzyme Myeloperoxidase. It is a potent component of Reactive Oxygen Species and contributes significantly to tissue damage during chronic Oxidative Stress. Biochemical Generation: The MPO-H₂O₂-Cl⁻ System Hypochlorous Acid is generated by Myeloperoxidase (MPO), a heme-containing enzyme stored in the azurophilic granules of Neutrophils and, to a lesser extent, in monocytes/macrophages. The two-electron oxidation reaction is: H₂O₂ + Cl⁻ + H⁺ → HOCl + H₂O The Hydrogen Peroxide (H₂O₂) substrate is primarily provided by the NADPH Oxidase (NOX2)-generated Superoxide Radicals (O₂⁻•) via spontaneous or Superoxide Dismutase-catalyzed dismutation. During the Respiratory Burst, activated Neutrophils consume oxygen at rates 10–20 times above basal levels, producing micromolar concentrations of HOCl locally at sites of Inflammation. Chemical Reactivity and Targets HOCl is a potent two-electron oxidant (E°′ = 1.28 V for HOCl/Cl⁻) that reacts preferentially with sulfur-containing amino acids and nitrogen centers. Reaction with Thiols and Thioethers Cysteine residues: HOCl oxidizes cysteine thiols (−SH) to sulfenic acid (−SOH), then to sulfinic (−SO₂H) and sulfonic acid (−SO₃H) derivatives. Sulfenic acid intermediates can form disulfide cross-links, inactivating enzymes such as Glutathione Peroxidase and Protein Tyrosine Phosphatases Methionine residues: Oxidized to methionine sulfoxide (MetSO), which can be repaired by methionine sulfoxide reductases (MsrA/MsrB) Glutathione: Rapidly consumed by HOCl (k ≈ 10⁷ M⁻¹s⁻¹), depleting the major intracellular antioxidant HOCl reacts with primary amines to form chloramines (RNHCl): RNH₂ + HOCl → RNHCl + H₂O These chloramines retain oxidizing capacity and serve as longer-lived secondary oxidants that propagate tissue damage. The major chloramine species include: Taurine chloramine: A relatively stable mediator that modulates Macrophage function Ammonia chloramine (monochloramine, NH₂Cl): Membrane-permeable and highly cytotoxic Protein chloramines: Formed on lysine side chains, leading to protein cross-linking and dysfunction Reaction with Aromatic Amino Acids Tyrosine: HOCl chlorinates tyrosine at the ortho-position to form 3-chlorotyrosine, a specific biomarker of MPO activity detected in atherosclerotic plaques Tryptophan: Oxidized to N-chlorotryptophan and further to kynurenine derivatives Lipid and Nucleic Acid Oxidation Chlorinated lipids: HOCl generates chlorohydrins from unsaturated fatty acids, disrupting membrane integrity Cholesterol: Forms cholesterol chlorohydrins, implicated in Lipid Peroxidation within atherosclerotic lesions Nucleic Acids: HOCl chlorinates DNA bases (particularly guanine to 8-chloroguanine) and induces strand breaks Physiological Role: Pathogen Killing HOCl is the primary microbicidal oxidant of the innate immune system. It kills pathogens through: Membrane permeabilization: Chlorination of bacterial lipid bilayers Inactivation of bacterial chaperones: Preventing protein folding Oxidation of bacterial Iron-sulfur cluster proteins: Disrupting respiration DNA damage: Inducing lethal chlorinated base adducts Flagellar and motility protein oxidation: Impairing bacterial invasion Pathogens have evolved countermeasures, including AhpC (alkyl hydroperoxide reductase) and Ohr (organic hydroperoxide resistance) proteins, as well as MPO-inhibitory virulence factors in organisms like Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Pathological Significance: Host Tissue Damage When MPO activity is excessive or dysregulated, HOCl contributes to inflammatory tissue pathology: Cardiovascular Disease HOCl-modified Apolipoprotein B in LDL enhances foam cell formation, and 3-chlorotyrosine levels are elevated 6–10 fold in atherosclerotic plaques compared to healthy arteries. HOCl also impairs ABCA1-mediated cholesterol efflux, promoting lipid accumulation. In Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease and Asthma, MPO activity in airway Neutrophils generates HOCl that: Inactivates Alpha-1 Antitrypsin: Destroying the major antiprotease shield, leading to Emphysema Impairs Catalase and Glutathione Peroxidase: Depleting airway antioxidant defenses Induces Mucus hypersecretion: Through direct irritation and NF-κB activation Renal Disease In chronic kidney disease, HOCl-modified proteins (advanced oxidation protein products, AOPPs) accumulate and serve as biomarkers of oxidative damage and predictors of cardiovascular mortality. In Rheumatoid Arthritis, HOCl modifies cartilage Proteins and Proteoglycans, contributing to joint destruction, and activates MMP (matrix metalloproteinases) via oxidative activation of their pro-enzymes. basal_ganglia.description:
The Basal Ganglia are a set of interconnected subcortical nuclei that regulate motor control, procedural learning, and aspects of executive function. Core components include the striatum (Caudate Nucleus and Putamen), globus pallidus (internal and external segments), subthalamic nucleus, and Substantia Nigra Pars Compacta (with its reticulata output). The Nigrostriatal System—the dopaminergic projection from SNpc to striatum—is the pathway whose degeneration defines Parkinson's Disease.

Circuit Organization

Information flows through the "direct" (facilitatory) and "indirect" (inhibitory) striatal output pathways that converge on the thalamus to modulate cortical motor commands. Dopamine from SNpc D1 receptors excite the direct pathway and D2 receptors inhibit the indirect pathway; the net effect is facilitated movement. Loss of dopamine produces relative overactivity of the indirect pathway, increasing basal ganglia output inhibition of thalamus and causing hypokinesia.

Motor, Cognitive, and Limbic Roles

Beyond movement, the basal ganglia contribute to habit learning (dorsal striatum), executive control (cognitive striatum in the caudate), and motivation/reward (ventral striatum/nucleus accumbens). Their dysfunction underlies not only parkinsonism but also Huntington's disease, dystonia, and components of Addiction.

Relation to Neuromelanin

The SNpc neurons that project to the striatum are among the most heavily Neuromelanin-pigmented cells in the brain. Their selective loss in PD disconnects the basal ganglia motor circuit, producing the classic triad of resting tremor, rigidity, and Bradykinesia. Neuromelanin's role as a metal buffer and toxin sink may explain why precisely these pigmented neurons—rather than other dopamine cells—degenerate.

Pathology & Clinical Relevance

Deep brain stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus or globus pallidus internus restores circuit balance in advanced PD. L-DOPA and dopamine agonists compensate for lost nigral input. Understanding basal ganglia physiology is essential for interpreting both the motor and non-motor features of parkinsonism and for designing circuit-based therapies.

keratinocyte_growth_factor.description:
Keratinocyte growth factor (KGF, FGF7) is a member of the fibroblast growth factor family that signals through FGFR2IIIb. It is critical for fetal thymus organogenesis and has been identified as a key factor in thymic rejuvenation.

Structure and Signaling
Gene: FGF7
Receptor: FGFR2IIIb (epithelial cell-specific)
Signaling: Ras/MAPK and PI3K/AKT pathways → proliferation and differentiation
Expression: Mesenchymal cells; acts on epithelial cells in a paracrine manner

Thymic Effects

Fetal development
Critical for thymus organogenesis via FGFR2IIIb signaling
Required for initial TEC proliferation and differentiation

Increases thymus size and thymocyte production in aged animals
Restores defined cortical and medullary compartments
Increases output of naïve phenotype CD4 T cells
Enhances humoral responses to T-dependent antigens

[!info] KGF efficacy in aged mice
Min et al. demonstrated that a single course of KGF treatment in aged mice increased thymic cellularity for two months. Monthly follow-up administration sustained this improvement, with restoration of thymic architecture and enhanced immune function.

Clinical Development

KGF (as Palifermin or Kepavance) has advanced to human clinical trials:
Cambridge University (NCT01712945) — Testing KGF to prevent secondary autoimmunity after Campath-1H treatment for multiple sclerosis
Indiana University (NCT00593554) — Phase II study of KGF in haplotype-mismatched hematopoietic stem cell (CD34+) transplant
Fred Hutchinson/UW (NCT01233921) — Pharmacodynamics of palifermin in adult stem cell transplant for hematologic cancer; testing whether KGF prevents chronic graft-versus-host disease

Limitations
KGF has multiple targets outside the thymus
Mechanisms of action in the postnatal thymus are still under investigation
Functional quality of the thymus after KGF-induced rebound requires further study

Documents
Thymic Rejuvenation and Aging
Reviews KGF's role in thymic rejuvenation, pre-clinical evidence in aged mice, and ongoing clinical trials for thymic regeneration.

ido1.description:
IDO1 (Indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 1) is a heme-containing enzyme that catalyzes the first and rate-limiting step in the Kynurenine Pathway (KP) of Tryptophan (Trp) catabolism. It oxidizes L-tryptophan to N-Formylkynurenine in an O₂-dependent reaction.

Structure & Domains

IDO1 is a monomeric cytosolic protein (~45 kDa, 403 amino acids) encoded by the IDO1 gene on human chromosome 8p11.21. It belongs to the heme-dependent dioxygenase family (EC 1.13.11.52). Crystal structures (PDB: 2D0T, 5EK2, 6E40) reveal:
A large catalytic domain with a deep heme-binding pocket containing a ferrous iron center that coordinates O₂
A smaller immunoglobulin-like domain that contributes to substrate recognition and active-site plasticity
A flexible active-site loop that accommodates multiple indoleamine substrates

Mechanism

The catalytic cycle requires reduction of the inactive ferric (Fe³⁺) heme to the active ferrous (Fe²⁺) form, typically coupled to NADH or ascorbate-dependent reductases. The ferrous-oxy complex performs oxidative cleavage of the indole ring of Tryptophan at the 2,3-position, producing N-Formylkynurenine, which is rapidly deformylated to Kynurenine by kynurenine formamidase.

IDO1 can act on multiple substrates including L-Trp, D-Trp, 5-hydroxy-Trp, tryptamine, and Serotonin, though L-Trp is the preferred physiological substrate.

Regulation

Transcriptional induction: Strongly induced by pro-inflammatory cytokines, particularly Interferon-gamma (IFNγ) via the JAK/STAT1 signaling pathway. TNF-α, IL-1β, LPS, and glucocorticoids can synergize in certain cellular contexts.

Post-translational control: Phosphorylation of ITIM (immunoreceptor tyrosine-based inhibitory motif) domains recruits SOCS3, promoting ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation — a negative feedback mechanism. IDO1 can also transduce non-enzymatic signaling through ITIM-dependent PI3K activation, exerting immunomodulatory effects independently of catalytic activity.

Expression pattern: Constitutively high in placenta, lymph nodes, lungs, and small intestine. Inducible in dendritic cells, macrophages, monocytes, endothelial cells, and fibroblasts during Inflammation.

Immunological Functions

IDO1 is a central immunoregulatory enzyme operating through two synergistic mechanisms:
Local tryptophan depletion: IDO1-mediated Trp consumption creates a Trp-deficient microenvironment. Effector T cells (which require Trp for proliferation) activate the GCN2 stress kinase in response to amino acid starvation, leading to cell-cycle arrest, anergy, or Apoptosis.
Kynurenine-dependent signaling: Accumulated Kynurenine and downstream KP metabolites (Kynurenic Acid, Quinolinic Acid, 3-Hydroxykynurenine) activate the Aryl Hydrocarbon Receptor (AhR). AhR signaling promotes regulatory T cell (Treg) differentiation, suppresses Th17 responses, and inhibits NK-cell and CD8⁺ T-cell effector functions.

This dual mechanism creates an immunosuppressive microenvironment exploited by cancers and critical for maternal-fetal tolerance.

Clinical Relevance

Immuno-oncology: IDO1 is frequently upregulated in tumors and tumor-draining lymph nodes, where it suppresses antitumor immunity. Epacadostat, navoximod, and linrodostat (BMS-986205) are IDO1 inhibitors tested in clinical trials (often combined with checkpoint inhibitors), though results have been mixed due to compensatory pathways (TDO, IDO2).

Diabetes: Type 1 diabetes involves altered Trp-Kyn profiles linked to IDO1 genotype and reduced IFNγ responsiveness. T2D is associated with elevated KP activity in the context of chronic inflammatory Insulin Resistance.

Neurodegeneration: KP metabolites (particularly Quinolinic Acid) are neurotoxic and implicated in Neurodegeneration, Depression, and HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders.

Primary source document covering IDO1 structure, regulation, immunological roles, diabetes context, and therapeutic targeting.

mitochondrial_derived_peptide.description:
Mitochondrial-Derived Peptide (MDP) refers to a family of small bioactive peptides encoded within the mitochondrial genome that are transcribed and translated independently of the canonical 13 mitochondrial-encoded proteins. These peptides function as both intracellular survival factors and endocrine signaling molecules, representing a novel layer of mitochondrial communication with the cell and distant tissues.

Paradigm Shift

[!important] From End-Function Organelle to Signaling Hub
The discovery of MDPs fundamentally changed the understanding of Mitochondria from passive "end-function" organelles that merely produce ATP and regulate Apoptosis to active signaling centers that communicate metabolic status to the nucleus and to distant tissues. MDPs are unique among retrograde signals because they are encoded within the mitochondrial genome itself, unlike other retrograde signals (Ca²⁺, ROS, Cytochrome c) that are secondary products of mitochondrial metabolism.

Known MDPs

The MDP family includes:

 Peptide    Encoding Locus    Length    Key Functions 
:--- :---
 Humanin    MT-RNR2 (16S rRNA)    24 aa    Neuroprotection, anti-apoptosis, metabolic regulation 
 MOTS-c    MT-RNR1 (12S rRNA)    16 aa    Glucose metabolism, exercise response, longevity 
 SHLP1-6    MT-RNR2 (16S rRNA)    Various    Cytokine-like functions, tissue-specific effects 
 Humanin-Like Peptides    Nuclear pseudogenes    Various    Similar to humanin, derived from NUMTs 

Molecular Mechanisms

MDPs exert their effects through multiple mechanisms:

Intracellular Actions
Direct protein-protein interactions (e.g., Humanin binding Bax, Bid, IGFBP3)
Mitochondrial function regulation


Secretion into circulation
Receptor-mediated signaling at distant tissues:
CNTFR/WSX-1/gp130 complex → STAT3 activation
FPRL1 (FPR2) → ERK1/2 activation



Mitochondrial stress: Mitochondrial Unfolded Protein Response, Complex I inhibition
Nutrient sensing: Upregulated by NAD+/SIRT1 and AMPK; suppressed by mTORC1
Aging: MDP levels decline with age, correlating with metabolic disease
Exercise: Acute exercise induces MDP expression

Biological Significance

MDPs regulate:
Longevity and lifespan (humanin overexpression extends lifespan 15–20% in mice)
Glucose metabolism and Insulin Sensitivity
Stress resistance and redox homeostasis
Apoptosis and cell survival
Inflammation modulation
Neuroprotection

Clinical Relevance

MDPs are implicated in:
Alzheimer's Disease: Humanin levels inversely correlate with disease severity
Type 1 and Type 2 Diabetes: Humanin improves glucose tolerance
Atherosclerosis: Humanin preserves endothelial function
Age-related decline: MDP levels decrease with age
MELAS and CPEO: MDPs are elevated as compensatory responses
Cancer: Humanin reduces incidence of age-related tumors in transgenic mice

Comprehensive review establishing the concept of mitochondrial-derived peptides, with Humanin as the prototypical member.

ccl2.description:
CCL2 (MCP-1)

CCL2 (C-C motif chemokine ligand 2), also known as MCP-1 (monocyte chemoattractant protein-1), is a CC chemokine that binds the receptor CCR2 and is the principal recruiter of monocytes and macrophages to sites of inflammation. It is one of the most conserved and well-characterized components of the Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype (Coppé et al., 2008, PMID 18948995; 2010, PMID 20723158).

Mechanism of Action & Signaling
Receptor binding: CCL2 signals chiefly through CCR2 (a Gαi-coupled GPCR), with minor activity at CCR4; it activates PI3K/Akt, p38 MAPK/ERK, and Ca2+ flux to drive chemotaxis and adhesion of monocytes.
Cell sources: Released by senescent fibroblasts, endothelial cells, macrophages, and epithelial cells under stress.
Transcriptional regulation: Transcription is driven by NF-κB, AP-1, STAT1/STAT3, and the C/EBP family, and is potently induced by the SASP cytokines IL-1α and IL-1β — a feed-forward loop because recruited macrophages further inflame tissue.
Downstream cellular effects: Recruits classical monocytes, macrophages, memory T cells, and dendritic cells; promotes M2-like polarization and tissue remodeling.

Role in Senescence / SASP
CCL2 is a core SASP chemokine whose expression is tightly linked to the IL-1α/IL-1β arm of the secretome.
It mediates immune recruitment to senescent cells that can be beneficial (macrophage-mediated clearance, immune surveillance) or detrimental (chronic monocyte infiltration, tissue damage).
In senescent mesenchymal stromal cells, the Polycomb protein Bmi-1 negatively regulates CCL2 through an IL-1α-mediated mechanism, tempering the SASP.
Urine CCL2 is used as a non-invasive readout of SASP burden in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, linking the chemokine to fibrotic aging.
In cancer, CCL2 recruits CCR2+ myeloid-derived suppressor cells, enabling immune evasion.

Clinical / Pathological Relevance
Elevated CCL2/CCR2 signaling is found in obesity, atherosclerosis, IPF, and multiple cancers, and correlates with senescence burden in human studies.
CCR2 antagonists (e.g., CCX872, MK-0812) are being tested to limit SASP-driven inflammation and tumor immunosuppression.
CCL2 is a candidate circulating/tissue biomarker of inflammaging and senolytic treatment response.

Documents
SASP Review 2024: The review describes CCL2 as one of the most conserved SASP chemokines, whose expression is tightly linked to the IL-1α/IL-1β arm of the secretome via NF-κB, AP-1, and C/EBP pathways. It recruits monocytes and macrophages to senescent cells, supporting either immune surveillance and clearance or, when chronic, monocyte infiltration and tissue damage.

Connections

Macrophages: CCL2 recruits macrophages to senescent cells
Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype: CCL2 is a key SASP chemokine

inflammasome.description: Inflammasomes are cytosolic supramolecular complexes of the innate immune system that assemble in response to pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs). They activate inflammatory caspases — primarily Caspase-1 in the canonical pathway — which proteolytically process pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 into their mature, secreted forms, and cleave gasdermin D (GSDMD) to trigger pyroptosis, a highly inflammatory form of programmed cell death. Inflammasome activity is central to host defence against infection, but when chronically activated by sterile stimuli (e.g., cellular senescence, metabolic stress, mitochondrial damage), it drives persistent Inflammation and contributes to age-related diseases, neurodegeneration, cardiovascular disease, and Cancer. Composition and Assembly Core Components An inflammasome typically consists of three elements: Sensor protein — detects the activating stimulus (e.g., NLRP3, AIM2, NLRC4, NLRP1, pyrin) Adaptor protein ASC (apoptosis-associated speck-like protein containing a CARD) — bridges sensor to effector via PYD–PYD and CARD–CARD interactions Effector caspase — most commonly Caspase-1 (canonical); Caspase-4, Caspase-5, or Caspase-11 (noncanonical) Assembly Mechanism Upon ligand binding, sensor proteins undergo conformational change and oligomerize. PYD-containing sensors (NLRP3, AIM2, pyrin) recruit ASC through PYD–PYD interactions, forming helical filaments known as ASC specks — large supramolecular organizing centers (SMOCs). ASC then recruits caspase-1 through CARD–CARD interactions, inducing caspase-1 dimerization and auto-proteolytic activation. The active caspase-1 p33/p10 heterodimer cleaves its substrates. [!info] Structural Insights Cryo-EM studies have revealed that the active NLRP3–NEK7–ASC complex comprises ~10–11 NLRP3 subunits forming a disc-shaped structure, with NEK7 bound at the periphery. The PYD filament protrudes orthogonally from the disc center, recruiting ASC through helical polymerization (Fu et al., Nat Rev Immunol, 2024). Major Inflammasome Types The most extensively studied inflammasome. NLRP3 is expressed in myeloid cells (macrophages, dendritic cells, neutrophils) and is activated by a remarkably diverse set of stimuli: PAMPs: bacterial toxins, viral RNA, fungal hyphae DAMPs: ATP, uric acid crystals, cholesterol crystals, mtDNA, HMGB1 Endogenous signals: amyloid-β, α-synuclein, protein aggregates Metabolic stress: ceramides, saturated fatty acids, glucose NLRP3 activation requires a two-step process: Priming (Signal 1): NF-κB-dependent transcriptional upregulation of NLRP3 and pro-IL-1β (e.g., via TLR ligation, LPS) Activation (Signal 2): Assembly triggered by K⁺ efflux, Ca²⁺ flux, reactive oxygen species, lysosomal destabilization, or mitochondrial dysfunction [!tip] NLRP3 and Senescence NLRP3 inflammasome activation is linked to immune senescence and is a plausible driver of the SASP. Senescent cells accumulate DAMPs (HMGB1, mtDNA, oxidized lipids) that can activate NLRP3 in neighbouring macrophages, amplifying the inflammatory milieu (Spadaro et al., 2016). Senses cytoplasmic double-stranded DNA (bacterial, viral, or self-DNA from damaged nuclei or mitochondria). AIM2 forms a direct CARD-containing complex that recruits caspase-1 without requiring ASC for cell death induction, though ASC is needed for maximal IL-1β processing. Activated by cytoplasmic bacterial flagellin and type III secretion system components. NAIP proteins act as co-receptors that directly bind bacterial ligands and recruit NLRC4 through NACHT–NACHT interactions. NLRC4 can directly recruit caspase-1 via its CARD, but ASC recruitment is required for full IL-1β processing. Contains a C-terminal CARD that recruits ASC directly. Activated by Bacillus anthracis lethal toxin and muramyl dipeptide. Human NLRP1 also responds to the intracellular danger signal UDP via the protease DPP9. Senses bacterial RhoA inactivation (e.g., by Clostridium difficile toxin B). Pyrin forms an ASC-dependent inflammasome that activates caspase-1. Downstream Effectors All inflammatory caspases (caspase-1, -4, -5, -11) cleave GSDMD between the N-terminal pore-forming domain and the C-terminal inhibitory domain. The liberated N-terminal fragment oligomerizes in the plasma membrane, forming pores (~10–20 nm) that cause osmotic swelling, membrane rupture, and pyroptosis. Together with NINJ1, GSDMD pores induce a highly inflammatory form of cell death that releases cytoplasmic contents — including mature IL-1β, IL-18, and DAMPs — into the extracellular space. [!warning] Pyroptosis Amplifies Inflammation Pyroptotic cell death releases intracellular IL-1α, HMGB1, mtDNA, and other DAMPs that activate surrounding cells, creating a feedforward inflammatory loop. In the context of Senescent Cells, this can amplify the SASP-driven inflammatory microenvironment.

quinolinic_acid.description:
Quinolinic acid (QA) is a dicarboxylic acid intermediate of the Kynurenine Pathway (KP) formed from 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid by the enzyme 3-hydroxyanthranilate 3,4-dioxygenase (HAAO). It is a precursor for de novo NAD+ biosynthesis and also acts as a selective NMDA receptor agonist with potent excitotoxic properties.

Dual Role
NAD+ precursor: QA is converted to nicotinic acid mononucleotide (NaMN) by quinolinate phosphoribosyltransferase (QPRT), entering the Preiss-Handler pathway for NAD+ synthesis.
Excitotoxin: QA is an endogenous NMDA receptor agonist with approximately 100-fold greater potency than glutamate. It promotes calcium influx, Oxidative Stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and Apoptosis in neurons.

Clinical Relevance

Elevated QA levels are implicated in neurodegenerative conditions including:


HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND)
Huntington's disease

QA also contributes to the immunosuppressive Tumor Microenvironment by activating the Aryl Hydrocarbon Receptor and promoting Treg differentiation.

chromatin_remodeling.description:
Definition: Chromatin Remodeling is a fundamental biological process that maintains cellular and organismal homeostasis. It involves coordinated molecular events regulated by signaling pathways and environmental cues.

Mechanism: The process of Chromatin Remodeling is executed by specific protein complexes, organelles, and signaling cascades. Key regulatory nodes control its initiation, progression, and termination.

mir_24.description:
miR-24 is a microRNA family member (miR-24-1, miR-24-2 loci) with context-dependent roles in development and disease. In cancer, miR-24 is often described as oncogenic because it represses the expression of pro-death regulators—including by modulating XIAP networks—thereby lowering the Apoptosis threshold and supporting tumor cell survival and Chemotherapy resistance. Its precise target set varies by tissue, contributing to its pleiotropic effects.

Biogenesis & Regulation

miR-24 is transcribed as part of polycistronic clusters (e.g., miR-23b~27b~24-1), processed by Drosha/Dicer into the mature guide strand incorporated into RISC. Its expression is regulated by transcription factors responsive to proliferation and stress signals; in many tumors it is upregulated, where it reinforces survival and proliferative gene programs.

Mechanism of Action

A key anti-apoptotic action of miR-24 is repression of factors that normally restrain XIAP or promote death. By suppressing these checkpoints, miR-24 elevates effective XIAP activity and reduces caspase engagement, lowering the apoptotic threshold. (Relatedly, IKKε phosphorylates and degrades XIAP to sensitize cells, illustrating the opposite regulatory direction.) miR-24 also targets additional tumor-relevant transcripts (e.g., p27^Kip1^, MKi67-linked proliferation factors, and death receptors in some contexts), coupling survival to cell-cycle progression.

Physiological & Pathological Relevance

In malignancies such as breast, colorectal, and hematopoietic cancers, high miR-24 correlates with reduced apoptosis, enhanced proliferation, and poorer response to cytotoxic therapy. Conversely, inhibition of miR-24 (antagomirs) can restore death sensitivity. Its dual nature—pro-survival in cancer but pro-apoptotic in some normal stress contexts—underscores the importance of cellular context.

Clinical & Research Relevance

miR-24 is investigated both as a prognostic biomarker and as a therapeutic target (antagomirs) to resensitize resistant tumors. Because it converges on the XIAP/apoptosis-threshold axis, combining miR-24 inhibition with XIAP antagonists or death-ligand therapies is a rational strategy under exploration to overcome resistance.

Connections

Apoptosis - Death threshold lowered by miR-24 in cancer cells.
IKKε - Kinase that opposes miR-24's survival effect by degrading XIAP.
Chemotherapy - Resistance often associated with miR-24 overexpression.
Oncogene - Functional class miR-24 can act within in cancer.

platelet_aggregation.description:
Overview

Platelet aggregation is the process whereby activated platelets bind to one another, primarily through fibrinogen bridging the integrin receptor Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa (αIIbβ3) on adjacent platelets. It is the terminal common pathway of primary hemostasis and the basis of pathological arterial thrombosis.

Mechanism
Platelet activation exposes/activates αIIbβ3, enabling fibrinogen- and von Willebrand factor-mediated cross-linking.
Secondary mediators (thromboxane A2, ADP, serotonin) amplify recruitment and aggregation.
The resulting aggregate is stabilized by the coagulation cascade (thrombin, fibrin).

Physiological & Pathological Relevance

Physiologically essential for wound sealing; pathologically, excessive aggregation underlies myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, and peripheral vascular disease. Antiplatelet agents (aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitors, GPIIb/IIIa antagonists) target this process. Aggregation is commonly quantified by light-transmission aggregometry.

toluidine_blue_o.description:
Toluidine Blue O (TB, tolonium chloride) is a phenothiazine thiazine dye structurally related to Methylene blue, differing mainly by methyl groups at positions 3 and 7 of the phenothiazine nucleus. In the structure-activity study of methylene blue derivatives, TB was the most potent compound tested for neuroprotection and mitochondrial antioxidant action in HT-22 hippocampal neurons .

Structure & Chemistry

TB retains the free position-10 nitrogen and position-5 sulfur of the phenothiazine scaffold that are required for the methylene blue-like alternative electron-transfer phenotype. Like Methylene blue, TB has a negative redox potential (E1/2 ≈ −0.012 V vs NHE, the most negative of the series), consistent with its ability to enhance cellular oxygen consumption .

Mechanism of Action

Alternative mitochondrial electron transfer

In isolated mitochondrial assays, TB — together with Methylene blue — was one of only two compounds that significantly increased the rate of Cytochrome c reduction using NADH as the electron donor (the Complex I→Complex III shunt), bypassing the need for Coenzyme Q10 . TB therefore acts as an alternative electron carrier that sustains electron flow when Complex I/III are compromised.

Cellular bioenergetics

TB increased cellular oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and decreased extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) in Seahorse XF24 assays, mirroring Methylene blue and indicating enhanced oxidative phosphorylation with suppressed anaerobic glycolysis .

Antioxidant / neuroprotection

Against glutamate insult in HT-22 cells, TB showed:
Viability EC50 ≈ 1.75 nM
ROS EC50 ≈ 0.11 nM (most potent of all tested)
Mitochondrial membrane potential EC50 ≈ 1.54 nM

TB protected against Rotenone, IAA, and glutamate neurotoxicity, and (like MB) provided no protection against direct extracellular H2O2 from Glucose Oxidase — confirming it is not a classical chain-breaking antioxidant but acts upstream on mitochondrial electron flow .

Complex IV

TB, like Methylene blue, increased Complex IV expression/activity at low nanomolar concentrations .

[!info] Why TB is the most potent
The 3,7-dimethyl substitution preserves the free 10-nitrogen and position-5 sulfur while tuning the redox potential to the most negative in the series, which correlates with the strongest OCR enhancement and lowest EC50s for neuroprotection .

Most potent MB analog; shares the alternative electron-transfer carrier mechanism, upregulates Complex IV, and protects against glutamate/rotenone/IAA but not direct H2O2.

metabolic_syndrome.description:
Metabolic syndrome is a cluster of interconnected metabolic abnormalities — central obesity, insulin resistance, hypertension, and dyslipidemia — that collectively increase the risk of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus, Cardiovascular Disease, and Non-alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease. Its development involves genetic, environmental, and lifestyle risk factors. Chronic Inflammation and Oxidative Stress underpin its metabolic dysregulation.

Etiology & Pathophysiology

Metabolic syndrome arises from the combination of visceral adiposity, insulin resistance, and dysregulated lipid and glucose metabolism, creating a state of systemic low-grade inflammation and oxidative stress. These disturbances drive progression to diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

Sirtuin Involvement (Wu et al., 2022)
SIRT1: Downregulated in metabolic syndrome. Post-transcriptional stabilization by the RNA-binding protein HuR represses inflammation and hyperglycemia to counter metabolic syndrome. SIRT1 modest overexpression protects from hepatic steatosis (via MnSOD/Nrf1 induction, PGC-1α activation, NF-κB downregulation).
SIRT6: Downregulated in lipid metabolism-related diseases; overexpression improves hypercholesterolemia (FoxO3 recruitment to the SREBP2 promoter → H3K9/H3K56 deacetylation).

Therapeutic Implications

Enhancing SIRT1/HuR stability and SIRT6 activity are candidate strategies to combat metabolic syndrome by dampening inflammation, hyperglycemia, and dyslipidemia.

peroxisome_biogenesis_network.description:
The Peroxisome Biogenesis Network (PBN) is a dynamic, interconnected pool of precursor peroxisomes primarily residing in the cytosol and closely interacting with the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). The PBN is critical for the generation of new Peroxisomes. During Selective Autophagy, damaged peroxisomes are broken down and their recycled fragments, along with new lipids and proteins supplied by the ER, are incorporated into the PBN to form new precursors. This constant turnover and amplification within the PBN ensure a healthy population of peroxisomes. Dysfunction in genes like PEX1 or PEX3 severely impairs the PBN and peroxisome biogenesis.

Pathway

The PBN involves PEX genes for peroxisome membrane assembly, matrix protein import, and proliferation. Defects cause Zellweger syndrome.

heterochromatin.description:
Heterochromatin is a tightly packed form of DNA or condensed Chromatin, which is typically transcriptionally inactive. It plays a vital role in maintaining the structure of chromosomes and protecting the genome from instability.
   Gene Silencing: It keeps genes that are not needed for a specific cell type "turned off."
   Protecting Repetitive Elements: It silences Transposable Elements like LINE-1, preventing them from jumping and causing Genomic Instability.
   Structural Support: Constitutive heterochromatin is found at the centromeres and telomeres, providing mechanical strength to chromosomes during cell division.
The "Heterochromatin Loss Model of Aging"
One of the earliest and most influential theories in Epigenetics is that Aging is driven by the progressive loss of heterochromatin.
   "Relaxation": As cells age, tightly packed regions begin to unravel and become more like Euchromatin.
Consequences: This leads to the inappropriate activation of repetitive elements and pro-aging genes, driving inflammation and cellular decline.
Molecular Markers
Heterochromatin is typically marked by specific histone modifications, such as H3K9me3 (trimethylation of histone H3 lysine 9), and is maintained by enzymes like HDACs and HMTs.

mtorc1.description: mTORC1 (mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1) is a multi-protein signaling complex that integrates nutrient, energy, and growth factor signals to coordinate Cell Growth, Protein Synthesis, Lipid Synthesis, Ribosome Biogenesis, and Autophagy. It is the central node of the mTOR signaling network and a master regulator of anabolic-catabolic balance in eukaryotic cells. Structure and Subunits mTORC1 is a large (~300 kDa) multiprotein assembly built around the mTOR serine/threonine kinase (catalytic core), with five core subunits: mTOR — the catalytic subunit belonging to the PIKK family; contains N-terminal HEAT repeats, a FAT domain, an FRB domain (rapamycin-binding), and a C-terminal kinase domain Raptor (regulatory-associated protein of mTOR) — scaffolding protein that recruits mTORC1 substrates (S6K1 and 4E-BP1) via TOS motifs mLST8 (mammalian lethal with SEC13 protein 8) — binds the mTOR kinase domain and stabilizes catalytic activity PRAS40 (proline-rich Akt substrate of 40 kDa) — inhibitory subunit; dissociates upon Akt-mediated phosphorylation to relieve repression Deptor (DEP domain-containing mTOR-interacting protein) — negative regulator that binds mTOR and inhibits kinase activity; itself suppressed by growth factor signaling Raptor is the defining mTORC1-specific subunit (distinguishing it from mTORC2). The complex localizes to the Lysosome surface in its active state, where it encounters its upstream activator Rheb. Regulation and Activation mTORC1 integrates signals from four major inputs: Growth Factors (PI3K-Akt-TSC axis) Growth Factor binding to Receptor Tyrosine Kinases activates Class I PI3K, producing PIP3, which recruits Akt to the plasma membrane. Akt phosphorylates and inhibits the TSC1-TSC2 complex, a GTPase-activating protein (GAP) toward Rheb. Rheb-GTP directly activates mTORC1 at the lysosomal surface. Akt also phosphorylates PRAS40, relieving its inhibition of mTORC1. Amino Acids (Rag GTPase axis) Amino Acids, particularly Leucine and Arginine, signal through the Ragulator-Rag GTPase system to recruit mTORC1 to the Lysosome. The Rag heterodimer (RagA/B bound to RagC/D) tethers mTORC1 to the lysosomal surface via Raptor interaction, bringing it into proximity of Rheb-GTP. This amino-acid sensing mechanism is mediated by the GATOR1-GATOR2 complexes, Sestrins, and CASTOR1. Energy Status (AMPK-TSC2 / AMPK-Raptor) Low cellular energy (high AMP/ATP ratio) activates AMPK, which phosphorylates: TSC2 — enhancing its GAP activity toward Rheb, suppressing mTORC1 Raptor — directly inhibiting mTORC1 by promoting 14-3-3 binding This provides a direct energy checkpoint preventing anabolic processes when ATP is limiting. Stress and Hypoxia (REDD1 / BNIP3) Hypoxia and DNA Damage induce REDD1/DDIT4, which activates TSC2 and suppresses mTORC1. Hypoxia also induces BNIP3 and BNIP3L, promoting Mitophagy and indirectly suppressing mTORC1. p53 (the guardian of the genome) represses mTORC1 activity under genotoxic stress. Downstream Effectors mTORC1 phosphorylates two major substrate families to drive anabolism: S6 Kinase 1 mTORC1 phosphorylates and activates S6K1 at Thr389. S6K1 in turn phosphorylates: S6 ribosomal protein — promotes translation of 5'-TOP mRNAs eIF4B — enhances helicase activity for mRNA unwinding PDCD4 — promotes its degradation, relieving eIF4A inhibition IRS1 — negative feedback to PI3K-Akt signaling 4E-BP Family mTORC1 phosphorylates 4E-BP1, 4E-BP2, and 4E-BP3, causing their release from eIF4E. Free eIF4E assembles into the eIF4F initiation complex (eIF4E, eIF4A, eIF4G) to initiate cap-dependent translation. Hypophosphorylated 4E-BPs sequester eIF4E, blocking translation initiation. Additional Targets Lipin-1 — phosphorylation blocks nuclear translocation, promoting Lipid Synthesis TFEB — mTORC1 phosphorylates TFEB, retaining it in the Cytosol; mTORC1 inhibition permits TFEB nuclear translocation and Lysosomal Biogenesis SREBP-1c — mTORC1-S6K1 signaling activates SREBP-1c, driving Lipid Synthesis and Cholesterol biogenesis HIF-1α — mTORC1 promotes HIF-1α translation, enabling Glycolysis and angiogenesis Physiological Functions Cell Growth and Proliferation mTORC1 drives Cell Growth by increasing protein and lipid synthesis. Cells lacking mTORC1 signaling are smaller and proliferate more slowly. In Quiescence, mTORC1 is suppressed and cells maintain a state of reduced anabolism. Autophagy Regulation mTORC1 inhibits Autophagy by phosphorylating ULK1 and ULK2 at Ser757, disrupting the ULK1-AMPK interaction. mTORC1 also phosphorylates TFEB and TFE3, preventing Lysosomal Biogenesis. Pharmacological mTORC1 inhibition with Rapamycin or Torin is a potent inducer of autophagy.

ptdins_3_5_p2.description:
Phosphatidylinositol 3,5-bisphosphate (PtdIns(3,5)P2) is a low-abundance, dynamically regulated phosphoinositide present predominantly on endolysosomal membranes. Synthesized from PtdIns3P by the lipid kinase PIKfyve, it orchestrates lysosomal membrane dynamics, ion channel regulation, and organelle reformation, serving as a central lipid signal that links nutrient sensing to Autophagy and Lysosome homeostasis.

Biosynthesis & Turnover

PtdIns(3,5)P2 is produced by PIKfyve (phosphoinositide kinase, FYVE finger-containing), which phosphorylates the 5-position of PtdIns(3)P. Its levels are tightly controlled: the phosphoinositide 5-phosphatase FIG4 (and its yeast homolog Fig4/Sac3) dephosphorylates PtdIns(3,5)P2 back to PtdIns3P, while the 3-phosphatase MTMR (myotubularin) can also consume it. The opposing activities of PIKfyve and FIG4 maintain a low but critical steady-state pool; loss of either enzyme causes profound lysosomal swelling and storage, underscoring the lipid's essential role.

Mechanism of Action

PtdIns(3,5)P2 acts as a membrane identity mark that recruits effector proteins and activates lysosomal ion channels. Most notably, it directly binds and activates TRPML1 (MCOLN1), the lysosomal Ca2+ release channel; TRPML1 opening elevates cytosolic Ca2+ that drives membrane fission, tubule scission, and the Autophagic Lysosome Reformation/Phagocytic Lysosome Reformation processes that rebuild lysosomes after degradation. PtdIns(3,5)P2 also recruits ESCRT and sorting nexin proteins, regulates v-ATPase function and lysosomal acidification, and supports autophagosome-lysosome fusion and Autophagic Flux. Through these actions it integrates with mTORC1 nutrient sensing at the Lysosome.

Physiological & Pathological Relevance

Because PtdIns(3,5)P2 is indispensable for lysosomal morphology and reformation, its dysregulation underlies human disease: FIG4 mutations cause Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 4J and Yunis-Varon syndrome, and PIKfyve dysfunction produces fleck cornea with pigmented maculopathy—both manifesting as Lysosomal Storage Disorders. Defective PtdIns(3,5)P2 signaling collapses autophagic clearance, contributing to Neurodegeneration and proteostatic failure in Aging. Pharmacologically, PIKfyve inhibitors such as apilimod raise PtdIns(3)P while depleting PtdIns(3,5)P2, disrupting lysosomal reformation and exhausting lysosomes in Cancer cells to amplify therapy-induced stress. Thus PtdIns(3,5)P2 is both a disease locus and a therapeutic interface bridging lipid signaling to the autophagy-lysosome network.

tnf_alpha.description: Pro-inflammatory cytokine involved in systemic inflammation and the acute phase response. Tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-alpha) is a cell signaling protein (cytokine) involved in systemic Inflammation and is one of the cytokines that make up the acute phase reaction. It is a potent activator of the NF-κB pathway and can induce Apoptosis and the production of other cytokines like IL-1β. Oxidative Stress and TNF-α Signaling TNF-α exerts its biological effects through two receptors: TNFR1 (p55; ubiquitously expressed) and TNFR2 (p75; restricted to immune and endothelial cells). Upon TNF-α binding, TNFR1 recruits the adaptor protein TRADD (TNFR-associated death domain protein), which serves as a platform for the assembly of two sequential signaling complexes. Complex I — formed at the plasma membrane — includes RIPK1 (receptor-interacting protein kinase 1), TRAF2 (TNF receptor-associated factor 2), and cIAP1/cIAP2, leading to NF-κB activation. Mitochondria ROS production is an early and obligatory event in TNFR1 signaling: TRAF2 recruits the E3 ligase TRIM21, which ubiquitinates p65 (NDUFS1) of Respiratory Chain Complex I, causing electron leak and Superoxide Radicals generation. This mitochondrial ROS (mtROS) is required for sustained JNK activation and IL-1β production. ROS in TNF-Induced NF-κB Activation and Its Feedback NF-κB activation by TNF-α is both facilitated and regulated by Oxidative Stress. Low-level ROS promote the phosphorylation and degradation of IkappaBalpha (the inhibitory subunit of NF-κB) by the IκB kinase (IKK) complex, allowing p65/p50 nuclear translocation. NF-κB then transcriptionally upregulates a battery of antioxidant genes that create a negative feedback loop: MnSOD (SOD2) — mitochondrial superoxide dismutase that dismutes O₂⁻• to H₂O₂ Ferritin heavy chain (FTH1) — sequesters free iron, reducing Fenton Reaction-driven •OH production Heme oxygenase-1 (HMOX1) — degrades pro-oxidant Free heme to biliverdin/Bilirubin (antioxidant) and CO (anti-inflammatory) Glutathione Peroxidase — reduces lipid hydroperoxides Catalase — converts H₂O₂ to H₂O This antioxidant gene program represents a critical mechanism limiting TNF-α-induced tissue damage. Defects in this NF-κB-driven antioxidant response sensitize cells to TNF-α-induced Apoptosis. Complex II Formation, ROS, and Necroptosis When NF-κB activation is blocked or insufficient, TNF-α signaling shifts from cytoprotective to pro-death. Complex I disassembles and RIPK1 associates with FADD and Caspase-8 to form Complex II (the death-inducing signaling complex, DISC). If Caspase-8 is inhibited (e.g., by viral inhibitors or pharmacological blockade), RIPK1 interacts with RIPK3 and MLKL, forming the necrosome — a signaling platform that executes Necroptosis, a lytic and highly pro-inflammatory form of cell death. ROS — particularly mitochondrial O₂⁻• and Hydrogen Peroxide — are critical for necrosome assembly. RIPK3 enhances mitochondrial metabolism and ROS production by activating pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) and Glutamine Metabolism, creating a feed-forward oxidative burst. MLKL oligomers also directly permeabilize the plasma membrane, allowing further ROS influx. TNF-α in Insulin Resistance and Metabolic Syndrome TNF-α is a major mediator of Insulin Resistance in Obesity and Diabetes Mellitus. TNF-α impairs insulin signaling by Serine phosphorylation of IRS1 (insulin receptor substrate-1) via JNK and IKKbeta. Both JNK and IKKβ are activated by TNF-α-induced ROS. Adipose tissue macrophages from obese individuals secrete elevated TNF-α, which generates a local oxidative environment that suppresses Adiponectin (an insulin-sensitizing, antioxidant adipokine) and promotes lipolysis. This TNF-α/ROS/adiponectin axis is a central driver of metabolic inflammation. Therapeutic Targeting of TNF-α and Oxidative Stress Anti-TNF biologics — Infliximab (chimeric monoclonal), Adalimumab (human monoclonal), Etanercept (TNFR2-Fc fusion), Certolizumab pegol, and Golimumab — are widely used in Rheumatoid Arthritis, Inflammatory bowel disease, Psoriasis, and Ankylosing spondylitis. Beyond neutralizing TNF-α, these agents reduce systemic Oxidative Stress: treated patients show decreased serum Malondialdehyde, increased Glutathione, and improved total antioxidant capacity. Xanthine oxidase inhibitors (Allopurinol) and N-Acetylcysteine have been proposed as adjuncts to enhance anti-TNF efficacy by reducing the ROS burden that perpetuates TNF-α production through NF-κB activation. SIRT1 deacetylation of NF-κB downregulates pro-inflammatory cytokines including TNF-α. SIRT7 kidney-specific knockout reduces TNF-α and other inflammatory factors.

yap1.description:
YAP1 (Yes-associated protein 1) is a potent transcriptional co-activator and the chief downstream effector of the Hippo Signaling Pathway, which governs organ size, tissue homeostasis, and regeneration. When Hippo signaling is off, YAP1 escapes phosphorylation, translocates to the nucleus, and with TEAD factors drives expression of genes promoting proliferation, survival, EMT, and Metastasis — endowing YAP1 with clear oncogenic properties.

Structure and Regulation

YAP1 contains a WW domain that binds PPxY motifs (e.g., in TEADs) and a transcriptional activation domain. The Hippo kinase cascade (MST1/2 → LATS1/2) phosphorylates YAP1 at Ser127, inducing 14-3-3 binding and cytoplasmic retention; further phosphorylation (Ser381) primes Ubiquitination and degradation. Mechanical cues (cell density, stiffness, junctional tension) and GPCR/PI3K signals modulate this gate, so YAP1 integrates both biochemical and biomechanical inputs.

Oncogenic Role in Cancer

YAP1 is overexpressed or hyperactive in Gastric Cancer, Lung Cancer, liver, ovarian, and many other malignancies, where it fuels tumor growth, stemness, and therapy resistance. Nuclear YAP1 correlates with poor prognosis and aggressive EMT. Because YAP1 lacks a classic druggable pocket, targeting focuses on upstream regulators and downstream partners.



Repurposed Ivermectin inhibits YAP1-mediated oncogenic signaling — suppressing YAP1 expression/activity and thereby blocking proliferation in cancers such as gastric and lung carcinoma. Sensitivity to ivermectin in some models depends on baseline YAP1 levels, suggesting YAP1 status as a biomarker for ivermectin selection. Other strategies include TEAD inhibitors, LATS agonists, and vertical inhibition of upstream PI3K/SRC nodes.
