glial_cells.description:
Glial cells are the non-neuronal supporting cells of the central nervous system, comprising astrocytes, microglia, oligodendrocytes, and NG2 glia. In the context of Neuromelanin and Parkinson's Disease, glia are critical both as mediators of Neuroinflammation and as metabolic converters that activate exogenous neurotoxins.

Types and Roles
Astrocytes maintain homeostasis, regulate extracellular glutamate and potassium, support the blood-brain barrier, and store glycogen. They also express monoamine oxidase B (Monoamine oxidase B), the enzyme that converts the protoxin MPTP into its active toxic metabolite MPP+.
Microglia are the resident immune cells of the brain; they surveil for damage and, when activated, release cytokines, reactive oxygen and nitrogen species that can both clear debris and exacerbate neuronal injury.
Oligodendrocytes produce myelin and, increasingly appreciated, also participate in metabolic support of axons.


MPTP itself is not directly toxic; it crosses the blood-brain barrier and is taken up by astrocytes and other cells, where Monoamine oxidase B oxidizes it to MPP+ (1-methyl-4-phenylpyridinium). MPP+ is then released and selectively accumulated by dopaminergic terminals via the dopamine transporter, where it inhibits mitochondrial complex I, depleting ATP and precipitating oxidative stress. This glial "activation" step explains why MPTP so selectively destroys the Substantia Nigra and why MAO-B inhibitors are partially protective.

Physiological Function
Under basal conditions glia nurture neuromelanin-containing neurons through metabolic coupling, antioxidant supply (e.g., glutathione transfer), and clearance of extracellular catecholamines and quinones. Astrocytic networks buffer the redox environment around pigmented neurons, potentially mitigating damage from Dopamine o-quinone and Iron-mediated reactions.

Pathology and Clinical Relevance
In PD, chronic microglial activation and astrogliosis are observed in the substantia nigra, often colocalized with Neuromelanin-laden neurons and Lewy Bodies. Activated glia release pro-inflammatory mediators (TNF-α, IL-1β, ROS) that may drive the selective vulnerability of pigmented neurons, and impaired glial clearance of alpha-synuclein may perpetuate pathology. Glia are thus both a therapeutic target (anti-inflammatory strategies, MAO-B inhibitors) and a potential delivery vehicle for neuroprotective agents. The interplay between glial metabolism of toxins and neuromelanin neuron loss remains a central theme in experimental parkinsonism models.

caspase.description:
Overview

Caspases (cysteine aspartate-specific proteases) are a conserved family of proteolytic enzymes that function as central regulators of cell death and inflammation. They are synthesized as inactive zymogens and activated by proteolytic cleavage, then cleave cellular substrates after aspartate residues. The family is conventionally divided into initiator caspases, which sense and amplify death or inflammatory signals, and executioner caspases, which dismantle the cell. Caspases therefore sit at the heart of both Apoptosis and inflammatory cell-death programs relevant across cancer biology.



Caspases share a catalytic cysteine and a conserved substrate specificity for aspartate, but they diverge functionally:
Initiator caspases (e.g., Caspase-2, Caspase-10) contain large prodomains that recruit them into activation platforms such as the PIDDosome or death-receptor complexes, where induced proximity drives autocleavage and activation.
Executioner caspases (e.g., Caspase-6) have short prodomains and are activated by initiator caspases; they then cleave structural and regulatory substrates — for example, caspase-6 cleaves nuclear lamins, driving the structural collapse of the nucleus during apoptotic execution.
Inflammatory caspases process cytokine precursors (e.g., pro-IL-1β) and, via gasdermin cleavage, drive pyroptosis.

[!info] Taxonomy vs. mechanism
"Caspase" is the overarching family; individual members such as Caspase-2, Caspase-6, Caspase-10, and Caspase-12 are specific types with distinct activation platforms and substrates. The family framework clarifies how a single enzymatic architecture is repurposed for death, inflammation, and developmental remodeling.

Role in Cell Death and Cancer

Within the architecture of cancer biology, caspases are the effector machinery of apoptotic elimination and a frequent target of dysregulation. Initiator caspases transduce DNA damage (Caspase-2 via the PIDDosome, responding to genotoxic stress and mitotic catastrophe) and death-receptor signals (Caspase-10 amplifying caspase-8 in the extrinsic pathway; its silencing is common in tumors). Executioner caspases such as Caspase-6 carry out the ordered proteolysis that produces the apoptotic morphology. Loss or silencing of these enzymes contributes to evasion of apoptosis, a hallmark of malignancy.

Clinical & Research Significance

Because caspases execute the cell-death programs that chemotherapy and radiotherapy aim to engage, they are both biomarkers of treatment response and targets for modulation. Restoring caspase-dependent apoptosis in resistant tumors and understanding context-specific caspase roles (initiator versus executioner versus inflammatory) remain active research fronts. The family's diversity — from ER-localized Caspase-12 to lamina-cleaving Caspase-6 — underscores that "caspase" denotes a functional superfamily rather than a single pathway.

Documents
Knowledge-graph triple contexts establishing Caspase-2, Caspase-6, Caspase-10, and Caspase-12 as specific members of the Caspase family, with caspase-2 activated by the PIDDosome and caspase-6 cleaving nuclear lamins, were the source.

Connections
Caspase-2: An initiator caspase activated by the PIDDosome in response to DNA damage.
Caspase-6: An executioner caspase that cleaves nuclear lamins during apoptotic execution.
Caspase-10: An initiator caspase related to caspase-8 that amplifies death-receptor signaling.
Caspase-12: An ER-localized caspase subtype within the family.
Apoptosis: The cell-death program executed by apoptotic caspases.

mdl_800.description:
MDL-800 is a highly potent, selective, and cell-permeable synthetic allosteric activator of SIRT6. It binds to a structurally conserved, distal allosteric hydrophobic pocket of SIRT6, enhancing its deacetylase and de-fatty-acylase activity. MDL-800 is the parent compound from which the more potent derivative MDL-801 was developed.

Chemical Properties & Classification
Class: Bis-benzenesulfonamide-based sirtuin allosteric activator.
Target Selectivity: Highly selective for SIRT6 over other sirtuin isoforms.
Potency: Exhibits an $EC_{50}$ of approximately $10.3\ \mu\text{M}$ for SIRT6 activation.
Cell Permeability: Readily cell-permeable, enabling use in cellular and in vivo models.

Pharmacodynamics & Pharmacokinetics

Mechanism of Action

MDL-800 binds to an elongated hydrophobic channel on the surface of SIRT6, stabilizing the active conformation when bound to NAD+ and acetylated/acylated peptide substrates. This promotes:
Increased deacetylation of histone H3 lysine 9 (H3K9ac) and lysine 56 (H3K56ac).
Chromatin compaction at targeted promoter regions, leading to transcriptional repression of pro-inflammatory and pro-fibrotic genes.

Pathological & Therapeutic Effects
Anti-Fibrotic Actions: MDL-800 inhibits myofibroblast differentiation by activating SIRT6, deacetylating $\beta$-catenin, and downregulating the pro-fibrotic TGF-β/Smad3 pathway, decreasing extracellular matrix production.
Wound Healing: Promotes angiogenesis and accelerates cutaneous wound healing in mouse models.
Oncology: Represses cancer-associated aerobic glycolysis by suppressing HIF-1α through SIRT6-dependent histone deacetylation, inhibiting tumor proliferation and stemness.

Applications
Fibrosis Research: Studied in models of skin, kidney, and lung fibrosis.
Cancer Biology: Used as a chemical tool to study SIRT6 activation effects on glycolysis inhibition, chromatin compaction, and tumor suppression.

gastric_cancer.description:
Gastric cancer (stomach cancer) is a malignant tumor of the gastric epithelium and remains one of the leading causes of cancer mortality worldwide, particularly in East Asia, Eastern Europe, and parts of Latin America. The vast majority are adenocarcinomas arising from chronic inflammation of the gastric mucosa.

Etiology & Pathophysiology

The dominant etiological factors are infection with Helicobacter pylori, dietary carcinogens (high salt, smoked foods, low fruit/vegetable intake), smoking, and hereditary syndromes (e.g., CDH1 germline mutations causing diffuse Hereditary Diffuse Gastric Cancer). A metaplasia–dysplasia–carcinoma sequence driven by Inflammation and oxidative DNA damage underlies intestinal-type tumors. Molecularly, gastric cancer is heterogeneous, encompassing EBV-positive, microsatellite-instable, genomically stable, and chromosomal-instable subtypes (TCGA classification). Key drivers include HER2 amplification, MET alterations, TP53 loss, and activation of the Wnt/β-catenin and PI3K/Akt pathways.

Clinical Presentation & Biomarkers

Early disease is often asymptomatic; advanced symptoms include dyspepsia, weight loss, early satiety, and anemia. Diagnosis relies on endoscopy with biopsy and Helicobacter pylori testing. Biomarkers guiding therapy include HER2 (for trastuzumab), PD-L1 (for immune checkpoint inhibitors), and MSI status. Circulating tumor DNA and serum pepsinogen are investigational tools.

Therapeutic Landscape

Curative resection with lymphadenectomy is the mainstay for localized disease; perioperative Chemotherapy and chemoradiotherapy improve outcomes. Targeted agents include trastuzumab (HER2+), ramucirumab (anti-VEGF receptor 2), and pembrolizumab in MSI-high/PD-L1+ tumors. Ivermectin has demonstrated inhibitory effects on gastric cancer proliferation in preclinical models, where its activity depends on YAP1 expression — cells with high YAP1 are more sensitive. Repurposing ivermectin, possibly with existing targeted drugs, is an active investigational avenue.

Sirtuin Involvement (Wu et al., 2022)

GC is the fifth most frequently diagnosed cancer (5.6% incidence) and fourth most common cause of cancer death (7.7%). SIRT1 is upregulated while SIRT4/SIRT6 are downregulated — low SIRT4/SIRT6 negatively correlates with tumor size/pathological grade → poor prognosis:
SIRT1: Depletion promotes progression via STAT3/MMP-13.
SIRT4: Inhibits proliferation/migration/invasion via EMT.
SIRT5: Enhances autophagy via the AMPK/mTOR pathway; SIRT5-induced deacetylation of lactate dehydrogenase B triggers hyperactivation of autophagy, a key event in tumorigenesis.
SIRT6: Inhibits JAK2/STAT3 pathway → suppresses growth; silencing overcomes sorafenib resistance by promoting ferroptosis.

epicatechin.description:
Epicatechin is a polyphenolic flavonoid found in various plants, such as green tea and cocoa, known for its antioxidant and therapeutic properties.

Overview

Epicatechin has been identified as a potent breaker of Advanced Glycation End Products (AGEs). It can destroy preformed protein cross-links, such as those in glycated Serum albumin. The nucleophilic carbons (C6 and C8) on its A-ring are thought to attack and break the side chains of AGE structures.

Beneficial Effects
Retinoprotective: Decreases AGE accumulation in retinal tissues.

Anti-glycation: Inhibits the formation of new AGEs.

ldhb.description:
LDHB (Lactate Dehydrogenase B subunit) encodes the heart-type (H) subunit of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), a tetrameric enzyme that catalyzes the reversible conversion of pyruvate to lactate with concomitant reduction of NADH to NAD+. LDHB preferentially converts lactate to pyruvate, favouring oxidative metabolism and gluconeogenic flux.

Structure and Isozymes

LDH is a homo- or heterotetramer composed of LDHA (M, muscle) and LDHB (H, heart) subunits. The five LDH isozymes (LDH-1 through LDH-5) differ in subunit composition. LDH-1 (B4 homotetramer) predominates in heart and brain, tissues reliant on aerobic respiration, whereas LDH-5 (A4) dominates glycolytic muscle and many tumors.

Mechanism

The reaction pyruvate + NADH + H+ ⇌ lactate + NAD+ is near-equilibrium. The A subunit favors lactate production (Warburg phenotype), while the B subunit favors lactate oxidation to pyruvate, feeding the TCA cycle. Tissue isozyme distribution therefore determines whether lactate is a waste product or a fuel.



SIRT5 deacetylates LDHB at specific lysine residues, enhancing its enzymatic activity beyond normal physiological levels. Hyperactivation of LDHB by SIRT5 shifts the intracellular lactate/pyruvate balance, leading to metabolic stress that triggers excessive autophagy. This non-canonical activation of autophagy contributes to tumorigenesis, providing cancer cells with recycled nutrients and resistance to metabolic stress. The SIRT5–LDHB axis therefore represents a pro-survival, tumour-promoting pathway linking a mitochondrial sirtuin to the autophagy machinery. SIRT5 is a lysine desuccinylase/demalonylase as well as a deacetylase, and LDHB is among its reported substrates whose succinylation state influences activity.

Clinical Implications

LDHB is overexpressed in multiple cancers and supports the reverse Warburg effect, where lactate generated by stromal cells is imported and oxidized by cancer cells. Targeting SIRT5-mediated LDHB deacetylation could suppress the autophagic survival response and sensitize tumours to therapy. Serum LDH (including LDHB-rich isozymes) is a prognostic marker in lymphoma and other malignancies.

Connections

Autophagy — Cellular recycling process hyperactivated by the SIRT5–LDHB axis in tumorigenesis
LDHA — Muscle-type LDH subunit; together with LDHB determines lactate metabolism
NADH — Co-substrate of LDH; balance affected by LDHB hyperactivation
Warburg Effect — Aerobic glycolysis typical of cancer cells; LDHB modulates the reverse Warburg effect

Linking Summary
Suggested new entity notes to create: Reverse Warburg effect, LDH-1, Cori cycle
Strong connections to strengthen: SIRT5 ↔ LDHB

fibrosis.description:
Fibrosis is a pathological biological process defined by the excessive accumulation of extracellular matrix (ECM) components — principally Collagen, fibronectin, and proteoglycans — within tissues, resulting in scarring and progressive architectural distortion. It is the common终点 of chronic injury across virtually every organ system, including the liver (cirrhosis), lung (pulmonary fibrosis), kidney (nephrosis), heart (myocardial fibrosis), and skin (keloids/scleroderma). Rather than being a single disease, fibrosis represents a conserved wound-healing response that has failed to resolve, shifting from physiological repair toward maladaptive tissue remodeling.

Mechanism and Cellular Basis

The central effector cell is the activated Fibroblast, and its transdifferentiated derivative, the myofibroblast, which expresses α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) and is the principal source of Extracellular Matrix. Myofibroblasts arise not only from resident fibroblasts but also through Epithelial-to-Mesenchymal Transition (EMT) of epithelial cells, endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EndMT), and recruitment of fibrotic progenitor cells. The master profibrotic cytokine is TGF-β, which drives collagen synthesis, inhibits ECM degradation by suppressing matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), and stimulates tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs). Additional mediators include PDGF, CTGF, IL-13, and angiotensin II.

Physiological vs. Pathological Function

In acute wound healing, transient fibroblast activation and matrix deposition restore barrier integrity — a beneficial Biological Process. Fibrosis becomes pathological when the inciting stimulus (persistent Inflammation, toxins, mechanical stress, or metabolic injury) is not removed and the myofibroblast niche is not dismantled via apoptosis. Chronic Inflammation sustains a feed-forward loop: immune cells secrete TGF-β and ROS, perpetuating fibroblast activation. Epigenetic reprogramming — DNA methylation, histone modification, and non-coding RNAs — locks fibroblasts into a persistent activated state, explaining why established fibrosis is often irreversible.

Clinical and Research Relevance

Fibrosis contributes to an estimated 45% of all deaths in the developed world, yet antifibrotic therapies remain limited. Approved agents include pirfenidone and nintedanib for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, which slow decline without reversing scarring. Research frontiers target myofibroblast senescence, the TGF-β pathway, and epigenetic "reversal" of the activated fibroblast state. The interplay between Inflammation and fibrogenesis makes dual anti-inflammatory/antifibrotic strategies an active area, as is the role of mechanical tension and the matrisome in sustaining the fibrotic niche.

information_theory_of_aging.description:
The Information Theory of Aging is a conceptual framework advanced by David Sinclair positing that aging arises primarily from the loss of epigenetic and nuclear-architectural information — a "software" problem — rather than from irreversible "hardware" damage such as mutations. Because epigenetic information is, in principle, rewritable, the theory implies that aging may be reversible at the information level.

Relationship to RCM

The Relocalization of Chromatin Modifiers (RCM) Hypothesis is a mechanistic instantiation of this theory: repeated recruitment of chromatin modifiers to DNA repair sites progressively degrades the epigenetic landscape, eroding cellular identity.

Supporting Lines of Evidence
The ICE mouse model induces DSBs without mutations yet produces epigenetic aging.
Partial reprogramming with Yamanaka factors can reset epigenetic marks and restore youthful phenotypes.
Epigenetic clocks track age-associated drift that can be advanced or reversed experimentally.

retrograde_signaling.description:
Retrograde signaling refers to pathways of communication from Mitochondria to the cell nucleus and cytoplasm that regulate cellular and organismal activities. This concept challenges the traditional view of mitochondria as passive "end-function" organelles, revealing them as active participants in determining cell fate, stress response, and metabolic adaptation.

Mechanisms of Communication

Mitochondria communicate with the cell through several classes of retrograde signals:
ROS: Superoxide, hydrogen peroxide, and hydroxyl radicals generated by the Mitochondrial Electron Transport Chain serve as signaling molecules at low concentrations, activating stress-response pathways including NRF2 and AMPK.
Ca²⁺: Mitochondrial calcium uptake and release modulates Apoptosis, ATP production, and cytoplasmic calcium oscillations.
Cytochrome c: Release from the mitochondrial intermembrane space is a critical trigger for Intrinsic Apoptosis.
Nitric Oxide: Diffusible gas that modulates mitochondrial respiration and vasodilation.
Mitochondrial-derived peptides (MDPs): Small peptides encoded within the mitochondrial genome, such as Humanin, that act as endocrine and intracellular survival signals.
mtDNA: Released mtDNA can activate innate immune responses via the NALP3 inflammasome.

Biological Significance

Retrograde signaling coordinates mitochondrial function with nuclear gene expression to maintain cellular homeostasis. Key processes regulated by retrograde signals include:
Stress resistance: Activation of cytoprotective programs during Oxidative Stress
Energy metabolism: Adaptation of oxidative phosphorylation to substrate availability
Apoptosis: Determination of cell fate in response to irreversible damage
Aging: Age-related decline in mitochondrial function correlates with diminished retrograde signaling capacity

Evolutionary Conservation

Retrograde signaling is well conserved from yeast to humans. In C. elegans, neuron-specific mitochondrial dysfunction induces a systemic longevity signal mediated by mitochondrial unfolded protein response (UPR^mt), suggesting that retrograde signals can act non-cell-autonomously as endocrine factors.

[!tip] Key Insight
The identification of Humanin and other MDPs as retrograde signals that function as circulating endocrine factors has expanded the definition of retrograde signaling beyond cell-autonomous responses to include systemic inter-organ communication.




Alzheimer's Disease: Impaired mitochondrial calcium handling and increased ROS
Atherosclerosis: Mitochondrial dysfunction in endothelial cells
Type 2 Diabetes: Defective mitochondrial insulin signaling
Age-related decline: Diminished Humanin levels correlate with metabolic disease

ruxolitinib.description:
Ruxolitinib (INCB018424) is a selective ATP-competitive inhibitor of Janus kinase 1 (JAK1) and JAK2, and the first JAK inhibitor approved by the FDA (2011 for myelofibrosis; 2014 for polycythemia vera). It is a senomorphic therapy that targets the JAK–STAT3 pathway to suppress the pro-inflammatory SASP.

Mechanism of Action & Signaling

Ruxolitinib inhibits JAK1 and JAK2, the tyrosine kinases that transduce signals from interferon, hematopoietic, and many cytokine receptors. By blocking JAK catalytic activity it prevents phosphorylation and nuclear translocation of downstream STAT3 (and STAT5), shutting off transcription of inflammatory target genes. In senescent cells, JAK–STAT is a major amplifier of the SASP; ruxolitinib abrogates secretion of IL-6 and IL-8 and blunts the broader pro-fibrotic and immunomodulatory secretome without killing the cells.



Ruxolitinib is a prototypic senomorphic agent: it does not eliminate senescent cells but suppresses their inflammatory output via JAK–STAT blockade. By quelling the SASP it reduces the senescence-associated chronic inflammation that drives Inflammaging and age-related tissue dysfunction, and it has been used experimentally to "rejuvenate" aspects of the aged phenotype in several models.

Clinical / Pathological Relevance

FDA-approved for myelofibrosis, polycythemia vera, and steroid-refractory acute graft-versus-host disease; a topical formulation (ruxolitinib cream, Opzelura) is approved for atopic dermatitis and vitiligo. Repurposing trials are exploring its senomorphic potential in age-related and fibrotic diseases (e.g., pulmonary fibrosis), leveraging its established safety and JAK–STAT suppression.

Documents
SASP Review 2024: The review discusses ruxolitinib as a prototypic senomorphic agent that suppresses the SASP by inhibiting JAK1/2 and blocking STAT3/5 phosphorylation downstream of cytokine receptors. It abrogates secretion of IL-6 and IL-8 and the broader pro-fibrotic secretome without killing senescent cells, illustrating JAK–STAT blockade as a route to dampen inflammaging.

wrn.description:
Overview

WRN is a member of the RecQ family of DNA helicases and the protein mutated in Werner Syndrome, a human progeroid disorder of premature aging. WRN possesses both helicase and exonuclease activities and functions in DNA replication, recombination, and repair.

Mechanism

SIRT1 deacetylates and activates the Werner syndrome helicase WRN, linking SIRT1 to DNA Repair and genomic stability. Acetylation represses WRN's helicase activity; SIRT1-dependent deacetylation relieves this inhibition, enabling WRN to participate in resolving DNA structures during repair.

[!important] SIRT1–WRN axis
SIRT1 deacetylation activates WRN helicase, coupling NAD+/sirtuin status to genome maintenance. Loss of this regulation mimics aspects of premature aging.

Physiological Function

WRN promotes resolution of double-strand breaks and replication-associated DNA structures (e.g., via Homologous Recombination and base-excision repair pathways). By activating WRN, SIRT1 coordinates DNA repair with metabolic state, protecting genome integrity during stress and aging.

Clinical Relevance

Werner syndrome is characterized by accelerated aging, genomic instability, and cancer predisposition. The SIRT1–WRN connection suggests that maintaining NAD+ levels and sirtuin activity may support genome maintenance and counteract age-related DNA damage.

intestinal_ischemia_reperfusion_injury.description:
Intestinal ischemia-reperfusion injury is mucosal damage that occurs when blood flow is restored to an ischemic gut segment — relevant to mesenteric ischemia, bowel transplantation, and hemorrhagic shock. Reperfusion drives epithelial reactive-oxygen accumulation, mitochondrial oxidative damage, apoptosis, and loss of barrier integrity, which can propagate systemic inflammation.

Sirtuin Axis
SIRT1: Suppresses epithelial ROS accumulation and apoptosis (e.g., via miR-34a-5p modulation); resveratrol protects through the SIRT1–NF-κB–iNOS–NO pathway.
SIRT3: Alleviates mitochondrial oxidative damage and apoptosis via deacetylation of Peroxiredoxin 3.
SIRT6: Downregulation by miR-351-5p aggravates injury via oxidative stress, inflammation, and apoptosis.

Clinical Relevance

Protection of the mucosal barrier during reperfusion reduces bacterial translocation and systemic inflammatory sequelae. Sirtuin activation (especially SIRT1/SIRT3) is a candidate intestinal-protective strategy.

insulin_signaling.description:
Insulin signaling is a conserved growth factor pathway that regulates metabolism, growth, and lifespan. It is a central suppressor of Autophagy via PI3K-Akt Signaling-dependent activation of mTORC1.
Pathway Architecture
Insulin binds the IGF1R/InsR receptor tyrosine kinase, recruiting IRS1/IRS2 to activate PI3K → PIP3 → PDK1 → Akt. Akt phosphorylates TSC2 (inhibiting the TSC1/TSC2 complex), PRAS40, and FOXO transcription factors, all converging to activate mTORC1 and suppress autophagy.
Autophagy Regulation
Insulin signaling suppresses Autophagy through mTORC1-dependent phosphorylation of ULK1 (inactivating the initiation complex) and TFEB/TFE3 (promoting cytosolic retention via 14-3-3 protein). Reduced insulin/IGF-1 signaling—through Dietary Restriction, Intermittent Fasting, or genetic reduction of DAF-2 (in C. elegans)—derepresses autophagy and extends lifespan across species.
Longevity Connection
Reduced IIS is among the most robust lifespan-extending interventions. In C. elegans, mutations in DAF-2 (insulin/IGF-1 receptor) double lifespan via DAF-16/FOXO and autophagy activation. In mammals, IGF1 reduction and insulin sensitivity enhancement are associated with longevity.
Pathological Relevance
Hyperinsulinemia in Metabolic Syndrome and Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus chronically suppresses autophagy, contributing to proteotoxicity, mitochondrial dysfunction, and accelerated aging. Conversely, autophagy impairment exacerbates insulin resistance.

diabetic_retinopathy.description:
Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a microvascular complication of diabetes mellitus affecting the retinal capillaries. Hyperglycemia drives capillary pericyte and endothelial cell apoptosis, formation of degenerative capillaries, retinal inflammation, and pathological neovascularization, ultimately causing visual impairment and blindness.

Sirtuin Axis
SIRT1: Overexpression prevents capillary cell apoptosis and degenerative capillary formation, reduces diabetes-induced retinal inflammation, and improves visual function.

Clinical Relevance

DR is the leading cause of blindness in working-age adults. SIRT1 activation offers a retinal-protective strategy targeting apoptosis and inflammation of the retinal vasculature.

ml385.description:
ML385 is a selective small-molecule inhibitor of NRF2 (NF-E2-related factor 2). It binds directly to the NRF2 Cap'n'Collar (CNC) basic-leucine zipper (bZIP) domain, blocking its heterodimerization with small Maf proteins and preventing transcriptional activation of antioxidant response element (ARE)-containing genes. Unlike earlier NRF2 inhibitors that operate upstream by disrupting the Keap1–NRF2 interaction or promoting NRF2 degradation, ML385 acts at the level of DNA binding, making it a precise chemical probe for distinguishing NRF2 transcriptional output from the broader antioxidant network in which Sirtuins participate.

Overview

NRF2 is the master transcription factor coordinating the cellular antioxidant and detoxification response. Under basal conditions it is tethered in the cytoplasm by Keap1 and targeted for proteasomal degradation. Upon oxidative or electrophilic stress, NRF2 stabilizes, translocates to the nucleus, heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins, and drives expression of cytoprotective enzymes including heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NQO1, glutathione biosynthetic enzymes, and glutathione. ML385 was identified through structure-based screening as a compound that occupies the CNC-bZIP interface, preventing the NRF2–Maf complex from engaging ARE sequences without altering NRF2 protein stability.

Mechanism of Action

ML385 interferes with NRF2's DNA-binding activity without affecting NRF2 protein stability or Keap1-mediated degradation. It selectively inhibits the NRF2 transcriptional program, including induction of heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NQO1, and glutathione synthesis genes, without directly affecting NF-κB or AP-1 signaling. Biochemically, ML385 acts as a non-competitive inhibitor with respect to DNA: it binds the transcription factor rather than the promoter, so its effect persists irrespective of ARE copy number. This mechanism contrasts with the sirtuin-dependent regulation of antioxidant genes, which typically proceeds through NAD+-dependent deacetylation of downstream targets such as FOXO3a and SIRT3-mediated activation of MnSOD.

Physiological and Pathological Relevance

NRF2 hyperactivation is a hallmark of many cancers, where it confers chemoresistance and proliferative advantage by sustaining reductive capacity. Consequently ML385 has been explored as a means to sensitize tumor cells to therapy. At the same time, intact NRF2 signaling is protective in neurodegeneration, cardiovascular disease, and ageing, so NRF2 inhibition must be contextually controlled. The intersection with sirtuin biology is particularly relevant: SIRT6 can be transcriptionally induced via NRF2 binding to an ARE in its promoter, and SIRT3-dependent mitochondrial antioxidant defenses overlap functionally with the NRF2 program. ML385 therefore serves as a dissection tool to separate these axes.

Use in Sirtuin Research

ML385 is used as a chemical tool to dissect NRF2-dependent vs. NRF2-independent effects of redox-active compounds and sirtuin modulators:
Demonstrating whether agonists upregulate SIRT6 via NRF2 binding to the ARE in the SIRT6 promoter.
Testing whether suppression of CD38 transcription is mediated by NRF2-dependent antagonism of NF-κB.
Differentiating NRF2-dependent and independent mechanisms in hormetic preconditioning experiments, where Caloric Restriction and Resveratrol engage both sirtuin and NRF2 pathways.

h3k9ac.description:
H3K9ac denotes the acetylation of lysine 9 on the N-terminal tail of histone H3. As a euchromatic mark, H3K9ac neutralizes the positive charge of lysine, loosens nucleosome–DNA contacts, and is generally associated with open, transcriptionally permissive chromatin. Its removal (deacetylation) by NAD⁺-dependent sirtuins is a central mechanism by which sirtuins impose transcriptional silencing and reshape the epigenetic landscape.

Regulation by Sirtuins
SIRT1: Deacetylates histone H3 at lysine 9 (and K79), promoting tightly compacted chromatin and gene silencing — a hallmark of SIRT1 activity at telomeres, promoters (e.g., of AR, BRCA1, EZH2, EP300), and in dynamic chromatin association of DNA-repair factors.
SIRT6: A principal H3K9ac (and H3K56ac) deacetylase. SIRT6 deacetylates H3K9 at the promoters of NF-κB target genes, repressing inflammatory transcription; at ERK1/2 promoters, inhibiting ERK expression; and at the Nkx3.2 promoter, relieving repression of GATA5. H3K9 deacetylation also facilitates recruitment of DSB-repair factors (53BP1, BRCA1) to damage-flanking chromatin.
SIRT6 activators such as UBCS039/MDL-800 and Cyanidin decrease both H3K9ac and H3K56ac, compacting chromatin and promoting DNA double-strand break repair.

Physiological & Pathological Relevance
Inflammation: SIRT6-mediated H3K9 deacetylation at NF-κB promoters underlies its anti-inflammatory effect and organismal lifespan regulation (Kawahara et al., 2009).
Genome stability & senescence: SIRT6 loss leads to telomeric H3K9 hyperacetylation and senescence; SIRT6 preserves telomere integrity.
Viral replication: SIRT3 and SIRT6 reduce H3K9 acetylation on HBV covalently closed circular DNA, inhibiting viral transcription.
Cancer & fibrosis: SIRT6 activators that lower H3K9ac/H3K56ac induce autophagy and suppress myofibroblast activation.

Connections

SIRT1, SIRT6: Major sirtuin deacetylases of H3K9ac.
NF-κB: NF-κB target promoters deacetylated by SIRT6 at H3K9.

metformin.description: Metformin is the world's most widely prescribed medication for type 2 diabetes. Beyond its role in controlling blood sugar, metformin has gained significant attention in Geroscience as a potential "geroprotector"—a drug that can slow the fundamental processes of aging. Metformin is a first-line medication for type 2 diabetes that also acts as a caloric restriction mimetic and Autophagy Inducer by activating AMPK. Mechanisms of Action Metformin's effects are systemic and pleiotropic: Activation of AMPK: Metformin activates the AMPK pathway, which mimics the effects of Caloric Restriction by promoting energy efficiency and cellular repair. Inhibition of mTOR: By activating AMPK, metformin indirectly inhibits the mTOR pathway, leading to increased Autophagy and reduced cellular growth. Reduction of Inflammation: Metformin has been shown to reduce the production of pro-inflammatory factors, including those associated with the Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype. Research indicates that metformin can influence the Epigenome: Epigenetic Clock: Studies have shown that metformin treatment can slow the rate of the Epigenetic Clock (e.g., DNAmGrimAge), indicating a slower rate of biological aging. DNA Methylation: Metformin may help maintain youthful DNA methylation patterns by influencing the activity of enzymes like DNMT1. The TAME Trial The potential anti-aging effects of metformin are currently being tested in the "Targeting Aging with Metformin" (TAME) trial, the first clinical trial designed to see if a drug can delay the onset of multiple age-related diseases in humans. Mechanism of Action Metformin's primary molecular target is Mitochondrial Complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase), where it acts as a mild, reversible inhibitor. This inhibition produces a transient decrease in mitochondrial ATP production, increasing the cellular AMP/ATP ratio, which activates AMP-Activated Protein Kinase (AMPK). AMPK activation orchestrates a metabolic shift from anabolic (lipogenesis, gluconeogenesis) to catabolic (fatty acid oxidation, glucose uptake) pathways. The Complex I inhibition is concentration-dependent: at therapeutic portal vein concentrations (100–500 µM), inhibition is approximately 10–30%, producing hormetic — not cytotoxic — metabolic stress. Metformin also inhibits mitochondrial Glycerol-3-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (mGPDH), altering the cytosolic redox state and suppressing gluconeogenesis from lactate and glycerol. Additional targets include Fructose-1,6-Bisphosphatase, Glucagon Signaling via AMPK-independent modulation of Adenylate Cyclase, and Lysosome-dependent Rag GTPases pathways that converge on mTORC1 suppression. Effects on AGE Formation Metformin reduces circulating Advanced Glycation End Products through multiple convergent mechanisms. Directly, metformin traps Methylglyoxal (MG) and other reactive dicarbonyl species through its biguanidine moiety, forming triazepinone adducts that are excreted in urine. In clinical studies, metformin treatment reduces plasma Methylglyoxal levels by 30–50% in patients with type 2 diabetes, correlating with reduced Carboxymethyllysine (CML) and MG-derived Hydroimidazolone (MG-H1) levels. Indirectly, metformin's AMPK-mediated suppression of gluconeogenesis reduces glycolytic flux, the primary source of Methylglyoxal production. By lowering blood glucose, metformin also decreases substrate availability for the Maillard Reaction. Furthermore, metformin upregulates Glyoxalase I expression through NRF2/ARE activation, enhancing endogenous dicarbonyl detoxification capacity. In diabetic animal models, metformin reduces renal and vascular AGE accumulation and attenuates RAGE expression. Anti-Aging Properties and Healthspan Extension Compelling preclinical evidence suggests metformin extends healthspan across multiple model organisms. In C. elegans, metformin extends lifespan by 20–40% via AMPK- and SKN-1/NRF2-dependent mechanisms. In Mus musculus, metformin delays the onset of age-related pathologies, including Hepatocellular Carcinoma, Alzheimer's Disease, and Atherosclerosis, though lifespan extension is inconsistent and more pronounced in female mice and mice on high-fat diets. Mechanistically, metformin mimics aspects of Caloric Restriction at the transcriptional level, reducing mTORC1 signaling, enhancing Autophagy, attenuating Senescence, and reducing Inflammaging. Metformin also modulates the gut microbiome, enriching Akkermansia muciniphila populations that improve metabolic health independently of glucose lowering. The landmark Targeting Aging with Metformin (TAME) trial — a multi-center, placebo-controlled study — is currently evaluating whether metformin can delay the onset of age-related multimorbidity in non-diabetic older adults. Connection to Mitohormesis Metformin's Complex I inhibition represents a canonical example of Mitohormesis: mild mitochondrial stress that activates adaptive cytoprotective programs. The transient reduction in NADH oxidation elevates the mitochondrial NADH/NAD+ ratio, which is then resolved through SIRT1-dependent deacetylation of PGC-1α and FOXO transcription factors.

dopamine_o_quinone.description:
Dopamine o-quinone (DAQ) is a highly reactive ortho-quinone oxidation product of the neurotransmitter Dopamine, arising through the one-electron or two-electron oxidation of dopamine. It is the central reactive intermediate in the spontaneous non-enzymatic polymerization pathway that builds the pigment Neuromelanin within catecholaminergic neurons of the Substantia Nigra and Locus Coeruleus.

Overview
Under normal conditions dopamine is a relatively stable catecholamine, but its catechol ring is highly susceptible to autoxidation and to oxidation by tyrosinase-related and ferric/iron-dependent mechanisms. Once oxidized, dopamine loses two electrons and two protons to form dopamine o-quinone, a cyclizable electrophile. DAQ is not an end product but a branchpoint molecule: it can either (a) be reduced back to dopamine (redox cycling), (b) react with cysteine residues on proteins via Michael addition, or (c) undergo intramolecular cyclization to the leukoaminochrome (aminochrome), which then rearranges and further oxidizes to the 5,6-indolequinone unit that is incorporated into the growing neuromelanin polymer.

Chemical Process and Structure
The pathway proceeds as follows: dopamine → dopamine o-quinone → leucoaminochrome (via intramolecular 1,4-Michael addition/cyclization) → aminochrome (5,6-indolequinone, also called Aminochrome) → further oxidation/polymerization into indolic and benzothiazine oligomers. Dopamine o-quinone and its downstream quinone/indolequinone species are electrophilic and bind covalently to nucleophilic residues (cysteine, lysine, histidine) on proteins, which may explain the protein-adduct burden observed in neuromelanin granules. The redox cycling of DAQ/semiquinone radicals also generates Reactive Oxygen Species, contributing to the local oxidative milieu.

Physiological Function
In melanized neurons, the continuous formation and sequestration of DAQ into neuromelanin is considered a protective disposal route: by polymerizing the reactive quinone, the neuron traps potentially toxic catechol-quinone species and redox-active metals (iron, copper) within insoluble granules, blunting oxidative damage and buffering cytosolic dopamine turnover. This "sink" hypothesis holds that neuromelanin accumulation is largely a by-product of lifelong dopamine metabolism and a detoxification strategy.

Pathology and Clinical Relevance
The same chemistry that protects can also injure. DAQ and downstream 5,6-indolequinone are toxic to non-melanized cells, and in vitro studies show DAQ induces apoptosis in dopaminergic neuron models, particularly when glutathione defenses are depleted. The imbalance between dopamine oxidation (driven by Tyrosinase-like activity and Iron-mediated Fenton chemistry) and antioxidant buffering is hypothesized to contribute to selective vulnerability in Parkinson's Disease. Moreover, neuromelanin's propensity to bind and release iron means that its quinone-rich matrix can become a source rather than a sink of Oxidative Stress as neurons age. DAQ-derived adducts and aminochrome are therefore studied as biomarkers of catecholamine oxidative stress and as contributors to Lewy Bodies pathology via cross-linking of Alpha-synuclein.

When Dopamine is oxidized to Dopamine o-quinone, Aminochrome and 5,6-indolequinone are formed and typically undergo polymerization to form the dark pigment, Neuromelanin (Munoz et al., 2012).

5_azacytidine.description: 5-Azacytidine (5-aza-CR; trade name Vidaza) is a ribose nucleoside analog of cytidine that functions as a dual DNA methyltransferase (DNMT) inhibitor and RNA incorporation agent. It is the prototypical epidrug and a first-line therapy for myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS). Beyond its epigenetic effects, it is also a potent inducer of Stress-Induced Premature Senescence in vitro. Mechanism of Action The therapeutic efficacy of 5-Azacytidine arises from its ability to interfere with both DNA and RNA metabolism through its incorporation as a nucleotide analog. DNA Methylation Inhibition: 5-Azacytidine is phosphorylated by Uridine-cytidine kinase to its triphosphate form. During DNA Replication, it is incorporated into the nascent DNA strand in place of cytidine. When the enzyme DNMT1 attempts to methylate the DNA at these sites, it forms a covalent bond with the 5-azacytidine residue. This interaction irreversibly traps the DNMT enzyme, leading to its depletion via proteasomal degradation. As the cell undergoes subsequent divisions, the lack of available DNMT leads to passive DNA Demethylation at CpG sites, potentially reactivating silenced genes. RNA Incorporation and Epigenetic Modulation: Unlike its deoxyribose counterpart Decitabine, 5-Azacytidine is also incorporated into RNA during transcription. This incorporation disrupts various aspects of RNA metabolism, including: Inhibition of tRNA methylation, which can impact translation efficiency. Impairment of rRNA processing. Alteration of mRNA splicing patterns. These RNA-level effects contribute to the overall cytotoxicity and may play a role in its unique epigenetic profile. Induction of Senescence and DNA Damage: The incorporation of 5-Azacytidine into DNA can trigger a DNA Damage Response due to replication fork stalling at the trapped DNMT-DNA adducts. This stress, combined with the re-expression of hypermethylated tumor suppressor genes (such as p15^INK4b^ and CDH1), can drive cells into Stress-Induced Premature Senescence. This senescence is often characterized by the elaboration of a Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype (Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype), including the secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines like IL-6 and IL-8. Clinical Use 5-Azacytidine is primarily indicated for the treatment of high-risk MDS: Myelodysplastic Syndrome (MDS): The FDA-approved regimen involves 75 mg/m² administered via subcutaneous or intravenous injection daily for 7 consecutive days in a 28-day cycle. It is particularly effective in patients with TET2 mutations. Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML): It is also used in certain subtypes of AML, often in combination with other agents. The clinical response in MDS involves the reactivation of silenced tumor suppressor genes, which can lead to improved hematopoiesis or the induction of terminal differentiation and senescence in leukemic cells. Several factors limit the clinical utility and contribute to resistance against 5-Azacytidine: Chemical Instability: 5-Azacytidine is highly unstable in aqueous solutions, with a half-life of approximately 4 hours at 37°C and pH 7.4. This requires it to be freshly prepared for clinical administration. Metabolic Inactivation: It is rapidly inactivated in the plasma by Cytidine deaminase (CDA), with a half-life of approximately 20 minutes. Resistance Mechanisms: Resistance can arise through the downregulation of the activating enzyme Deoxycytidine kinase (dCK), the upregulation of Cytidine deaminase (CDA), or compensatory methylation by DNMT3a and DNMT3b. Connections DNA Methylation — 5-Azacytidine causes passive demethylation by inhibiting DNMTs. RNA — The drug is incorporated into both DNA and RNA. Epigenetic Modifiers — It is a prototypical epidrug. Myelodysplastic Syndrome — It is a first-line therapy for this condition. Stress-Induced Premature Senescence — It can induce senescence in vitro. Uridine-cytidine kinase — The enzyme responsible for its phosphorylation. DNA Replication — The process where its incorporation into DNA occurs. DNMT1 — The enzyme that is covalently trapped by the drug. DNA Demethylation — The resulting state of the genome after DNMT depletion. tRNA — RNA incorporation inhibits tRNA methylation. rRNA — RNA incorporation impairs rRNA processing. mRNA — RNA incorporation alters mRNA splicing. DNA Damage Response — Triggered by replication fork stalling at adducts. CDKN2B — A tumor suppressor gene that can be reactivated. CDH1 — A tumor suppressor gene that can be reactivated. Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype — The secretory profile associated with induced senescence.

oncogene_induced_senescence.description: Oncogene-Induced Senescence (OIS) is a biological process in which normal cells expressing activated oncogenes enter a state of permanent cell cycle arrest, functioning as an intrinsic tumor-suppressive barrier. First described by Manuel Serrano in 1997, OIS is triggered by hyperproliferative signals from oncogenes such as RAS (HRAS^G12V^), BRAF (BRAF^V600E^), and MYC. Molecular Mechanism Constitutive oncogenic signaling pushes cells into a state of "hyper-replication," where DNA replication forks are initiated at excessive frequency from overdriven E2F transcriptional programs. This leads to: DNA Replication Stress: Stalled/dysfunctional replication forks generate single-strand DNA gaps. DNA Damage Response activation: ATR-CHK1 and ATM-CHK2 cascades are engaged, converging on p53 stabilization. p16INK4A transcriptional activation: The CDKN2A locus is derepressed via loss of PRC1/2-mediated H3K27me3. RB1-dependent arrest: Both p21 (p53-dependent) and p16^INK4a^ enforce hypophosphorylated RB1 activity, silencing E2F targets. OIS shares features with Replicative Senescence but also has distinctive hallmarks: Oncogene-induced hyperproliferation phase: A transient burst of proliferation precedes arrest, unlike the gradual slowdown of replicative senescence. SAHF formation: Senescence-associated heterochromatin foci are particularly prominent in OIS, especially in BRAF V600E-induced lesions. Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype with distinct signature: OIS-associated SASP is enriched for IL-1-dependent cytokines, CXCR2 chemokines, and Notch signaling, which recruit immune cells for senescent cell clearance. Active DNA Methylation changes: OIS is accompanied by focal hypermethylation of PRC2 target genes, establishing a cancer-prone epigenetic landscape. Tumor-Suppressive Role and Bypass OIS acts as a fail-safe mechanism against malignant transformation. In vivo, OIS is observed in benign human lesions such as melanocytic nevi (moles), where BRAF V600E-expressing melanocytes are arrested. OIS bypass — through loss of p53, p16INK4A, or PTEN; or activation of TERT — is a prerequisite for progression to malignancy. Interactions with Senolytics OIS cells are susceptible to Senolytic Drugs like Navitoclax (Bcl-2/Bcl-xL inhibitor). However, eliminating OIS cells in premalignant lesions may paradoxically promote tumor growth by removing a cell-autonomous cancer barrier — the Senolytic Paradox. An open question is whether transient OIS cell clearance can reduce the pro-tumorigenic Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype without compromising tumor suppression. List of documents that mention this entity Oncogene-Induced Senescence represents another complex senescence phenotype that depends on activation and/or overexpression of oncogenes (Serrano et al., ; Bianchi‐Smiraglia & Nikiforov, ). document - The role of the dynamic epigenetic landscape in senescence_orchestrating SASP expression Review shows OIS undergoes B-to-A compartment switching at SASP genes (condensin-bound), enhancer remodeling at the TAD scale, and HMGB2 protection of SASP loci from SAHF silencing; AP-1/BRD4/EZH2/KDM4 orchestrate the SASP epigenetically. Demonstrated that OIS cells transmit senescence to neighbouring normal cells via SASP factors (paracrine senescence). Identified the inflammasome–IL-1α axis as the master SASP regulator and TGF-β family ligands as major paracrine mediators. Showed in vivo paracrine senescence in mouse liver, skin, and human SSA models.

telomere.description:
Telomeres are nucleoprotein structures capping the ends of linear chromosomes, composed of tandem TTAGGG repeats bound by the shelterin protein complex. They solve the "end-replication problem," preventing exonuclease erosion of coding DNA and distinguishing natural chromosome ends from double-strand breaks.

Structure & Biology

Telomeric repeats are maintained by Telomerase, a reverse transcriptase expressed in stem and germ cells but largely absent in somatic tissue. With each cell division, telomeres shorten until they reach a critical length that triggers replicative Senescence or apoptosis — a phenomenon known as the Hayflick limit.

Mechanism & Pathology

Critically short or dysfunctional telomeres activate DNA-damage-response pathways (ATM, p53) and promote Genomic Instability, a recognized hallmark of aging. Telomere attrition therefore couples cellular aging to Aging systemically and is linked to Age-Related Diseases including pulmonary fibrosis and immune aging.

Longevity Relevance

Telomere length is a candidate biomarker of biological age, though it is less consistent than epigenetic clocks such as the Horvath Clock. Interventions that preserve telomere integrity — Caloric Restriction, sirtuin activity, reduced Oxidative Stress — are active geroscience targets.

[!warning] Causality Caveat
Telomere shortening correlates with aging but is not proven to be a primary driver; excessively elongating telomeres risks oncogenesis.

Documents
Epigenetic Changes in Aging
Discusses telomere dynamics and reprogramming in the context of age-related epigenetic drift.
Epigenetic Alterations Indicator
Examines telomere attrition as an early aging signal and health-risk marker.
Gut Microbiome, Aging, Longevity
Reviews microbial and dietary associations with telomere length in aging.
OSKM Reprogramming Events
Covers reprogramming approaches that reset telomere and epigenetic aging marks.

DNA Damage: Dysfunctional telomeres are sensed as DNA damage.

ammonium_persulfate.description: Ammonium Persulfate (APS, (NH₄)₂S₂O₈) is a Persulfate salt widely used as a strong oxidizing agent and free radical initiator in biochemistry, molecular biology, and industrial chemistry. In the context of Adrenochrome research, APS is employed as a convenient chemical oxidant to convert Epinephrine to Adrenochrome in vitro, a reaction commonly used to model Oxidative Stress and catecholamine oxidation under controlled laboratory conditions. Chemical Properties APS is a white crystalline solid with a molecular weight of 228.20 g/mol that is highly soluble in water (approx. 558 g/L at 20 °C). It acts as a powerful two-electron oxidizer with a standard reduction potential of E° = 2.01 V for the half-reaction S₂O₈²⁻ + 2e⁻ → 2SO₄²⁻ — one of the highest among common peroxygen compounds, exceeding that of Hydrogen Peroxide (1.78 V). In aqueous solution, APS decomposes slowly via hydrolysis to form Hydrogen Peroxide and ammonium bisulfate; this decomposition is accelerated by heat, transition metal ions, and alkaline pH. Beyond its specialized use in adrenochrome chemistry, APS is widely employed as a free radical initiator in Polymerization reactions, most notably in Acrylamide gel polymerization for SDS-PAGE and other electrophoretic techniques. During gel casting, APS reacts with TEMED (tetramethylethylenediamine) to generate persulfate free radicals that crosslink acrylamide monomers into a polyacrylamide matrix. Additional applications include chemical oxidation of organic substrates in synthetic chemistry, etching of copper in printed circuit board manufacturing, bleaching agents in hair cosmetic formulations, and as a disinfectant in wastewater treatment. Use in Epinephrine Oxidation In biochemical and cell biology experiments, APS serves as a rapid and reproducible chemical oxidant to convert Epinephrine to Adrenochrome. The reaction proceeds through a two-electron oxidation of the catechol ring to the corresponding o-quinone intermediate (Adrenaline-quinone), which then undergoes rapid intramolecular cyclization via Michael-type addition of the secondary amine to form the indoline-like tricyclic adrenochrome chromophore. Adrenochrome formation can be monitored spectrophotometrically by its characteristic absorbance maximum at 480 nm, enabling real-time kinetic measurements of the oxidation reaction. Beyond tracking adrenochrome synthesis, this reaction is employed experimentally to generate Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS) and study redox cycling dynamics. During the one-electron reduction of adrenochrome back to the leuco-adrenochrome semiquinone radical, superoxide and subsequent ROS are produced, linking APS-driven epinephrine oxidation to models of Oxidative Stress, Apoptosis, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Variations of this assay have been used as a surrogate measure of Superoxide Dismutase (SOD) activity, where SOD inhibits the rate of adrenochrome formation by scavenging superoxide — an approach known as the epinephrine-adrenochrome SOD assay. The simplicity and colorimetric readout of this method make it a useful tool for screening antioxidant compounds and characterizing oxidant-antioxidant balance in cellular systems. Safety & Handling APS is a strong irritant to the skin, eyes, and respiratory tract. It is classified as a skin sensitizer, and repeated or prolonged exposure can lead to allergic contact dermatitis and respiratory hypersensitivity. As a strong oxidizer, APS can cause ignition of combustible materials and may react violently with reducing agents, powdered metals, and organic compounds. APS should be stored in a cool, dry environment away from heat sources, direct sunlight, and incompatible materials. When handling, appropriate personal protective equipment (chemical-resistant gloves, safety goggles, and a lab coat) is required. Spills should be contained with inert absorbents and never mixed with organic waste due to fire risk. Connections Adrenochrome: APS is used as an in vitro oxidant to convert Epinephrine to Adrenochrome. Epinephrine: The catecholamine substrate oxidized by APS in the adrenochrome synthesis reaction. Oxidative Stress: APS-driven epinephrine oxidation generates ROS and is used to model oxidative stress. Polymerization: APS serves as a free radical initiator for acrylamide gel polymerization in SDS-PAGE. Redox cycle: The conversion of epinephrine to adrenochrome by APS initiates redox cycling. o-quinone: The initial two-electron oxidation product of epinephrine prior to cyclization to adrenochrome. Hydrogen Peroxide: A decomposition product of APS in aqueous solution and a related oxidant.

adiposity.description:
Overview

Adiposity refers to the accumulation of body fat, particularly in white adipose tissue, and is a central driver of metabolic disease and age-related morbidity. Protein restriction (PR) is a well-characterized dietary intervention that reduces adiposity while simultaneously increasing energy expenditure — an effect that occurs despite increased food intake, distinguishing it from conventional caloric restriction.

Mechanisms

Dietary protein restriction lowers body fat and improves Glucose homeostasis in young and aged rodents, with benefits most pronounced in males but also present in females, and remains effective when initiated late in life (18–20 months). The metabolic effects are largely mediated by FGF21, which is induced during low-protein feeding and promotes energy expenditure through UCP1-dependent thermogenic beiging of white adipose tissue and increased thermogenesis in Brown Adipose Tissue. PR also shifts central brain signaling toward protein appetite, reinforcing protein-seeking behavior over energy intake.

[!info] Protein appetite trade-off
PR increases food intake to compensate for low protein, yet fat mass still falls — energy expenditure rises faster than intake because FGF21-driven thermogenesis outweighs the caloric surplus.

Clinical Evidence

Randomized controlled trials in humans confirm that low-protein diets reduce body weight and fat mass despite increased caloric intake, mirroring the rodent findings. The effects scale with the magnitude of protein restriction and interact with Energy Expenditure, Obesity, and insulin sensitivity, positioning PR as a candidate strategy for metabolic healthspan extension alongside Protein Restriction and Aging research.

uv_light.description:
Overview

Ultraviolet (UV) light is high-energy electromagnetic radiation that generates Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS), which drive the oxidation of Catecholamines such as Epinephrine. Because ROS can steal electrons from the catechol hydroxyls, producing the o-quinone intermediate, light exposure accelerates the pathway that converts adrenaline into Adrenochrome.

[!info]
 Factor    Effect 
---  ---
 UV-generated ROS    Oxidation of catechol hydroxyls 
 o-quinone intermediate    Accelerated adrenochrome formation 
 Temperature    Kinetic energy controlling reaction rate 

Relevance to Drug Stability

This photochemical sensitivity is why pharmaceutical epinephrine is stored in amber vials away from light: preventing light-induced ROS formation slows the oxidation and cyclization reactions that degrade the drug. The same principle applies more broadly to catecholamine biochemistry, where photo-oxidation can convert adrenaline solutions pink.

[!warning]
Temperature and light, as factors governing kinetic energy and radical generation, are environmental controls that determine whether epinephrine remains stable or proceeds toward adrenochrome and its toxic downstream chemistry.

Broader Context

UV-induced oxidative chemistry also underlies photoaging and UV-mediated tissue damage, connecting this entity to the broader oxidative stress and ROS biology of the vault.

signaling_molecules.description: Definition Signaling molecules (or chemical messengers) are molecules that transmit information between cells or within a single cell to coordinate biological processes. Role in Oxidative Stress While often viewed as harmful, low levels of Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS) and Reactive Nitrogen Species (RNS) function as critical signaling molecules. This process is known as redox signaling. Key Messengers Hydrogen Peroxide: A stable ROS that acts as a second messenger in insulin signaling and growth factor pathways. Nitric Oxide: A gasotransmitter involved in Vasodilation and neurotransmission. Superoxide Radicals: Can modulate the activity of Iron-Sulfur Clusters in proteins. Connections Apoptosis: ROS levels determine the threshold for programmed cell death. Immunity: ROS are used to signal the presence of pathogens. Differentiation: Redox state influences stem cell fate. Thioredoxin: Primary system for reducing oxidized cysteine switches. Glutathione: Maintains general thiol redox buffering and participates in S-glutathionylation signaling. NADPH Oxidase: The major enzyme family producing signaling ROS. Aquaporins (AQP3, AQP8): Peroxiporins that channel H2O2 across membranes. PTEN: Redox-sensitive tumor suppressor; oxidized PTEN activates PI3K/Akt. Protein Kinase G: Mediates NO-cGMP signaling in vasodilation. S-Nitrosylation: The equivalent of phosphorylation for NO signaling. mTOR: Downstream target of PI3K/Akt, activated when PTEN is oxidized. HIF-1α: Stabilized by mitochondrial ROS, linking metabolism to gene expression. Cancer: Dysregulated redox signaling drives proliferation, survival, and metastasis. Insulin: Insulin signaling generates H2O2 that amplifies the signaling cascade through PTP oxidation. Linking Summary New links added in this revision: Thioredoxin, Glutathione, Protein Tyrosine Phosphatases, PTEN, Aquaporins, NADPH Oxidase, Mitochondria, Mitochondrial ROS, HIF-1α, PGC-1α, Unfolded Protein Response, AMPK, mTOR, PI3K, Akt, S-Nitrosylation, Parkin, GAPDH, Caspase-3, Protein Kinase G, Catalase, Peroxiredoxin, EGF Receptor, Receptor Tyrosine Kinases, Cancer, Metabolic Syndromes, Neurodegenerative Diseases, Insulin, Metabolism, Apoptosis Suggested new entity notes to create: Peroxiporins, Sulfenic Acid, Cysteine Redox Code, Sulfenylamide, Denitrosylases, GSNOR, ERO1, UPRmt, Redox Signalosome New links added: Reactive Oxygen Species, Reactive Nitrogen Species, Hydrogen Peroxide, Nitric Oxide, Vasodilation, Superoxide Radicals, Iron-Sulfur Clusters, Apoptosis, Immunity, Differentiation Suggested new entity notes to create: Iron-Sulfur Clusters, Vasodilation Strong connections to strengthen: Signaling Molecules ↔ Hydrogen Peroxide The Cysteine Code: Redox-Sensitive Protein Switches The primary mechanism by which H2O2 transduces signals is through reversible oxidation of cysteine thiols (Cys-SH) in target proteins. Specific cysteine residues are "redox-sensitive" because their local electrostatic environment lowers the thiol pKa from the typical value of ~8.5 to as low as ~4.5–5.5, making them ionized to thiolate (Cys-S−) at physiological pH. Thiolates are ~10^8-fold more reactive toward H2O2 than protonated thiols, enabling rapid and selective oxidation. The initial oxidation product is a sulfenic acid (Cys-SOH), which is unstable and either condenses with a nearby thiol to form a disulfide bond or is further oxidized to sulfinic (Cys-SO2H) or sulfonic (Cys-SO3H) acid. While sulfenylation and disulfide formation are reversible (by Thioredoxin and Glutathione/glutaredoxin systems), sulfinic and sulfonic acids are irreversible modifications that require proteolytic removal. This "cysteine redox code" — the pattern of reversible versus irreversible oxidation — determines whether the signaling event is transient (regulatory) or permanent (damage-associated). The best-characterized targets include Protein Tyrosine Phosphatases (PTP1B, SHP-2, PTEN), whose active-site cysteine (Cys-215 in PTP1B) is oxidized to sulfenic acid upon H2O2 exposure, transiently inactivating phosphatase activity and allowing tyrosine kinase signaling to proceed unchecked. H2O2 Diffusion and Gradients: The Peroxiporin Model For H2O2 to act as a second messenger, it must be generated in specific cellular compartments and reach defined targets without being consumed by the abundant Glutathione peroxidases (GPx) and peroxiredoxins that maintain nanomolar steady-state H2O2 levels. The discovery that specific Aquaporins (AQP3, AQP5, AQP8, and AQP11) function as "peroxiporins" — channels that facilitate H2O2 diffusion across lipid bilayers — revolutionized our understanding of compartmentalized redox signaling. AQP3 and AQP8 are localized to the plasma membrane and mitochondrial membrane, respectively, allowing H2O2 produced by NADPH Oxidase (at the plasma membrane) or by the mitochondrial electron transport chain to exit into the cytosol without dissolving in or damaging the lipid bilayer.

cyanidin.description:
Cyanidin is a natural anthocyanidin (a class of flavonoid pigments) widely found in red, blue, and purple berries and fruits. Its glycoside form, cyanidin-3-glucoside (C3G), is one of the most prevalent and bioavailable anthocyanins in the human diet. Cyanidin has emerged as a potent natural activator of SIRT6, with reported activity increases of over 50-fold in certain in vitro assays.

Mechanism of Action — SIRT6 Activation

SIRT6 features a unique elongated hydrophobic pocket designed to accommodate long-chain fatty acyl groups (myristoyl, palmitoyl). Cyanidin interacts with SIRT6 to stabilize its catalytically active conformation:
Allosteric activation: Cyanidin (and related anthocyanidins) bind to the SIRT6 allosteric pocket, stabilizing the NAD⁺ co-substrate and the acylated/acetylated histone substrate.
Enhanced deacetylase/deacylase activity: Leads to increased deacetylation of H3K9ac and H3K56ac, compacting chromatin and facilitating DNA repair.
Potency: Reported 50-fold+ activation in vitro — among the highest for natural SIRT6 activators.

Physiological Impacts
Genomic stability: SIRT6 activation deacetylates H3K9 and H3K56, improving DNA double-strand break repair recruitment.
Tumor suppression: SIRT6 suppresses glycolysis (Warburg effect) and promotes autophagy in tumor cells — cyanidin-mediated SIRT6 activation may contribute to anti-cancer effects.
Anti-inflammatory: Broadly anti-inflammatory via NF-κB suppression and antioxidant activity.
Cardiometabolic: Anthocyanins improve endothelial function, reduce LDL oxidation, lower blood pressure, and improve insulin sensitivity.

Dietary Sources and Dose Estimates

Cyanidin/C3G is one of the most realistically achievable SIRT6 activators through diet:

 Source    C3G Content    Quantity for ~300 mg C3G 
---  ---  ---
 Black elderberries (Sambucus nigra)    ~300–450 mg/100g    ~70–100 g (~½ cup raw) 
 Blackberries    ~80–95 mg/100g    ~315–375 g (~2–2.5 cups) 
 Black currants    ~150–300 mg/100g total anthocyanins    ~100–200 g 
 Blueberries    ~25–50 mg/100g    Large quantities required 

Note: Raw elderberries require cooking/processing (toxic saponins in raw form); elderberry syrup or extract is safer.

adp_ribosylation.description:
ADP-ribosylation is a reversible post-translational modification in which one or more ADP-ribose moieties from NAD+ are transferred to specific amino acid residues (such as glutamate, aspartate, lysine, arginine, or cysteine) on a target protein. 

It plays a crucial role in several cellular processes, including:
Cell signaling and transduction
DNA damage repair
Genomic stability and chromatin regulation
Apoptosis and cell death pathways

Types of ADP-ribosylation
Mono-ADP-ribosylation (MARylation): The addition of a single ADP-ribose unit to a protein. 
Poly-ADP-ribosylation (PARylation): The addition of multiple, polymerized ADP-ribose units to form long, branching chains. This is primarily catalyzed by Poly-ADP-ribose polymerases (PARPs), such as PARP1.

Sirtuins with ADP-ribosyltransferase Activity

While mammalian Sirtuins are most famously recognized for their deacetylase activities, several family members function as ADP-ribosyltransferases, using NAD+ to modify substrates:
SIRT4: Possesses primary mono-ADP-ribosyltransferase activity. For example, it ribosylates and inhibits Glutamate Dehydrogenase (GDH) in pancreatic β-cells, suppressing insulin secretion in response to glutamine.
SIRT6: Exhibits mono-ADP-ribosyltransferase activity alongside deacetylation and deacylation. Under DNA damage conditions, SIRT6 ribosylates proteins like PARP1, stimulating its double-strand break repair activity, and ribosylates Kap1 to suppress transposable elements.
SIRT7: Also exhibits weak ADP-ribosylation activity involved in nucleolar chromatin organization and transcriptional regulation.

shp1.description:
Overview
SHP1 (PTPN6, SH2 domain-containing phosphatase 1) is a non-receptor tyrosine phosphatase that plays critical roles in immune signaling and apoptotic regulation. SHP1 dephosphorylates Caspase-8 at Tyr380, removing the inhibitory phosphate placed by Src family kinases and restoring the cell's sensitivity to death ligands (TRAIL, FasL).

Structure & Activation
SHP1 contains two N-terminal SH2 domains that mediate recruitment to phosphotyrosine-containing motifs on receptors and signaling proteins, a catalytic phosphatase domain, and a C-terminal tail. SHP1 is autoinhibited by intramolecular interaction of the N-SH2 domain with the catalytic domain; binding of phosphotyrosine ligands to the SH2 domains relieves this autoinhibition.

Mechanism of Action & Pathways
Caspase-8 Dephosphorylation: SHP1 removes inhibitory phosphate groups from Caspase-8 at Tyr380 (and related Tyr397/Tyr465), restoring Caspase-8's ability to undergo proteolytic cleavage and maturation. This re-engages the extrinsic apoptotic pathway.

[!important] Epigenetic Silencing of SHP1 in Cancer
Many tumors epigenetically silence PTPN6 (SHP1) via promoter hypermethylation. This maintains Caspase-8 in its pro-migratory, anti-apoptotic phosphorylated state, enabling tumor cells to resist death ligand-induced apoptosis while promoting metastasis through the scaffolding functions of phosphorylated Caspase-8.
Immune Regulation: SHP1 is a negative regulator of signaling through immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motifs (ITAMs) in T cells, B cells, and NK cells. It limits cytokine signaling and prevents autoimmunity.
Other Substrates: SHP1 dephosphorylates JAK2, STAT3, ERK, and other signaling proteins, modulating inflammatory and growth signaling.

Pathology & Clinical Relevance
Cancer: SHP1 is frequently silenced in cancers (colon, glioblastoma, leukemia, breast cancer) through promoter methylation. Loss of SHP1 correlates with poor prognosis and resistance to TRAIL-based therapies.
Autoimmunity: Loss-of-function mutations in SHP1 cause autoimmune-like inflammation in mice (motheaten mice) and potentially in humans.
Therapeutic Potential: Demethylating agents that restore SHP1 expression or small molecules that activate SHP1 could sensitize tumors to death ligand therapy.

Documents
Molecular Mechanisms of Caspase and Bcl-2 Family Regulation
Details SHP1 as the phosphatase that dephosphorylates Caspase-8 at Tyr380, restoring apoptotic sensitivity and opposing Src-mediated inhibition.

retinal_photoreceptors.description:
Retinal photoreceptors are the light-sensitive neurons of the retina — rods for dim-light vision and cones for color and high-acuity vision. They have extremely high metabolic demand and densely packed Mitochondria, making them exceptionally vulnerable to energetic and oxidative stress.

Mitochondrial Dependence
Photoreceptors rely on Oxidative Phosphorylation for the ATP required for phototransduction and outer segment renewal. SIRT3 and SIRT5 are both critical for the health of retinal photoreceptors. SIRT3 is a mitochondrial NAD+-dependent deacetylase that supports ATP homeostasis, ROS detoxification, and neuroprotection.

NAD+ and Degeneration
SIRT3 activity is sensitive to the reduction of NAD+ content detected in multiple disorders with retinal degeneration, including age-associated dysfunction, Diabetic Retinopathy, and light-induced degeneration in mice.

[!info] NAD+–SIRT3 in Photoreceptor Survival
Increasing mitochondrial NAD+ to support SIRT3 is one proposed mechanism of Nicotinamide Riboside's neuroprotective effects. This suggests a potential therapeutic role for NR in disorders that include photoreceptor degeneration.

Clinical Relevance
Photoreceptor loss underlies the irreversible vision loss of retinitis pigmentosa, macular degeneration, and Diabetic Retinopathy. Strategies that maintain mitochondrial NAD+, such as NAD+ precursor supplementation, are being investigated to preserve photoreceptor viability and function.



List of documents in the wiki that mention this entity

Describes SIRT3 and SIRT5 as critical for photoreceptor health, with SIRT3 activity sensitive to NAD+ reductions in retinal degeneration, supporting NR's potential as therapy.

ku70.description:
Ku70 (encoded by the XRCC6 gene; also known as Lupus autoantigen p70) is a highly conserved nuclear protein that forms a heterodimer with Ku80. The Ku70/Ku80 complex binds to double-stranded DNA ends and is essential for the non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) pathway of DNA double-strand break repair. Ku70 is also an autoantigen in systemic lupus erythematosus and scleroderma.

Structure & Mechanism

Ku70 and Ku80 together form a ring-shaped heterodimer that threads onto DNA ends, serving as the recruitment platform for the DNA-PK catalytic subunit (DNA-PKcs) and downstream NHEJ factors (XRCC4, Ligase IV, XLF). Beyond repair, Ku70 modulates telomere maintenance, V(D)J recombination, and Bax-dependent apoptosis.



In addition to its role in DNA repair, Ku70 acts as an important regulator of apoptosis, a function post-translationally modulated by SIRT1:
Bax Sequestration: Under normal physiological conditions, Ku70 physically associates with the pro-apoptotic BCL-2 family protein Bax, sequestering it in the cytoplasm and preventing it from translocating to the mitochondria, where Bax would otherwise trigger mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP) and apoptosis.
SIRT1 Deacetylation: Under stress, Ku70 is acetylated, which disrupts its interaction with Bax, releasing Bax to trigger apoptosis. SIRT1 physically interacts with and deacetylates Ku70 on key lysine residues. Deacetylated Ku70 binds Bax with high affinity, thereby preventing stress-induced cell death and promoting cell survival.

Physiological & Pathological Function

The Ku70–Bax interaction thus couples DNA repair competence to cell death decisions: cells with intact Ku70 retain a survival advantage, while acetylation (e.g., by p300/CBP) tips the balance toward apoptosis. The SIRT1–Ku70 axis intersects with the broader p53 tumor-suppressor network, as SIRT1 also deacetylates p53, jointly enforcing a stress-adapted survival program.

Clinical Relevance

Augmenting SIRT1 to preserve Ku70–Bax sequestration is being explored for neuroprotection (where excessive apoptosis drives degeneration), whereas disrupting the axis could sensitize cancer cells to therapy. Ku70 itself is a biomarker of radiosensitivity and a lupus autoantigen.

caspase_5.description:
Caspase-5

Caspase 5 is a human inflammatory (non-canonical) caspase, paralogous to Caspase-11 (mouse) and Caspase-4 (human). It is best known for its role in the non-canonical inflammasome: in response to cytosolic danger signals it oligomerizes and cleaves Gasdermin D, generating plasma-membrane pores that drive Pyroptosis and release of inflammatory mediators. In the context of senescence, caspase 5 (and its orthologs) also contributes to IL-1α processing, a regulatory step embedded in the Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype.

Mechanism of Action & Signaling
Non-canonical inflammasome: Caspase 5 is activated by cytosolic stimuli (e.g., microbial products, potassium efflux) that promote its oligomerization and auto-cleavage.
Gasdermin D cleavage: Active caspase 5 cleaves Gasdermin D at its linker, releasing the N-terminal pore-forming domain, which oligomerizes in the plasma membrane to form lytic pores.
IL-1α processing: Caspase 5 cleaves IL-1α, an alarmin that can transit from the cell surface to the nucleus in a copper/calcium-dependent manner, modulating SASP composition and IL-1–biased signaling.
Caspase-1 cooperation: Pore formation and K+ efflux downstream of caspase 5 can license canonical Caspase-1 activation, amplifying maturation of IL-1β/IL-18.

Role in Senescence
Caspase 5 is essential for certain IL-1α activation events within the SASP, linking inflammasome signaling to SASP regulation.
Through gasdermin-D pores it can enforce an inflammatory, lytic cell state that overlaps functionally with senescence-associated inflammation.
Caspase 5-mediated IL-1α cleavage feeds forward into NF-κB– and IL-1–driven SASP factor expression.

Clinical / Pathological Relevance
Caspase 5 is a candidate target in inflammatory and autoinflammatory diseases where non-canonical inflammasome signaling dominates.
Inhibitors of caspase 5/gasdermin-D may modulate the SASP and attenuate Inflammaging.
It is implicated in sepsis and age-related inflammation.

Documents
SASP Review 2024: The review notes that caspase 5, part of the non-canonical inflammasome, contributes to SASP regulation by cleaving the alarmin IL-1α, which then transits to the nucleus to license NF-κB–dependent SASP transcription. Through gasdermin-D pores it can also enforce a lytic, inflammatory cell state that overlaps with senescence-associated inflammation.

7_ketocholesterol.description:
7-Ketocholesterol (7-KC, 7-oxocholesterol) is the most abundant non-enzymatic oxysterol formed by ROS-mediated oxidation of Cholesterol at the C7 position. It is a major component of oxidized LDL and a potent inducer of apoptosis.

Formation & Properties

7-KC is produced via cholesterol 7-hydroperoxide intermediates formed by Singlet Oxygen or free radical attack. It accumulates in atherosclerotic plaques (up to 10% of total sterol), oxidized LDL, and in cells under oxidative stress. Its mechanism of cytotoxicity involves ROS-dependent mitochondrial membrane permeabilization, cytochrome c release, and Caspase-3 activation.

Biological Effects
Pro-apoptotic: Induces cell death in endothelial cells, macrophages, vascular smooth muscle cells, and neurons.
Pro-inflammatory: Activates NF-κB, upregulates IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-alpha, and MCP-1.
Ferroptosis Sensitization: 7-KC can synergize with iron to promote lipid peroxidation and ferroptotic death.
Anti-angiogenic: Inhibits endothelial tube formation and VEGF signaling at high concentrations.

Clinical Relevance

7-KC is a biomarker and mediator of Atherosclerosis, plaque vulnerability, and Cardiovascular Disease. It is also elevated in Alzheimer's Disease brains, age-related macular degeneration, and NASH. PON1 (paraoxonase 1) can hydrolyze 7-KC and other oxidized lipid species, contributing to HDL's anti-atherogenic effects.
