dopamine.description: Dopamine is a critical catecholamine neurotransmitter in the brain and peripheral nervous system, playing key roles in reward, motivation, motor control, and executive function. Dopamine is a neurotransmitter that plays several important roles in the brain and body, and the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the Substantia Nigra is the hallmark of Parkinson's Disease. Dopamine is a catecholamine neurotransmitter that plays a central role in the brain's reward, motivation, and motor control systems. Dopamine is a major Neurotransmitters in the brain that plays a critical role in reward, motivation, motor control, and Executive Function. Oxidation and Pigmentation Like other Catecholamines, Dopamine can undergo Oxidation (spontaneous or enzymatic) to form reactive intermediates: Dopaminochrome: The aminochrome intermediate analogous to Adrenochrome. It is produced by the oxidation of the catechol ring to an o-quinone followed by cyclization. Neuromelanin: Dopaminochrome and its derivatives polymerize to form the dark pigment found in the substantia nigra. Clinical Relevance Parkinson's Disease: Characterized by the death of dopaminergic neurons and loss of Neuromelanin. Excess oxidation of dopamine to Dopaminochrome is linked to neuronal stress. Oxidative Stress: High levels of ROS promote the oxidation of dopamine, bypassing normal enzymatic degradation by COMT and MAO. Parkinson's Disease: Characterized by a lack of dopamine in certain brain regions. Schizophrenia: Associated with dysregulated dopamine signaling. Working Memory: Dopamine levels in the Prefrontal Cortex are critical for optimal working memory performance. Biosynthesis Dopamine is synthesized from the amino acid tyrosine. The process involves two main steps: Tyrosine to L-DOPA: Catalyzed by the enzyme Tyrosine Hydroxylase (TH). L-DOPA to Dopamine: Catalyzed by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (AADC). In the Substantia Nigra Pars Compacta, dopamine is produced and then encapsulated into synaptic vesicles by Vesicular Monoamine Transporter 2 (VMAT2). Role in Parkinson's Disease The hallmark of Parkinson's Disease is the progressive degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the Substantia Nigra. The resulting deficiency in dopamine leads to the characteristic motor symptoms of the disease. Oxidation: Cytosolic dopamine can undergo auto-oxidation or enzymatic oxidation to form Neuromelanin. While this is initially a protective mechanism to remove reactive quinones, it leads to the lifelong accumulation of pigment. Vulnerability: Neurons with high dopamine turnover and low VMAT2 expression are particularly vulnerable to neurodegeneration. Clinical Use L-DOPA is the primary pharmacological treatment for PD, acting as a prodrug that is converted into dopamine in the brain to replenish depleted levels. Metabolism Dopamine is primarily degraded by two enzymes: COMT (Catechol-O-methyltransferase) Monoamine oxidase (MAO) In the Sirtuins, the Dopamine Transporter (DAT) is responsible for rapid uptake, whereas in the Prefrontal Cortex (Prefrontal Cortex), COMT and the Norepinephrine transporter (NET) play more dominant roles in clearance. Genetic Influence The COMT Val158Met Polymorphism significantly affects dopamine levels by altering the rate of degradation. List of documents that mention this entity COMT How to Optimize Your Supplements for Your COMT Genotype Catechols include Neurotransmitters such as Dopamine, Epinephrine, and Norepinephrine. Other Catechols include Estrogen metabolites as well as drugs and Natural Substances with a catechol structure. Genetic variation in COMT activity impacts learning and dopamine release capacity in the striatum A common genetic Polymorphism that results in increased activity of the Dopamine regulating enzyme COMT (the COMT Val 158 allele) has been found to associate with poorer Cognitive Performance and increased susceptibility to develop Psychiatric Disorders. Neuromelanin, aging, and neuronal vulnerability in Parkinson's disease The loss of nigral pigmented neurons, which we now know produce the neurotransmitter Dopamine, leads to the classical motor symptoms of PD and constitutes the only robust clinico‐pathological correlation associated with the disease. Neuromelanin, one of the most overlooked molecules in modern medicine, is not a spectator Neuromelanin (NM) in the pre-synaptic terminal of Dopamine neurons is emerging as a primary player in the etiology of Neurodegenerative Diseases including PD. COMT × Fisetin Research Evaluation Fisetin-mediated COMT inhibition could augment prefrontal dopamine tone, particularly in Val/Val (fast COMT) individuals.

phenothiazine.description:
Phenothiazine is a tricyclic heterocyclic compound consisting of two benzene rings fused to a central thiazine ring containing a position-5 sulfur and a position-10 nitrogen. It is the parent scaffold of a large family of derivatives — most famously the antipsychotic Chlorpromazine and Promethazine, the dye Methylene blue and Toluidine Blue O, and the antihistamine/antiemetic phenothiazines. It has been called "pharmacology's first lead structure," giving rise to diverse clinical agents across psychiatry, anesthesia, antimicrobial therapy, and mitochondrial medicine .

Structure & Chemistry

The phenothiazine nucleus presents three substitution positions critical to biological activity:
Positions 3 and 7 — typically bear amine/alkylamine side chains in bioactive derivatives (e.g., methyl groups in Toluidine Blue O, dimethylamino groups in Methylene blue).
Position 10 nitrogen — when free (unsubstituted), the heterocyclic nitrogen is essential for methylene blue-like alternative electron-transfer function; substitution with a bulky side chain (as in Chlorpromazine and Promethazine) abolishes this activity .
Position 5 sulfur — required for the electron-carrier phenotype; replacement with nitrogen converts the scaffold to a phenazine (e.g., Neutral Red) and destroys mitochondrial electron-shuttling .

[!info] Redox character
Phenothiazine and its derivatives are redox-active dyes. The oxidized (cationic) form is reduced to a colorless leuco form, enabling electron shuttling. Derivatives such as Methylene blue and Toluidine Blue O show negative redox potentials (≈ −0.1 V vs NHE) that correlate with their ability to enhance cellular oxygen consumption .

Biological & Pharmacological Actions

Neuroprotection and mitochondrial redox cycling

Phenothiazine itself — without amine side chains — is a potent, direct free-radical scavenger. In HT-22 hippocampal neurons it protects against glutamate, Rotenone, and iodoacetic acid (IAA) neurotoxicity with nanomolar EC50s (viability EC50 ≈ 18.99 nM; ROS EC50 ≈ 57.21 nM) . Unlike Methylene blue, phenothiazine does not enhance cellular oxygen consumption, inhibit anaerobic glycolysis, or act as an alternative electron carrier between Complex I and Cytochrome c; its protection is a direct, mitochondria/NADH-independent antioxidant action .

In C. elegans models of Parkinson's Disease, phenothiazine is highly efficacious against rotenone- and MPP+-induced dopaminergic neurodegeneration, outperforming Chlorpromazine , .

Other clinical phenotypes
Antipsychotic (position-10 substituted): Chlorpromazine pioneered the dopamine-receptor blockade treatment of psychosis.
Antihistamine / antiemetic: Promethazine and related phenothiazines block H1 receptors.
Antimalarial & antimicrobial: Methylene blue and phenothiazine-derived compounds inhibit parasitic disulfide reductases , .
Mitochondrial enhancer: Methylene blue and Toluidine Blue O improve brain oxidative metabolism and memory , , .

Structure–Activity Relationships (from the MB derivative study)

The study "Neuroprotective Actions of Methylene Blue and Its Derivatives" divided phenothiazine-related compounds into four groups :
Naked phenothiazine nucleus (Phenothiazine, 2-Chlorophenothiazine) — nanomolar neuroprotection via direct scavenging; no OCR/electron-shunt effect.
3,7-amine-substituted (Methylene blue, Toluidine Blue O) — nanomolar neuroprotection + alternative electron-transfer carrier (bypass of Complex I/Complex III) + OCR enhancement + Complex IV upregulation.
10-nitrogen side-chain substituted (Chlorpromazine, Promethazine) — ~1000-fold potency loss, no electron shunt, pro-oxidative in cell-free assays.
Phenazine (S5→N) (Neutral Red) — OCR enhancement but no electron-carrier function and weak neuroprotection.

[!important] Two structural features define MB-like mitochondrial protection
A free 10-nitrogen and the position-5 sulfur are both required for the alternative electron-transfer phenotype. Substituting either destroys the mitochondrial electron-carrier action while often preserving (or converting to) a direct antioxidant effect .

Neuroprotective Actions of Methylene Blue and Its Derivatives

noise_induced_hearing_loss.description:
Noise-induced hearing loss (NIHL) is sensorineural hearing loss caused by exposure to loud sound, which damages cochlear hair cells and auditory nerve fibers through mechanical and metabolic stress, including Oxidative Stress and mitochondrial dysfunction.

Pathophysiology
Acoustic overstimulation generates excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) in the cochlea, triggering hair cell apoptosis, synaptic loss between hair cells and spiral ganglion neurons, and neurite retraction. The resulting Axonal Degeneration of auditory nerve fibers contributes to permanent threshold shifts.

NAD+ and Prevention
Nicotinamide Riboside (NR) prevents noise-induced hearing loss and neurite retraction from hair cells in the inner ear through a SIRT3-dependent mechanism, in which the NR-induced increase in NAD+ supports the activity of the mitochondrial deacetylase SIRT3.

[!info] SIRT3-Mediated Protection
NR's elevation of cochlear NAD+ activates the mitochondrial deacetylase SIRT3, which supports ATP homeostasis and ROS detoxification, protecting hair cells and their neurites from noise-induced degeneration.

Broader Relevance
This illustrates the broader neuroprotective and therapeutic potential of NR, which also protects neurons from excitotoxicity-induced Axonal Degeneration. SIRT3 activity is sensitive to NAD+ reductions seen in retinal degeneration disorders, and NR may therefore have applications for a variety of sensory and neurodegenerative conditions, including Diabetic Retinopathy and retinal ganglion cell dysfunction.

drp1.description:
DRP1 (Dynamin-Related Protein 1; gene DNM1L) is a cytosolic dynamin-like GTPase that executes mitochondrial fission in mammals. Recruited to the outer mitochondrial membrane by adaptor proteins, it oligomerizes into a ring, hydrolyzes GTP, and severs the organelle. Balanced against MFN1/MFN2/OPA1-mediated fusion, DRP1 controls mitochondrial morphology, Mitophagy, and Apoptosis, and is implicated in Parkinson's Disease, Atherosclerosis, Left Ventricular Hypertrophy, and Cancer.

Structure and Domains

DRP1 contains an N-terminal GTPase domain, a middle domain, a variable (B-insert) domain, and a C-terminal GTPase-effector domain (GED). It is recruited from the cytosol to mitochondria by OMM adaptors MFF, MID49, MID51, and FIS1, forming a ring-like structure that constricts the organelle. After DRP1, Dynamin 2 (DNM2) assembles at the constriction site to complete division (though DRP1 alone can constrict and sever, making DNM2 dispensable).

Initiation by ER and Actin

Fission is initiated where ER tubules contact mitochondria, reducing diameter to ~150 nm. The ER-bound formin Inverted Formin 2 (INF2) and mitochondria-anchored Spire1C drive actin assembly for constriction. IMM constriction is Ca2+-dependent, and Cardiolipin binds DRP1 to stimulate its oligomerization and GTPase activity.

Regulation

[!info] Source: document - The role of mitochondrial dynamics in disease
DRP1 is the key mediator of mitochondrial fission, recruited to the OMM by adaptors MFF, FIS1, MID49, and MID51. It is regulated by multiple post-translational modifications: phosphorylation at Ser616 (stimulatory) and Ser637 (inhibitory) by kinases including PKA, AMPK, and SIRT. However, Ser637 phosphorylation can paradoxically promote fission in podocytes under high glucose, and Ser637 phosphorylation may promote subsequent Ser616 phosphorylation — indicating context-dependent regulation where no single modification determines outcome.
CDK1/Cyclin B phosphorylates DRP1 at Ser585 during mitosis, promoting fission.
ERK2 (MAPK1) phosphorylates DRP1 at Ser616, activating fission — a central node in MAPK-driven tumor growth.
Protein Kinase A phosphorylates DRP1 at Ser637, retaining it cytosolic and inhibiting fission during starvation.
Calcineurin dephosphorylates Ser637, enabling mitochondrial translocation and fission.
SUMOylation by MAPL stabilizes ER–mitochondrial contacts and promotes cytochrome c release in apoptosis.
S-nitrosylation (by nitric oxide) and O-GlcNAcylation increase fission activity.
Ubiquitination by Parkin targets DRP1 for proteasomal degradation.

Pathological Significance
Parkinson's Disease — excess fission via OPA1 cleavage and DRP1 hyperphosphorylation; DRP1 inhibition reduces fragmentation and ROS in sporadic PD.
Atherosclerosis — DRP1 inhibition (or Mdivi-1) reduces endothelial dysfunction and lesion progression.
Left Ventricular Hypertrophy — DRP1 is upregulated; Mdivi-1 ameliorates dysfunction.
Cancer — ERK/DRP1 Ser616 signaling and hypoxia-driven DRP1 promote tumorigenesis and metastasis; Mdivi-1 attenuates migration.

f2_isoprostanes.description:
F2-Isoprostanes (F2-IsoPs) are prostaglandin-like compounds formed non-enzymatically by free radical-mediated Lipid Peroxidation of Arachidonic acid, and are widely considered the gold-standard biomarker for endogenous Oxidative Stress.

Formation Chemistry

Unlike cyclooxygenase-derived prostaglandins, F2-IsoPs are generated independently of COX enzymes, in situ on esterified phospholipids within cell membranes. The mechanism begins with free-radical hydrogen abstraction from the bis-allylic C7, C10, or C13 positions of arachidonic acid (20:4, n-6). The resulting carbon-centered radical undergoes endocyclic addition of O₂ and rearrangement to a bicyclic endoperoxide (PGG₂-like), which is reduced to the F-ring prostane. After phospholipase A₂ (PLA₂) release, free F2-IsoPs enter plasma and urine. Because formation requires radical attack on intact membrane lipids, F2-IsoPs report cumulative, non-enzymatic oxidative modification rather than enzymatic eicosanoid signaling.

Isoform Diversity

Over 60 F2-IsoP isomers exist. The most frequently measured are 8-iso-PGF₂α (iPF₂α-III, also called 15-F₂t-IsoP), which is used as the reference biomarker in both plasma and urine. Other regioisomers (e.g., ent-7-epi-iso-PGF₂α) are also quantified in research settings.

Analytical Detection

F2-IsoPs are measured by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC-MS) or liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), with the latter offering superior specificity and throughput. Rigorous sample handling (antioxidant addition, cold processing, avoidance of air exposure) is mandatory to prevent ex vivo autoxidation, a major source of artefactual elevation in older studies.

Biological Activity

Beyond being biomarkers, F2-IsoPs possess biological activity. They act as weak vasoconstrictors of pulmonary and systemic vessels and can potentiate platelet activation and smooth-muscle proliferation through thromboxane receptor (TP) binding, linking oxidative lipid damage to vasomotor and thrombotic pathology.

Clinical Relevance

Elevated F2-IsoPs are found in virtually every disease involving oxidative stress: Cardiovascular Disease (atherothrombosis, reperfusion injury), Neurodegeneration (Alzheimer's Disease, Parkinson's Disease), Diabetes Mellitus, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease, Rheumatoid Arthritis, and Aging. They correlate with disease severity and decline with effective antioxidant or lifestyle intervention, supporting their use as pharmacodynamic endpoints in redox trials.

mitochondrial_respiration.description:
Mitochondrial respiration is the oxygen-consuming process by which the Mitochondria convert nutritional reducing equivalents into ATP. Reducing equivalents (NADH, FADH2) generated by the TCA cycle donate electrons to the Mitochondrial Electron Transport Chain (Complexes I–IV); electron flow drives proton pumping that builds the Mitochondrial Membrane Potential across the inner membrane, and the return of protons through ATP Synthase powers Oxidative Phosphorylation and ATP production. This coupled process supplies the majority of cellular ATP.

Control & Regulation

Respiration is tightly controlled by ADP availability (respiratory control): active ATP demand accelerates electron flux, whereas low ADP slows it. Key regulators include PGC-1α (mitochondrial biogenesis), AMPK (energy sensing), and mTORC1 (anabolic control). A small fraction of electrons "leak" at Complex I and III, producing mtROS; modest leak underpins Mitohormesis, an adaptive program that strengthens respiratory capacity.

Pharmacological Modulation

Methylene blue is an electron cycler that can accept electrons from NADH and donate them downstream, effectively bypassing impaired Complex I/III. This restores mitochondrial respiration and oxygen consumption while reducing superoxide, a mechanism relevant in Mitochondrial Dysfunction and certain neurodegenerative states. Uncouplers and inhibitors (e.g., oligomycin, rotenone) are classical tools that dissect coupling versus ATP synthesis.

Relevance

Age-related decline in respiratory capacity contributes to fatigue, metabolic disease, and cellular senescence. Preserving efficient respiration is a core goal of Longevity and metabolic-health interventions.

Describes how MB enhances mitochondrial respiration and oxygen consumption, reducing superoxide.

Frames low-level respiratory stress as an adaptive, longevity-promoting signal.

Links NAD+ repletion to sustained mitochondrial respiratory function.

adma.description:
ADMA (Asymmetric dimethylarginine) is an endogenous inhibitor of nitric oxide synthase (NOS) produced by post-translational methylation of arginine residues in proteins by PRMTs and released during proteolysis. It is a central mediator linking Oxidative Stress, endothelial dysfunction, and cardiovascular disease through impairment of nitric oxide bioavailability.

Formation & Metabolism

ADMA is generated when protein arginine methyltransferase enzymes (PRMT1 primarily) methylate arginine side chains on nucleolar and other cellular proteins. During normal protein turnover, methylated arginines are released as free ADMA, symmetric dimethylarginine (SDMA), and monomethylarginine (MMA). ADMA is cleared almost exclusively by dimethylarginine dimethylaminohydrolase (DDAH), which hydrolyzes it to dimethylamine and L-citrulline; a minor fraction is excreted renally. SDMA, by contrast, is not a NOS inhibitor but competes for cationic amino acid transport, indirectly raising ADMA.

Mechanism of NOS Inhibition

ADMA competitively inhibits all NOS isoforms (eNOS, nNOS, iNOS) at the L-arginine binding site, with an inhibition constant (Ki) in the low micromolar range. At physiologically elevated concentrations (~0.5–1 μM, versus ~0.3 μM in healthy subjects), ADMA significantly reduces eNOS activity. Critically, partial eNOS inhibition promotes eNOS uncoupling: when tetrahydrobiopterin (BH₄) is limiting, the enzyme shifts from NO synthesis to superoxide generation, converting a protective vasodilator enzyme into a pro-oxidant source. This represents a switch from redox-protective to redox-damaging signaling.

The Oxidative Stress Feed-Forward Loop

ADMA levels rise in conditions of Oxidative Stress because reactive oxygen species inactivate DDAH via oxidation of its cysteine residues, reducing ADMA clearance. The resulting ADMA accumulation further suppresses eNOS and promotes uncoupling, generating more superoxide—a self-amplifying cycle: oxidative stress → DDAH inactivation → ADMA accumulation → eNOS uncoupling → more ROS. This loop is central to the progression of endothelial dysfunction.

Clinical & Research Relevance

Elevated ADMA is an independent risk factor for Cardiovascular Disease, Endothelial Dysfunction, Diabetes Mellitus, Hypertension, and chronic kidney disease. The plasma L-arginine:ADMA ratio is a biomarker of NO bioavailability and cardiovascular risk. ADMA predicts adverse outcomes in chronic renal failure, pulmonary hypertension, and preeclampsia. Therapeutic strategies aimed at lowering ADMA include enhancing DDAH activity (e.g., via Folic Acid or_statins), increasing L-arginine substrate availability, and reducing oxidative stress directly. Allopurinol and MitoQ-style interventions that lower XO-derived ROS indirectly improve the ADMA–DDAH axis.

c_abl.description:
c-ABL (gene ABL1) is a ubiquitously expressed non-receptor tyrosine kinase that transmits stress, DNA-damage, and adhesion signals. In the apoptotic response to genotoxic injury, c-ABL regulates Caspase-9 autocleavage and activation, linking DNA damage to the Intrinsic Pathway of Apoptosis. Its oncogenic fusion BCR-ABL (the Philadelphia chromosome) drives chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) and is the target of tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib.

Structure & Activation

c-ABL contains an N-terminal tyrosine kinase domain, an SH2/SH3 module, and a C-terminal actin-binding region. It is normally restrained in the nucleus/cytoplasm; genotoxic stress (activated p53, ATM/ATR) phosphorylates and activates c-ABL, enabling it to phosphorylate substrates including p73, p53, and Caspase-9.

Mechanism in Apoptosis

c-ABL phosphorylates and enhances Caspase-9 autocleavage/activation downstream of mitochondrial commitment, amplifying the Apoptosome-driven cascade. It also cooperates with the p73 tumor suppressor to induce apoptosis independent of p53, positioning c-ABL as a tumor-suppressive stress responder.

Physiological Function

Beyond apoptosis, c-ABL governs cell adhesion, cytoskeletal remodeling, and oxidative stress responses. It integrates cues from the extracellular matrix and growth factors.

Cancer Relevance
Oncogenesis: BCR-ABL is constitutively active, proliferative, and anti-apoptotic; its inhibition by imatinib/nilotinib/dasatinib is a paradigm of targeted Cancer therapy.
Therapeutic Resistance: ABL kinase-domain mutations confer TKI resistance, necessitating next-generation inhibitors.
Apoptotic Priming: c-ABL activation by DNA-damaging Chemotherapy (e.g., genistein, doxorubicin) can sensitize tumors; combining TKIs with BH3 mimetics is explored to overcome survival signaling.

beclin1.description: Beclin1 (also known as Atg6 and BECN1) is a key regulatory protein in the initiation and regulation of Autophagy. It functions as a molecular scaffold that assembles the class III PI3K complex, which produces phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PI3P) to nucleate autophagosome formation. Structure and Domains Beclin1 is a 450-amino-acid protein containing several conserved domains: BH3 Domain (Bcl-2 homology 3): Mediates interaction with anti-apoptotic Bcl-2 family members (Bcl-2, Bcl-xL, Mcl-1). Binding of Bcl-2 to the BH3 domain sequesters Beclin1 and inhibits autophagy. CCD (Coiled-Coil Domain): Mediates homodimerisation and interaction with UVRAG (UV radiation resistance-associated gene). adrenaline_quinone.description:
Adrenaline-quinone is a highly reactive, electrophilic intermediate formed during the oxidation of Epinephrine.

Formation
It is the first major intermediate in the "side pathway" of epinephrine metabolism. Under Oxidative Stress or alkaline conditions, the Catechol ring of Epinephrine loses two electrons to become a Quinone.

Role in Adrenochrome Pathway
Once formed, adrenaline-quinone is extremely unstable and rapidly undergoes intramolecular Michael addition (cyclization) to form Leuco-adrenochrome.

Significance
As a potent Electrophile, adrenaline-quinone can damage cellular proteins and DNA if not quickly neutralized by antioxidants like Glutathione.

respiratory_chain_complex_i.description:
Complex I (NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase) is the first and largest enzyme of the mitochondrial Electron Transport Chain, embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

Structure & Mechanism
L-shaped assembly of ~45 subunits (14 core, conserved from bacteria) with a hydrophilic peripheral arm and a membrane arm.
Redox chemistry: oxidizes NADH at a flavin mononucleotide (FMN) site, passing electrons through a chain of iron–sulfur clusters to reduce Ubiquinone (coenzyme Q) to ubiquinol.
Proton pumping: the exergonic electron transfer drives translocation of ~4 H⁺ across the membrane, contributing to the Mitochondrial Membrane Potential that powers ATP Synthase.
ROS production: electron leak at the FMN and Q sites makes Complex I a principal source of superoxide and Mitochondrial ROS.

Physiological & Pathological Relevance

[!info] Aging, disease, and inhibitors
Complex I activity declines with age and contributes to Mitochondrial Dysfunction and Oxidative Stress. Genetic deficiency causes Leigh syndrome and mitochondrial encephalopathies, and Complex I inhibition is central to Parkinson's Disease models. The pesticide Rotenone and the biguanide Metformin both inhibit Complex I, while Methylene blue can act as an alternative electron carrier bypassing a defective complex.

Discusses methylene blue as an alternative electron donor/acceptor that reroutes electrons around Complex I to preserve mitochondrial respiration.

Connects NAD+/NADH supply to Complex I function and mitochondrial bioenergetics.

atgl.description:
ATGL (adipose triglyceride lipase, encoded by PNPLA2) is the first and rate-limiting enzyme of catabolic lipolysis, hydrolyzing triacylglycerol in lipid droplets to diacylglycerol and free fatty acids. Its activity determines the rate of free fatty acid release from adipose tissue and therefore systemic lipid mobilization.

Function and Regulation
Cytosolic Lipolysis: ATGL localizes to the surface of lipid droplets and hydrolyzes triglycerides into diacylglycerols and free fatty acids, providing substrate for Lipophagy and fatty acid oxidation.
Nutrient Status: Activated during Starvation and Fasting to mobilize energy reserves.
Independence from Lipophagy: In C. elegans, ATGL (encoded by atgl-1) acts in parallel to the lipophagy pathway involving LIPL-1 and LIPL-3.

SIRT1 promotes lipolysis in white adipocytes partly through FOXO1-dependent induction of ATGL expression, enhancing triglyceride hydrolysis.
SIRT6 promotes adipose lipolysis and prevents ectopic lipid accumulation through FOXO1-dependent induction of ATGL, protecting against lipotoxic insulin resistance.
Together with HSL (hormone-sensitive lipase) and MGL (monoacylglycerol lipase), ATGL governs the stepwise mobilization of stored fat used for energy and thermogenesis.

resting_metabolic_rate.description: Resting Metabolic Rate (RMR) is the energy expended per unit time by a subject at rest in a post-absorptive state, at thermoneutral temperature, typically measured in the morning after an overnight fast using Indirect Calorimetry. It is closely related to, but slightly higher than, the basal metabolic rate (BMR), which is measured under stricter conditions (awake, supine, fasting, thermoneutral). In most human societies RMR is the largest single component of the daily energy budget, accounting for roughly 60 % of daily energy expenditure. Determinants Fat-Free Mass is the dominant determinant, accounting for between 50 and 70 % of the individual variation in RMR (Westerterp et al. 1992; Heshka et al. 1993; Zhang et al. 2002). Residual variation beyond lean mass is substantial — two individuals of identical fat-free mass can differ by up to 3 MJ/d — and is biological rather than methodological in origin, given a measurement precision of ~3 % (≈200 kJ/d). Residual RMR is heritable and correlates with thyroid status and circulating Triiodothyronine, protein turnover, mitochondrial proton leak (Rolfe & Brand, 1996), UCP2/UCP3 polymorphisms (Bouchard et al. 1997; Astrup et al. 1999), β3-adrenoreceptor and sulphonylurea-receptor variants, circulating Leptin (Toth et al. 1999), and ribosomal protein L3. [!info] Source: Speakman & Selman (2003) The 2003 review compiles the determinants of RMR and its residual variance, and reviews the acute (EPOC) and chronic (training) responses of RMR to physical activity in animals and humans. Physiological Role RMR sustains the metabolic activity of internal organs, brain, and resting muscle (the "cost of living"). It sets the baseline against which physical activity level (DEE:RMR) is computed. The comparative physiology literature shows that free-living small mammals average a daily energy expenditure of 2·6 × RMR (range 1·4–7·5), whereas contemporary Western adults average only 1·66 × RMR — meaning modern humans expend ~60 % of daily energy at rest (Black et al. 1996; Speakman, 2000). Two distinct effects of physical activity on RMR are recognized: Long-term (training): increases in lean tissue mass raise RMR, and residual metabolism may also increase as tissue-specific metabolic intensity rises (e.g., induction of aerobic enzymes such as cytochrome-c oxidase and citrate synthase in skeletal muscle and heart). Acute (single bout): transient elevations in RMR after exercise, termed EPOC, lasting from < 2 h up to ~48 h. Results are heterogeneous: many training studies raise RMR, others find no effect, and intensive or forced regimens can paradoxically lower RMR despite gains in lean mass (Byrne & Wilmore, 2001), possibly via down-regulation of muscle UCP3 or compensatory responses to overly demanding protocols. Clinical Relevance RMR is the basis of predictive equations for human energy requirements (Harris & Benedict, 1919; Schofield et al. 1985). These equations modestly overestimate the energy demands of tropical and sub-tropical populations (≈0·5 MJ/d), and modern Western populations show no evidence of reduced BMR relative to predictions — implicating reduced physical activity rather than a lowered resting metabolism in the obesity epidemic. Low RMR relative to Fat-Free Mass has been proposed as a risk factor for body weight regain. Documents Speakman & Selman (2003) — Physical activity and resting metabolic rate This document is the primary source for this note: it defines RMR, reviews its determinants (fat-free mass, thyroid status, proton leak, UCP2/UCP3), and synthesizes the animal and human evidence on how exercise affects resting metabolism. cross_linking.description:
Cross-linking is the formation of covalent bonds that bridge adjacent protein molecules (or within a single molecule), creating large, inert macromolecular networks. In the context of aging and metabolic disease, the dominant pathological form is non-enzymatic protein cross-linking driven by Glycation and the accumulation of Advanced Glycation End Products (AGEs).

Overview

Cross-linking reactions are familiar in everyday life — they cause cut fruit to toughen and brown, and food proteins to yellow. In the body, the continuous reaction of reducing sugars with the free amino groups of proteins proceeds through Schiff-base and Amadori intermediates to stable cross-links such as Glucosepane and Pentosidine. Because sugar–protein adducts persist for months to years, cross-linking accumulates progressively with age.

Mechanisms and Pathology
Extracellular matrix stiffening: Cross-links between structural proteins such as Collagen and elastic fibers reduce tissue elasticity. This is a leading mechanism behind Arterial Stiffness, Cardiac Hypertrophy, and senile Cataract.
Vascular disease: AGE cross-linking of vessel-wall matrix, together with glycation of LDL and Very Low Density Lipoprotein, promotes Atherosclerosis and impairs blood flow.
Diabetic complications: Cross-linking product levels in diabetics are two to three times those of non-diabetics, implicating cross-linking in nephropathy, retinopathy, and neuropathy.
Cancer and immunity: Cross-linking–mediated damage to the Immune System and to DNA (via glucose–DNA adducts) is proposed to raise infection susceptibility and malignancy risk.

Prevention and Reversal
Inhibitors such as Aminoguanidine and Carnosine trap reactive carbonyl intermediates and prevent new cross-links from forming.
Breakers such as ALT-711 (a thiazolium salt) are claimed to cleave pre-existing AGE cross-links, representing a potential "reverse-aging" strategy.

Documents
Aminoguanidine: An AGE Product Inhibitor
Frames protein cross-linking as a central mechanism of aging and details aminoguanidine's ability to prevent AGE-induced cross-linking of the extracellular matrix.

Connections
Glycation: The non-enzymatic sugar–protein reaction that initiates cross-linking.
Advanced Glycation End Products: Stable end-products that form covalent cross-links.
Collagen: A primary substrate whose cross-linking drives tissue stiffening.
Aminoguanidine: A carbonyl-trapping inhibitor of cross-link formation.
Alagebrium: A cross-link "breaker" claimed to cleave established links.

etoposide.description:
Etoposide (also known as VP-16) is a chemotherapy medication used for the treatment of a number of types of cancer, including testicular cancer, lung cancer, Lymphoma, and leukemia.
Mechanism of Action
Etoposide belongs to the class of drugs known as topoisomerase inhibitors. It works by forming a ternary complex with DNA and the enzyme topoisomerase II, preventing the re-ligation of DNA strands. This leads to the accumulation of DNA double-strand breaks, triggering cell cycle arrest and Apoptosis.
Role in Combination Therapy
Etoposide is frequently used in combination with other agents to enhance its efficacy. For example, synergistic effects have been reported when combined with Caspase-3 gene therapy in liver tumor models.

non_alcoholic_fatty_liver_disease.description:
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is the most common liver disease, with a worldwide prevalence of ~25%. It encompasses a spectrum from simple hepatic steatosis to non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), fibrosis, and cirrhosis in the absence of significant alcohol consumption. Its development involves genetic, environmental, and lifestyle risk factors.

Etiology & Pathophysiology

NAFLD arises from lipid metabolic dysregulation, oxidative stress, inflammation, and fibrosis. Key drivers include de novo lipogenesis, impaired fatty acid oxidation, insulin resistance, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Lipid metabolic homeostatic factors such as PPARα, PGC-1α, and NF-κB play protective roles.

Sirtuin Involvement (Wu et al., 2022)

Sirtuin expression is decreased in NAFLD/fibrosis patients (SIRT1–3, SIRT5, SIRT6):
SIRT1: Protective — deacetylates ChREBP and SREBP-1c to maintain hepatic lipid homeostasis; antagonizes liver fibrosis by blocking hepatic stellate cell activation. However, intestinal SIRT1 can be harmful by intensifying hepatic ferroptosis/inflammation via gut microbiota imbalance.
SIRT6: Deacetylates ChREBP/SREBP-1c; hepatocyte-specific knockout elevates fibrosis and oxidative stress in NASH mice.
SIRT2: Prevents NAFLD by deacetylating hepatocyte nuclear factor 4α; deleterious in hepatic fibrosis via the SIRT2/ERK/c-Myc axis.
SIRT3: Improves mitochondrial function via deacetylation of mitochondrial trifunctional proteins and LCAD.
SIRT5: Systemic knockout impairs medium-chain fatty acid oxidation → periportal macrovascular steatosis.
SIRT4: Upregulation inhibits HFD-induced lipid accumulation/inflammation/fibrogenesis via the SIRT4/Smad4 axis; but can be harmful in NAFLD by deacetylating/destabilizing mitochondrial trifunctional protein-α.
SIRT7: High expression in alcoholic hepatitis/NAFLD is harmful.

Therapeutic Implications

NAD⁺-sirtuin axis modulation (e.g., SIRT1/SIRT6 activators) represents a candidate strategy for restoring hepatic lipid homeostasis and limiting progression to NASH and fibrosis.

vegfc.description:
VEGFc (VEGF-C)

VEGFc denotes VEGF-C (vascular endothelial growth factor C), a member of the VEGF (vascular endothelial growth factor) family of cysteine-knot growth factors. VEGF-C is a potent lymphangiogenic and angiogenic factor that signals primarily through VEGFR-3 (FLT4) on lymphatic endothelium and, at higher concentrations or via proteolytic processing, through VEGFR2 (KDR/FLK1) on blood vascular endothelium. It is a component of the Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype, secreted by senescent cells and implicated in Paracrine Senescence and tumour-associated vascular remodeling.

Mechanism of Action & Signaling
Receptors: VEGF-C binds VEGFR-3 (its primary lymphatic-endothelial receptor) and, after N- and C-terminal proteolytic maturation, also VEGFR2. Receptor binding activates VEGFR kinase activity, triggering PI3K/Akt, MAPK/ERK, and PLCγ pathways that drive endothelial proliferation, survival, migration, and tube formation.
Lymphangiogenesis vs angiogenesis: Full-length VEGF-C preferentially activates VEGFR-3 and promotes lymphatic vessel sprouting; fully processed VEGF-C additionally engages VEGFR-2 to support blood-vessel angiogenesis.
Transcriptional regulation: In senescence, VEGF-C expression is induced downstream of RAS/RAF/MEK oncogenic signalling and reinforced by the SASP transcriptional program governed by IL-1α and NF-κB.
Extracellular processing: Proteases (e.g., ADAMTS3, CCBE1-assisted) cleave the VEGF-C pro-peptide to generate high-affinity receptor-binding forms, tuning its receptor selectivity.

Role in Senescence / SASP

[!info] Source: Acosta et al., 2013 (PMID 23636316)
Quantitative SILAC proteomics of the OIS secretome identified VEGF family ligands as top SASP hits. VEGF-C (notated VEGFc) was induced as early as 2–3 days after RAS activation, together with CXCL1, IL-8, CCL20, and activin A. Among the SASP mediators of paracrine senescence, VEGF family factors (alongside TGFβ family ligands, CCL2, and CCL20) were validated by receptor-inhibition: a VEGFR2/FLT3 inhibitor suppressed paracrine senescence in vitro and, combined with IL-1R, CCR2, and TGFBR1 inhibitors, reduced senescent hepatocyte burden in vivo in an NrasG12V liver model.
VEGF-C is a secreted SASP growth factor that, like VEGF-A, contributes to the pro-angiogenic and paracrine signaling milieu of senescent cells.
It supports the SASP's dual character: reinforcing the tumour-suppressive senescence arrest microenvironment while simultaneously promoting angiogenesis that can aid tumour growth and immune evasion in the Tumor Microenvironment.
In Paracrine Senescence, VEGF family signaling is one of the branches (together with TGF-β, CCL2, CCL20) whose receptor blockade partially rescues paracrine arrest.

Clinical / Pathological Relevance
Cancer: VEGF-C drives tumour lymphangiogenesis and lymphatic metastasis and is a prognostic marker in several cancers; its presence in the SASP links senescence to pro-metastatic vascular remodeling.
Lymphatic / vascular disease: VEGF-C is investigated therapeutically to stimulate lymphatic growth in lymphedema and for therapeutic angiogenesis in ischemia.
Senescence-related aging: As a pro-angiogenic SASP component, VEGF-C contributes to the age-associated vascular changes and the pro-tumorigenic microenvironment generated by accumulating Senescent Cells.

adrenaline_catabolism.description:
Adrenaline catabolism

The metabolic process by which adrenaline is broken down in the body.



List of documents that mention this entity
The Adrenochrome Pathway
Linking Summary: - New links added: Adrenochrome Pathway, Heart disease, Reactive Oxygen Species, Neutrophils, Epinephrine, Adrenochrome, Adrenolutin, HPLC, Serum, Myocardial infarction, Cardiotoxicity, Cell necrosis, Arrhythmias, Coronary artery constricti...
neutrophil and erthrocyte
This is described as a major pathway for Adrenaline catabolism in these cells.

Connections
Neutrophils: Actively oxidize adrenaline to Adrenochrome as a pathway for catabolism.
MAO: Enzyme involved in the breakdown of Catecholamines.
COMT: Enzyme involved in the breakdown of Catecholamines.

Major Routes of Catabolism

Epinephrine is metabolized through three principal routes, each competing for the same substrate pool:
O-Methylation by COMT: COMT (catechol-O-methyltransferase) transfers a methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine to the 3-hydroxyl of the catechol ring, producing Metanephrine. This is the predominant initial step in peripheral tissues, particularly in the liver and kidney. Metanephrine is subsequently deaminated by MAO to 3-methoxy-4-hydroxymandelic acid (VMA), the major urinary endpoint metabolite.
Deamination by MAO: MAO (monoamine oxidase) oxidatively deaminates epinephrine to 3,4-dihydroxymandelaldehyde, which is further reduced or oxidized to 3,4-dihydroxymandelic acid or, following COMT action, to VMA. In the central nervous system, MAO-A is the primary isoform responsible for epinephrine and norepinephrine metabolism, while MAO-B preferentially acts on dopamine.
Oxidative Cyclization (Adrenochrome Pathway): Under conditions of elevated oxidative stress, epinephrine undergoes two-electron oxidation of the catechol ring to form Adrenaline-quinone, which cyclizes to Leuco-adrenochrome and then Adrenochrome. This route bypasses both COMT and MAO entirely and represents a shunt toward highly reactive oxidation products.

Relative Flux Under Normal vs Stress Conditions

Under basal physiological conditions, COMT-mediated O-methylation accounts for approximately 60–70% of peripheral epinephrine clearance, with MAO-mediated deamination contributing 20–30% and the oxidative cyclization pathway representing less than 5% of total flux. However, during acute inflammatory states, tissue ischemia, or conditions with robust neutrophil infiltration, the oxidative pathway can become markedly upregulated. In Rheumatoid synovial fluid, for instance, adrenochrome and its conjugates are detected at concentrations suggesting that 15–30% of local epinephrine may be routed through the oxidative cyclization pathway. The presence of Myeloperoxidase, NADPH Oxidase, and transition metals released from damaged tissues all shift flux toward adrenochrome formation.

Tissue-Specific Differences

The relative activity of these catabolic routes varies considerably across tissues:
Liver and kidney: High COMT and MAO activity; epinephrine clearance is rapid, with minimal adrenochrome formation.
Heart and vascular tissue: Moderate COMT activity; susceptibility to oxidative cycling is increased during ischemia-reperfusion, contributing to adrenochrome-mediated cardiotoxicity.
Brain: COMT and MAO are both active; the blood-brain barrier limits peripherally formed adrenochrome entry, but local production is possible under neuroinflammatory conditions.
Blood and myeloid cells: Erythrocytes contain abundant hemoglobin that can oxidize epinephrine, and activated Neutrophils release MPO and generate ROS, creating a highly favorable microenvironment for adrenochrome synthesis.
Synovial fluid: Largely acellular but accumulates MPO from infiltrating neutrophils, creating conditions for sustained epinephrine oxidation.

Factors Shifting Flux Toward Adrenochrome Formation

Several biochemical parameters divert epinephrine away from COMT/MAO and toward the oxidative cyclization pathway:
Elevated ROS/RNS: Superoxide, H₂O₂, HOCl, and peroxynitrite directly oxidize the catechol ring.
Metal ion availability: Fe³⁺, Cu²⁺, and heme iron accelerate autoxidation.
GSH depletion: Glutathione normally reduces adrenaline-quinone back to epinephrine; when GSH is consumed, the quinone accumulates and cyclizes.
pH elevation: Alkaline conditions (e.g., during alkalosis or in secretory vesicles) accelerate the cyclization rate by deprotonating the amine nucleophile.
Enzyme inhibition: Genetic or pharmacological inhibition of COMT (e.g., by entacapone) or MAO (e.g., by phenelzine) extends epinephrine half-life and increases substrate availability for oxidative cycling.
Ascorbate deficiency: Vitamin C efficiently reduces the semiquinone radical back to epinephrine; deficiency removes this protective recycling pathway.

cerebellum.description:
The Cerebellum ("little brain") is a major hindbrain structure situated posterior to the brainstem, comprising the cerebellar cortex, deep nuclei, and extensive white matter. Though it contains more neurons than the rest of the brain combined, it is best known for refining motor output—coordinating voluntary movement, maintaining posture and balance, and calibrating the timing and precision of skilled actions.

Structure & Functional Subdivisions

The cerebellar cortex is a uniform three-layered architecture (molecular, Purkinje, granular layers) organized into longitudinal zones receiving input from spinal, vestibular, and cortical pathways via climbing and mossy fibers. Output through deep nuclei (dentate, interposed, fastigial) shapes motor commands. Beyond motor control, the cerebellum contributes to cognitive and affective processing, though its dopaminergic innervation is sparse compared with the Prefrontal Cortex or striatum.


Catecholamine signaling in the cerebellum is modest. The enzyme COMT is expressed at low levels here relative to forebrain regions, and—critically for experimental design—the CamKIIα promoter used to overexpress COMT in transgenic models is not active in cerebellar Purkinje or granule cells. In COMT-overexpressing (COMT-OE) mice, therefore, cerebellar COMT activity remains at baseline, making the cerebellum a built-in negative control against which forebrain (cortical, hippocampal) effects of elevated COMT can be compared. This dissociation helps attribute cognitive and synaptic phenotypes specifically to cortical COMT elevation rather than global enzyme excess.



Because motor coordination depends little on the COMT-driven dopamine clearance that dominates cortical physiology, cerebellar-sparing designs preserve normal locomotor behavior while isolating prefrontal and hippocampal deficits (e.g., impaired Working Memory). This contrasts with disorders such as Parkinson's Disease, where midbrain dopamine loss produces prominent motor signs, and with Schizophrenia, where cortical dopamine and COMT variation are more relevant.

Clinical & Research Relevance

The cerebellum is a model system for studying synaptic plasticity (long-term depression) and, increasingly, for its role in cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome. Its use as a control region in COMT transgenic work illustrates how anatomical promoter specificity enables region-targeted genetic manipulation.

aspirin.description:
Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid, ASA) is a salicylate derivative and one of the most widely used medications globally. It irreversibly acetylates cyclooxygenase-1 and -2 (COX-1/COX-2), blocking the conversion of arachidonic acid to prostaglandins and thromboxanes for the lifetime of the platelet (~7–10 days). This gives aspirin both anti-inflammatory/analgesic properties and a durable antiplatelet effect that underlies its use in cardiovascular prophylaxis.

Mechanism of Action

Aspirin's acetyl group covalently modifies a serine residue (Ser529 in COX-1, Ser516 in COX-2) in the enzyme's active channel, permanently disabling prostaglandin G/H synthase activity. COX-derived prostaglandins (especially PGI2 from endothelium and TxA2 from platelets) normally balance vasodilation/anticoagulation against vasoconstriction/aggregation. By suppressing TxA2 synthesis in platelets—which cannot resynthesize COX—aspirin shifts hemostasis toward reduced clot formation at low (75–325 mg) doses.

Interaction with COMT Genotype

Beyond COX, emerging pharmacogenetic evidence links aspirin response to COMT variation. The Val158Met polymorphism (rs4680) determines catecholamine and dopamine clearance efficiency and influences vascular tone and platelet reactivity. Observational and subgroup analyses suggest a stratified effect on Cardiovascular Disease risk:
Slow COMT (rs4680 A/A, Met/Met): Preserved assumptions of benefit; aspirin appears effective for primary and secondary prevention of atherosclerotic events.
Fast COMT (rs4680 G/G, Val/Val): Some reports indicate aspirin may fail to confer protection and, in certain cohorts, may be associated with increased cardiovascular event rates, possibly reflecting differences in endothelial catecholamine signaling and oxidative stress handling.

These findings remain debated and are not yet standard in guideline-driven prescribing, but they illustrate the broader principle that methylation and catecholamine metabolism modulate drug response.

Clinical Relevance

Aspirin is indicated for secondary prevention of myocardial infarction and stroke, and (at low dose) for preeclampsia prophylaxis and colorectal cancer risk reduction. Consideration of COMT status adds a personalized layer to the long-standing balance between bleeding risk and thrombotic prevention. Notably, aspirin itself is not a catechol and does not require COMT for metabolism, distinguishing it from polyphenols such as Quercetin or Green tea catechins.

cell_necrosis.description: Cell necrosis is a form of cell injury that results in the premature death of cells in living tissue by autolysis. Unlike Apoptosis, which is a tightly regulated, energy-dependent program of cellular suicide, necrosis is traditionally viewed as an unregulated, passive process triggered by overwhelming environmental stress. However, specific forms of regulated necrosis (e.g., Necroptosis) blur this distinction. Overview Feature Necrosis Apoptosis --- --- --- Trigger Severe injury, hypoxia, toxins Physiological signals, mild stress Energy requirement ATP-depleted ATP-dependent Cell size Swelling (oncosis) Shrinkage Membrane integrity Early rupture Preserved (blebbing) DNA fragmentation Random, smeared Inter-nucleosomal (ladder) Inflammation Prominent (pro-inflammatory) Minimal (anti-inflammatory) Fate Phagocytosis by scavengers Apoptotic body clearance Oncosis and Autolysis Oncosis (from Greek onkos = swelling) describes the pre-lethal morphological phase preceding necrotic cell death, characterized by cellular swelling, organelle edema, and bleb formation due to failure of ion pumps. Autolysis refers to the post-mortem degradation of cells by their own hydrolytic enzymes released from lysosomes, accelerating after membrane rupture. While oncosis is the process leading to necrotic cell death, autolysis is the post-mortem consequence. The hallmark features of necrosis include: Cell swelling — Loss of ionic homeostasis causes water influx and cytoplasmic vacuolation. Membrane rupture — Loss of plasma membrane integrity releases intracellular contents. Organelle breakdown — Mitochondrial swelling, lysosomal leakage, and nuclear pyknosis → karyorrhexis → karyolysis. Release of Damage-Associated Molecular Patterns (DAMPs) — Cytosolic and nuclear components spill into the extracellular space, triggering Inflammation. Type Tissue Key Features --- --- --- Coagulative necrosis Heart, kidney, liver (ischemia) Denatured proteins preserve tissue architecture; eosinophilic cytoplasm; nuclear loss Liquefactive necrosis Brain, abscesses Enzymatic digestion liquefies tissue; pus formation; cystic cavitation Caseous necrosis Mycobacterium tuberculosis Soft, friable, cheese-like; granuloma formation; surrounded by epithelioid macrophages Fat necrosis Pancreas, breast, omentum Lipases hydrolyze triglycerides → free fatty acids + calcium → saponification (chalky white deposits) Gangrenous necrosis Limbs, GI tract Coagulative + liquefactive necrosis; secondary bacterial infection; dry (ischemic) or wet (infected) Fibrinoid necrosis Arteries (Hypertension, vasculitis) Deposition of fibrin-like material in vessel walls; immune complex-mediated damage Mechanisms ATP Depletion and Ionic Collapse Ischemia or mitochondrial poisons deplete Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP), disabling the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump. Intracellular sodium and water accumulate, causing cell swelling (oncosis). Calcium ions enter via reverse-mode Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchange and voltage-gated channels, precipitating widespread Ca²⁺ overload. Ca²⁺ Overload and Calpain Activation Cytosolic Calcium overload activates Calpains — Ca²⁺-dependent cysteine proteases that cleave Cytoskeleton components (spectrin, talin), plasma membrane proteins, and Bid (linking to Apoptosis crosstalk). Prolonged calpain activity leads to membrane blebbing and loss of integrity. Reactive Oxygen Species and mPTP Opening Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS), generated from leaky mitochondria, NADPH Oxidase, and Xanthine Oxidase, attack membrane phospholipids, proteins, and DNA. Mitochondrial permeability transition pore (mPTP) opening collapses the mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨₘ), halting ATP synthesis and releasing Cytochrome c and other pro-death factors. Lysosomal membrane permeabilization (LMP) releases hydrolytic Cathepsins (B, D, L) into the cytosol. Cathepsin B and Cathepsin D amplify the death signal by cleaving Bid to tBid, activating Caspase cascades, and directly degrading cellular structures. LMP is a critical point of no return in necrotic cell death. Pathophysiology: DAMP Release and Sterile Inflammation Necrotic cell rupture releases Damage-Associated Molecular Patterns (DAMPs) that activate innate immunity: HMGB1 — Nuclear protein; when released, binds TLR2/TLR4 and RAGE, promoting NF-κB-dependent Inflammation. ATP — Extracellular ATP acts on P2X7 Receptor to trigger NLRP3 Inflammasome assembly and IL-1β secretion. Uric Acid — Released purine metabolite; activates NLRP3 as a danger signal. DNA — Self-DNA engages TLR9 (endosomal) and cGAS-STING Pathway (cytosolic), driving type I Interferon responses. Other DAMPs — S100 proteins, Heat Shock Proteins, Calreticulin, Histones. This cascade defines sterile inflammation — inflammation triggered by cell stress and death in the absence of microbial infection — which underlies pathologies such as Ischemia-reperfusion Injury, Myocardial infarction, and Neurodegenerative Diseases.

nnmt.description:
NNMT (nicotinamide N-methyltransferase) is a cytosolic S-adenosylmethionine–dependent methyltransferase that converts Nicotinamide into 1-methylnicotinamide (1-MNA) and S-adenosylhomocysteine. In doing so it withdraws nicotinamide from the NAD+ Salvage Pathway (which requires NAMPT to recycle nicotinamide into NMN), acting as a sink that limits NAD+ biosynthesis.

Role in NAD+ Homeostasis and Sirtuin Activity
NNMT expression and activity strongly influence the intracellular pool of NAD+ precursors; high NNMT flux lowers available nicotinamide for salvage and thus can indirectly restrain NAD+-dependent enzymes such as the Sirtuins.
Because all sirtuins require NAD+ as an obligate co-substrate, NNMT is positioned as an upstream modulator of sirtuin network activity through its control of precursor availability.
Dysregulated NNMT is implicated in metabolic disorders (obesity, metabolic syndrome), multiple cancers, and cardiovascular disease, where it contributes to metabolic reprogramming and altered NAD+ handling.

endothelial_dysfunction.description: Endothelial dysfunction is a systemic pathological state of the vascular endothelium characterized by reduced bioavailability of Nitric Oxide, impaired vasodilation, increased inflammatory adhesion molecule expression, and a pro-thrombotic phenotype. It is an early hallmark of Atherosclerosis and Cardiovascular Disease. Mechanisms Reduced eNOS activity and Nitric Oxide production Increased oxidative stress from NADPH Oxidase and mitochondrial ROS Inflammatory cytokine activation (TNFα, Interleukin 1β) Impaired Insulin Signaling Clinical Assessment Measured by flow-mediated dilation (FMD), Pulse Wave Velocity, and circulating biomarkers (VCAM-1, ICAM-1, E-selectin). eNOS Uncoupling: The Central Molecular Mechanism The primary driver of endothelial dysfunction is reduced bioavailable Nitric Oxide (NO), which occurs through multiple convergent mechanisms. The endothelial isoform of Nitric Oxide Synthase (eNOS, NOS3) normally dimerizes to catalyze the NADPH-dependent oxidation of L-arginine to citrulline and NO, requiring the cofactors Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4), FAD, and FMN. Under conditions of elevated oxidative stress, BH4 is oxidized to dihydrobiopterin (BH2) by Peroxynitrite, a process termed "BH4 deficiency." In the absence of sufficient BH4, eNOS undergoes "uncoupling" — the enzyme's electron transfer becomes uncoupled from L-arginine oxidation, and the oxygenase domain instead reduces molecular oxygen to Superoxide Radicals rather than producing NO. This converts eNOS from a protective NO-generating enzyme into a pro-oxidant source of Reactive Oxygen Species, creating a feed-forward loop: superoxide from uncoupled eNOS rapidly reacts with any remaining NO (diffusion-limited rate constant of ~6.7 × 10^9 M^−1·s^−1) to form Peroxynitrite, which further oxidizes BH4 and perpetuates uncoupling. While uncoupled eNOS is a major source, endothelial dysfunction involves a network of interconnected ROS-producing systems. NADPH Oxidase (particularly the NOX1 and NOX4 isoforms in endothelial cells) generates superoxide in response to Angiotensin II, TNF-alpha, and mechanical shear stress. Xanthine Oxidase, which is highly expressed in the vascular endothelium and circulates bound to endothelial glycosaminoglycans, produces both Superoxide Radicals and Hydrogen Peroxide during purine catabolism. Mitochondrial electron transport chain complexes I and III also contribute significantly; in the dysfunctional endothelium, elevated mitochondrial membrane potential favors superoxide production at complex III (the Q-cycle), particularly when NO levels are low and cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV) is not NO-inhibited. The interplay between these sources is non-additive — XO-derived superoxide activates ROS-sensitive signaling pathways that upregulate NOX expression, while NOX-derived Hydrogen Peroxide can stabilize HIF-1α and induce hypoxic gene programs that remodel endothelial function. Asymmetric Dimethylarginine (ADMA) and Endogenous NOS Inhibition The endogenous NOS inhibitor asymmetric dimethylarginine (ADMA) accumulates in oxidative stress states because ROS directly inhibit the enzyme dimethylarginine dimethylaminohydrolase (DDAH), which degrades ADMA. DDAH contains a critical cysteine residue (Cys-249) in its active site that is susceptible to oxidation and S-nitrosylation, rendering the enzyme inactive. Elevated ADMA competitively inhibits eNOS, promoting uncoupling and exacerbating endothelial dysfunction. Plasma ADMA levels are a robust independent predictor of cardiovascular events and all-cause mortality in patients with coronary artery disease, type 2 diabetes, and chronic kidney disease. Clinical Assessment and Diagnostic Markers Endothelial dysfunction is most commonly quantified non-invasively by Flow-Mediated Dilation (FMD) of the brachial artery, a technique where reactive hyperemia-induced shear stress triggers NO-mediated vasodilation that is measured by ultrasound. Reduced FMD (<5–7% dilation) is an independent predictor of future cardiovascular events. Circulating biomarkers include elevated levels of von Willebrand Factor (vWF), soluble ICAM-1, soluble VCAM-1 (both products of NF-κB activation), E-Selectin, and ADMA. In the microcirculation, reactive hyperemia index (RHI) measured by peripheral arterial tonometry (PAT) provides an alternative assessment of small-vessel endothelial function. SASP Milieu and Cellular Senescence as Drivers [!info] Source: Mahoney et al. 2025 The circulating SASP milieu was established as a causal driver of age-related endothelial dysfunction through Senescence induction. Fisetin (a senolytic) improved endothelial function by eliminating senescent endothelial cells and reducing circulating CXCL12. Key mechanisms: Cellular Senescence: ECs are the most senescence-susceptible vascular cell type; aging increases senescent EC burden 10.7-fold Circulating SASP milieu: Plasma from old mice directly impaired EDD (−17%), induced EC senescence (6.1-fold SA-β-Gal), reduced NO (−24%), and increased mitochondrial superoxide (3.

febuxostat.description:
Pharmacodynamics

Febuxostat is a non-purine, selective inhibitor of Xanthine Oxidase. Unlike Allopurinol, which only inhibits the reduced form of the enzyme, febuxostat blocks both the oxidized and reduced forms, achieving more complete suppression of urate production. It is a reversible, mixed-type inhibitor that binds in the molybdenum-pterin channel of the enzyme.

[!important]
Febuxostat carries cardiovascular black-box warnings in some populations, and like allopurinol it does not address pre-existing urate crystal deposits immediately.

Pharmacokinetics

Febuxostat is primarily metabolized by the liver (glucuronidation and oxidation), which permits its use in some renally impaired patients. This hepatic route distinguishes it from allopurinol and its renally cleared metabolite oxypurinol.

Applications

Febuxostat is used for the management of hyperuricemia and Gout. By inhibiting Xanthine Oxidase, it lowers Uric Acid production and concurrently reduces Reactive Oxygen Species generated by the enzyme, potentially conferring antioxidant benefits beyond urate lowering. However, cardiovascular safety concerns have limited broad adoption relative to allopurinol.

aif.description:
AIF (Apoptosis-inducing factor, gene AIFM1) is a flavoprotein normally resident in the mitochondrial intermembrane space, where it functions as an NADH oxidase contributing to oxidative phosphorylation and maintenance of mitochondrial structure. Upon severe cellular stress it is released and translocates to the nucleus, where it executes a caspase-independent form of programmed cell death — a distinct arm of Apoptosis and Cell Death.

Structure & Localization

AIF contains an N-terminal mitochondrial targeting sequence, a central flavin-binding domain related to oxidoreductases, and a C-terminal nuclear localization sequence exposed after proteolytic cleavage. In healthy mitochondria, AIF supports respiratory complex I assembly and stability. Its redox activity is independent of its lethal nuclear function.

Mechanism of Action

Following mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (see Intrinsic Pathway), AIF is cleaved by calpains or cathepsins and translocates to the nucleus. There it binds to DNA and, together with Cyclophilin A, induces large-scale (~50 kb) chromatin fragmentation and chromatin condensation. This caspase-independent route ensures death execution even when caspases are inhibited (e.g., by IAPs or viral inhibitors), providing a fail-safe lethal program.

Physiological Function

Beyond cell death, AIF is essential for life: AIFM1 loss causes a severe mitochondrial encephalopathy (combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency) in humans. In development, AIF-mediated caspase-independent death shapes cavitation during lumen formation and removes superfluous cells in select tissues.

Pathological & Cancer Relevance
Tumor Cell Death: AIF contributes to the lethality of many Chemotherapy agents and radiotherapy, particularly when they inflict catastrophic oxidative damage. Agents that trigger reactive oxygen species (Oxidative Stress) can engage AIF as a backup death route.
Resistance: Caspase-deficient or Apoptosis-resistant tumors may still be killed via AIF, making it a therapeutic target of interest. Conversely, AIF downregulation can confer resistance to certain cytotoxic drugs.
Neuroprotection Interface: Because AIF release also occurs in excitotoxic and ischemic injury, AIF inhibitors are explored neuroprotectively — a balance relevant where tumor and normal tissue share apoptotic vulnerability.

silver_compounds.description:
Overview

Silver compounds are derivatives of metallic Silver, produced for antimicrobial, electronic, and synthetic applications. Silver(I) Oxide is used to prepare other silver compounds, serving as a versatile silver precursor in synthetic chemistry.

Preparation & Types

Because silver(I) oxide is a stable, readily handled oxidant and silver source, it can be converted into soluble Silver salts, coordination complexes, and metal Silver nanoparticles, including the silver oxide nanoparticle dispersions used in antimicrobial and electronic applications.

Aldo-Keto Reductases (AKRs) are a superfamily of NAD(P)H-dependent oxidoreductases that catalyze the reduction of various carbonyl substrates, including aldehydes and ketones, to their corresponding alcohols.

malondialdehyde.description:
Malondialdehyde (MDA) is a reactive dialdehyde end-product of Lipid Peroxidation and a widely used Biomarker of chronic Oxidative Stress and oxidative damage to lipids, proteins, and DNA.



MDA is generated primarily from peroxidation of polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) with ≥3 double bonds—arachidonic acid (20:4, n-6), eicosapentaenoic acid (22:5, n-3), and docosahexaenoic acid (22:6, n-3). During Lipid Peroxidation, bicyclic endoperoxide intermediates cyclize and fragment to yield MDA as a three-carbon dialdehyde (CH₂(CHO)₂). The yield is non-stoichiometric—roughly 1 MDA per 20–40 fatty acids oxidized. MDA is also a byproduct of Thromboxane A₂ and Prostacyclin biosynthesis via the COX pathway (PGH₂ fragmentation), so not all MDA reflects oxidative damage—relevant to biomarker interpretation.

Chemical Reactivity and Adduct Formation

At neutral pH MDA exists mainly as its enolate and is highly electrophilic. Its best-characterized DNA adduct is M₁dG (pyrimidopurinone deoxyguanosine), formed with the exocyclic amino group and N1 of deoxyguanosine. M₁dG is mutagenic (G→T transversions, frameshifts), repaired mainly by Nucleotide Excision Repair but not Base Excision Repair; elevated M₁dG occurs in colorectal cancer and Helicobacter pylori gastritis, linking MDA to carcinogenesis. MDA forms stable, fluorescent MDA-lysine cross-links on proteins (lysine/histidine), recognized by RAGE receptors, triggering inflammation. MDA modification of LDL yields MDA-LDL, taken up by Macrophage scavenger receptors (SR-A, CD36 Receptor) like Oxidized LDL in Atherosclerosis; anti-MDA-LDL autoantibodies track cardiovascular severity.

Measurement and Biomarker Utility

MDA is classically measured as thiobarbituric acid reactive substances (TBARS), but TBA cross-reacts with 4-HNE, acrolein, and glycated proteins, and processing can artifactually generate MDA—so TBARS overestimates true MDA. Specific methods include HPLC, GC-MS, and LC-MS/MS with deuterated MDA-d₂ internal standard (current gold standard). Healthy plasma MDA by LC-MS/MS is ~0.5–1.5 μM (TBARS 1–4 μM). Elevated MDA is reported in Cardiovascular Disease, Diabetes Mellitus (correlating with HbA1c), Neurodegenerative Diseases (Alzheimer's, Parkinson's), Chronic Kidney Disease, and Cancer (breast, lung, colorectal, liver).

Therapeutic Implications

Interventions lowering MDA include Statins (pleiotropic antioxidant effects), Metformin (AMPK-dependent mitochondrial ROS reduction), Vitamin E, and N-Acetylcysteine (replenishing Glutathione). Lifestyle measures—Caloric Restriction, Exercise, and the Mediterranean Diet rich in Polyphenols—reduce serum MDA in trials.

chromatin.description:
Chromatin is the complex of DNA and proteins (primarily histones) that packages the genome within the cell nucleus. In young, healthy cells, chromatin is organized into a precise landscape of tightly packed Heterochromatin (transcriptionally silent) and open Euchromatin (transcriptionally active). During Aging, this structure undergoes significant remodeling, often referred to as epigenetic drift.

One of the most consistent hallmarks of aging is the global loss of heterochromatin, known as the Heterochromatin Loss Model of Aging.
   Mechanism: Regions of the genome that are normally permanently silenced, such as centromeres and repetitive DNA sequences, become "leaky" and less condensed.
   Consequences: This leads to the activation of Transposable Elements (jumping genes) and increased Genomic Instability.
   SAHF (Senescence-Associated Heterochromatin Foci): Paradoxically, while global heterochromatin decreases, senescent cells often form dense, localized clusters of heterochromatin to permanently silence cell-cycle genes.
Histone Modifications and Loss
Histones are the structural proteins around which DNA is wound to form Nucleosomes. Aging affects both the quantity and the chemical "tags" on these proteins.
   Histone Loss: The total amount of core histone proteins often decreases with age, leading to a more "open" but disorganized chromatin state.
   Altered Marks: Aging is associated with a reduction in repressive marks (e.g., H3K9me3) and an increase in certain active marks (e.g., H4K16ac) that promote a less stable chromatin structure.
DNA Methylation Changes
Predictable shifts in DNA methylation patterns are central to chromatin remodeling during aging.
   Global Hypomethylation: Older cells generally show a decrease in overall DNA methylation, contributing to the activation of repetitive elements.
   Focal Hypermethylation: Conversely, specific promoter regions—often those of tumor suppressor genes—can become hypermethylated and silenced.
   Epigenetic Clock: These consistent shifts in methylation are used by epigenetic clocks to accurately measure biological age.
3D Genome Disorganization
The physical folding of chromatin into loops and domains changes with age.
   Loss of Compartmentalization: The separation between active and inactive regions of the genome blurs.
   Structural Defects: Changes in the proteins that maintain DNA architecture can lead to "miswiring," where enhancers interact with the wrong genes, causing them to turn on or off inappropriately.

cholangiocarcinoma.description:
Cholangiocarcinoma is a malignant tumor originating from the bile duct epithelium (cholangiocytes), occurring inside or outside the liver. It is the second most common primary liver cancer after hepatocellular carcinoma. Because it is typically diagnosed at advanced stages and is refractory to conventional therapy, cholangiocarcinoma carries a dismal prognosis, driving intense interest in repurposed agents such as Ivermectin.

Subtypes & Etiology

Cholangiocarcinoma is anatomically classified into intrahepatic (iCCA), perihilar (pCCA, Klatskin tumors), and distal (dCCA) forms, each with distinct biology and risk factors. Established risk factors include primary sclerosing cholangitis, liver fluke infection (Opisthorchis viverrini, Clonorchis sinensis), chronic biliary inflammation, cirrhosis, hepatitis B/C, and metabolic syndrome. Recurrent Inflammation and bile acid–driven injury promote cholangiocyte proliferation and Oxidative Stress, fostering malignant transformation. Driver alterations commonly involve IDH1/2, FGFR2 fusions, BRAF, KRAS, and TP53.

Mechanism & Pathobiology

Tumor cholangiocytes (e.g., the KKU cell lines) display constitutive proliferative and survival signaling through EGFR, MAPK Signaling, PI3K–AKT, and IL-6/STAT3 axes. The desmoplastic stroma secretes factors that further drive invasion and chemoresistance. These features render cholangiocarcinoma notoriously resistant to the backbone agent Gemcitabine combined with cisplatin.



Ivermectin has shown potent anticancer activity against cholangiocarcinoma in preclinical models. Mechanisms include: (1) inhibition of proliferation in a dose- and time-dependent manner in KKU214 and related lines; (2) cell-cycle arrest in S phase accompanied by induction of Apoptosis; and (3) overcoming resistance, as gemcitabine-resistant cells remain highly sensitive to ivermectin. Ivermectin's pleiotropic actions — PAK1 inhibition, mitochondrial depolarization, and disruption of survival signaling — make it a candidate repositioned therapy, especially for refractory or drug-resistant disease.

Clinical & Research Relevance

Standard care is surgical resection for localized disease, with systemic Chemotherapy (gemcitabine/cisplatin) for advanced cases and emerging targeted agents (FGFR2 inhibitors, IDH1 inhibitors) for molecularly defined subsets. Repurposing Ivermectin alone or with chemotherapy is under investigation to bypass resistance. Biomarkers such as CA19-9 aid monitoring, and liquid biopsy for FGFR2 or IDH alterations guides precision approaches.

flavones.description:
Flavonoids are divided into subclasses; flavones are characterized by a 2-phenylchromen-4-one backbone without a 3-hydroxyl group (unlike flavonols). Major dietary flavones include Apigenin (parsley, celery, chamomile), Luteolin, and Chrysin. They share the generic C6-C3-C6 polyphenolic structure and are especially abundant in parsley and celery.

Biological Activities

Flavones exert antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anticancer effects. Apigenin inhibits breast cancer proliferation through the Akt/FOXO3a pathway and induces proteasomal degradation of HER2/neu; Chrysin synergizes with apigenin to induce apoptosis and inhibit migration in breast and liver cancers. Flavones generally act as weaker direct antioxidants than flavonols (lack of 3-OH) but retain strong kinase-modulating and epigenetic activities.

bax.description:
Overview
BAX (Bcl-2-associated X protein) is a pro-apoptotic effector of the Bcl-2 protein family localized predominantly in the cytosol and loosely bound to the outer mitochondrial membrane in healthy cells. Upon apoptotic signaling, BAX undergoes conformational activation, inserts into the outer mitochondrial membrane, and oligomerizes with BAK to form pores that commit the cell to apoptosis.

Structure & Activation
BAX shares the conserved Bcl-2 homology (BH1–BH3) domains. Activation is governed by the balance between anti-apoptotic proteins such as Bcl-2 and BH3-only activators (e.g., Bid). Transcriptionally, p53 upregulates BAX, linking genotoxic stress to the death program.

Mechanism of Action & MOMP
Activated BAX translocates to mitochondria, where it cooperates with BAK to permeabilize the membrane. This releases Cytochrome c and Smac DIABLO into the cytosol, triggering Caspases and the execution phase of Apoptosis. The threshold of MOMP is also implicated in Minority MOMP, which can induce survival signaling without immediate death.

Phosphorylation-Dependent Regulation

[!important] ERK-Pin1 Survival Switch at Thr167
In response to survival cytokines (e.g., GM-CSF), the ERK2 pathway phosphorylates BAX at Thr167. This creates a pThr-Pro motif recognized by the peptidyl-prolyl isomerase Pin1. Pin1 binding catalyzes a conformational change that locks Bax in an inactive state, preventing its translocation to mitochondria and subsequent oligomerization. This mechanism protects cells (notably eosinophils) from apoptosis.


While ERK-mediated Thr167 phosphorylation is pro-survival, the same site can be targeted by JNK or p38 MAPK under stress to promote apoptosis. Pin1 acts as the critical switch for the pro-survival outcome. Disruption of the ERK-Bax-Pin1 complex or inhibition of Pin1 triggers BAX activation and MOMP.

Physiology, Redox & Longevity
Beyond classical apoptosis, BAX/BAK-mediated leakage intersects with Mitophagy and Parkin-dependent quality control, and with Reactive Oxygen Species amplification in Mitochondrial Dysfunction. Senescent cells that evade BAX-dependent death can persist and secrete the Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype, driving Inflammaging. Compounds such as Fisetin and Urolithin A modulate these death/cleanup pathways, making BAX a node connecting apoptosis, mitophagy, and longevity.

BAK: Closely related effector that hetero-oligomerizes with BAX at the mitochondrial membrane.

glutamate.description:
Overview
Glutamate is the principal excitatory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system, essential for learning and synaptic plasticity. However, uncontrolled extracellular accumulation produces Excitotoxicity, a core mechanism in Neurodegeneration and aging.

Synthesis & Clearance
Glutamate is derived from glutamine via glutaminase and from the tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediate α-ketoglutarate. Termination of signaling depends on Na+-dependent excitatory amino-acid transporters (EAATs) on astrocytes and neurons, which clear synaptic glutamate and sustain low extracellular tone.

Mechanism of Action & Excitotoxicity
Excess glutamate overactivates ionotropic receptors, causing sustained Ca2+ influx. Calcium overload stresses Mitochondrial Dysfunction, drives Reactive Oxygen Species generation, and activates proteases that damage neurons. This cascade contributes to Parkinson's Disease, Alzheimer's Disease, and stroke injury. Glutamate also feeds into Glutathione biosynthesis via cysteine availability, coupling excitotoxic redox cost to antioxidant capacity.

Redox, Sirtuins & Longevity
Excitotoxic injury elevates Oxidative Stress and depletes NAD+-dependent resilience, whereas Sirtuins and Methylene blue can buffer downstream mitochondrial failure. Creatine supports neuronal bioenergetics against glutamate challenge. Maintaining glutamate homeostasis is therefore a longevity-relevant neuroprotective target; senotherapeutic and mitohormetic strategies indirectly limit excitotoxic burden.

avermectin.description:
Avermectins are a family of 16-membered macrocyclic lactones produced by the soil actinomycete Streptomyces avermectinius. Discovered through the pioneering work of Satoshi Ōmura and William C. Campbell — recognized by the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine — avermectins are among the most important anthelmintic and insecticidal natural products ever developed. Ivermectin is the best-known semi-synthetic derivative.

Chemical Structure & Classification

Avermectins consist of a macrocyclic lactone ring fused to a disaccharide (α-L-oleandrose)₂. Naturally occurring avermectins (A1a, A2a, B1a, B2a and their minor homologs) differ in substitution; the B1a component is the precursor to ivermectin (22,23-dihydroavermectin B1). They act as agonists of glutamate-gated and γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-gated chloride channels in invertebrates.

Pharmacological Action

In parasites, avermectins bind invertebrate glutamate- and GABA-gated chloride channels, causing sustained Cl⁻ influx, paralysis, and death. Mammalian CNS channels are structurally distinct and poorly penetrated (especially with the blood–brain barrier intact), underpinning their selectivity and safety margin.

Relevance to Cancer Research

Beyond its antiparasitic role, avermectin itself shows direct anticancer activity — it inhibits cancer-cell proliferation and, like ivermectin, engages the Glutamate-gated Cl- channels target that underlies the class's selective safety. Ivermectin, the flagship avermectin, is under active investigation for anticancer repositioning:
Inhibits the Wnt/β-catenin, AKT/mTOR, and PAK1 oncogenic pathways.
Impairs Mitochondrial Respiration and promotes Apoptosis in tumor cells.
Enhances the efficacy of conventional Chemotherapy and may overcome Multidrug Resistance.
Decades of safe use (via programs like the African Programme for Onchocerciasis Control) support repurposing trials.

History & Development

Avermectin discovery emerged from a systematic screen of soil microbes at the Kitasato Institute and was developed commercially by Merck & Co. Inc. The drug donation program underpinned global elimination efforts against onchocerciasis and lymphatic filariasis.
