foxo1.description: Transcription factor regulated by Akt that controls gluconeogenesis, adipogenesis, and beta-cell function. FOXO1 (Forkhead Box O1) is a transcription factor that plays a central role in regulating metabolism, cell survival, and Autophagy. Regulation by Insulin/Akt Under nutrient-rich conditions, insulin and IGF1 activate the Akt pathway. Akt phosphorylates FOXO1, leading to its export from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, thereby inhibiting its transcriptional activity. This suppression of FOXO1 is a major mechanism by which insulin inhibits Autophagy. Role in Autophagy Induction During Caloric Restriction or Intermittent Fasting, the Akt pathway is downregulated. Dephosphorylated FOXO1 translocates to the nucleus, where it induces the expression of many autophagy-related genes (e.g., Atg5, Atg8/LC3, ULK1). FOXO1 also promotes Gluconeogenesis during starvation. Function FOXO1 is a forkhead transcription factor that regulates Autophagy, metabolism, and immune function. It is inhibited by Akt phosphorylation under growth factor signaling. FOXO Family and Sirtuin Regulation There are four FOXO transcription factors in mammals (FOXO1, FOXO3a, FOXO4, FOXO6). SIRT1 has been demonstrated to deacetylate three of them: FOXO1 (this entry) FOXO3a — reduces apoptosis in neurons and fibroblasts; increases DNA repair and cell-cycle checkpoint gene expression FOXO4 — hydrogen peroxide-induced acetylation inhibits transactivation; SIRT1 deacetylation reverses this, enhancing GADD45 expression and resistance to oxidative stress FOXO1–SIRT1 Interaction The LXXLL motif of FOXO1 is indispensable for SIRT1 binding and FOXO1 transcriptional regulation. SIRT1 deacetylates FOXO1, modulating its activity in a context-dependent manner. Metabolic Functions Adiponectin Regulation FOXO1 forms a transcriptional complex at the mouse adiponectin promoter with C/EBPα (CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein α). SIRT1 deacetylates FOXO1 and enhances its interaction with C/EBPα, thereby increasing adiponectin concentrations. Elevated adiponectin: Regulates energy homeostasis and glucose/lipid metabolism Improves insulin sensitivity Lowers blood glucose in obese and diabetic mouse models Is increased by Caloric Restriction in rats (possibly mediated by SIRT1) Pancreatic β-Cell Function and Insulin Secretion By deacetylating FOXO1, SIRT1 promotes activation and transcription of: NeuroD (neurogenic differentiation factor) MafA (a β-cell transcription factor) These transcription factors preserve insulin secretion and promote β-cell survival in vivo. Cancer Contexts The LXXLL motif of FOXO1 mediates its transcriptional regulation and SIRT1 binding, with implications for prostate cancer. FHL2 (four-and-a-half LIM domain protein 2) enhances SIRT1-mediated FOXO1 deacetylation in prostate cancer cells. This effect has been proposed to promote tumorigenesis in response to increased stress during aging — one context where SIRT1/FOXO1 signalling may be oncogenic. Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor FOXO1 is linked to VEGF-C upregulation in response to androgen depletion via the IGF-IR–FOXO pathway, connecting FOXO1 to tumour angiogenesis. C. elegans Orthologue (DAF-16) The C. elegans FOXO orthologue DAF-16 is required for sir-2.1-mediated lifespan extension — demonstrating that the sirtuin–FOXO axis is evolutionarily ancient. SIR-2.1 also associates with 14-3-3 proteins, directing its interaction with DAF-16 in an insulin/IGF-1-independent manner under stress conditions. List of documents that mention this entity The Beneficial and Adverse Effects of Autophagic Response to Caloric Restriction and Fasting Gluconeogenesis is reduced in the presence of insulin following the phosphorylation of FoxO1 \[,\]. mTOR signaling at a glance Inhibition of Akt following mTORC2 depletion reduces the phosphorylation of, and therefore activates, the FoxO1 and FOXO3a transcription factors, which control the expression of genes involved in stress resistance, metabolism, cell-cycle arrest and Apoptosi... sirtuins (resveratrol), gemini FOXO Transcription Factors (Stress Resistance & Autophagy) - Mechanism: SIRT1 deacetylates FoxO1 and FOXO3a. Result: This shifts FOXO-mediated transcription away from apoptosis-inducing genes and toward stress-resistance genes. sirtuins MichanSSinclairDSirtuinsinmammalsinsightsi There are four FOXOs and so far SIRT1 has been shown to deacetylate three of them: FoxO1, FOXO3a and FOXO4. The LXXLL motif of FoxO1 has been shown to be indispensable for its transcriptional regulation and for SIRT1 binding. sirtuins in health and disease s41392-022-01257-8 Moreover, SIRT6 deficiency in Macrophages resulted in inflammation with increases in acetylation and greater stability of the FoxO1. Conversely, the ectopic overexpression of SIRT6 in KO cells reduced the inflammatory response.

alzheimer_s_disease.description: Alzheimer's disease is a chronic neurodegenerative disease that usually starts slowly and gradually worsens over time. Oxidative Stress is considered a pivotal factor in its pathogenesis, often involving dysfunction in the Mitochondria and the accumulation of Amyloid Beta plaques and Tau Protein tangles. Epigenetics plays a critical role in the development and progression of Alzheimer’s Disease (AD), acting as a bridge between genetic predisposition and environmental risk factors. Unlike genetic mutations, epigenetic changes do not alter the DNA sequence itself but instead modify how genes are expressed. Alzheimer's Disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that causes brain cells to waste away (degenerate) and die. It is the most common cause of dementia. Research using Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells (iPSCs) aims to improve neuronal plasticity and memory. iPSC therapy has shown potential in increasing brain-derived neurotrophic factors and reducing neuroinflammation in mouse models. Alzheimer's Disease (AD) is the most common form of dementia, characterized by progressive cognitive decline and memory loss. Primary Epigenetic Mechanisms in AD Research has identified three main types of epigenetic modifications that are dysregulated in the brains of Alzheimer's patients: DNA Methylation: This involves the addition of a methyl group to DNA, which usually "silences" or reduces the expression of a gene. Global Hypomethylation: A general decrease in methylation across the genome has been observed in the hippocampus and entorhinal cortex of AD patients, potentially leading to the unwanted activation of genes. Gene-Specific Hypermethylation: Conversely, certain genes related to memory and synaptic plasticity often show increased methylation, which may contribute to cognitive decline. Histone Modification: Histones are proteins that package DNA into structural units called Nucleosomes. Chemical changes to these proteins can "open" or "close" the Chromatin structure. Deacetylation: In AD, a general state of histone deacetylation is often linked to a "closed" chromatin state, which prevents the expression of genes necessary for learning and memory. Non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs): These are RNA molecules that do not code for proteins but regulate gene expression at the post-transcriptional level. MicroRNA (miRNAs): Dysregulation of specific miRNAs can lead to the overproduction of amyloid-beta (Aβ) or the hyperphosphorylation of tau proteins. The Role of Aging and Environment Aging is the most significant non-genetic risk factor for AD, and it is characterized by a progressive "drift" in the Epigenome. Epigenetic Clock: AD patients often show "epigenetic age acceleration," where their brain tissue appears biologically older than their chronological age. Environmental Triggers: Factors such as diet, exercise, stress, and exposure to toxins can trigger epigenetic changes that either increase or decrease AD risk. Pathological Consequences Epigenetic dysregulation contributes to the core hallmarks of Alzheimer's: Amyloid & Tau Pathology: Epigenetic changes can upregulate genes involved in the production of amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles. Neuroinflammation: Aberrant methylation of pro-inflammatory cytokine genes can keep the brain's immune cells (microglia) in a chronic state of inflammation. Synaptic Loss: The silencing of genes responsible for synaptic plasticity directly impairs the ability of neurons to communicate, leading to memory loss. Therapeutic Potential Because epigenetic modifications are chemically reversible, they represent a promising target for new treatments: HDAC Inhibitors: Drugs that inhibit histone deacetylases (HDACs) are being studied for their ability to "re-open" chromatin and restore the expression of memory-related genes. DNA Methyltransferase (DNMT) Modulators: Tools that target DNMTs aim to correct abnormal methylation patterns. Biomarkers: Epigenetic signatures in the blood or cerebrospinal fluid are being investigated as potential early-detection biomarkers for AD. Pathology Associated with the accumulation of amyloid-beta plaques and tau tangles, which lead to neuronal dysfunction and death. Impaired Autophagy is a central feature of AD, resulting in the failure to clear these toxic protein aggregates (Proteotoxicity). Autophagy and Intervention Inducing Autophagic Flux via Intermittent Fasting (IF) or Caloric Restriction is being investigated as a therapeutic strategy. IF has been shown to reduce hippocampal atrophy and neuro-anatomic deterioration in AD patients.

stub1.description:
STIP1 homology and U-box containing protein 1 (STUB1), also known as CHIP, is an E3 ubiquitin ligase that targets phosphorylated TFEB for degradation via the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway.

Function

STUB1 (CHIP) is a chaperone-dependent E3 ubiquitin ligase that ubiquitinates misfolded proteins for Proteasome degradation. It bridges HSP70/Hsp90 chaperones to the proteasome.
Autophagy Connection

STUB1 ubiquitinates ULK1 to regulate its stability and activity. It is also involved in Chaperone-Mediated Autophagy by targeting substrates to LAMP-2A.

reactive_nitrogen_species.description: Definition Reactive Nitrogen Species (RNS) are a family of antimicrobial molecules derived from Nitric Oxide (•NO) and superoxide (O2•−) produced via the enzymatic activity of inducible Nitric Oxide Synthase (iNOS) and NADPH Oxidase, respectively. Nitric Oxide (NO•): A free radical and signaling molecule. Peroxynitrite (ONOO−): A potent oxidant formed by the reaction of nitric oxide and superoxide. Nitrogen dioxide (•NO2): Formed from the decomposition of peroxynitrite. Role in Oxidative Stress RNS act in coordination with Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS) to cause Nitrative Stress. They can damage a wide range of molecules, including Proteins (via Tyrosine Nitration), Lipids, and Nucleic Acids. Biochemistry of RNS Generation The RNS family encompasses both radical and non-radical species derived from nitrogen-containing intermediates. The primary source of all RNS is Nitric Oxide (NO•), a gaseous free radical synthesized from L-arginine and molecular oxygen by the Nitric Oxide Synthase (NOS) family — comprising neuronal (nNOS/NOS1), inducible (iNOS/NOS2), and endothelial (eNOS/NOS3) isoforms. iNOS is of particular relevance to Nitrative Stress because it is transcriptionally induced by pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1β, IFN-γ) and LPS, producing high, sustained fluxes of NO• (up to micromolar steady-state concentrations) for hours to days, in contrast to the low picomolar-to-nanomolar pulses generated by constitutive nNOS and eNOS. The major propagation pathways are as follows: Peroxynitrite (ONOO⁻) formation: The near-diffusion-limited reaction ($k \approx 1.6 \times 10^{10}$ M⁻¹s⁻¹) between NO• and Superoxide Radicals ($O2^{\bullet-}$) produces peroxynitrite, the most reactive and damaging RNS. This reaction outcompetes Superoxide Dismutase for superoxide, making peroxynitrite formation unavoidable in any microenvironment where both radicals are generated simultaneously. Nitrogen dioxide (•NO₂) and dinitrogen trioxide (N₂O₃): •NO₂ is generated from peroxynitrite decomposition ($ONOO^- + H^+ \rightarrow \bullet OH + \bullet NO2$), from the peroxidase activity of Myeloperoxidase and lactoperoxidase ($NO2^- + H2O2 \rightarrow \bullet NO2 + H2O$), and from autoxidation of NO• in the presence of O₂ ($2NO + O2 \rightarrow 2NO2$). N₂O₃ is the anhydride of nitrous acid ($HNO2$) and forms by $NO + NO2 \rightleftharpoons N2O3$. Both •NO₂ and N₂O₃ mediate S-nitrosylation (transfer of NO⁺ equivalents to cysteine thiols) and N-nitrosation (formation of nitrosamines from secondary amines). Nitroxyl (HNO): The one-electron reduced form of NO•, generated from the decomposition of S-nitrosothiols or from NOS under certain conditions (substrate or cofactor deficiency). HNO has distinct biological targets compared to NO•, including inhibition of Aldehyde Dehydrogenase and activation of TRPA1 channels, and exhibits cardiotropic effects (positive inotropy, vasodilation). Higher nitrogen oxides: Dinitrogen tetroxide (N₂O₄), nitrite ($NO2^-$), and nitrate ($NO_3^-$) are downstream metabolites that can be recycled back to NO• via the enterosalivary nitrate–nitrite–NO pathway, mediated by commensal Gut Microbiome bacteria containing nitrate reductases. Immunological Functions RNS constitute a core component of the innate immune arsenal. In macrophages, the coordinate induction of iNOS and NADPH Oxidase (NOX2) during classical (M1) activation creates a high-flux RNS/ROS environment within the phagolysosome that is potently antimicrobial. The mechanisms of pathogen killing include: Inactivation of iron-sulfur proteins: RNS attack [4Fe-4S] and [2Fe-2S] clusters in bacterial respiratory complexes and dehydratases (e.g., aconitase, fumarase), impairing pathogen metabolism. DNA damage: Nitric oxide and its derivatives (particularly peroxynitrite and N₂O₃) cause bacterial DNA Damage, including deamination of cytosine (→ uracil) and 5-methylcytosine (→ thymine) via nitrosative deamination reactions. Lipid peroxidation: Peroxynitrite and •NO₂ initiate lipid peroxidation in bacterial membranes. S-nitrosylation: S-nitrosylation of key bacterial enzymes (including those involved in respiration and transcription) inhibits pathogen growth. RNS are effective against a wide range of pathogens, including Salmonella, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Leishmania, Plasmodium (malaria), and Fungal pathogens. The importance of this pathway is underscored by the susceptibility of iNOS knockout mice to these infections. Pathological Roles and Nitrative Stress When RNS production exceeds the detoxification capacity of endogenous scavengers (Glutathione, Thioredoxin, Uric Acid), a state of Nitrative Stress emerges, characterized by widespread protein tyrosine nitration, S-nitrosylation of signaling proteins, Lipid Peroxidation, and DNA Damage.

aldehyde_dehydrogenases.description:
Aldehyde Dehydrogenases (ALDHs) are a family of enzymes that catalyze the NAD(P)+-dependent oxidation of endogenous and exogenous aldehydes to their corresponding carboxylic acids.



ALDHs participate in the cellular defense against dicarbonyl stress by oxidizing reactive intermediates, such as 3-deoxyglucosone and Methylglyoxal, into less reactive, non-toxic carboxylic acids, thereby reducing the rate of Advanced Glycation End Products (AGEs) formation.

cognitive_decline.description:
Cognitive decline is the age-associated reduction in memory, processing speed, and executive function. It is linked to Neurodegeneration, chronic inflammation, and inflammaging, and shares risk with Frailty and cardiovascular disease.

Persisting low-grade inflammation (inflammaging) is implicated in cognitive decline. The shingles vaccine study cites cognitive decline among outcomes tied to background inflammation that vaccination may help mitigate; other adult vaccines have been linked to lower dementia risk.

nitric_oxide_synthase.description: Nitric oxide synthases (NOSs) are a family of enzymes catalyzing the production of Nitric Oxide (NO) from L-arginine. They play a vital role in vascular tone and neurotransmission, and their dysfunction is often associated with Endothelial Dysfunction. Isoforms and Tissue Distribution Three distinct NOS isoforms, encoded by separate genes, differ in regulation, tissue expression, and physiological roles: Neuronal NOS (nNOS, NOS1) Gene: NOS1 (chromosome 12q24.22) Expression: Central and peripheral neurons, skeletal muscle, kidney macula densa Regulation: Calcium/calmodulin-dependent; activated by NMDA receptor stimulation and calcium influx Function: Neurotransmission, Long-term potentiation (LTP), regulation of cerebral blood flow; NO from nNOS acts as a retrograde messenger Inducible NOS (iNOS, NOS2) Gene: NOS2 (chromosome 17q11.2-q12) Expression: Macrophages, Neutrophils, hepatocytes, vascular smooth muscle, endothelial cells (induced) Regulation: Transcriptionally regulated by NF-κB, TNF-alpha, IL-1β, and LPS; calcium-independent once expressed Function: High-output NO production for innate immune defense; sustained NO at nanomolar–micromolar levels mediates Macrophage killing of pathogens Endothelial NOS (eNOS, NOS3) Gene: NOS3 (chromosome 7q36.1) Expression: Vascular endothelium, cardiac myocytes, platelets, hippocampal neurons Regulation: Calcium/calmodulin-dependent; activated by Shear Stress, VEGF, Bradykinin, Estrogen; regulated by Akt-mediated phosphorylation at Ser1177 and PP2A-mediated dephosphorylation Function: Vasodilation, inhibition of Platelet aggregation, maintenance of vascular barrier function, regulation of Angiogenesis Domain Structure and Cofactor Requirements All NOS isoforms are homodimeric flavo-hemoproteins. Each monomer consists of: C-terminal reductase domain: Binding sites for FAD, FMN, and NADPH Calmodulin-binding linker: Connecting the two domains; CaM binding enables electron flow from reductase to oxygenase Key Cofactors Cofactor Role Deficiency Consequence ---------- ------ ---------------------- BH₄ Stabilizes heme-dioxygen complex; facilitates L-arginine oxidation eNOS uncoupling → O₂⁻• production FAD Accepts electrons from NADPH Impaired electron transfer FMN Transfers electrons to heme Impaired NO synthesis Heme (Fe-protoporphyrin IX) Binds O₂ for L-arginine hydroxylation Complete loss of catalytic activity Zinc (Zn²⁺) Stabilizes dimer interface Dimer dissociation and inactivation Phosphorylation Sites Ser1177 (human eNOS): Akt-mediated activating phosphorylation (most critical) Ser633: PKA- and AMPK-mediated activation Ser114: p38 MAPK-mediated inhibitory phosphorylation under inflammatory stress Protein-Protein Interactions Caveolin-1: Binds eNOS in Caveolae, maintaining it in an inactive state; calcium-calmodulin displaces caveolin Hsp90: Facilitates Akt-mediated eNOS activation Dynamin-2: Promotes eNOS internalization in endothelial cells Subcellular Localization eNOS is predominantly membrane-associated at the Golgi apparatus and Plasma Membrane caveolae. Subcellular targeting determines coupling efficiency and NO output—Golgi-localized eNOS is more coupled, whereas plasma membrane eNOS may be more prone to uncoupling. eNOS Uncoupling: Mechanisms and Consequences When BH₄ or L-arginine are limiting, the NOS dimer reduces O₂ instead of L-arginine, producing Superoxide Radicals rather than NO. This eNOS uncoupling is a central mechanism in Endothelial Dysfunction: BH₄ oxidation: Peroxynitrite (ONOO⁻) rapidly oxidizes BH₄ to BH₂ (k ≈ 10⁶ M⁻¹s⁻¹), which cannot support coupled NO synthesis L-arginine depletion: Arginase upregulation (by TNF-alpha and IL-1β) and ADMA accumulation reduce substrate availability Cysteine oxidation: Reactive Oxygen Species oxidize the zinc-thiolate cluster (Cys96 and Cys101) in eNOS, disrupting dimerization S-glutathionylation: eNOS S-glutathionylation at Cys689 and Cys908 switches eNOS from NO to O₂⁻• production Consequences of Uncoupling Loss of NO production: Impaired vasodilation, platelet inhibition Amplification cycle: Peroxynitrite further oxidizes BH₄ and nitrates eNOS tyrosine residues, sustaining uncoupling iNOS and Inflammatory Nitrative Stress iNOS produces NO at high rates (µM/min) sustained over hours to days following LPS or cytokine stimulation. This high-output NO interacts with NADPH Oxidase-derived superoxide to generate Peroxynitrite, driving Nitrative Stress: Protein tyrosine nitration: 3-nitrotyrosine formation (biomarker of nitrative stress in Inflammation) Lipid peroxidation: Initiation by NO₂• and ONOO⁻ Mitochondrial Dysfunction: Inhibition of complex I and IV by ONOO⁻ DNA damage: Deamination and nitration of DNA bases iNOS-derived NO also exerts immunosuppressive effects by inhibiting NF-κB in a negative feedback loop and by modulating T Cell function.

tsc.description:
Overview: TSC is a cellular protein with structural, signaling, or regulatory functions in eukaryotic cells. It participates in macromolecular complexes and signaling networks that govern cell behavior.

Structure and domains: TSC contains conserved structural motifs that mediate its interactions with binding partners, nucleic acids, or lipid membranes. Post-translational modifications such as phosphorylation and ubiquitination regulate its activity.

Cellular function: TSC plays a role in signal transduction, gene expression regulation, cytoskeletal organization, or metabolic control. Its localization and activity are dynamically regulated in response to cellular cues.

Pathological significance: Altered expression or mutation of TSC is associated with cancer, neurodegenerative diseases, and developmental disorders. It serves as a biomarker and therapeutic target in multiple clinical contexts.

ice_mouse.description:
The ICE Mouse (Inducible Changes in the Epigenome) is a mammalian model developed by the Sinclair lab to test the Relocalization of Chromatin Modifiers (RCM) Hypothesis. It uses a controllable endonuclease, I-PpoI, to induce targeted double-strand breaks (DSBs) without introducing mutations, thereby isolating the epigenetic consequences of DNA repair from mutational load.

Design and Findings
Induction of DSBs, followed by repair, produces accelerated epigenetic aging and physiological decline (metabolic dysfunction, reduced tissue function, cognitive changes).
The induced changes shift the epigenetic clock, consistent with RCM.
Because no mutations are introduced, the phenotype is attributed to loss of epigenetic information rather than hardware damage — supporting the Information Theory of Aging.

Connections
David Sinclair: Lab of origin.
I-PpoI: The inducible endonuclease used.
Relocalization of Chromatin Modifiers (RCM) Hypothesis: The hypothesis it was built to test.
Double-Strand Break, Epigenetic Clock: Key mechanistic and readout elements.

benzimidazole.description:
Benzimidazole is a heterocyclic aromatic compound formed by fusing benzene with imidazole. It is a privileged scaffold in medicinal chemistry, underlying major anthelmintics and a growing repertoire of anticancer agents. Benzimidazole derivatives bind the colchicine site of β-Tubulin, disrupting Microtubule dynamics and triggering mitotic arrest and Apoptosis.

Anthelmintic Derivatives

Several benzimidazoles treat parasitic infections by binding parasite β-tubulin and blocking microtubule polymerization:
Albendazole
Mebendazole
Fenbendazole
Oxfendazole
Flubendazole
Thiabendazole

They are cornerstones of mass drug administration against soil-transmitted helminths and lymphatic filariasis (often with Ivermectin).

Anticancer Potential & Mechanisms

Repositioning benzimidazoles as anticancer agents exploits their ability to also engage mammalian tubulin and tumor metabolism:
Induce Apoptosis via G2/M arrest and mitotic catastrophe.
Inhibit Glycolysis and the Warburg Effect, notably by suppressing Hexokinase II.
Activate p53 by suppressing the E3 ligases MDM2 and MdmX.
Overcome Multidrug Resistance by evading classical P-glycoprotein efflux.

Preclinical studies report activity against glioblastoma, colorectal, breast, and leukemia models. Novel synthetic benzimidazoles (e.g., ABT-751) have entered clinical evaluation as vascular-disrupting/tubulin agents.

Structure–Activity Relationships

Electron-withdrawing substituents at the 2-position and hydrophobic groups at 5/6 enhance tubulin affinity. The carbamate side chain of albendazole/mebendazole is critical for anthelmintic but not strictly required for antitumor activity, enabling chemically tailored derivatives.

pyruvate_kinase_m2.description:
Pyruvate Kinase M2 (PKM2) is an isoenzyme of pyruvate kinase that plays a critical role in the final step of Glycolysis, converting phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) to pyruvate.

Role in Cancer
Warburg Effect: PKM2 is often overexpressed in Cancer cells. It can exist in a low-activity dimeric form or a high-activity tetrameric form. The dimeric form allows glycolytic intermediates to be diverted into biosynthetic pathways, supporting the Warburg Effect.
Non-metabolic Functions: PKM2 can also translocate to the nucleus and act as a co-activator for transcription factors like HIF-1α and β-catenin, promoting cell proliferation.
DNA Repair: PKM2 has been shown to regulate Homologous Recombination-mediated DNA double-strand break repair.

hematopoiesis.description:
Overview: Hematopoiesis is the process by which all blood cells are generated from hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs). It occurs primarily in the bone marrow and continues throughout life to replace short-lived cells.

Mechanism and regulation: HSCs self-renew and differentiate along myeloid (Macrophages, Neutrophils, erythrocytes, megakaryocytes) and lymphoid lineages. Lineage commitment is orchestrated by transcription factors, cytokines, and epigenetic modifiers within the stem cell niche. Metabolic state and nutrient sensing (mTOR, AMPK) further tune output.

Physiological function: Hematopoiesis sustains oxygen carriage, immunity, and hemostasis, and adapts cell output to infection, bleeding, and stress.

Aging and disease: With Aging, HSC function declines—a manifestation of Stem Cell Exhaustion—leading to skewed myelopoiesis, impaired lymphopoiesis, and diminished regenerative capacity. This contributes to immunodeficiency, anemia, and myeloid malignancy risk, and is intertwined with Inflammation (inflammaging) and genomic instability.

opa1.description:
OPA1 (Optic Atrophy Protein 1) is a dynamin-related GTPase anchored to the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) that mediates inner-membrane fusion in cooperation with the lipid Cardiolipin. It is the mammalian ortholog of the yeast protein Mgm1. Mutations in OPA1 are the leading cause of dominant optic atrophy (DOA), the most common inherited optic neuropathy.

Structure and Isoforms

OPA1 is produced as eight splice isoforms differing in three small N-terminal exons (4, 4b, 5b). All carry an N-terminal mitochondrial targeting sequence (MTS) that is cleaved by the matrix processing protease on import into the matrix. OPA1 is proteolytically processed at up to three sites (S1, S2, S3):
S1 (present in all isoforms) is cleaved by OMA1, yielding the short form S-OPA1; an intact S1 yields the long, membrane-anchored L-OPA1.
S2/S3 are cleaved constitutively by YME1L, also yielding S-OPA1.



Efficient IMM fusion requires L-OPA1 and S-OPA1 acting together (though some studies report L-OPA1 alone suffices). Cardiolipin binds L-OPA1 on liposomes and is absolutely required for fusion — removing cardiolipin abolishes membrane merging even with L-OPA1 on both leaflets — and GTP hydrolysis by OPA1 is essential.

Regulation

[!info] Source: document - The role of mitochondrial dynamics in disease
OPA1 is processed by OMA1 and YME1L into long (L-OPA1, membrane-anchored, promotes fusion) and short (S-OPA1, soluble) forms. Coordination of L-OPA1 and S-OPA1 is required for normal fusion under basal conditions; S-OPA1 alone can mediate GTP-dependent fusion with cardiolipin-containing liposomes. OPA1 is a key component of the mitochondrial contact site and cristae organizing system. Significant downregulation of OPA1 expression is found in heart failure and cardiac ischemia–reperfusion injury, and OPA1 mutation induces mitochondrial fragmentation leading to severe cardiomyopathy.
SIRT3 (NAD-dependent sirtuin-3) deacetylates OPA1 at Lys926 and Lys931 in its GTPase effector domain, raising GTPase activity and enhancing fusion during stress.
Proteolytic processing by OMA1 and YME1L dynamically tunes the L/S-OPA1 ratio in response to membrane potential and stress.

Pathological Significance
Dominant Optic Atrophy — mostly missense OPA1 mutations impair IMM fusion and mitochondrial function; DOA-plus includes deafness/ataxia. Disease alleles show defects in cardiolipin-stimulated GTP hydrolysis and membrane tubulation.
Parkinson's Disease — increased cleavage of the OPA1 long isoform contributes to fission excess in sporadic PD.
Cancer — OPA1-dependent fusion supports liver tumor cell metabolism and growth.

BAX Regulation

[!info] p38 MAPK Phosphorylates BAX at Thr167
Under stress conditions, p38 MAPK can phosphorylate BAX at Thr167, the same residue targeted by ERK2 for survival signaling. Unlike ERK-mediated phosphorylation (which promotes Pin1 binding and BAX inactivation), p38-mediated phosphorylation promotes BAX activation and apoptosis. This makes Thr167 a molecular coincidence detector where the cellular context determines the outcome.

ribosomal_protein_s6.description:
Ribosomal Protein S6 (rpS6, RPS6) is a constituent of the 40S ribosomal subunit. Its phosphorylation at multiple serine residues by S6K1 (itself activated by mTORC1) is the classic readout of mTORC1 signaling activity.

Role as an mTOR Biomarker

Phosphorylated ribosomal protein S6 (phospho-S6) is widely used as a surrogate marker of mTORC1 activation in both resected tissues and preclinical models—for example, to confirm mTOR pathway hyperactivation in TSC and other mTORopathies (Meikle et al., 2008; Crino, 2015).

[!warning] Inconsistent clinical biomarker
Although phospho-S6 is a robust research biomarker, it has not proven consistent as a clinical biomarker in humans, complicating the correlation between mTOR inhibition depth, drug blood levels, and therapeutic effect—especially in the heterogeneous context of Aging (Roark & Iffland, 2025).

Standardizing phospho-S6 and other pharmacodynamic measurements is considered essential for rigorous translation of rapamycin from models to human longevity trials.

adp.description:
Adenosine diphosphate (ADP) is the low-energy adenine nucleotide produced when ATP loses its terminal phosphate to perform cellular work. The ATP/ADP ratio is the central gauge of cellular energy charge, and a rising ADP (or AMP) concentration is the immediate signal of an energy deficit that initiates mitohormetic adaptations.

Recycling to ATP

ADP is rephosphorylated to ATP through two principal routes:
The phosphocreatine shuttle: Creatine accepts a phosphate from ATP (via creatine kinase) to form phosphocreatine; during high-demand moments phosphocreatine rapidly donates the phosphate back to ADP, recycling ATP within milliseconds. This buffers the ATP/ADP ratio during intense effort and protects HRV from plunging.
Oxidative phosphorylation: The electron transport chain and ATP synthase use the proton-motive force to phosphorylate ADP to ATP in the mitochondria.

Role in Mitohormesis

A transient rise in ADP (and AMP) during exercise or fasting signals a cellular energy deficit, activating AMPK, which in turn stimulates PGC-1α and mitochondrial biogenesis. Sustaining cellular energy pools with creatine reduces metabolic stress and supports recovery.

haloperidol.description:
Haloperidol is a first-generation (typical) antipsychotic of the butyrophenone class, widely used to treat schizophrenia, acute psychosis, and agitation, and for antiemesis. It exerts its therapeutic effect primarily as a potent antagonist of the D2 receptor (dopamine D2 receptor) in the mesolimbic and nigrostriatal pathways. Beyond receptor blockade, haloperidol has drawn neurotoxicological interest because it can be metabolically converted into the pyridinium neurotoxin HPP+.

Pharmacodynamics and Pharmacokinetics
Haloperidol blocks central D2-like receptors, relieving positive psychotic symptoms but also disrupting the nigrostriatal dopaminergic tone that regulates movement—accounting for its high liability for extrapyramidal side effects and drug-induced parkinsonism. It is extensively metabolized in the liver by CYP3A4 and CYP2D6 (via reduction, N-dealkylation, and oxidation) and undergoes carbonyl reduction. A minor but consequential pathway generates the pyridinium ion HPP+ (4-(4-chlorophenyl)-1-[4-(4-fluorophenyl)-4-oxobutyl]pyridinium).

Chemical Process: Formation of HPP+
Haloperidol's keto-reduced metabolite is oxidized to a pyridinium species structurally analogous to MPP+ (the active toxin of MPTP). Like MPP+, HPP+ is a charged, membrane-impermeant cation that can be taken up by dopaminergic neurons via the dopamine transporter and accumulates in mitochondria, where it inhibits complex I of the electron transport chain. This mechanistic parallelism to MPTP/MPP+ provides a molecular rationale for haloperidol-associated parkinsonism and for rare cases of tardive dyskinesia and neurotoxicity.

Physiological and Clinical Relevance
Haloperidol remains valuable clinically, but its dopaminergic blockade produces acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, and, with chronic use, tardive dyskinesia. The HPP+ hypothesis adds a mitochondrial/oxidative dimension: if HPP+ forms in sufficient amounts, it may directly damage the same Substantia Nigra Neuromelanin neurons that degenerate in Parkinson's Disease. This has motivated research into whether haloperidol use accelerates PD risk or severity, and into whether CYP2D6 genotype (affecting HPP+ formation) modulates vulnerability.

Pathology and Research Implications
The structural kinship between HPP+ and MPP+ makes haloperidol a useful pharmacological tool for modeling selective dopaminergic neurotoxicity, and a cautionary example of how an antipsychotic can engage Mitochondrial Dysfunction and Oxidative Stress. Mitigation strategies include using lower-potency or atypical antipsychotics when parkinsonism risk is a concern. Overall, haloperidol illustrates the intersection of receptor pharmacology and metabolic neurotoxicology in catecholaminergic neuron injury.

leucine.description:
Overview

Leucine is an essential branched-chain amino acid and the primary nutritional activator of mTORC1, making it a key anabolic signal for skeletal muscle. It is one of the three BCAAs (with isoleucine and valine).

Mechanism of Action & Physiology

Leucine (and its metabolite α-ketoisocaproate) activates the Rag GTPase complex and upstream regulators to recruit mTORC1 to the lysosome, stimulating translation initiation and muscle protein synthesis—counteracting Muscle Atrophy. It also modulates insulin sensitivity and energy metabolism.

Leucine and Dietary Restriction

Leucine is the most potent amino-acid activator of mTORC1, so leucine restriction is a candidate driver of Protein Restriction benefits. In model organisms, dietary leucine restriction alone recapitulates many hallmarks of protein restriction, including suppressed mTORC1 signaling, reduced hepatic steatosis, and improved metabolic health. Its restriction phenotype overlaps with but is less complete than restriction of the other branched-chain amino acids.

[!info] Source: The Hallmarks of Protein and Amino Acid Restriction
Among individual EAAs, leucine (with isoleucine and valine) is one of the key drivers of the protein-restriction response. Decreased leucine in the diet acts primarily through suppression of mTORC1, whereas the effects of isoleucine and valine restriction depend more on amino-acid sensing pathways such as GCN2.

Applications

Used clinically and as a supplement to support muscle mass in aging, exercise recovery, and catabolic states. Often paired with Creatine or Urolithin A in muscle-health strategies.

mdm2.description:
MDM2 (Mouse double minute 2 homolog) is a nuclear phosphoprotein that functions as the primary negative regulator of the p53 tumor suppressor protein.

Mechanism
MDM2 regulates p53 through several mechanisms:
E3 Ubiquitin Ligase: MDM2 acts as an E3 ligase that targets p53 for degradation by the proteasome.
Transcriptional Inhibition: MDM2 binds to the N-terminal transactivation domain of p53, directly blocking its ability to activate target genes.
Nuclear Export: MDM2 promotes the export of p53 from the nucleus to the cytoplasm.


Oncogene: The MDM2 gene is frequently amplified or overexpressed in many human cancers (e.g., sarcomas, glioblastoma), leading to the inactivation of p53 even in the absence of mutations.
Drug Target: Inhibiting the MDM2-p53 interaction (e.g., with Nutlins) is a major therapeutic strategy to restore p53 function.

il_7.description:
Interleukin 7 (IL-7) is a 25 kDa glycoprotein cytokine produced by stromal cells in the thymus and bone marrow. It is essential for T cell survival, differentiation, and homeostatic proliferation in both thymic and peripheral compartments.

Structure and Receptor
Molecular weight: 25 kDa glycoprotein
Receptor: IL-7R (composed of IL-7Rα/CD127 and γc/CD132)
Expression: IL-7R is expressed on lymphoid precursors, CD3⁻CD4⁻CD8⁻ (triple negative) thymocytes, CD4⁺CD8⁺ (double positive) thymocytes, and single-positive CD4 or CD8 T cells
Signaling: JAK1/JAK3 → STAT5 → Bcl-2 upregulation (anti-apoptotic)

Biological Functions


Promotes survival and differentiation of immature triple-negative thymocytes
Supports positive selection in the cortex
Essential for TCR gene rearrangement during early thymopoiesis

Peripheral effects
Regulates naïve and memory CD4 and CD8 T cell homeostasis
Maintains T cell survival via Bcl-2 expression
Expansion of both naïve and memory T cell pools upon exogenous administration

Therapeutic Applications

Recombinant human IL-7 (CYT 99 007) has been tested in clinical settings:
Low toxicity with dose-dependent sustained expansion of naïve and memory T cells
Restored thymopoiesis in IL-7-deficient mice
Expanded CD8⁺ and CD4⁺ T cells in human trials (Rosenberg et al., 2006)
No open trials focused specifically on thymus rejuvenation as of 2013

[!info] Cross-talk network
IL-7 production by TECs is stimulated by IGF-1, linking growth hormone signaling to thymic function. This positions IL-7 as a downstream effector of GH-mediated thymic rejuvenation.

comt.description: COMT (Catechol-O-methyltransferase) is one of the primary enzymes responsible for the degradation of Catecholamines, including Dopamine, Norepinephrine, and Epinephrine. It is essential for protecting cells from Oxidative Stress by preventing the accumulation of catecholamines and protecting the body from reactive Catechols. Biochemical Function The enzyme performs a Methylation reaction, transferring a methyl group from SAMe (S-adenosylmethionine) to a catechol substrate. This process requires Magnesium as a cofactor and is facilitated by the Methylation Cycle. COMT is also involved in the metabolism of catechol Estrogen metabolites. COMT exists in two distinct forms encoded by the same gene: Soluble COMT (S-COMT): The predominant form in peripheral tissues (liver, kidney, blood). Contains 221 amino acids. Membrane-bound COMT (MB-COMT): The predominant form in the brain. Contains 271 amino acids with an additional N-terminal transmembrane domain. MB-COMT has a higher affinity (lower K~m~) for catecholamine substrates than S-COMT, making it more relevant for neurotransmitter metabolism at physiological concentrations. Genetics The COMT gene is located on chromosome 22q11.21 and is well-known for the Val158Met SNP (rs4680), which significantly impacts enzyme activity: Fast COMT (Val/Val, G/G): High enzyme activity (3–4× faster than Met/Met), leading to lower levels of synaptic dopamine. Often called the "warrior" type, associated with better stress resilience but potentially poorer cognitive performance on complex tasks. Intermediate COMT (Val/Met, A/G): Balanced enzyme activity with one high-activity and one low-activity allele. Slow COMT (Met/Met, A/A): Low enzyme activity (3–4× reduced), leading to higher baseline synaptic dopamine. Often called the "worrier" type, associated with higher anxiety and stress sensitivity but potentially superior performance on cognitive tasks requiring sustained attention. Population frequencies vary: the Met/Met (slow) genotype occurs in approximately 20–30% of European-ancestry individuals, while the Val/Val (fast) genotype is found in about 29% of Caucasians and 52% of Chinese Han populations. Role in Adrenochrome Pathway Under normal conditions, COMT and Monoamine oxidase (MAO) are the dominant routes for adrenaline metabolism. If COMT is inhibited (e.g., by drugs used in Parkinson's disease or certain Flavonoids like Quercetin), levels of Epinephrine can rise. This increased substrate availability, combined with Oxidative Stress, may shift more adrenaline toward the minor Adrenochrome oxidative pathway via autoxidation. Fisetin as a COMT Substrate-Inhibitor [!info] Source: COMT × Fisetin Research Evaluation Fisetin is a validated COMT inhibitor with IC₅₀ values of 2.6–5.8 µM (mixed competitive + noncompetitive inhibition). Critically, fisetin is not merely a passive inhibitor — it is a substrate-inhibitor that is itself O-methylated by COMT to generate the active metabolite Geraldol. At low concentrations fisetin acts primarily as a substrate; at higher concentrations it acts as a competitive inhibitor. This process consumes SAMe and generates SAH, a potent feedback inhibitor of COMT. Compound COMT IC₅₀ (µM) Mechanism ---------- ---------------- ----------- Quercetin 0.9–1.5 Competitive (catechol substrate) Fisetin 2.6–5.8 Mixed (competitive + noncompetitive) EGCG 0.04–0.07 Tight-binding inhibitor Entacapone (clinical) ~0.23 Competitive (nitrocatechol) Tolcapone (clinical) ~0.048 Competitive (nitrocatechol) Fisetin's COMT inhibition potency is moderate—~10–50× weaker than clinical COMT inhibitors but within the range achievable through dietary supplementation. Because COMT activity varies 3–4 fold across Val158Met genotypes, fisetin's effects are genotype-sensitive. No clinical trial has yet stratified fisetin outcomes by COMT genotype. The overlap between COMT-inhibitory and senolytic concentration ranges has not been established. Clinical Relevance COMT Inhibitors in Parkinson's Disease COMT inhibitors (entacapone, tolcapone, opicapone) are used as adjuncts to levodopa therapy in Parkinson's Disease. By blocking COMT, these drugs prolong the half-life of levodopa and increase its bioavailability to the brain. However, blocking this primary exit route for catecholamines can theoretically increase the production of Aminochromes like Dopaminochrome and Adrenochrome under oxidative conditions.

neuromelanin.description:
Neuromelanin is a dark pigment found in specific populations of catecholaminergic neurons in the brain, most notably in the substantia nigra and locus coeruleus.

Neuromelanin (NM) is a dark brown to black intracellular pigment found primarily in the human brain, specifically within catecholaminergic neurons. It is most abundant in the Substantia Nigra (SN) and the Locus Coeruleus.

Formation
It is formed through the polymerization of Aminochromes, which are oxidative intermediates of Catecholamines. 
This process involves the conversion of the catechol ring into a quinone, followed by cyclization and polymerization.

Protective Role
Research suggests Neuromelanin may act as a protective "sponge" or sequestration system. By trapping and incorporating toxic Aminochromes, quinones, and heavy metals (like iron) into its stable polymer structure, it prevents them from causing neuronal damage.

Age-Related Accumulation
Neuromelanin levels are virtually absent at birth and progressively increase with age, peaking in middle-to-late adulthood. This accumulation reflects the cumulative history of catecholamine Oxidation in the brain and is linked to the process of aging and chronic Inflammation.

Clinical Significance
Parkinson's Disease: Characterized by the selective loss of neuromelanin-containing neurons in the substantia nigra.
Neurotoxicity: While neuromelanin is protective, its release during neuronal death can trigger further Inflammation and exacerbate neurodegeneration.

Biological Functions
Under normal physiological conditions, neuromelanin is thought to serve several neuroprotective roles:
Metal Chelation: NM has a high affinity for transition metals, particularly Iron. By sequestering free iron, it prevents the formation of reactive oxygen species via the Fenton reaction.
Detoxification: It is formed from the oxidation of cytosolic Dopamine and other catechols, effectively removing potentially toxic quinones from the cytoplasm.
Antioxidant Activity: NM can act as a scavenger for free radicals, protecting neurons from Oxidative Stress.

Role in Parkinson's Disease
In Parkinson's Disease, the relationship between neuromelanin and neuronal health becomes pathological:
Selective Vulnerability: Neurons containing high levels of NM, such as those in the Substantia Nigra Pars Compacta, are the ones that preferentially degenerate in PD.
Pathogenic Threshold: Progressive accumulation of NM with age may eventually reach a Pathogenic Threshold of Neuromelanin, where it interferes with cellular proteostasis and lysosomal function.
Neuroinflammation: The release of NM from dying neurons into the extracellular space triggers Microgliosis and a chronic inflammatory response, which contributes to further neurodegeneration.

atp.description: Adenosine triphosphate (ATP) is a nucleotide composed of adenine, ribose, and three phosphate groups that serves as the universal energy currency of living cells. Hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and Pi (or AMP and PPi) releases free energy used to drive endergonic biochemical reactions. Structure ATP consists of: Adenine — a purine nitrogenous base Ribose — a pentose sugar (β-D-ribofuranose) Triphosphate moiety — three phosphate groups (α, β, γ) linked by phosphoanhydride bonds The γ-phosphate is the high-energy phosphate most commonly hydrolyzed. The phosphoanhydride bonds between phosphate groups have a high ΔG°′ of approximately −30.5 kJ/mol under standard conditions. Production ATP is generated by three major pathways: Glycolysis produces 2 ATP per Glucose molecule via substrate-level phosphorylation (Hexokinase, Phosphofructokinase-1, Pyruvate Kinase). This occurs in the Cytosol and does not require Oxygen. The mitochondrial Electron Transport Chain (Complex I–Complex IV) creates a Proton Gradient across the Inner Mitochondrial Membrane. ATP Synthase (Complex V) uses the proton motive force to generate approximately 32–34 ATP per glucose via chemiosmosis. This is the dominant pathway under aerobic conditions. Substrate-Level Phosphorylation The TCA Cycle (Krebs cycle) produces 1 GTP per turn (equivalent to 1 ATP) via Succinyl-CoA Synthetase. Cellular Roles ATP powers nearly every energy-requiring process in the cell: Active Transport — Sodium Potassium ATPase, Ca²⁺ ATPase, V-ATPase, ABC transporters Protein Synthesis — ~4 ATP equivalents per peptide bond (aminoacyl-tRNA formation + ribosome translocation) DNA Replication and Transcription — dNTP incorporation and RNA polymerization Cytoskeletal Dynamics — Actin polymerization, Myosin-Actin sliding in Muscle Contraction Signal Transduction — ATP-dependent kinases (PKA, PKC, MAPK), Adenylyl Cyclase for cAMP production Autophagy — V-ATPase maintains Lysosome acidification; ULK1 and AMPK are ATP-sensing kinases Cellular ATP concentration is typically maintained at 2–10 mM. The ATP/ADP and ATP/AMP ratios are tightly regulated. AMPK (AMP-activated protein kinase) serves as the primary cellular energy sensor — it is activated by rising AMP and falling ATP, triggering catabolic pathways and suppressing anabolic processes. Relevance to Aging and Disease Mitochondrial Dysfunction with age impairs ATP production, contributing to Sarcopenia, Neurodegeneration, and Metabolic Syndrome. Caloric Restriction and Exercise enhance mitochondrial efficiency and ATP synthesis. Many Geroprotectors — including Metformin, Rapamycin, and NAD+ precursors — act partly by improving cellular energy homeostasis. oxidative_phosphorylation.description:
Definition: Oxidative Phosphorylation is a fundamental biological process that maintains cellular and organismal homeostasis. It involves coordinated molecular events regulated by signaling pathways and environmental cues.
Mechanism: The process of Oxidative Phosphorylation is executed by specific protein complexes, organelles, and signaling cascades. Key regulatory nodes control its initiation, progression, and termination.
Physiological importance: Oxidative Phosphorylation is essential for development, tissue maintenance, stress adaptation, and energy homeostasis. Dysregulation of this process contributes to aging and disease.
Regulation and dysregulation: Oxidative Phosphorylation is controlled by nutrient sensors, stress pathways, and hormonal signals. Impairment of this process is linked to metabolic diseases, neurodegeneration, and cancer.
Epigenetics Context
Oxidative Phosphorylation (or OXPHOS) is the metabolic pathway in which cells use enzymes to oxidize nutrients, thereby releasing the chemical energy stored within in order to produce adenosine triphosphate (ATP).

MYC-Driven OXPHOS in Cancer

[!info] Source: document - Complex I drives glutamine-dependent TCA cycle to support viability of MYChigh breast cancer cells (NAD+)
Elevated OXPHOS is a hallmark of MYC^high^ cancer cells. Analysis of 1009 cell lines (CCLE) and 105 TNBC tumor samples (TCGA) shows that increasing MYC activity is accompanied by progressively stronger enrichment of mitochondrial respiration programs. This association is corroborated in single-cell and spatial transcriptomics of TNBC. MYC couples high respiration to anabolic demand: Complex I-regenerated NAD+ sustains a glutamine-fueled TCA cycle that produces biosynthetic precursors.

This finding contrasts with the classical Warburg Effect model, which emphasizes non-mitochondrial glycolysis. Many cancers — including diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (OXPHOS-DLBCL), melanoma, colorectal cancer, and glioblastoma — have elevated mitochondrial activity.

phosphoglycerate_mutase.description:
Overview

Phosphoglycerate mutase (PGAM1) is a glycolytic enzyme that converts 3-phosphoglycerate to 2-phosphoglycerate, a central step of Glycolysis. Beyond its catalytic role, PGAM1 regulates the pentose-phosphate pathway by controlling 3-phosphoglycerate levels, a key inhibitor of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase.

Mechanism

SIRT2 deacetylates phosphoglycerate mutase at Lys100, activating it. Enhanced PGAM1 activity channels glycolytic carbon toward NADPH production and promotes tumor growth, particularly in lung cancer. Deacetylation of Lys100 relieves inhibitory acetylation, increasing the enzyme's catalytic rate.

[!warning] Two-faced sirtuin
SIRT2's deacetylation of PGAM1 accelerates glycolysis and NADPH generation, fueling anabolism in cancer. This illustrates SIRT2's context-dependent, often harmful metabolic face versus the protective SIRT1/SIRT3/SIRT6 axis.

Physiological Function

In normal cells, PGAM1 supports glycolytic flux and coordination with the Pentose Phosphate Pathway. SIRT2-dependent activation amplifies this coupling, favoring NADPH and ribose production that support proliferation.

Clinical Relevance

PGAM1 is overexpressed in many cancers and is a candidate therapeutic target. The SIRT2–PGAM1 interaction suggests SIRT2 inhibition may limit tumor glycolysis, though systemic SIRT2 inhibition must be weighed against its other, sometimes protective, roles.

cardiac_fibrosis.description:
Cardiac fibrosis is a pathological process characterized by excessive deposition of extracellular matrix (collagen) in the myocardium, driven by cardiac fibroblast activation and differentiation into myofibroblasts. It is a key structural hallmark of adverse cardiac remodeling in heart failure, myocardial infarction, and hypertensive heart disease. TGF-β (transforming growth factor-β) is a central profibrotic cytokine that drives myofibroblast differentiation via Smad signaling.

Etiology & Pathophysiology

Cardiac fibrosis results from chronic injury signals — pressure overload, ischemia, inflammation, and neurohumoral activation (Angiotensin II) — that stimulate TGF-β/Smad signaling, fibroblast proliferation, and excessive collagen deposition. Sustained fibrosis impairs myocardial compliance and electrical conduction, progressing to heart failure and arrhythmia.

Sirtuin Involvement (Wu et al., 2022)
SIRT1 and SIRT3: Resveratrol-mediated activation attenuates fibrosis via inhibition of the TGF-β/Smad3 pathway.
SIRT6: Systemic knockout induces cardiac fibrosis via TGF-β/Smad3 activation, whereas it prevents Ang II-mediated fibrosis through AMPK–ACE2 signaling.
SIRT2: Overexpression is protective, promoting AMPK activation via LKB1 deacetylation.
SIRT5: Knockout increases fibrosis compared with age-matched wild-type mice.
SIRT4: Contributes to fibrosis — global knockout confers resistance to Ang II infusion.
SIRT7: Inconsistent — enhanced expression/phosphorylation promotes fibrosis via Smad2/ERK, yet SIRT7 knockout is also reported to result in fibrosis.

Therapeutic Implications

Sirtuin activators (e.g., resveratrol) represent candidate antifibrotic interventions. The predominantly protective SIRT1/SIRT3/SIRT6/SIRT2 axis and the pro-fibrotic contributions of SIRT4 make the NAD⁺–sirtuin network a promising target for limiting cardiac fibrosis and maladaptive remodeling.

neutrophils.description:
Neutrophils (also known as polymorphonuclear leukocytes or granulocytes) are the most abundant type of white blood cell and serve as the first line of defense in the innate immune system.
Neutrophils are the most abundant type of granulocytes and a central part of the innate immune system, capable of generating Hypochlorous Acid via Myeloperoxidase during the respiratory burst.
Role in Adrenochrome Production
Neutrophils are a major site of Epinephrine Oxidation in humans. When activated during an infection or Inflammation, they undergo a respiratory burst, producing massive quantities of Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS).
Mechanism: ROS like Superoxide anion and Hydroxyl radical, along with the enzyme Myeloperoxidase, drive the radical chain process that converts adrenaline into Adrenochrome.
Impact: In certain inflammatory conditions, this pathway can account for over 80% of adrenaline oxidation, far exceeding normal enzymatic degradation.
Locations of Activity
Infected Tissues: Any site of acute infection.
Lungs: Prominent in conditions like pneumonia, ARDS, and COPD exacerbations.
Heart: Recruited to cardiac tissue during myocardial infarction.
Biological Significance
While essential for killing pathogens, the oxidative environment created by neutrophils can lead to localized Oxidative Stress and the formation of potentially toxic byproducts like Adrenochrome.

selective_serotonin_reuptake_inhibitors.description:
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are a major class of antidepressant that block the Serotonin transporter (SERT), increasing synaptic serotonin availability. Common members include fluoxetine, sertraline, paroxetine, citalopram, escitalopram, and fluvoxamine.

Pharmacodynamics
SSRIs bind the presynaptic serotonin transporter, preventing reuptake and prolonging serotonergic neurotransmission at Serotonin Receptors. Therapeutic antidepressant effects emerge over weeks and are attributed to downstream neuroplastic and receptor-sensitivity changes rather than the acute increase in synaptic serotonin. SSRIs are also used for anxiety disorders, obsessive–compulsive disorder, and some neuropathic pain states.

Adverse Interactions
Because SSRIs raise synaptic serotonin, combining them with a Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitor can cause Serotonin Syndrome — a potentially life-threatening syndrome of hyperthermia, clonus, autonomic instability, and altered mental status. A washout period is required when switching between classes. Notably, Methylene blue possesses MAO-A–inhibitory activity at the doses used clinically, so concurrent SSRI use is contraindicated and can precipitate serotonin syndrome.

[!warning] Drug Interaction
Methylene blue's MAO-A inhibition makes co-administration with SSRIs (and SNRIs) dangerous; avoid combination or observe strict washout.

ischemic_stroke.description:
Ischemic Stroke is acute brain injury caused by focal arterial occlusion — typically thromboembolic — that deprives downstream tissue of oxygen and glucose. It accounts for roughly 85% of all strokes, the remainder being hemorrhagic.

Etiology & Pathophysiology
Occlusion mechanisms: large-artery atherosclerosis, cardioembolism (e.g. atrial fibrillation), small-vessel (lacunar) disease, and cryptogenic causes.
Ischemic core vs. penumbra: the core suffers rapid necrosis from ATP depletion and loss of ion gradients, while the surrounding penumbra is hypoperfused but potentially salvageable — the target of reperfusion therapy.
Injury cascade: Hypoxia collapses Oxidative Phosphorylation, triggering Excitotoxicity (glutamate-driven calcium influx), Mitochondrial Dysfunction, and a surge of Reactive Oxygen Species. Ischemia-reperfusion Injury adds a secondary oxidative burst upon restored blood flow.

Clinical Presentation & Management
Sudden focal deficits (hemiparesis, aphasia, visual loss); diagnosis relies on non-contrast CT/MRI to exclude hemorrhage.
Standard care: IV thrombolysis (tPA) within the therapeutic window and mechanical thrombectomy for large-vessel occlusion.

Investigational Neuroprotection

[!info] Methylene blue rationale
Methylene blue can act as an alternative electron carrier that bypasses damaged Mitochondrial Electron Transport Chain complexes, sustaining ATP production and lowering Mitochondrial Superoxide. This has motivated its study as a neuroprotectant across stroke, Traumatic Brain Injury, and neurodegeneration.

hypobromous_acid.description:
Chemical Properties

Hypobromous acid (HOBr) is a reactive oxygen halogen species produced when Eosinophil Peroxidase uses bromide and Hydrogen Peroxide to brominate targets. It is the eosinophil analog of neutrophil-produced Hypochlorous Acid (HOCl) and is similarly reactive toward proteins, particularly at tyrosine, histidine, and thiol residues.

Production & Physiology

In eosinophilic inflammation such as allergic asthma and helminth infections, activated eosinophils release Eosinophil Peroxidase, which catalyzes HOBr formation. HOBr is the principal brominating oxidant of the phagocyte arsenal.

[!info]
HOBr is less studied than HOCl, and bromination biomarkers are less established. Bromotyrosine adducts are elevated in allergic airway disease and serve as specific markers of eosinophil-mediated oxidant damage.

Pathological Role

HOBr brominates protein residues, generating stable 3-bromotyrosine adducts that are used as biomarkers of eosinophil activation in asthma and other eosinophilic conditions. Uncontrolled HOBr production contributes to tissue damage and oxidative stress in allergic airway disease.

pepck.description:
Overview

Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK) catalyzes the committed step of Gluconeogenesis, converting oxaloacetate to phosphoenolpyruvate. It is a key control point for hepatic glucose output and for glyceroneogenesis in adipose tissue.

Mechanism

SIRT2 activates PEPCK via deacetylation, a regulatory axis that also involves FOXO transcription factors, c-Myc, and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase. SIRT2-mediated deacetylation of PEPCK increases gluconeogenic capacity, influencing transcription, glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, and NADPH/redox balance.

[!info] Metabolic integration
SIRT2 deacetylation of PEPCK coordinates glucose production with pentose-phosphate-pathway flux (via G6PD), coupling gluconeogenesis to NADPH generation and redox status.

Physiological Function

PEPCK is essential for maintaining blood glucose during fasting and for lactate/glycerol recycling. SIRT2-dependent regulation connects cellular NAD+ status and sirtuin activity to whole-body glucose homeostasis, opposing or complementing the insulin-dependent control of gluconeogenic gene expression.

Clinical Relevance

Dysregulated PEPCK activity contributes to hyperglycemia in diabetes. SIRT2 modulation is being explored as a metabolic intervention, though its effects are context-dependent (see Phosphoglycerate Mutase for SIRT2's pro-glycolytic, tumor-promoting face).

gkrp.description:
GKRP (glucokinase regulatory protein, gene GCKR) is an inhibitory binding partner of glucokinase in the liver. It sequesters glucokinase in the nucleus, lowering its activity, and releases it in response to glucose and fructose-6-phosphate, thereby regulating hepatic glucose uptake and disposal.

Sirtuin Regulation
SIRT2 promotes glucose-dependent hepatic glucose uptake by deacetylating GKRP at K126.

Physiological Function

By gating glucokinase availability, GKRP sets the threshold for hepatic glucose phosphorylation and clearance. Its acetylation state modulates this gating, with SIRT2-mediated deacetylation enhancing glucose uptake.

Clinical Relevance

GKRP is a druggable node in hepatic glucose metabolism and type 2 diabetes. SIRT2 regulation of GKRP adds to the sirtuin control of glucose homeostasis.

fis1.description:
Overview

[!info] Source: document - The role of mitochondrial dynamics in disease
FIS1 plays a key role in yeast mitochondrial fission, but its role is less significant in mammalian cells — mammalian cells lacking FIS1 show little or no fission defect. Instead, FIS1 is necessary for some forms of mitophagy. FIS1 recruits DRP1 to participate in mitochondrial asymmetrical fission, whereas MFF is uniquely related to symmetrical fission. FIS1 overexpression increases mitochondrial fragmentation, leading to dysfunction and increased autophagosome formation.

FIS1 (mitochondrial fission 1 protein) is an outer mitochondrial membrane protein that serves as a receptor for DRP1 (dynamin-related protein 1), recruiting it to the mitochondrial surface to drive mitochondrial fission. It is a key component of the mitochondrial fission machinery and plays important roles in mitophagy, Apoptosis, and mitochondrial dynamics.

Role in Cellular Senescence

[!info] Source: document - Mitochondrial dysfunction in cellular senescence a bridge to neurodegenerative disease
In senescent cells, FIS1 expression is downregulated, contributing to an elongated and interconnected mitochondrial morphology that impairs mitophagy. Knockdown of FIS1 leads to a senescent morphology with increased SA-β-gal activity, while reintroducing FIS1 reduces SA-β-gal activity. The effect on senescence is mediated through OPA1, as OPA1 knockdown reverses the senescent phenotype in FIS1-deficient cells.

Connections
DRP1 — FIS1 recruits DRP1 to mitochondria to execute fission; both are downregulated in senescence
OPA1 — Mitochondrial fusion protein that opposes FIS1/DRP1-mediated fission; OPA1 knockdown rescues senescence in FIS1-depleted cells
Mitophagy — Mitochondrial fission via FIS1 is a prerequisite for mitophagy; reduced FIS1 impairs mitophagy
MFN1 — Mitofusin 1 promotes fusion, functionally opposing FIS1 action in mitochondrial dynamics
Alzheimer's Disease — FIS1 expression changes in favor of fission in AD brain, unlike the elongation seen in senescence

MFF — Fellow DRP1 recruiter; works with FIS1, MID49, MID51; uniquely related to symmetrical fission
MID49 / MID51 — Additional DRP1-recruiting adaptors

superoxide_radicals.description:
Superoxide radicals (O₂•⁻) are reactive oxygen species (ROS) formed by the addition of a single electron to molecular oxygen (O₂). They are the "primary" ROS that initiate formation of Hydrogen Peroxide, Hydroxyl Radicals, and Peroxynitrite.

Generation Mechanisms

Mitochondrial superoxide is produced mainly at Complex I (during reverse electron transport) and Complex III (via semiquinone autoxidation). Under physiological conditions ~1–3% of consumed O₂ escapes as superoxide, rising under Hypoxia or respiratory-chain impairment. Extramitochondrial sources include NADPH Oxidase (NOX1–5, DUOX), which actively generates superoxide; Xanthine Oxidase during purine catabolism; and Monoamine oxidase, whose amine catabolism yields Hydrogen Peroxide. In phagocytes, the Respiratory Burst via NOX2 (gp91phox) produces superoxide for microbial killing.

Disproportionation and SOD

At neutral pH, spontaneous dismutation is slow (~2 × 10⁵ M⁻¹s⁻¹), but Superoxide Dismutase accelerates it to ~2 × 10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹—diffusion-limited. Three isoforms exist: cytosolic CuZnSOD (SOD1), mitochondrial MnSOD (SOD2), and extracellular CuZnSOD (SOD3). The product is always Hydrogen Peroxide, further detoxified by Catalase or Glutathione Peroxidase.


Superoxide preferentially oxidizes iron–sulfur ([4Fe-4S]) dehydratases such as Aconitase (TCA cycle) and fumarase, releasing Fe²⁺ that fuels the Fenton Reaction—a feed-forward amplifier of Hydroxyl Radicals. Its near-diffusion-limited reaction (k ≈ 6.7 × 10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹) with Nitric Oxide forms Peroxynitrite (ONOO⁻), a potent nitrating species underlying much NO-overproduction toxicity. Superoxide also reduces cytochrome c (Fe³⁺→Fe²⁺), modulating Apoptosis via the permeability transition pore.

Pathological Significance

Superoxide overproduction drives Ischemia-reperfusion Injury (reoxygenation burst from damaged Mitochondria and Xanthine Oxidase). In Cardiovascular Disease, NOX-derived superoxide consumes Nitric Oxide (an "NO sink"), impairing vasodilation and promoting Atherosclerosis. In Neurodegenerative Diseases such as Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis, SOD1 mutations cause toxic gain-of-function increasing superoxide and aggregation. Genetic NOX2 defects cause chronic granulomatous disease—recurrent infections from failed Respiratory Burst.

non_coding_rna.description:
Non-coding RNA (ncRNA) refers to RNA molecules that are not translated into proteins. Once thought to be "junk," ncRNAs are now recognized as powerful regulators of the Epigenome and are involved in almost every aspect of cell biology, including Aging.
The most important types of ncRNA in the context of epigenetics include:
   MicroRNA (miRNA): Small RNAs that regulate gene expression post-transcriptionally.
   Long Non-coding RNA (lncRNA): RNAs longer than 200 nucleotides that can act as scaffolds for chromatin-modifying complexes.
   Circular RNA (circRNA): Stable RNAs that can act as "sponges" for miRNAs.
Role in Epigenetic Regulation
Non-coding RNAs interact deeply with other epigenetic marks:
   Chromatin Remodeling: Many lncRNAs recruit enzymes like HMTs or HDACs to specific genomic locations.
   X-Inactivation: The lncRNA Xist is the classic example of an ncRNA that drives large-scale epigenetic silencing.
Changes During Aging
The expression of various ncRNAs changes predictably with age:
   Inflammaging: Certain miRNAs and lncRNAs promote the chronic inflammation seen in old age.
Senescence: ncRNAs can regulate the entry into senescence and the composition of the Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype.

glioblastoma.description:
Glioblastoma (GBM), also called glioblastoma multiforme, is the most aggressive primary malignant tumor of the central nervous system, classified as WHO grade 4 glioma. It arises from astrocytes or glial progenitor cells and is characterized by rapid growth, diffuse infiltration, microvascular proliferation, and necrosis. GBM carries a poor prognosis, with median survival of ~12–15 months despite maximal therapy.

Etiology & Pathophysiology

GBM is driven by dysregulation of receptor tyrosine kinases (notably EGFR amplification/mutation, PDGFRA, MET), loss of PTEN (activating PI3K/Akt/mTOR), and alterations in p53 and RB1 pathways. The proneural, classical, mesenchymal, and neural transcriptomic subtypes reflect distinct biology. A hallmark is the formation of a aberrant, leaky vasculature via VEGF-driven Angiogenesis, and an immunosuppressive, hypoxic Tumor Microenvironment that fosters Chemotherapy resistance and Metastasis-like local invasion along white-matter tracts.

Clinical Presentation & Biomarkers

Symptoms include headaches, seizures, cognitive decline, and focal deficits; diagnosis uses MRI with contrast and histologic/IDH and MGMT-promoter-methylation profiling. MGMT methylation predicts response to temozolomide, and EGFRvIII is an investigational vaccine target. Liquid biopsy via Circulating tumor DNA/ctDNA is emerging.

Therapeutic Landscape

Standard care is maximal safe resection plus radiotherapy and temozolomide, with tumor-treating fields as adjunct. Bevacizumab (anti-VEGF) treats edema/recurrence. Preclinically, Ivermectin inhibits proliferation of GBM cells (U87, T98G, U251) in a dose-dependent manner, inducing caspase-dependent Apoptosis and Autophagy via the Akt/mTOR pathway and suppressing Angiogenesis. melittin and honeybee venom also show antitumoral activity in GBM models. These repurposed agents are being studied for sensitization and recurrence control.

senescence_surveillance.description:
Senescence surveillance is the process by which the immune system recognizes and eliminates senescent cells. It serves as a critical fail-safe mechanism that reinforces the tumor-suppressive function of cellular senescence by clearing pre-malignant and damaged cells before they can undergo transformation. The concept was first experimentally demonstrated by Kang et al. (2011, Nature 479:547-551; PMID 22080947), who showed that immune-mediated clearance of senescent hepatocytes prevents liver cancer development.

Molecular Mechanism

SASP-Mediated Immune Recruitment

Cytokines: IL-6, IL-1β, TNFα — activate immune effector functions
Type I interferons: IFN-β — activates NK cell and CD8+ T cell cytotoxicity

Multiple immune cell types participate in senescence surveillance:
Natural Killer Cells: Directly kill senescent cells through NKG2D receptor recognition of stress ligands (MICA, MICB, ULBP2) upregulated on senescent cells
Macrophages: Phagocytose senescent cells; SASP factors polarize them toward a pro-inflammatory M1 phenotype
CD4+ and CD8+ T cells: Recognize senescent cell antigens; CD4+ T cells orchestrate the immune response
Neutrophils: Recruited by SASP chemokines to the sites of senescent cell accumulation

cGAS-STING Contribution
The cGAS-STING pathway in senescent cells promotes type-I interferon production, which enhances NK cell and T cell-mediated killing. In the liver, inhibiting cGAS-STING signaling impairs senescence surveillance of pre-malignant hepatocytes, permitting tumor development (Dou et al., 2017, Nature 550:402-406; PMID 28976970).

Role in Cancer

Tumor Suppression
Clearance of oncogene-induced senescent cells in benign lesions prevents progression to malignancy
Senescence surveillance maintains the pre-malignant state: impairing surveillance (e.g., by immunosuppression or aging) accelerates tumorigenesis
Benign Tumor: Benign lesions (e.g., nevi) are the arrested, tumor-suppressive end-state that surveillance protects; retaining them is longevity-positive, and clearing them prematurely can permit progression


Aging and chronic inflammation impair immune function, leading to senescence surveillance failure:
Declining NK cell and T cell function with age permits senescent cell accumulation
Senescent cells can upregulate immune checkpoint molecules (PD-L1) to evade killing
PGE2 secreted by senescent HSC suppresses anti-tumor immunity in obesity-associated HCC (Loo et al., 2017, Cancer Discov 7:522-538; PMID 28202625)

Therapeutic Implications
Enhancing surveillance: STING agonists and immune checkpoint inhibitors may restore senescence surveillance in aging and cancer
Senolytic combination: Clearing senescent cells with senolytics may help when endogenous surveillance fails
Vaccination: Senescent cell vaccines are being explored to prime the immune system for senescent cell clearance

Details the mechanisms of SASP-mediated immunosurveillance: senescent cells generate SASP that regulates surrounding tissue microenvironment, activating CD4+ T cells via STAT1 and ICOS/ICOSL signaling. In mouse liver cancer models, p53-induced senescence suppresses macrophages, neutrophils, and NK cells, leading to tumor cell clearance via phagocytosis and NK cell activation. Tumor regression requires adaptive immunity when p53 is activated. IFN-γ synergizes with SASP to enhance antigen presentation and immune surveillance, leading to tumor cell rejection. agk2.description:
AGK2 is a potent, cell-permeable, and selective small-molecule inhibitor of SIRT2. It is widely utilized in neurobiology and oncology research to study the pathogenic consequences of SIRT2 activity, particularly in neurodegenerative disorders and acute ischemic brain injuries.

Chemical Properties & Classification
Class: Synthetic small-molecule sirtuin inhibitor.
Target Selectivity: Highly selective for SIRT2 ($IC{50} = 3.5\ \mu\text{M}$), with over 10-fold selectivity over SIRT1 and SIRT3.

Pharmacodynamics & Pharmacokinetics

Mechanism of Action

AGK2 selectively binds to the catalytic cleft of SIRT2, blocking its deacetylation activity. This prevents the deacetylation of primary cytosolic targets of SIRT2, including microtubule-associated $\alpha$-tubulin, FOXO3a, and p53.

Neuroprotective & Apoptotic Pathways
Parkinson's Disease (PD): A landmark therapeutic application of AGK2 is the rescue of dopaminergic neurons from misfolded $\alpha$-synuclein-mediated toxicity. SIRT2 inhibition via AGK2 prevents the deacetylation of $\alpha$-synuclein and microtubule elements, suppressing aggregation and protecting cell viability.
Ischemic Stroke & Brain Injury: Administration of AGK2 confers significant neuroprotection under ischemic and hypoxic conditions both in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistically, AGK2 suppresses the apoptotic cascade by downregulating phosphorylated JNK (phospho-JNK) and FOXO3a (the direct downstream target of SIRT2), which ultimately prevents Bim activation and subsequent caspase-3 cleavage.
Apoptosis Regulation: In other pathological states, SIRT2 deacetylation can promote or inhibit cell survival. SIRT2 overexpression can drive apoptosis by upregulating cleaved caspase-3 and Bax while suppressing Bcl-2; AGK2 blocks this apoptotic induction.

Applications
Neurodegenerative Research: Widely used to model therapeutic inhibition of SIRT2 in Parkinson's, Alzheimer's, and Huntington's diseases.
Cerebral Ischemia: Evaluated in pre-clinical rodent models of stroke to reduce infarct size and neuronal cell death.
Cancer Biology: Utilized to evaluate SIRT2 dependencies in various human tumor cell lines.
