leukemia.description:
Leukemia is a heterogeneous group of blood cancers that originate in the bone marrow and hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells, resulting in the accumulation of large numbers of abnormal white blood cells that impair normal hematopoiesis. Major categories include acute lymphoblastic (ALL), acute myeloid (AML), chronic myeloid (CML), and chronic lymphocytic (CLL) leukemias. Beyond conventional Chemotherapy and targeted agents, leukemia cells have been shown vulnerable to natural products such as honeybee venom, its principal peptide melittin, and the antiparasitic Ivermectin.

Etiology & Pathophysiology

Leukemogenesis arises from acquired mutations in genes controlling proliferation, differentiation, and Apoptosis—e.g., the BCR-ABL fusion in CML, FLT3 mutations in AML, and TP53 loss. These lesions produce clonal expansion of immature blasts, bone marrow failure (anemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia), and tissue infiltration. The malignant clone often exhibits heightened dependence on survival kinases such as Akt and on anti-apoptotic proteins, creating therapeutic vulnerabilities.

Role of Bee Venom & Ivermectin

Both honeybee venom and melittin display cytotoxic potency against leukemia cells. Bumblebee venom induces apoptosis in human chronic myelogenous leukemia cells by inhibiting phosphorylation of Akt, a key survival kinase. Ivermectin preferentially kills leukemia cells at low concentrations through chloride-dependent membrane hyperpolarization and ROS production, engaging mitochondrial dysfunction. It shows synergistic lethality with conventional antileukemic agents cytarabine and Daunorubicin, suggesting repositioning potential in combinatorial regimens.

Clinical & Research Relevance

Standard therapy combines cytotoxic nucleosides (cytarabine, daunorubicin) with targeted approaches (tyrosine kinase inhibitors for BCR-ABL, venetoclax for BCL-2). The demonstrations that melittin and ivermectin selectively stress leukemia cells via Akt and chloride/ROS axes provide mechanistic footholds for adjunct strategies and for overcoming resistance. Research continues into delivery (e.g., nanoparticle-encapsulated melittin) to spare normal marrow.

inos.description: iNOS (Inducible Nitric Oxide Synthase, NOS2) is a calcium-independent isoform of Nitric Oxide Synthase that produces high, sustained fluxes of Nitric Oxide (micromolar range) in response to inflammatory and immunological stimuli. Expression & Activation iNOS is not constitutively expressed; its transcription is induced by pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1β, IFN-gamma) and microbial products (LPS) through NF-κB, STAT1, and IRF1-dependent pathways. Unlike eNOS and nNOS, iNOS activity is independent of intracellular Ca²⁺ transients because it binds calmodulin tightly even at resting Ca²⁺ levels, enabling sustained NO production lasting hours to days. iNOS is expressed in macrophages, neutrophils, hepatocytes, cardiomyocytes, vascular smooth muscle cells, and glial cells. Physiological Functions Innate Immunity: Micromolar NO is a potent antimicrobial agent, inhibiting microbial respiration, DNA replication, and Fe-S cluster proteins in pathogens phagocytosed by macrophages. Wound Healing: iNOS-derived NO regulates angiogenesis, fibroblast proliferation, and collagen deposition. Tumor Immunity: iNOS activity in tumor-associated macrophages can have both tumoricidal and tumor-promoting effects depending on concentration and context. Pathological Roles Nitrative Stress: iNOS-derived NO rapidly reacts with Superoxide Radicals to form Peroxynitrite, driving 3-nitrotyrosine formation, protein nitration, and oxidative damage. Septic Shock: Excessive iNOS-derived NO causes systemic vasodilation, hypotension, and vascular hyporeactivity to vasoconstrictors. Cardiovascular Disease: Vascular iNOS contributes to endothelial dysfunction and atherosclerotic plaque instability. Neurodegenerative Diseases: Glial iNOS produces sustained NO bursts that contribute to neuronal injury in Alzheimer's Disease, Parkinson's Disease, Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis, and Multiple Sclerosis. Diabetes Mellitus: iNOS upregulation in pancreatic islets and Peroxynitrite formation damage β-cells. Chronic Inflammatory Diseases: iNOS is elevated in Rheumatoid Arthritis synovium, inflammatory bowel disease, and Asthma. bet_inhibitors.description:
Overview

BET (Bromodomain and Extra-Terminal) inhibitors are a class of epigenetic drugs that target the bromodomains of BRD2, BRD3, BRD4, and BRDT. These proteins recognize acetylated lysine residues on histone tails and regulate transcription of oncogenes (e.g., MYC, BCL2), inflammatory genes, and Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype factors.

Mechanism
BET proteins (especially BRD4) bind acetylated histones at super-enhancer regions.
BET inhibitors (e.g., JQ1, OTX015/Birabresib, ABBV-075/Mivebresib) displace BET proteins from chromatin.
This selectively downregulates MYC and its transcriptional program.
Also suppresses NF-κB-dependent transcription of inflammatory cytokines.

Role in Senescence

BET inhibitors can suppress the Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype by displacing BRD4 from the promoters of SASP genes including IL-6, IL-8, and MMP family members. This has been proposed as a Senomorphic strategy to block the harmful effects of SASP without eliminating senescent cells.

Role in Cancer
Downregulate MYC in MYC-driven cancers (e.g., leukemia, lymphoma, multiple myeloma).
Show synergy with Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors in preclinical models.
OTX015 and ABBV-075 have been evaluated in Phase I/II clinical trials for hematologic and solid malignancies.

Documents
Cellular senescence and SASP via cGAS-STING
BET inhibitors are referenced as a strategy to suppress SASP at the transcriptional level, acting as senomorphic agents.

Senomorphic: Class of drugs that suppress SASP without killing senescent cells
MYC: Downstream target downregulated by BET inhibition
JQ1: Prototypical BET inhibitor widely used in research

urea_cycle.description:
Overview

The urea cycle is a Liver mitochondrial and cytosolic pathway that converts toxic ammonia (from amino-acid catabolism) into urea for excretion. It consists of five enzymes: carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 (CPS1), ornithine transcarbamylase, argininosuccinate synthetase, argininosuccinate lyase, and arginase.

Mechanism

SIRT5, a mitochondrial desuccinylase/demalonylase, participates in urea cycle regulation. As a desuccinylase/demalonylase it regulates urea cycle enzymes (notably CPS1), ketogenesis, and redox enzymes (Du 2011 PMID 22076378; Nakagawa 2009 PMID 19410549). SIRT5-mediated desuccinylation of CPS1 activates the enzyme, coupling ammonia detoxification to mitochondrial NAD+ and acylation status.

[!info] Acylation control
SIRT5 removes succinyl and malonyl groups from urea cycle enzymes such as CPS1, tuning ammonia handling and connecting protein acylation to nitrogen metabolism.

Physiological Function

The urea cycle is essential for nitrogen balance during fasting and high-protein feeding. SIRT5-dependent regulation adapts urea production to metabolic demand, while also influencing ketogenesis and mitochondrial redox homeostasis.

Clinical Relevance

Urea cycle defects cause hyperammonemia with severe neurological consequences. Understanding SIRT5-mediated acylation control of the cycle informs metabolic interventions and the biology of liver dysfunction in aging and disease.

acat1.description:
Acetyl-CoA acetyltransferase 1 (ACAT1, also known as thiolase) is a mitochondrial enzyme canonically known for catalyzing the condensation of two acetyl-CoA molecules into acetoacetyl-CoA — the first committed step of Ketogenesis and the mevalonate/cholesterol pathway. More recently, ACAT1 has been identified as a lysine acetyltransferase that post-translationally acetylates the master lysosomal transcription factor TFEB at multiple lysines (K91, K103, K116, and K430). This acetylation enhances TFEB nuclear translocation and its DNA-binding affinity at CLEAR Element loci, thereby promoting Lysosome biogenesis and Autophagy.

Structure & Enzymatic Activity

ACAT1 is a homotetrameric enzyme localized primarily to the mitochondrial matrix, with its catalytic Cys89 residue forming a thioester intermediate during acetoacetyl-CoA synthesis. Although classically a thiolase, ACAT1 also transfers acetyl groups from acetyl-CoA to lysine ε-amino groups on protein substrates, functioning as a non-canonical acetyltransferase. This dual activity links intermediary metabolism directly to epigenetic/transcriptional control of autophagy.

Mechanism in TFEB Regulation

Under conditions of increased acetyl-CoA availability (e.g., fatty acid oxidation or ketogenic states), mitochondrial ACAT1 acetylates TFEB. Acetylation at K430 and other sites reduces TFEB interaction with cytosolic retention factors such as 14-3-3 protein and enhances its nuclear import and promoter occupancy. Acetylated TFEB drives coordinated expression of lysosomal hydrolases and autophagic machinery, raising Autophagic Flux. The opposing enzyme, the deacetylase SIRT1, removes these marks, placing ACAT1 and SIRT1 in a metabolic rheostat that tunes autophagic capacity to nutrient state.

Physiological & Pathological Relevance

Because ACAT1 bridges ketone-body metabolism and autophagic clearance, it has implications for Aging and Neurodegeneration, where declining TFEB activity impairs proteostasis. Pharmacological promotion of ACAT1-mediated TFEB acetylation is being explored as a strategy to boost lysosomal degradation in proteinopathy models. Conversely, ACAT1's canonical role in cholesterol/mevalonate metabolism links it to Cancer lipid homeostasis and statin-responsive pathways. ACAT1 deficiency (beta-ketothiolase deficiency) is a rare inborn error of metabolism causing ketoacidotic crises.

lysosomal_exocytosis.description:
Lysosomal Exocytosis is a regulated secretory pathway in which late endosomes/lysosomes dock at and fuse with the plasma membrane, releasing luminal hydrolases and membrane components into the extracellular space and expanding the plasma membrane. In neurons, this pathway is essential for membrane repair, clearance of damaged organelles, and the extracellular disposal of undigestible material. Because Neuromelanin is a non-degradable polymer that accumulates in lysosomes throughout the life of dopaminergic neurons, lysosomal exocytosis has been proposed as a "last-resort" mechanism by which the cell can offload pigment it cannot break down, thereby relieving Lysosomal Dysfunction and Macromolecular Crowding.

Mechanism and Regulation

The process is initiated by a rise in cytosolic Ca²⁺, which triggers the recruitment of the v-SNARE VAMP7 (and VAMP8) on the lysosomal membrane to pair with plasma-membrane t-SNAREs (Syntaxin 4 and SNAP23). The small GTPase Rab27a and the effector Slp2-a help tether lysosomes to the cortex. Before fusion, lysosomes must first be regenerated and mobilized through TFEB-driven transcriptional programs—the CLEAR (Coordinated Lysosomal Expression and Regulation) network—which upregulate lysosomal biogenesis, exocytosis, and autophagy genes. Thus lysosomal exocytosis is coupled to the broader Proteostasis machinery coordinated by TFEB.

Physiological and Pathological Relevance

In the healthy nervous system, lysosomal exocytosis supports synaptic membrane recycling and reseals pores in the lysosomal and plasma membranes after injury. In aging and in Parkinson's Disease, chronic cargo overload—including Alpha-synuclein aggregates, lipofuscin, and Neuromelanin—impairs this pathway. When exocytosis is blocked, pigment-laden lysosomes swell, oxidative reactions within the lysosome generate Reactive Oxygen Species, and the neuron becomes increasingly vulnerable. Experimental enhancement of lysosomal exocytosis (e.g., TFEB overexpression, or pharmacologic stimulation via LAMP2A-associated pathways) reduces intracellular neuromelanin accumulation and improves dopaminergic survival in models, making it a candidate Medical Treatment strategy for disease modification.

Research Implications

Targeting lysosomal exocytosis offers a complementary approach to Autophagy induction: whereas autophagy degrades material intracellularly, exocytosis exports it. Because Neuromelanin resists lysosomal hydrolysis, exocytosis may be the more relevant route for pigment clearance. Biomarkers of exocytic flux (e.g., extracellular lysosomal enzymes) are under investigation as proxies for neuronal Lysosomal Dysfunction.




Neuromelanin, aging, and neuronal vulnerability in Parkinson's disease

fucoidan.description:
Fucoidan is a sulfated polysaccharide extracted from brown seaweeds such as Fucus vesiculosus (Fucoidan-FV). It has been identified as a SIRT6 activator that elevates SIRT6 protein levels and enhances its mono-ADP-ribosyltransferase (mADPr) activity[48,49], mimicking the biochemical effects of the centenarian SIRT6 variants (N308K/A313S).

Mechanism of Action

Fucoidan-FV activates SIRT6 by increasing SIRT6 protein abundance and enhancing its mADPr activity[48]. Unlike most existing SIRT6 activators that primarily target deacetylase activity, fucoidan preferentially stimulates the ADP-ribosyltransferase function of SIRT6 — an activity profile that aligns with centenarian SIRT6 variants.

Biological Effects
LINE1 Repression: Fucoidan-FV treatment (50–100 µg/mL) reduces LINE-1 ORF1p and ORF2p protein levels in HGPS patient-derived fibroblasts, mimicking the transposable element suppression conferred by centenarian SIRT6 variants.
DNA Repair: Fucoidans enhance SIRT6-dependent DNA Repair and act as senotherapeutics[48].
Healthspan & Lifespan: SIRT6 activator fucoidan extends Healthspan and lifespan in aged wild-type mice[49].

excess_post_exercise_oxygen_consumption.description:
Excess Post-Exercise Oxygen Consumption (EPOC), historically the "oxygen debt", is the sustained elevation of metabolic rate above resting levels following a bout of physical activity. Because the energy equivalent of this extra oxygen consumption is counted beyond the exercise itself, omitting EPOC from energy-cost calculations can substantially underestimate the total energetic cost of an exercise bout.

Phases
Rapid component (< 2 h): driven largely by replenishment of muscle and blood O₂ stores and ATP resynthesis (phosphocreatine regeneration), plus restoration of tissue oxygen stores.
Prolonged component (up to 48 h): a smaller but longer-lasting elevation, involving a shift from carbohydrate to fat metabolism, increased fat oxidation, protein turnover, and β-adrenergically mediated metabolic stimulation (Borsheim et al. 1998).

Magnitude and Dependence on Intensity
For long-duration, low-intensity activity EPOC is markedly less than the energy of the activity itself.
For short, high-intensity activity EPOC can be 80–90 % of the total energy expended (Baker & Gleeson, 1998, 1999; Edwards & Gleeson, 2001).
In mice sprinting maximally for 5–60 s, total costs including EPOC were 1·5–2·5-fold higher than activity energy alone; the level of EPOC was independent of duration or intensity below 60 s.

[!info] Source: Speakman & Selman (2003)
The review highlights EPOC as the acute route by which physical activity raises resting metabolism, and warns that training studies failing to allow the long-phase EPOC to resolve may confound long-term RMR measurements. In dogs, the long-term EPOC is sensitive to β-antagonists, implicating the β-adrenergic system — a parallel to human post-exercise metabolism.

Negative EPOC After Flight

An instructive exception: in small insectivorous bats forced to fly, post-flight RMR fell to a nadir (~0·33 W vs. ~0·55 W pre-flight) and recovered only after ~2·5 h — i.e., negative EPOC — with the post-flight suppression nearly matching the energy cost of flight (Speakman & Racey, 1991). Forced flights in birds similarly produce compensatory suppression of resting metabolism overnight (Deerenberg et al. 1998). These findings indicate that EPOC direction depends on the voluntary vs. forced nature and intensity of exercise.

Connections
Resting Metabolic Rate — EPOC is a transient post-exercise elevation of RMR
Energy Expenditure — EPOC adds to the total energy cost of an exercise bout
ATP — Rapid EPOC component involves ATP and phosphocreatine resynthesis
Fat Oxidation — Prolonged EPOC involves a switch toward fat metabolism
Beta-Adrenergic Receptor — β-adrenergic blockade abolishes long-term EPOC in dogs
Exercise — EPOC is the acute mechanism linking exercise to increased resting metabolism

Primary source: reviews the two-phase nature of EPOC, its intensity dependence, and negative EPOC after flight in bats and birds.

benign_tumor.description: A benign tumor (benign neoplasm) is a localized cellular proliferation that does not invade surrounding tissue or metastasize. In the longevity and cancer-biology literature, "benign" does not mean "functionally neutral or good." Benign growths sit on a spectrum between two opposite relationships to healthspan: Tumor-suppressive fail-safe — a benign lesion is the end product of a growth program that was deliberately halted (Oncogene-Induced Senescence). The growth event itself is what triggers the arrest that contains a potentially malignant clone. Pathological growth — a benign lesion (e.g., a hamartoma) is the manifestation of an overactive growth program (mTORC1 hyperactivation) and is itself disease. The decisive factor for longevity is whether the growth is capped and arrested (beneficial) or ongoing and driven by nutrient/growth signaling (detrimental). Benign Lesions as Tumor-Suppressive Barriers The clearest case where "benign tumor growth" is positive for longevity is Oncogene-Induced Senescence (OIS). A cell carrying a driver mutation (BRAF V600E, RAS, MYC) launches a hyperproliferative burst that generates DNA Replication Stress and engages the DNA Damage Response, driving permanent Cell Cycle Arrest via p53/p21 and p16INK4A/Rb. In vivo, this produces benign melanocytic nevi (moles) — oncogene-bearing cells locked in a non-dividing state rather than progressing to Melanoma (see src/notes/senescence/Oncogene-Induced Senescence.md:40). [!important] The growth is the trap, the arrest is the benefit The "benign tumor" here is not benign because it grew — it is benign because growth triggered a permanent halt. The lesion is the body's way of putting a potentially malignant clone into custody. This is reinforced by Senescence Surveillance: the immune system (Natural Killer Cells, Macrophages, CD8+ T cells) clears oncogene-induced senescent cells in benign lesions, preventing progression to malignancy (src/notes/senescence/Senescence Surveillance.md:44). Experimental evidence: p16/p21 double-knockout increases cancer rates, and senescence surveillance failure permits tumor development (Kang et al., 2011, Nature 479:547-551, PMID 22080947). The senolytic paradox Because OIS cells are senescent, they are vulnerable to Senolytic Drugs such as Navitoclax. But clearing OIS cells from premalignant lesions "may paradoxically promote tumor growth by removing a cell-autonomous cancer barrier" (Oncogene-Induced Senescence.md:44). In other words, retaining a benign, arrested lesion can be longevity-positive; aggressively clearing every senescent/benign focus can backfire. Benign Tumors as Research Tools Teratoma — a benign, well-differentiated germ-cell tumor — is the gold-standard in vivo assay of Pluripotency and underpins safety benchmarking of Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells and Embryonic Stem Cells for regenerative and Rejuvenation medicine (src/notes/epigenetics/Teratoma.md:21). Its value is instrumental, confirming trilineage differentiation capacity before clinical translation. Benign Tumors as Pathological Growth (the counter-case) Not all benign growth is protective. Loss of TSC1/TSC2 causes Tuberous Sclerosis, a disorder marked by numerous benign tumors (hamartomas) driven by mTORC1 hyperactivation (src/notes/link/mTORC1.md:104; src/notes/autophagy/document - mTOR signaling at a glance.md:62). Here the benign growth itself is the disease (epilepsy, autism, renal Angiomyolipoma), with no anti-cancer benefit. Longevity Framing — the Hyperfunction View Under Blagosklonny's hyperfunction theory of aging (wiki's Rapamycin longevity article), aging is the quasi-programmed continuation of developmental growth signaling after growth should have stopped; suppressing mTOR with Rapamycin extends lifespan by dampening growth (src/notes/link/document - Rapamycin for longevity opinion article.md:113). This frames the issue precisely: the longevity-relevant "benign tumor" phenomenon is growth that is decisively halted — the frozen, arrested state (senescence) being protective, whereas unopposed proliferation is the engine of aging and disease. The pathological, growth-driven benign lesion — the Hamartoma (e.g., in mTORopathies) — is the counter-example, while the Senolytic Paradox warns that clearing protective benign lesions can backfire. Documents Oncogene-Induced Senescence Benign melanocytic nevi are the in-vivo archetype of OIS — a benign lesion that is the fail-safe end-state of an arrested oncogene-driven growth program. Immune clearance of senescent cells within benign lesions prevents malignant progression; surveillance failure accelerates tumorigenesis. Teratoma Benign tumor used as the canonical assay of pluripotency, linking benign growth to regenerative/rejuvenation research. mTORC1 TSC1/2 loss produces benign hamartomas via mTORC1 hyperactivation — the pathological counter-case where benign growth is disease.

melanoidins.description:
Chemical Properties

Melanoidins are the high-molecular-weight, brown-pigmented final products of the Maillard Reaction, formed during thermal food processing. They are found in bread crust, bakery products, and coffee, and are responsible for much of the color and flavor of cooked foods.

Biological Activity

Ames and colleagues found that melanoidins increased the number of anaerobes, clostridia, and bifidobacteria in cultures of human fecal bacteria. Borrelli and colleagues found that bread crust melanoidins can promote growth of some bifidobacterial strains, indicating a possible prebiotic effect.

[!info]
These findings show that not all Maillard products are detrimental: some dietary glycation products may support gut bacteria considered health-beneficial, in contrast to the pro-inflammatory effects of other Advanced Glycation End Products.

Relevance

Melanoidins are only partially absorbed and largely reach the colon, where they modulate the gut microbiota. Their antioxidant, antimicrobial, and prebiotic activities complicate the simple narrative that all Maillard products are harmful, informing balanced interpretation of dietary AGE research.

nmnh.description:
Overview

NMNH (dihydronicotinamide mononucleotide) is the reduced form of Nicotinamide Mononucleotide (NMN). It has been shown to promote NAD+ synthesis, joining NRH (reduced nicotinamide riboside) in an emerging class of reduced NAD+ precursors.

Mechanism

NMNH carries the reduced pyridine ring (dihydronicotinamide), which is converted to NAD+ through the salvage machinery, typically via NAD+ kinase/adenylylation steps in the NAD+ Salvage Pathway. Like NRH, NMNH bypasses some of the rate-limiting steps of the amidated routes, providing an alternative substrate for NAD+ replenishment.

[!info] Flexibility of NAD+ metabolism
Reduced precursors NMNH and NRH demonstrate that the NAD+ metabolic cycle is more flexible than initially recognized, offering alternative routes beyond the classic precursors Tryptophan, nicotinamide, nicotinic acid, NMN, and Nicotinamide Riboside.

Physiological Function

Reduced NAD+ precursors expand the toolkit for restoring NAD+ levels across tissues. Since NAD+ declines with Aging and is central to sirtuin activity, compounds such as NMNH are of interest for preventing age-related NAD+ loss.

Research Applications

NMNH and NRH are being investigated for their potency, oral bioavailability, and tissue distribution relative to NMN and NR. Adenosine Kinase-catalyzed phosphorylation of NRH to NMNH links these reduced precursors into a connected biosynthetic network.

cox_2.description:
Catalytic function: COX-2 is an enzyme that catalyzes biochemical reactions essential for cellular metabolism and homeostasis.

Mechanism: The catalytic activity of COX-2 is typically regulated by substrate availability, post-translational modifications, and allosteric effectors. Its active site contains key residues that coordinate substrate binding and transition state stabilization.

Physiological role: COX-2 participates in metabolic pathways that maintain cellular redox balance, energy production, and biosynthetic processes. Its expression and activity are tightly regulated across different tissues.

Clinical relevance: Dysregulation of COX-2 activity is implicated in metabolic disorders, oxidative stress-related pathologies, and cancer. Pharmacological modulation of this enzyme represents a therapeutic strategy for diseases involving its pathway.

bnip3.description:
Overview: BNIP3 (BCL2 Interacting Protein 3) is a single-pass transmembrane protein located on the outer mitochondrial membrane, belonging to the BH3-only subfamily of the BCL-2 family. It functions as a receptor for ubiquitin-independent mitophagy.

Structure and Function: BNIP3 directly interacts with the autophagy-related protein LC3 via its LIR motif, triggering the specific clearance of mitochondria. It is induced by HIF-1α under hypoxic stress and acts as an important receptor-mediated autophagy receptor.

[!info] Source: document - The role of mitochondrial dynamics in disease
BNIP3 is an OMM receptor for hypoxia-induced mitophagy via NIX/BNIP3-mediated HIF-1α stabilization. BNIP3 interacts directly with OPA1 to induce mitochondrial fragmentation, and with DRP1 to facilitate fission. BNIP3 protein levels are upregulated at early premalignant stages of various solid cancers (pancreatic, breast) but frequently decrease when tumors become invasive.

Role in Hypoxia-Induced Mitophagy: Following severe metabolic stress (such as hypoxia/ischemia), HIF-1α within neurons transcriptionally activates BNIP3. BNIP3 then inserts into the mitochondrial membrane, directly causing the loss of mitochondrial membrane potential and the opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore. This BNIP3-mediated cell death is delayed neuronal death. Knocking out the BNIP3 gene can significantly improve neuronal survival in damaged brain regions.

Pathological Significance: In Alzheimer's disease, BNIP3 expression is significantly lower in brain tissues compared to normal controls, contributing to mitochondrial clearance disorders. Excessively prolonged activation of BNIP3-mediated mitophagy disrupts neuronal energy metabolism and triggers apoptosis. Inhibiting BNIP3 represents a potential therapeutic target for preventing neuronal degenerative death.

iron.description:
Iron is an essential transition metal central to oxygen transport, electron transfer, and enzyme catalysis. In the brain, Neuromelanin is the principal iron-storage molecule within dopaminergic neurons of the Substantia Nigra and Locus Coeruleus, binding the metal via its catechol-quinone and indole moieties. While iron is required for normal metabolism, excess or miscompartmentalized iron promotes Oxidative Stress through Fenton chemistry, contributing to neurodegeneration in Parkinson's Disease.

Biological Roles
Iron exists physiologically as Fe2+ (ferrous) and Fe3+ (ferrous). It is incorporated into heme (cytochromes, hemoglobin) and iron-sulfur clusters (respiratory chain complexes I–III), and serves as a cofactor for enzymes such as tyrosine hydroxylase and Monoamine oxidase B. Tight regulation by ferroportin, transferrin, ferritin, and iron-regulatory proteins maintains safe pools and prevents free catalytic iron.


Neuromelanin granules bind substantial iron—up to ~30% of total nigral iron—acting as a neuronal metal reservoir. This sequestration is likely protective, detoxifying reactive free iron. However, the same strong binding means aged, iron-laden neuromelanin accumulates over decades, and the redox-active metal can participate in cycling reactions at the granule surface.

Chemical Process: Fenton Reaction and Oxidative Stress
Free or weakly bound Fe2+ reacts with hydrogen peroxide to generate the hydroxyl radical (•OH), a highly damaging species (Fenton reaction: Fe2+ + H2O2 → Fe3+ + •OH + OH−). Neuromelanin itself can both catalyze and buffer these reactions. When antioxidant defenses (glutathione, ferritin) are overwhelmed, iron-driven ROS damages lipids, proteins, and DNA. Iron also accelerates dopamine oxidation to Dopamine o-quinone, feeding the neuromelanin-building and quinone-toxic cycles.

Pathology and Clinical Relevance
Postmortem PD brains show elevated iron in the substantia nigra, with displaced iron from neuromelanin as neurons degenerate. Iron accumulation correlates with motor severity and with Lewy Bodies pathology. MRI-based铁 quantification (R2*/susceptibility mapping) is therefore studied as a PD biomarker and progression tracker. Therapeutically, iron chelators (e.g., deferiprone) and modulation of iron homeostasis are under investigation to slow nigral degeneration. Iron thus sits at the intersection of pigment biology, oxidative stress, and selective vulnerability: a necessary nutrient that, in the catecholaminergic neuron, becomes a liability amplified by neuromelanin's own metal affinity.

methionine.description:
Methionine is one of the nine essential amino acids and the only sulfur-containing essential amino acid in mammals. It is the precursor of S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), the universal methyl donor, placing it at the interface of diet, one-carbon metabolism, and the Epigenome. Dietary Methionine Restriction extends lifespan of many species and recapitulates many of the benefits of Protein Restriction.

Overview

Methionine is an endogenous metabolite involved in cellular energy metabolism, redox reactions, and biosynthetic pathways. Its cellular concentration reflects metabolic flux and energy status, and it participates as a substrate and intermediate in one-carbon metabolism, the methionine cycle, and transsulfuration. Intracellular levels are maintained through biosynthesis (in lower organisms), catabolism, and transport mechanisms, and its concentration serves as a metabolic signal regulating enzyme activity and gene expression.

Role in One-Carbon Metabolism and the Epigenome

Methionine is adenylated to form S-adenosyl-L-methionine, the universal methyl donor used by DNA and histone methyltransferases. Dietary methionine deprivation therefore reduces methyl-donor availability, altering the Epigenome:
Cells preserve heterochromatic stability through upregulation of H3K9 mono-methylation in the liver during methionine depletion
Methionine availability couples nutrient status to DNA Methylation and histone methylation programs
In humans, strict vegan diets reduce blood methionine and improve glucose homeostasis



Methionine Restriction (MR) extends lifespan of many species and, when initiated early or late in life, reduces body weight, increases lean mass, improves mitochondrial function and lipid metabolism, reduces Frailty, and extends lifespan of rodents. The metabolic response is partially dependent on FGF21 and also inhibits mTORC1. Most MR studies require Cysteine depletion — since cysteine can be synthesized from methionine via transsulfuration — for the metabolic benefits to be observed.

Among the individual essential amino acids, methionine is one of the primary drivers of protein restriction benefits, alongside the Branched-Chain Amino Acids. In humans, sulfur amino acid restriction increased FGF21, reduced leptin, and reduced body weight.

Clinical Significance

Altered methionine levels are observed in metabolic disorders, mitochondrial diseases, and nutritional deficiencies. Human studies link high circulating sulfur amino acids to cardiovascular and metabolic disease risk, while sulfur amino acid restriction improves biomarkers of metabolic health.

The Hallmarks of Protein and Amino Acid Restriction in Aging and Longevity

stemness.description:
Stemness describes the capacity of cells for self-renewal and differentiation potential that defines Stem Cells. It is governed by an interconnected transcription-factor network that maintains pluripotency and dedifferentiation competence, and its modulation underlies both regenerative plasticity and pathological cancer stemness.

IL-6/JAK/STAT3 and Reprogramming

IL-6 is a central driver of in vivo reprogramming toward pluripotency and stemness via JAK-STAT Signaling and STAT3. STAT3 transcriptionally sustains the core pluripotency factors Oct4, Nanog, and Sox2, promoting a dedifferentiated, stem-like state in recipient cells. This underlies both wound-healing plasticity and, pathologically, Cancer Stem Cell formation.

[!important] SASP as a Fate-Shaping Signal
Because IL-6 is a major Senescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype component, the senescent secretome can actively reprogram neighboring cells toward stemness — a dual-edged consequence linking senescence to tissue repair and cancer risk.

Role in Senescence & Tissue Context

Senescent cells, through SASP-mediated IL-6/JAK/STAT3 signaling, can induce stem-like properties in the tumor microenvironment, contributing to cancer stemness and therapy resistance. Conversely, the same signaling supports regenerative stemness during wound healing. Blocking IL-6/JAK/STAT3 signaling can interrupt this reprogramming, highlighting a targetable axis connecting senescence, inflammation, and cell-fate control.

Clinical Relevance

Manipulating stemness is central to Cellular Reprogramming and Partial Reprogramming strategies for regenerative medicine, while restraining cancer stemness is a therapeutic goal in oncology. The IL-6–STAT3–stemness axis is a validated point of pharmacological intervention.

silver_sulfide_albuminates.description:
Overview

Silver sulfide albuminates are soluble complexes in which silver sulfide is bound to albumin and other plasma proteins. They are formed in the body when insoluble Silver salts are transformed into soluble, protein-bound species.

Systemic Distribution

Insoluble silver salts are transformed in the body into soluble silver sulfide albuminates, which circulate bound to protein. This transformation is central to silver's systemic distribution because the albumin-bound species can travel through the blood to tissues.

[!info]
Formation of silver sulfide is chemically significant, paralleling the mineral argentite. The protein-bound silver then interacts with cellular RNA, DNA, and protein amino or carboxyl groups, or is reduced to metallic silver by Ascorbic Acid or Catecholamines.

Relevance

Albuminate transport is the key link between silver exposure and tissue deposition. It enables the silver to reach distant tissues where it interacts with biomolecules or precipitates, ultimately contributing to the permanent pigmentation of Argyria.

thymic_involution.description:
Thymic involution is the progressive age-related shrinkage and functional decline of the thymus, resulting in reduced thymopoiesis, decreased naïve T cell output, and impaired immune function. It is one of the most conspicuous and consistent features of mammalian aging and is a major contributor to immune aging.

Timeline
Onset: Begins in the first year of life
Puberty: Accelerated decline coinciding with increased sex steroid production

Post-middle age: ~1% annual decline throughout remaining life
Age 70: Thymic epithelial space constitutes <10% of total thymic tissue

Structural Changes

Thymic epithelial space (TES)
Progressive loss of cortical and medullary lymphoid tissue
Decreased thymic epithelial cell numbers and function
Disruption of thymic architecture
Reduced cytokine production (particularly IL-7)

Perivascular space (PVS)
Expansion of adipocytes, peripheral lymphocytes, and stroma
Progressive replacement of functional TES
Altered TES:PVS ratio

Functional Consequences
Reduced TCR gene rearrangement capacity
Decreased output of naïve T cells to the periphery
Restricted TCR repertoire diversity
Measurable decline in sjTREC levels (three-log decline across 80-year lifespan)
Increased susceptibility to infection, autoimmunity, and cancer
Impaired immune reconstitution after chemotherapy, radiation, or HIV-1 infection

Impact on Immune System
Results in a decrease in peripheral naïve adaptive immune cells
Contributes to Immune Aging and impaired immune reactions to new antigens
Perturbs memory responses in the Adaptive Immune Response

Evolutionary Hypotheses
Energy reallocation (Shanley et al.) — Thymic involution evolved to redirect energy from T cell production to reproduction once a diverse TCR repertoire is established
Peripheral selection (Dowling & Hodgkin) — Involution permits peripheral homeostatic proliferation of a well-adapted limited clone repertoire

Mouse Models

In BALB/c mice (aged 6–90 weeks):
Thymus weight and cellularity decrease significantly with age
Decrease detectable as early as 12 weeks of age
After 35 weeks, thymus weight stabilizes at ~45% of 6-week size
sjTREC per milligram of thymus tissue decreases significantly with age


Strategies to rejuvenate the aged Immune System often focus on counteracting the effects of thymic involution through autophagy induction.
Autophagy decline contributes to thymic aging, linking the two processes in age-related immune decline.

Therapeutic Reversal

Multiple strategies aim to reverse or attenuate thymic involution:
Sex Steroid Ablation — Surgical castration or LHRH analogues restore thymic architecture
IL-7 — Promotes thymocyte survival and differentiation
KGF — Stimulates TEC proliferation and differentiation
IL-22 — Drives TEC regeneration after injury
Growth hormone — Enhances hematopoiesis and thymic function
Ghrelin — Increases early thymic progenitors and recent thymic emigrants

fundc1.description:
FUNDC1 (FUN14 Domain-Containing Protein 1) is an outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM) protein that functions as a receptor for ubiquitin-independent mitophagy, particularly under hypoxic stress. It is a key mediator of receptor-mediated mitophagy and contributes to the maintenance of Mitochondria-Associated Endoplasmic Reticulum Membranes (MAMs).

Mechanism

[!info] Source: document - The role of mitochondrial dynamics in disease
FUNDC1 is a hypoxia-induced mitophagy receptor on the OMM. PGAM5 dephosphorylates FUNDC1 under hypoxic stimulation, promoting its interaction with LC3. FUNDC1 also interacts with both OPA1 and DRP1, regulated by Ser13 phosphorylation state during hypoxia or MMP loss. ULK1 phosphorylates FUNDC1 at Ser17, enhancing LC3 binding.

FUNDC1-mediated mitophagy is regulated by phosphorylation. Under normal conditions, Src kinase phosphorylates FUNDC1, keeping it inactive. During hypoxia, the mitochondrial kinase CK2 is inhibited, leading to dephosphorylation of FUNDC1 at the Ser13 site. This dephosphorylation activates FUNDC1, enabling it to recruit LC3 via its LIR motif and initiate mitophagy.

Role in MAMs

FUNDC1 is localized to MAMs and interacts with the IP3R2 receptor on the endoplasmic reticulum. The presence of FUNDC1 helps maintain the structural stability of MAMs. When FUNDC1 is absent, the MAM structure is disrupted, leading to impaired mitochondrial fission and abnormal calcium signaling. Given that MAMs are often dysfunctional in Alzheimer's disease, FUNDC1's fine-tuning of MAMs provides a mechanism for understanding calcium homeostasis imbalance in neurodegenerative diseases.

Role in Neuroprotection

Activating FUNDC1-mediated autophagy can clear damaged mitochondria, significantly reducing neuronal apoptosis and infarct volume following ischemia/hypoxia-reperfusion injury. Conversely, knockout of FUNDC1 significantly worsens neural damage.

ketogenic_diet.description:
A Ketogenic Diet is a high-fat, adequate-protein, low-carbohydrate dietary regimen that forces the body to burn fats rather than carbohydrates.

Metabolic State
The diet mimics the metabolic state of fasting by inducing Ketogenesis.
This results in elevated levels of ketone bodies in the blood, which serve as an alternative energy source.

Relationship with Autophagy
Ketogenic diets have been shown to stimulate Autophagy and increase Longevity in various animal models.
The induction of autophagy is thought to contribute to the neuroprotective effects of the diet.

Therapeutic Applications
Traditionally used to treat refractory epilepsy in children.
Investigated for its potential in treating neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer's Disease and Parkinson's Disease.
In Cancer research, its effects are complex; while it can enhance healing mechanisms, it may also contribute to conflicting outcomes depending on the tumor type and treatment regimen.

Metabolic Effects

KD induces Ketogenesis, increases β-hydroxybutyrate, and activates Autophagy via HDAC inhibition and FOXO signaling. It has therapeutic potential in epilepsy and neurodegeneration.

antagonistic_pleiotropy.description:
Antagonistic Pleiotropy is an evolutionary concept (notably developed by George C. Williams) in which a genetic trait or physiological program that enhances fitness early in life exerts deleterious effects later in life, after the period of peak reproduction. It explains why selection does not eliminate aging-causing mechanisms.

Application to the RCM Hypothesis

Within the Relocalization of Chromatin Modifiers (RCM) Hypothesis, antagonistic pleiotropy frames chromatin-modifier relocalization as a beneficial short-term response: recruiting modifiers to damage sites helps cells survive acute threats (rapid replication in microbes/embryos or injury) by prioritizing repair over normal gene regulation. This is advantageous in youth; across a lifetime, the cumulative "failure to reset" becomes detrimental and drives aging.

Connections

Aging: Late-life cost of the pleiotropic program.

zkscan3.description:
ZKSCAN3 is a zinc finger transcription factor that acts as a master transcriptional repressor of Autophagy and Lysosome biogenesis.

Function

ZKSCAN3 (ZNF306) is a zinc-finger transcription factor that represses lysosomal and autophagy genes. It binds directly to the promoters of TFEB, LC3, and lysosomal hydrolase genes.
Regulation

Under nutrient-replete conditions, ZKSCAN3 suppresses the CLEAR network. During Starvation, ZKSCAN3 is exported from the nucleus via CRM1, derepressing autophagy and lysosomal biogenesis.

udp_glucuronosyltransferases.description:
Overview

UDP-glucuronosyltransferases (UGTs) are a superfamily of phase II conjugating enzymes localized to the endoplasmic reticulum that transfer glucuronic acid from UDP-glucuronic acid to a wide range of lipophilic substrates, including polyphenols, drugs, and endogenous metabolites.

Role in Polyphenol Metabolism

Once absorbed, Fisetin is extensively conjugated by UGTs and sulfotransferases in the intestinal epithelium and liver, producing fisetin glucuronide and fisetin sulfate metabolites that circulate in the plasma.

[!warning]
 Effect    Consequence 
---  ---

 Rapid biliary/urinary excretion    Short plasma half-life 
 Low aglycone tissue levels    Poor oral bioavailability 

Because these conjugates have reduced biological activity and are rapidly excreted via bile and urine, the parent aglycone fisetin reaches only low concentrations in tissues.

Relevance

The extent of this phase II metabolism is a primary cause of fisetin's poor oral bioavailability and short plasma half-life, and it is one reason most preclinical efficacy studies have used intraperitoneal injection rather than oral dosing. UGT-mediated conjugation is a general bottleneck for dietary polyphenol bioactivity.



List of documents in the wiki that mention this entity
Fisetin—In Search of Better Bioavailability—From Macro to Nano Modifications A Review
Attributes fisetin's poor oral bioavailability to extensive UGT- and sulfotransferase-mediated conjugation.

Endoplasmic Reticulum: The subcellular site of UGT activity.

neuroprotection.description:
Neuroprotection encompasses the endogenous mechanisms and therapeutic strategies that preserve the structure and function of the central nervous system against injury, aging, and neurodegeneration. In Parkinson's Disease, neuroprotective (disease-modifying) approaches aim to slow or halt the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the Substantia Nigra Pars Compacta, contrasting with symptomatic treatments such as L-DOPA that merely replace Dopamine. Because Neuromelanin-containing neurons are selectively vulnerable, many strategies target the pigment-linked axes of oxidative, mitochondrial, and lysosomal stress.

Major Neuroprotective Strategies
Antioxidant defense: Boosting glutathione, mitochondrial antioxidants, or scavenging Reactive Oxygen Species to counter the oxidative burden amplified by neuromelanin-bound metals.
Mitochondrial support: Enhancing Complex I function and bioenergetics (e.g., Coenzyme Q10, Creatine) to resist toxin injury such as that from MPP+.
Lysosomal/autophagic clearance: Inducing Autophagy and Lysosomal Exocytosis to relieve Lysosomal Dysfunction and pigment crowding.
Anti-inflammatory modulation: Dampening Neuroinflammation and Microgliosis (NLRP3 inhibitors, MC1R agonists) to break the inflammatory cycle.
Trophic and regenerative support: Neurotrophic Factors (GDNF, BDNF) and α-synuclein-lowering approaches to preserve neuronal integrity.

Neuromelanin as a Therapeutic Node

The dual nature of Neuromelanin—redox buffer vs. pro-oxidant sink—makes it a strategic target. Approaches include limiting catecholamine auto-oxidation (MAO-B inhibitors like Selegiline), sequestering bound iron, or facilitating pigment export via lysosomal exocytosis. Determining whether to enhance or reduce pigment accumulation is an open question in the field.

Challenges and Biomarkers

True neuroprotection is hard to prove clinically; trials require sensitive progression biomarkers such as neuromelanin-sensitive Magnetic Resonance Imaging, DAT imaging, and α-synuclein assays. Most candidates (coenzyme Q10, creatine, rasagiline) have shown mixed results, underscoring the need for combination and earlier intervention.

Research Outlook

Repurposing toxin models (MPTP, 6-hydroxydopamine, Paraquat) and patient-derived neurons continues to identify targets. The convergence of pigment biology, immunity (Major histocompatibility complex class I), and bioenergetics frames a multipronged neuroprotective paradigm.





Suggested new entity notes to create: Neuroprotection, mTOR, Glucocerebrosidase, Lysosomal Exocytosis, Antigen Presentation. Strong connections to strengthen: Neuromelanin ↔ Parkinson's Disease, Neuromelanin ↔ Pathogenic Threshold of Neuromelanin.
Neuro-Modulating Effects of Honokiol: A Review
Honokiol protects neurons via Na+/K+-ATPase preservation, Akt pro-survival phosphorylation, mitochondrial protection, GABA_A receptor modulation, and suppression of ROS/inflammation; also disrupts PSD95–nNOS coupling at the NMDA receptor to prevent ischemic neurotoxicity.

Connections

melanoma.description: Melanoma is an aggressive malignant neoplasm arising from melanocytes — the pigment-producing cells of the skin and mucous membranes. It accounts for the majority of skin-cancer deaths due to its high propensity for early Metastasis and its capacity to evade immune surveillance. The incidence of melanoma has been rising steadily worldwide, with UV radiation exposure being the principal environmental risk factor. Melanoma is an aggressive skin cancer from melanocytes. MITF amplification drives proliferation; Autophagy supports melanoma survival under metabolic stress and contributes to melanoma progression and resistance to therapy. Etiology & Pathophysiology Melanoma development is driven by genetic and epigenetic alterations that activate proliferative signaling pathways: BRAF V600E mutations: Present in ~50% of cutaneous melanomas; constitutively activates the MAPK/ERK pathway. Paradoxically, BRAF activation in melanocytes of benign nevi (moles) induces oncogene-induced senescence (OIS), restraining progression — rare cell variants that bypass OIS evolve into melanoma. NRAS mutations: Present in ~20% of melanomas; activates RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT signaling. Loss of CDKN2A: The p16/p14ARF tumor suppressor locus is frequently inactivated, enabling escape from senescence. UV-induced DNA damage: Characteristic C>T transitions at dipyrimidine sites; defects in DNA repair promote mutagenesis. Epigenetic reprogramming: DNA methylation changes and histone modifications contribute to tumor heterogeneity and drug resistance. [!important] Senescence as a Double-Edged Sword Senescent melanocytes in nevi are held in check by OIS driven by BRAF V600E. However, the SASP produced by these senescent cells — particularly IL-8 and GROα — can stimulate the proliferation of rare premalignant cells that have escaped senescence, potentially driving melanoma development. Clinical Presentation & Biomarkers ABCDE criteria: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter >6 mm, Evolving shape Breslow thickness: Primary prognostic factor; determines staging and surgical margins LDH: Serum lactate dehydrogenase level; prognostic marker in metastatic disease Sentinel lymph node biopsy: Standard staging procedure for intermediate-thickness melanomas Molecular biomarkers: BRAF/NRAS mutation status, PD-L1 expression, tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) density Autophagy and Treatment Autophagy plays a significant role in melanoma progression and resistance to therapy. Fasting and Intermittent Fasting have been shown to sensitize melanoma cells to treatments like cold atmospheric plasma. These interventions induce apoptosis via the stimulation of the autophagic response, highlighting the therapeutic potential of modulating autophagy in melanoma. Both honeybee venom and melittin have demonstrated antitumoral effects in melanoma. Melittin has been shown to inhibit the MAPK signaling pathway in melanoma cells. Ivermectin inhibits melanoma activity and lung metastasis. It acts as a PAK1 inhibitor and induces Autophagy-dependent cell death. Ivermectin shows synergistic effects with dabrafenib. Therapeutic Landscape Surgery: Wide local excision with appropriate margins; sentinel lymph node biopsy for staging Immunotherapy: Checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1: nivolumab, pembrolizumab; anti-CTLA-4: ipilimumab) have transformed outcomes TIL therapy: Adoptive cell transfer of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes for advanced disease Radiation: Adjuvant radiation for high-risk disease; palliative for metastases [!tip] Senolytic Potential Senescent melanocytes accumulate in aging skin and may contribute to a pro-tumorigenic microenvironment via SASP. Senolytic strategies could potentially clear these cells and reduce melanoma risk in aging populations. Documents Autophagy and intermittent fasting the connection for cancer therapy? Autophagy was observed in melanoma under treatment with palladium complex drugs, indicating its importance in therapy. Lysosome biogenesis Regulation and functions In melanoma with the most prevalent BRAF(V600E) mutation, TFEB, but not TFE3, is phosphorylated and inactivated by ERK independently of mTOR. Inhibition of BRAF leads to TFEB activation via ERK inhibition. TFEB AND TFE3 LINKING LYSOSOMES TO CELLULAR ADAPTATION TO STRESS Microarray analysis of 51 melanoma lines revealed a strong correlation between expression of MITF-M (an isoform enriched in melanoma) and many lysosomal genes containing CLEAR elements. Apoptosis in cancer from pathogenesis to treatment Some target genes of p53 involved in apoptosis and cell cycle regulation are aberrantly expressed in melanoma cells, contributing to their proliferation. Caspase ERK2 phosphorylates an unidentified target at Ser77 (inactivation) in Melanoma; Bik is phosphorylated by ERK1_2 at Thr124.

myocardial_ischemia_reperfusion_injury.description:
Myocardial Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury

Myocardial ischemia-reperfusion (MI/R) injury is the paradoxical worsening of cardiac damage that occurs when blood flow is restored to a previously ischemic myocardium. Reperfusion triggers an oxidative burst, calcium overload, mitochondrial permeability transition, and inflammatory cell infiltration that together expand the zone of infarction.

Sirtuin Axis

Sirtuins are largely cardioprotective against MI/R injury:
SIRT1: Cardiac-specific knockout increases infarct size; overexpression upregulates FoxO1/MnSOD antioxidant pathways and downregulates pro-apoptotic caspase-3/Bax. Upstream regulation includes miR-132 inhibition → PGC-1α/Nrf2 and lncRNA Oip5-as1 acting via the SIRT1/AMPK/PGC-1α axis.
SIRT3: Deficiency exacerbates MI/R injury; as the primary mitochondrial deacetylase it sustains OXPHOS and mitochondrial quality control during reperfusion stress.
SIRT6: Protective via FoxO3α antioxidant defense and attenuation of CHMP2B accumulation.
SIRT4: Downregulated after MI/R; overexpression decreases infarct size through mitochondrial preservation and reduced apoptosis.
SIRT5: Loss increases infarct size via protein succinylation modulation.
SIRT2 and SIRT7: Few studies reported.

Clinical Relevance

MI/R injury is central to outcomes in reperfusion therapy for acute myocardial infarction and cardiac surgery. The protective sirtuin network (SIRT1/3/6) is a target for conditioning strategies that reduce infarct size.

Documents
Sirtuins in Health and Disease
MI/R injury is discussed under cardiovascular diseases with SIRT1/SIRT6 protective roles and the succinylation-linked SIRT5 effects.

Connections
SIRT1: Cardioprotective via FoxO1/MnSOD, PGC-1α/Nrf2
SIRT3: Mitochondrial protection during reperfusion
SIRT6: FoxO3α antioxidant defense
SIRT4: Overexpression reduces infarct size
SIRT5: Loss increases infarct size (succinylation)
Atherosclerosis: Coronary artery disease predisposes to ischemia

Strong connections to strengthen: SIRT1 ↔ Myocardial Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury, SIRT3 ↔ Myocardial Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury

nlrp3.description:
Overview: NLRP3 is a cellular protein with structural, signaling, or regulatory functions in eukaryotic cells. It participates in macromolecular complexes and signaling networks that govern cell behavior.

Structure and domains: NLRP3 contains conserved structural motifs that mediate its interactions with binding partners, nucleic acids, or lipid membranes. Post-translational modifications such as phosphorylation and ubiquitination regulate its activity.

Cellular function: NLRP3 plays a role in signal transduction, gene expression regulation, cytoskeletal organization, or metabolic control. Its localization and activity are dynamically regulated in response to cellular cues.

Pathological significance: Altered expression or mutation of NLRP3 is associated with cancer, neurodegenerative diseases, and developmental disorders. It serves as a biomarker and therapeutic target in multiple clinical contexts.

nucleus.description:
Overview

The Nucleus (cell nucleus) is the membrane-bound Nucleus that encloses the genome, organizing Chromatin and regulating transcription, DNA replication, and repair. Although cGAS is best known for cytosolic DNA sensing, a substantial pool localizes to the nucleus, where it performs noncanonical, STING-independent functions. Nuclear cGAS is tightly tethered to nucleosomes via histones H2A/H2B, a configuration that restricts aberrant activation while enabling roles in genome stability and RNA processing.

Noncanonical Nuclear cGAS Functions

Nuclear cGAS interacts with PARP1, disrupting the PARP1-Timeless complex and thereby suppressing homologous recombination and influencing DNA Damage repair (43). Its N-terminal intrinsically disordered region promotes LLPS, scaffolding RNA-binding proteins, the spliceosome, and the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodeling complex, implicating nuclear cGAS in gene expression regulation (77). Under homeostatic conditions, nucleosome tethering and N-terminal hyperphosphorylation keep nuclear cGAS restrained; however, viral infection or DNA Damage can license nuclear cGAS to produce cGAMP and elicit a STING-dependent IFN-I response.

Retrograde Signaling and Protective Roles

Nuclear cGAS also engages in Z-DNA sensing and retrograde signaling, and a pool of STING resides at the adjacent Nuclear Envelope, suggesting coordinated nuclear-envelope signaling. In long-lived species such as the naked mole rat, chromatin-retained cGAS actually enhances DNA repair, indicating that noncanonical nuclear cGAS can be protective. Differentiating inflammatory versus homeostatic nuclear cGAS functions remains a key open question for understanding Neurodegeneration in postmitotic neurons.

Documents
JCI cGAS-STING in Neuroinflammation
The review details noncanonical nuclear cGAS functions: binding nucleosomes/H3-histone, suppressing homologous recombination via PARP1, and scaffolding RNA-binding proteins, spliceosome, and SWI/SNF via IDR-LLPS, with nuclear Z-DNA sensing and retrograde signaling that may be protective.

Connections

Nuclear Envelope: Adjacent site where STING localizes and coordinates signaling.
Chromatin: Organized and potentially regulated by nuclear cGAS.

lymphocytes.description:
Lymphocytes are agranular white blood cells of the adaptive immune system, comprising B cells, T cells (CD4+ helper, CD8+ cytotoxic, regulatory), and natural killer (NK) cells. They mediate antigen-specific immunity through antibodies (B cells), cell-mediated cytotoxicity, and cytokine signaling (T cells). In Parkinson's Disease (PD), lymphocytes—particularly T cells—have been found to infiltrate the Substantia Nigra, especially in regions containing Neuromelanin, implicating adaptive immunity in neurodegeneration.

Types and Immune Functions
B cells produce antibodies (including Immunoglobulin G) and present antigen.
T cells coordinate responses and directly kill infected or stressed cells via MHC class I/II recognition.
NK cells provide innate-like cytotoxicity without prior sensitization.
Central to CNS immunity is the major histocompatibility complex (MHC), which presents peptide antigens to T-cell receptors; neurons under stress may upregulate MHC class I, becoming targets for CD8+ T cells.


Postmortem PD brains show perivascular and parenchymal T-cell infiltrates in the substantia nigra, often clustered around neuromelanin-laden neurons. Proposed mechanisms include:
Blood-brain barrier breach: Age and Oxidative Stress permit lymphocyte trafficking into the parenchyma.
Antigen presentation: Neuromelanin or Alpha-synuclein peptides presented on MHC may activate autoreactive T cells.
Cytotoxic attack: CD8+ T cells release perforin/granzyme or Fas ligand, killing stressed dopaminergic neurons.
Bystander inflammation: Lymphocyte cytokines amplify microglial Neuroinflammation, worsening injury.

This adaptive response complements the innate microglial activation long recognized in PD.

Physiological and Pathological Relevance
While immune surveillance is protective against infection and clears debris, maladaptive lymphocyte activity may accelerate the loss of pigmented neurons. Peripheral blood studies report altered T-cell subsets and alpha-synuclein-reactive T cells in PD patients, supporting an autoimmune component. The intimacy of lymphocytes with neuromelanin-rich regions suggests pigment-related antigens (quinone-modified proteins, iron-bound complexes) could be triggers.

Clinical and Research Implications
Lymphocyte profiling in blood or cerebrospinal fluid is being developed as a PD biomarker, and immunomodulatory strategies (e.g., suppressing autoreactive T cells, fostering regulatory T cells) are under investigation as disease-modifying approaches. Understanding the lymphocyte–neuromelanin interface also clarifies why Immunoglobulin G deposits colocalize with nigral degeneration. Ultimately, balancing protective versus destructive immunity is a frontier in PD therapeutics, with lymphocytes as both diagnostic signals and therapeutic targets.

Connections
Parkinson's Disease: Condition with nigral T-cell infiltration.
Substantia Nigra: Site of lymphocyte accumulation around pigmented neurons.
Neuromelanin: Pigment region where lymphocytes localize.
Immunoglobulin G: Antibody class tied to adaptive response in PD.
Alpha-synuclein: Potential autoantigen for T cells.
Neuroinflammation: Broad immune context of lymphocyte activity.
Oxidative Stress: Promotes barrier breach enabling infiltration.
Major histocompatibility complex class I: Presents antigens to cytotoxic T cells.

Linking Summary

srt2183.description:
SRT2183 is a synthetic small-molecule STAC (sirtuin-activating compound) developed by Sirtris Pharmaceuticals as a potent SIRT1 activator. It belongs to the imidazothiazole class and is discussed together with SRT1720 and SRT1460 as the potent second-generation STACs reported after the polyphenolic activators (compound 8 in Fig. 3 of the review).

Chemical Properties & Classification
Class: Imidazothiazole; second-generation synthetic STAC.
Target: SIRT1 activator.
Selectivity/Potency: More potent than resveratrol in deacetylase-based SIRT1 activation assays.

Pharmacodynamics & Pharmacokinetics
SRT2183 mimics many transcriptional effects of resveratrol (deacetylation of SIRT1 substrates such as p53), shifting cells toward stress resistance and oxidative metabolism.
Mechanism controversy: as with other STACs, activation was frequently only demonstrable with fluorescently tagged substrates. Given its metabolic similarity to resveratrol, SRT2183 may act in vivo partly through indirect pathways (e.g., the cAMP-Epac1-AMPK axis) rather than direct SIRT1 binding.

Applications
Research tool in metabolic and longevity research to model SIRT1-dependent effects.
STACs of this class were reported to possess anticancer activity, though the contribution of SIRT1 activation vs. off-target activity is unresolved.



List of documents in the wiki that mention this entity
Rejuvenating Sirtuins: The Rise of a New Family of Cancer Drug Targets
Describes SRT2183 (compound 8 of Fig. 3) as a potent synthetic STAC along with SRT1720 and SRT1460; notes the controversy over its mechanism and possible indirect cAMP-Epac1-AMPK-mediated activity.

SRT1460: Fellow second-generation STAC in the same series.

rspo1.description:
Rspo1 (R-spondin 1) is a secreted protein that potentiates canonical Wnt signaling by stabilizing the LGR5 receptor complex, thereby maintaining intestinal epithelial stem-cell function and tissue regeneration.

Sirtuin Regulation

Physiological Function

Rspo1 sustains the crypt stem-cell niche and intestinal barrier integrity, enabling rapid epithelial repair after injury.

Clinical Relevance

Maintaining Rspo1 via SIRT6 is a candidate strategy to protect the intestinal epithelium from inflammatory damage in IBD.

cdkn2b.description:
CDKN2B (p15^INK4b^)

CDKN2B encodes p15^INK4b^ (cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 2B), a member of the INK4 family of CDK inhibitors that specifically binds and inhibits CDK4 and CDK6, preventing their association with D-type cyclins. This maintains Rb in its hypophosphorylated, growth-suppressive state, enforcing G1 cell cycle arrest. CDKN2B is a key effector of TGFβ-mediated growth arrest and plays a critical role in paracrine senescence.

Mechanism of Action
CDK4/6 inhibition: p15^INK4b^ binds CDK4 and CDK6, preventing cyclin D–CDK complex formation and Rb phosphorylation.
G1 arrest: By maintaining hypophosphorylated Rb, p15^INK4b^ sequesters E2F transcription factors, silencing genes required for S-phase entry.
TGF-β target: CDKN2B is a direct transcriptional target of TGFβ signaling via SMAD3/SMAD4 complexes binding to SMAD-binding elements in the CDKN2B promoter.
Epigenetic regulation: The CDKN2B locus is subject to DNA Methylation and PRC2-mediated H3K27me3 silencing; its derepression is a hallmark of senescence.


The INK4 family comprises four members: p16^INK4a^ (CDKN2A), p15^INK4b^ (CDKN2B), p18^INK4c^ (CDKN2C), and p19^INK4d^ (CDKN2D). All specifically inhibit CDK4/6 but have distinct expression patterns and regulatory mechanisms. p15^INK4b^ is the primary CDK inhibitor induced by TGF-β, while p16^INK4a^ is the primary senescence-associated CDK inhibitor induced by oncogenic stress.

Role in Senescence

[!important] Source: Acosta et al., 2013 (PMID 23636316)
TGF-β family ligands (TGF-β1, activin A, BMP2, GDF15) are major mediators of Paracrine Senescence. They signal through TGFBR1/ALK4/ALK5/ALK7 and SMAD2/SMAD3 to induce p15^INK4b and p21^CIP1 in receiving cells. TGFBR1 inhibitors prevented SMAD2/3 phosphorylation, blunted paracrine arrest, and correlated with impaired p15^INK4b and p21^CIP1 induction. In a PanIN mouse model, conditional deletion of TGF-βR1 attenuated OIS — confirming that TGF-β → p15^INK4b/p21^CIP1 signaling is essential for senescence-mediated tumour suppression.
p15^INK4b^ is induced by TGF-β during paracrine senescence, acting as a key effector of the growth arrest signal.
It cooperates with p21^CIP1 (induced by both TGF-β and p53 pathways) to enforce the cell cycle arrest.
CDKN2B loss or silencing (e.g., by promoter methylation) is a mechanism of senescence bypass in some cancers.
CDKN2B is located on chromosome 9p21, adjacent to CDKN2A (p16^INK4a^/p14^ARF^), in a region frequently deleted or silenced in cancer.

Clinical / Pathological Relevance
Cancer: CDKN2B is frequently silenced by promoter methylation or deleted in leukaemias, lymphomas, gliomas, and other cancers. Its re-expression by demethylating agents (e.g., decitabine, 5-azacytidine) can restore growth arrest.
Myeloid malignancies: CDKN2B methylation is a prognostic marker in myelodysplastic syndromes and acute myeloid leukaemia.
Atherosclerosis: CDKN2B variants at the 9p21 locus are the strongest common genetic risk factor for coronary artery disease, though the mechanism involves regulation of neighbouring genes (ANRIL, CDKN2A) rather than p15^INK4b^ directly.
TGF-β pathway disorders: Loss of TGF-β → p15^INK4b^ signaling contributes to fibrosis, cancer progression, and impaired senescence-mediated tumour suppression.

Documents
Acosta et al., 2013 — Inflammasome controls paracrine senescence
Identified p15^INK4b as a key downstream effector of TGF-β-mediated paracrine senescence. TGFBR1 inhibitors impaired p15^INK4b induction and blunted paracrine arrest. TGF-βR1 knockout in a PanIN model attenuated OIS, confirming the TGF-β → p15^INK4b axis is essential for senescence-mediated tumor suppression.

Connections

raidd.description:
RAIDD (RIP-associated protein with a death domain), also known as CRADD, is a death-domain-containing adaptor protein that nucleates the PIDDosome—a multiprotein complex that activates Caspase-2 in response to genotoxic and mitotic stress. RAIDD bridges the sensor PIDD (p53-induced protein with a death domain) to the apical caspase, thereby initiating a defined branch of Apoptosis.

Structure & Mechanism

RAIDD contains an N-terminal caspase recruitment domain (CARD) and a C-terminal death domain (DD). The DD mediates homotypic interaction with the DD of PIDD, while the CARD recruits the CARD of pro-Caspase-2. Upon DNA damage or prolonged mitotic arrest, PIDD oligomerization creates a scaffold on which RAIDD assembles multiple Caspase-2 zymogens into the active PIDDosome, enabling Caspase-2 proximity-driven activation. Activated Caspase-2 can amplify death through Bid truncation and mitochondrial outer-membrane permeabilization.

Physiological & Pathological Function

The PIDD–RAIDD–Caspase-2 axis functions as a genomic-stress sensor that eliminates cells with irreparable DNA damage, guarding against transformation. In Cancer, this checkpoint is frequently attenuated (through PIDD or Caspase-2 silencing, or PP1/CaMKII tuning of Caspase-2 phosphorylation), allowing damaged cells to survive and acquire mutations—feeding the Hallmarks of Cancer. RAIDD thus acts as a tumor-suppressive conduit for stress-induced death.

Clinical & Research Relevance

RAIDD/PIDDosome integrity is a biomarker of apoptotic competence and a determinant of response to DNA-damaging Chemotherapy and radiation. Strategies that restore PIDDosome assembly or bypass Caspase-2 dependence are explored to overcome resistance. RAIDD remains a key experimental tool for dissecting apical caspase activation.



List of documents that mention this entity
Evading apoptosis in cancer
Of note, Caspase-2 is activated via formation of the PIDDosome, a complex which consists of the adaptor proteins PIDD (p53-induced death domain protein) and RAIDD (RIP-associated protein with a death domain).

Connections
PIDD - DNA-damage sensor that scaffolds RAIDD in the PIDDosome.
Caspase-2 - Apical caspase recruited and activated by RAIDD.
PIDDosome - Multiprotein complex assembled via RAIDD.
Apoptosis - Cell death program initiated by the PIDDosome.

mitochondrial_dysfunction.description:
Mitochondrial Dysfunction refers to the impairment of mitochondrial processes, particularly the production of ATP and the regulation of cellular metabolism.
In Parkinson's Disease
Mitochondrial dysfunction is a central feature of Parkinson's Disease and is thought to be both a cause and a consequence of other pathological processes.
Energy Failure: Neurons in the Substantia Nigra have high energy demands, making them particularly sensitive to mitochondrial impairment.
Oxidative Stress: Defective mitochondria are a major source of reactive oxygen species, leading to increased Oxidative Stress.
Link to Neuromelanin: The accumulation of Neuromelanin-filled autophagic structures may interfere with the turnover of damaged mitochondria, a process known as Mitophagy.
Toxin Sensitivity: Many neurotoxins associated with PD, such as MPTP, act by inhibiting the mitochondrial respiratory chain (specifically Complex I).

dolichol.description:
Dolichol is a long-chain polyisoprenoid lipid identified as a major lipid component of human Neuromelanin granules in the Substantia Nigra Pars Compacta. Its presence reshapes the view of neuromelanin from a simple pigment to a complex lipopigment organelle with membrane-like properties.

Structure & Biosynthesis

Dolichols are α-saturated polyisoprenols (typically 17–21 isoprene units in humans) synthesized via the mevalonate pathway and modified in the endoplasmic reticulum. Best known for serving as the lipid anchor for the oligosaccharide carrier in N-linked glycosylation (dolichol phosphate), free dolichol also accumulates in lysosomes and aging tissue as a marker of senescence.

Role in Neuromelanin Granules

Biochemical isolation of neuromelanin granules shows they are rich in dolichol and dolichyl esters, co-localized with protein, lipid, and the pigment polymer. Dolichol's long hydrophobic chain likely integrates into the granule membrane/matrix, influencing its fluidity, permeability, and interaction with catechol quinones such as Aminochrome and 5,6-indolequinone. Elevated granule dolichol may reflect altered isoprenoid metabolism or lysosomal storage in aging dopaminergic neurons.

Physiological & Pathological Implications

As neurons age, free dolichol rises in many tissues, and its accumulation in neuromelanin granules could alter granule stability and metal handling. Because dolichol synthesis shares the mevalonate pathway with Coenzyme Q10 and cholesterol, perturbations may couple pigment biology to mitochondrial and membrane homeostasis. Whether dolichol content differs in Parkinson's Disease substantia nigra is an open question with implications for granule fragility and Oxidative Stress.

Research & Clinical Relevance

Dolichol in neuromelanin highlights the organelle-like nature of pigment granules and their intersection with lysosomal and isoprenoid metabolism. It connects to Lysosomal Dysfunction and to the broader lipofuscin/pigment-aging literature, suggesting that granule lipid composition is a modifiable factor in neuronal resilience and a potential biomarker of dopaminergic aging.

nampt.description:
NAMPT (Nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase) is a key enzyme in the salvage pathway of NAD+ biosynthesis, whose levels decrease significantly in various tissues during aging.
Forms and Subcellular Localization
NAMPT exists in two distinct functional forms in mammals:
Intracellular NAMPT (iNAMPT): Localized in the cytoplasm and nucleus, iNAMPT is vital for maintaining cellular NAD⁺ pools. It is regulated by the circadian clock (via CLOCK:BMAL1 heterodimers binding to its promoter) to drive rhythmic NAD⁺ synthesis.
Extracellular NAMPT (eNAMPT / Visfatin / PBEF): Secreted primarily by adipose tissue, immune cells, and hepatocytes. eNAMPT acts as an adipokine and cytokine with pro-inflammatory and systemic insulin-mimetic effects, binding to receptors such as Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4).
Regulation of Sirtuin Activity
By controlling NMN synthesis and subsequently cellular NAD⁺ levels, NAMPT acts as a primary upstream master regulator of sirtuin-mediated deacetylation.
AMPK Activation: During energetic stress, activation of AMPK phosphorylates and activates NAMPT, elevating NAD⁺ levels to boost SIRT1 activity.
Resveratrol Indirect Axis: Resveratrol-mediated PDE4 inhibition leads to accumulation of cAMP, triggering calcium release and AMPK activation, which upregulates NAMPT to stimulate sirtuin activity.
Role in Aging and Disease
Age-Related Decline: Systemic and tissue-specific NAMPT expression declines with age, leading to NAD⁺ depletion, mitochondrial dysfunction, and diminished sirtuin activity (a key driver of the Hallmarks of Aging).
Metabolic Syndrome: Decreased NAMPT activity is associated with insulin resistance, obesity, and type 2 diabetes. Conversely, NAMPT overexpression or NMN supplementation improves glucose tolerance and lipid profiles in animal models.
Cancer Biology: Many cancer cells overexpress NAMPT to satisfy their high energetic and DNA repair demands (via PARPs). NAMPT inhibitors (e.g., FK866) are being investigated as anti-cancer agents to selectively deplete NAD⁺ and induce apoptosis in tumor cells.

microtubule.description:
Microtubules are polymers of Tubulin that form part of the cytoskeleton and provide structure and shape to eukaryotic cells. They are involved in many cellular processes, including Mitosis, cytokinesis, and vesicular transport.

Role in Cancer
Microtubules are critical for the formation of the mitotic spindle during cell division. Because Cancer cells divide rapidly, microtubules are a major target for chemotherapy.

Microtubule-Targeting Agents (MTAs)
Drugs that interfere with microtubule dynamics are classified into two groups:
Microtubule-Stabilizing Agents: (e.g., Taxanes like paclitaxel, docetaxel)
Microtubule-Destabilizing Agents: (e.g., vinca alkaloids like Vincristine, and Benzimidazoles like Fenbendazole, Albendazole, Mebendazole)

Fenbendazole acts as a moderate microtubule destabilizing agent, binding to tubulin and inhibiting its polymerization, which leads to cell cycle arrest and Apoptosis in cancer cells.

bim.description:
Bim (Bcl-2-like protein 11) is a potent pro-apoptotic BH3-only member of the Bcl-2 family. It is a major initiator of the Intrinsic Pathway of apoptosis.

Mechanism
Bim acts as a "direct activator" of the apoptotic effectors Bax and Bak. It can also bind and neutralize all anti-apoptotic members of the Bcl-2 family (e.g., Bcl-2, Bcl-xL, Mcl-1), thereby lowering the threshold for apoptosis.

Regulation
Bim activity and stability are tightly regulated by several signaling pathways:
ERK: Phosphorylates Bim at Ser69, promoting its degradation through the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway. This phosphorylation also prevents the interaction between Bim and Bax.
RSK: Phosphorylates Bim at S93/S94/S98, which is required for Beta-TrCP-mediated ubiquitination.
JNK / p38 MAPK: Phosphorylate Bim to promote its pro-apoptotic activity by enhancing binding to anti-apoptotic members.
PKA: Stabilizes Bim protein.
E3 Ligases: Bim is targeted for degradation by SCF Complex (Beta-TrCP), c-CBL, TRIM2, and the Elongin B/C-Cullin 2-CIS complex.


Reduced expression or loss of Bim is associated with tumor progression and resistance to therapy, particularly in lymphoid malignancies.

tnf.description: Tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα) is a pleiotropic pro-inflammatory cytokine produced primarily by activated Macrophages, T Cells, and Natural Killer Cells. It is a master regulator of the inflammatory response and a central mediator of both acute and chronic inflammation. Structure TNFα is synthesized as a 233-amino acid Type II Transmembrane Protein (26 kDa) forming homotrimers. The transmembrane form (mTNF) is cleaved by TACE/ADAM17 to release soluble TNFα (sTNF, 17 kDa), which also forms bioactive homotrimers. Both forms signal through two distinct Receptors: TNFR1 (p55) — expressed on nearly all cell types; signals primarily through TRADD to activate NF-κB and MAPK pathways and, under certain conditions, Apoptosis via Caspase-8 TNFR2 (p75) — expressed mainly on Endothelial Cells, T Cells, and Neurons; signals through TRAF2 to activate NF-κB and PI3K-Akt Signaling Pathways NF-κB Activation TNFα binding to TNFR1 recruits TRADD, RIPK1, and TRAF2. TRAF2 activates the IKK complex (IKKα, IKKbeta, IKKγ/NEMO), which phosphorylates IkappaBalpha, targeting it for proteasomal degradation. Released NF-κB (p50-p65 heterodimer) translocates to the Nucleus and transcriptionally activates hundreds of target genes including pro-inflammatory cytokines, chemokines, and anti-apoptotic factors. TNFα activates the JNK, p38 MAPK, and ERK cascades via TRAF2-ASK1-MKK4/7 signaling, regulating AP-1 transcription factor activity. Apoptosis Under conditions of NF-κB blockade or Protein Synthesis inhibition, TNFα signaling switches from survival to death. RIPK1 deubiquitination promotes formation of Complex II (FADD-Caspase-8), triggering Apoptosis via Caspase-3 activation. If caspases are inhibited, RIPK3-dependent Necroptosis can occur.
